    Lending Basics & Technology

    Lending Basics & Technology in Lending

    (Instructor: Ritesh Chandra — Modules 1 & 2)

    How to read this: You're an engineer, so wherever a finance idea maps to something you already know, I've said so. The MCQ-critical bits (exact numbers, exact definitions, "which of these is NOT…" traps) are in bold or in tables.

    1.1Fundamentals of Credit and Loan Types

    Credit = a promise. You give something of value today (money), expecting return later plus interest. Credit is fundamentally about trust.

    Why credit matters (exam-friendly list): - Fuel for the economy — enables home/car/education purchases → boosts real estate, autos, education sectors → positive cycle. - Fuels business growth — from a tea-stall kettle to a new factory. - Critical for MSMEs in India (e.g. Mudra Yojana). - Major driver of GDP — bank credit growth ≈ sign of a healthy, expanding economy. - Career: BFSI is a fast-growing segment; India targeting a $5 trillion economy. Credit skills are also a life skill (sales managers assessing customers, purchase managers assessing suppliers).

    Types of borrowers

    Two top-level buckets: Individuals and Businesses.

    Business structure Legal identity Who is liable on default?
    Proprietorship Owner and business are legally one and the same Owner personally liable; personal assets can be attached
    Partnership 2+ people share profits/losses All partners personally liable
    Company / Corporation Separate legal identity from shareholders Bank can go after company assets only — unless a shareholder has given a personal guarantee

    MCQ trap: "Limited liability" applies to the company form only. A personal guarantee is the exception that pierces it.

    Common loan products

    For individuals: - Home loan — large, long tenor (15–20 yrs), property is collateral (secured). - Personal loan — unsecured (no collateral) → therefore higher interest rate. For weddings, vacations, medical. - Car loan — vehicle is the security. - Education loan — funds higher education in India/abroad.

    For businesses: - Working capital loan — short-term, for day-to-day ops (raw material, salaries). Example: Surat textile factory buying cotton before festive season. - Term loan — long-term investment (machinery, factory building). Example: ₹5 cr machine repaid over 5–7 years.

    1.2Preliminary Assessment1

    Think of it as the doctor's first check-up before ordering expensive tests. Three questions:

    Q1: Who is the borrower?

    • Individual → ask: salaried or self-employed?
    • Salaried (esp. govt / stable company) = predictable monthly income = lower risk.
    • Self-employed (shop owner, consultant) = income varies → must look at business profits and cash flow.
    • Business → ask for vintage (how old the business is) and turnover (total sales).
    • New business = riskier (no track record). Mature business = analysable track record.
    • Stable/growing turnover = has customers, performing well.
    • Management / promoter quality — "the quality of management and the integrity of management is the single most important factor when lending to a business." remember this line, it's a classic MCQ answer

    Q2: What is the opportunity?

    Check three things: 1. Specific opportunity — Amount, Purpose, Repayment source, Tenor. 2. Is the request logical? Do amount/purpose/tenor align with each other? (Can't fund a factory with a 6-month loan.) 3. Is it aligned with the bank's own lending policy? (Legal + within institution's policy; some industries are excluded.)

    Q3: What is the cause of borrowing?

    Three borrowing causes — this is the heart of commercial credit:

    Cause Nature of need Correct facility Example
    Seasonal working capital Temporary — current assets rise for a season, then fall and the loan is repaid Short-term / revolving Sivakasi cracker maker, 3 months before Diwali
    Permanent working capital Permanent — sales grow year on year → inventory and receivables permanently higher Higher year-round working capital limit Consistently growing business
    Capital expenditure (CapEx) Multi-year fixed assets: machinery, land, building Term loan Nagpur e-commerce co. building a warehouse

    Why it matters: A loss-making company asking for working capital → decline. Someone buying machinery but proposing 6-month repayment → mismatch. The bank wants a logical, productive purpose + a clear repayment plan.

    1.3Credit Assessment — The 5 Cs of Credit

    C What it assesses Example
    Character Integrity, reputation, track record, business strategy of leadership Promoter with clean record, honours past commitments
    Capacity Ability to generate enough cash flow to service obligations. Cash flows from operations are the primary source of repayment. ₹2 L monthly cash flow vs ₹50 k EMI
    Capital How much money the owner has invested — skin in the game Founder puts ₹50 L own money then asks ₹1 cr > founder who puts ₹5 L
    Conditions Competitive environment, industry, economy, government regulation EV battery maker benefits from subsidies/tax benefits
    Collateral Secondary source of repayment — asset pledged as security Commercial property in Gurgaon

    Big idea: credit analysis is about (a) ability to pay and (b) willingness to pay. The 5 Cs cover both.

    Mapping 5 Cs to practice — practitioners split total risk into two: - Business risk (qualitative) — industry, business model, management quality → maps to Character + Conditions. - Financial risk (quantitative) — historical financials, debt obligations, projections, cash flows → maps to Capacity + Capital + Collateral.

    MCQ trap: which C maps to which risk bucket. Memorise: Business risk = Character & Conditions; Financial risk = Capacity, Capital, Collateral.

    1.4Industry Risk Analysis

    Industry risks are those faced by ALL companies in that industry. The type of industry is a key driver of credit profile.

    Two broad industry types

    Product industries (create/buy/sell physical goods):

    Player Value addition Margin Borrowing need
    Manufacturer Highest (raw material → finished good) Highest Heavy fixed assets → long-term / term loans
    Wholesaler Volume & logistics Lower Working capital (inventory + credit to customers)
    Retailer Availability at convenient place/time Lowest Working capital for inventory

    Service industries: - Capital-intensive services — cargo airline, power generation. High fixed costs, big fixed-asset investment → term loans. - Labour-intensive services — software development, consulting. Key asset = people → working capital to pay salaries.

    The 7 industry risk factors (memorise the list)

    1. Sales / revenue prospects — growing (EV), stagnant, or declining (fixed-line telephones)? Healthcare = growing (aging population, health awareness).
    2. Cyclicality — tied to the economic cycle. Construction = highly cyclical; FMCG (toothpaste, soap) = non-cyclical → smoother, more predictable cash flows.
    3. Seasonality — wedding/events industry peaks Oct–Feb; dairy is stable year-round.
    4. Capital intensity — steel manufacturing = high barrier to entry BUT high fixed costs → operating leverage: a 10% sales fall can cut profit 25–30%. Software = low capital intensity.
    5. Stability of technology — IT/telecom change fast (obsolescence risk); pickle manufacturing is stable.
    6. Regulatory susceptibility — telecom (licence, pricing), real-money online gaming (e.g. Dream11 hit by a blanket ban); home bakery ≈ zero regulatory risk.
    7. Nature of competition — price-only competition (cement) squeezes margins; brand/quality competition (luxury cars) supports higher margins.

    The single big idea: all seven exist to answer "how volatile are the cash flows of companies in this industry?" Credit analysis = assessing stability of the borrower's cash flows.

    1.5Business Risk and Competitive Advantage

    Same industry, different outcomes → depends on management strategy and capability. Case: Indian telecom — capital intensive + regulation-heavy + fierce price competition. Reliance Jio had deep pockets + a disruptive low-price strategy + pan-India 4G → dominant. Aircel lacked financial capacity and strategic vision → collapsed under the price war and unmanageable debt.

    Three sources of competitive advantage

    1. Cost efficiency — be the low-cost producer (budget airline: single aircraft type, high seat density, quick turnaround).
    2. Product differentiation — unique/superior product commanding a premium (premium smartphone: camera, display, brand).
    3. Market focus — serve a specific niche better than anyone (local South Indian restaurant in a residential area).

    Other business-risk factors

    • Market share — bargaining power over suppliers & customers (Maruti Suzuki).
    • Sales growth — consistent growth = healthy, more predictable future cash flows (Zomato).
    • Profitability — healthy margins allow reinvestment and debt service (Asian Paints).
    • Diversification — product diversification (Tata Motors: trucks + Tiago + Nexon) and customer diversification (a vendor selling only to Tata Steel is high risk).
    • Key-man / promoter dependence — Wipro & Infosys reduced key-man risk by professionalising management and building second-level leadership.

    1.6The Cash Flow Statement (heavily testable)1

    Core mantra: "Sales is vanity, profit is sanity, cash is the only reality."

    Worked illustration: Buy 10 laptops for ₹10 L cash; sell for ₹15 L on 90-day credit. - P&L: Revenue 15, COGS 10, Net profit ₹5 L, margin 33%. - Bank account: opening ₹10 L − ₹10 L paid = ₹0. Profit is trapped in accounts receivable. → Profitable on paper, out of cash. This gap is the cash flow gap.

    The three buckets

    Bucket What it captures Inflow example Outflow example
    CFO — Cash flow from Operating activities "Heartbeat": core business Cash from selling a T-shirt Paying the electricity bill
    CFI — Cash flow from Investing activities Long-term assets / investments (the future) Selling an old warehouse Buying a delivery van (CapEx)
    CFF — Cash flow from Financing activities Flows with lenders and shareholders Issuing new shares; new loan Paying dividends; repaying debt; buyback

    What analysts use it for

    • Liquidity — can the firm pay bills for the next 3–6 months without new debt?
    • Ability to invest in the future — is the core business funding its own maintenance/growth CapEx, or is it selling fixed assets to survive? (Positive cash flow only because they sold the main factory = big red flag: selling the future for today's survival.)
    • Dividend sustainability — is the dividend paid out of operating surplus or funded by fresh borrowing?
    • Quality of accounting — accrual profits are manipulable (extend asset life 5→10 yrs to cut depreciation and boost PAT; aggressive revenue recognition on a 3-year contract booked on day 1). Cash cannot be manipulated that way. Profits rising while CFO stagnant → red flag (channel stuffing, fake invoices).

    Direct vs Indirect method

    • They differ ONLY in the computation of CFO. CFI and CFF are identical in both. classic MCQ
    • Direct: list actual cash received from customers, paid to suppliers, etc. More intuitive but tedious.
    • Indirect: start with net profit, adjust for non-cash items and changes in balance sheet items. Industry standard — it shows the reconciliation between profit and cash. (Used in this course.)

    Sign rules (memorise)

    Balance-sheet movement Cash effect
    Asset ↑ Outflow (cash trapped in the asset)
    Asset ↓ Inflow
    Liability / Equity ↑ Inflow (someone financed you)
    Liability / Equity ↓ Outflow (settling an obligation)

    Note: buying inventory on credit is still treated as an outflow at the operating level — you'll pay for it later.

    Life-cycle signature (very likely MCQ)

    Stage CFO CFI CFF Why
    Startup / burn − − + Operations not yet break-even, heavy infra/R&D spend, survives on external equity/debt
    Growth / expansion + − + Model proven and generating cash, but aggressive CapEx exceeds internal generation
    Mature / cash cow + (highly) − (maintenance only) − Self-funded; returns surplus via dividends, buybacks, debt reduction
    Decline / harvesting +/− (declining) + − Not investing; liquidating assets; returning funds to lenders/owners

    Worked example — Vikas Electronics Ltd (₹ lakhs)

    Consumer electronics retailer. Revenue 1,000 → 1,200 (+20%); gross profit 400 → 500 (+25%).

    CFO (indirect):

    PAT                                    187.5
+ Depreciation (non-cash)              +50.0
− Gain on sale of assets (investing)   −10.0
+ Interest expense (financing)         +30.0
= FFO (Funds Flow from Operations)     257.5
  Δ Inventory      200 → 250           −50.0   (asset ↑ = outflow)
  Δ Receivables    120 → 160           −40.0   (asset ↑ = outflow)
  Δ Payables        80 → 110           +30.0   (liability ↑ = inflow)
= CFO                                  197.5

    FFO vs CFO: FFO is the subtotal before working-capital movements. CFO = FFO ± working-capital changes.

    CFI:

    Cash from sale of assets = Book value (15) + Gain (10)   = +25.0
Purchase of fixed assets:
   Closing NFA = Opening NFA − Depreciation − BV of assets sold + Purchases
   580 = 500 − 50 − 15 + Purchases  →  Purchases = 145
                                                   = −145.0
= CFI (net)                                          −120.0

    Rearranged form: Purchases = ΔNFA + Depreciation + BV of assets sold.

    CFF:

    Share capital 200 → 250                +50.0
Long-term debt 300 → 350               +50.0
Interest paid                          −30.0
Dividends (derived)                    −12.5
= CFF                                   +57.5

    Deriving dividends: Retained earnings is the bridge between the balance sheet and P&L. Expected RE = Opening RE (290) + PAT (187.5) = 477.5. Actual RE = 465. Difference = ₹12.5 L = dividend paid. Why retained earnings is NOT counted as financing inflow: it's already captured inside CFO via PAT — counting it again is double counting. Only share capital changes are financing.

    Reconciliation: CFO 197.5 + CFI (−120) + CFF 57.5 = +135 = closing cash (185) − opening cash (50). ✔ In the real world an exact match is rare — focus on materiality, not perfection.

    Interpretation — 5 lenses

    1. Quality of Earnings = CFO ÷ PAT. Here 197.5/187.5 ≈ 1.05×. Close to or above 1 is very good — the core business converts profit into cash.
    2. EBITDA bridge. Analysts treat EBITDA as a cash-flow proxy, but it isn't. EBITDA 320 vs CFO 197.5 → gap 122.5 = taxes 62.5 + working-capital changes 60. A widening EBITDA–CFO gap year after year = the company is getting worse at converting paper profit into cash.
    3. Free Cash Flow = CFO − CapEx. Here 197.5 − 145 = +52.5. Positive FCF = self-funded company; covers working capital and fixed-asset investment with cash left over. Strong credit quality.
    4. Cash conversion cycle — days to turn ₹1 of inventory investment into ₹1 of cash from sales. Cash flow statement tells you the direction: if inventory and receivables grow faster than revenue, CCC is lengthening (cash stuck longer).
    5. Red flags: - CFO persistently < PAT → poor collection, or fake/unrealisable profits. - Dividends > FCF → company liquidating itself to pay shareholders; unsustainable. - CFO persistently < interest expense → can't even service interest. - FFO positive but working-capital changes eat it all (spike in inventory/receivables) → channel stuffing or slow-moving inventory. - CFO −, CFI −, CFF + → surviving purely on investor money.

    1.7Loan Structuring

    Definition: designing the specific terms and conditions of a credit facility to fit both borrower and lender. Not just the amount — also facility type, pricing, disbursement/repayment method, and covenants.

    Elements of loan structuring

    1. Timing of disbursement and repayment — disburse in stages tied to milestones/CapEx (ensures end-use); repayment schedule tailored to the borrower's cash flow cycle (e.g. aligned to peak sales season).
    2. Restrictions / requirements (covenants) — audited financials within a prescribed period; annual budget/projections; no material business change, asset disposal or M&A without bank consent.
    3. Security and collateral — the secondary source of repayment (primary = cash flows). Home loan → mortgage on the house; business loan → hypothecation of machinery/inventory. Collateral value drives loan amount and risk appetite.
    4. Pricing — not just interest rate: interest can be fixed or floating, linked to the bank's MCLR or an external benchmark like the repo rate; plus upfront arrangement fees, annual renewal fees, penalties for covenant non-compliance. Risk-based pricing: riskier borrower → higher rate and fees.
    5. Selecting the appropriate credit facility (below).
    6. Covenants (below).

    Matching facility to need

    Need Facility
    Working capital build-up, cash-flow gaps, temporary liquidity mismatch, seasonal inventory Revolving short-term: CC (Cash Credit), OD (Overdraft), WCDL (Working Capital Demand Loan), business credit card
    CapEx: new machinery, factory expansion Term loan — defined drawdown schedule + fixed repayment over years
    • CC/OD: draw down up to a limit determined by the level of current assets. Principal often never repaid — the borrower only services interest and maintains adequate current assets, evidenced by a monthly stock and book debt statement.
    • WCDL: drawn against drawing power (based on current asset levels), then repaid and redrawn.
    • Drawing power = the banking term for how much you may actually draw, based on actual current assets.

    Mismatch consequences: funding a short-term need with a long-term loan gives the borrower more money than needed; funding a long-term need with short-term funds creates a liquidity crisis.

    Covenants

    By direction: - Affirmative covenants — promises to DO something: provide audited financials annually, maintain adequate insurance, notify the bank of material litigation. - Negative covenants — promises to NOT do something: no additional debt without consent, no sale of substantial assets, no dividends until the debt is repaid.

    By type:

    A. Financial covenants — three families

    Family Covenant Formula Threshold
    Gearing Gross debt gearing Total borrowing ÷ equity (tangible net worth) —
    Debt-to-earnings Debt ÷ EBITDA — (very popular in banking)
    Serviceability Interest cover EBITDA (or EBIT) ÷ gross interest expense —
    DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio) (EBITDA − taxes) ÷ (interest + principal repayment) 1.25× — standard; inevitable on any term loan
    Financial strength Minimum net worth Net worth floor —
    Current ratio Current assets (stock, book debt, cash) ÷ current liabilities (short-term loan, trade creditors) 1.33× — Indian standard

    Two numbers you must memorise: DSCR ≥ 1.25×, Current ratio ≥ 1.33×. Breach of DSCR → borrower may be asked to right-size the debt (reduce debt to restore the ratio).

    B. Non-financial covenants - Pari-passu ranking — "at the same level as others"; the security given to this bank cannot be inferior to what's given to any other bank. - Cross-default — the bank can declare a default on its loan because the borrower defaulted on someone else's loan. Prevents this lender being disadvantaged when another lender with a stronger covenant declares default first. - Negative pledge — the borrower will not create a security interest over any asset without the bank's consent. Common with unsecured loans; prevents dilution of the bank's position. - Material Adverse Change (MAC) — allows the bank to declare default on a significant adverse change in financial/trading position. Hard to enforce in practice, but useful to force a conversation.

    Why covenants exist: supplement the initial due diligence and act as an early warning system — the bank learns credit quality is deteriorating before the account becomes an NPA.

    1.8Post-Sanction Monitoring

    Rationale: creditworthiness is not static. Goal: prevent a good loan from turning bad; prevent slippage into NPA; verify end use of funds.

    Methods (on-site + off-site)

    1. Review of financial documents (off-site) — B/S, P&L, cash flow; day-to-day transactions in the borrower's account (abnormal transactions = early warning); stock and book debt statement, submitted monthly in India, to validate drawing power.
    2. Physical verification and inspection (on-site) — business premises, factory, project site; verifies operations and the existence/upkeep of secured assets. For project finance, a specialised monitoring agency may be appointed to prevent cost overruns and delays. Stock audit = valuation of charged inventory; check insurance, maintenance, storage.
    3. Compliance with loan covenants — financial ratios met, reports submitted on time.
    4. End-use verification — - Term loan example (Bharat Manufacturing, ₹5 cr CNC machine): bank pays the supplier directly, against a proforma invoice, after verifying supplier credentials and installation. Money never touches the borrower's account → no diversion. - Working capital example (Textile Innovation, ₹10 cr CC): no lump-sum; monthly stock & book debt statements set drawing power; monitor account for large transfers to unrelated third parties (e.g. a director's personal account) = red flag; physically inspect inventory.

    SMA framework (RBI early-warning system) — memorise the buckets

    Category Principal/interest overdue for
    SMA-0 1–30 days
    SMA-1 31–60 days
    SMA-2 more than 60 days (i.e. 61–90)
    NPA more than 90 days

    CRILC — Central Repository of Information on Large Credits, maintained by RBI. Banks must report all credit exposures of ₹5 crore and above, including SMA-classified and defaulted accounts. Purpose: shared database so other banks can spot stressed accounts and avoid lending to high-risk borrowers.

    Scenario: Techtronics, ₹20 cr loan, interest delayed 15 days for two consecutive months → auto-flagged SMA-0 → RM contacts company → learns a client payment was delayed → reworks the schedule / offers a temporary OD → prevents slide to SMA-1 and NPA.

    CERSAI — Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India. Centralised online registry of security interests over movable and immovable property. - Created to stop the fraud of mortgaging the same property to multiple banks. - Primarily a pre-sanction/disbursement check, but has a post-sanction role: lenders must register the security interest within a specified time frame or risk losing legal protection under the SARFAESI Act. - Scenario: Mr Sharma mortgages a Mumbai property to Bank A; two years later applies to Bank B; Bank B's CERSAI search reveals the existing charge → application rejected.

    Credit audit

    • Evaluation of the bank's credit portfolio and lending practices by an independent observer — typically the bank's internal audit team, not the RM.
    • Objective: compliance with internal credit policy + regulatory guidelines; assess portfolio quality. Part of the bank's risk-based internal audit framework.
    • Difference from day-to-day monitoring: monitoring is done by the RM/credit officer; credit audit is done by an independent team → impartial check on sanctioning authorities.
    • What it reviews: the sanctioning process (policy compliance, pre-disbursement conditions), post-sanction procedures, documentation adequacy (executed, stamped, charges filed with the RoC), and early warning signals.
    • Scenario (Future Tech, ₹50 cr): audit finds (a) an unapproved policy deviation on debt-to-equity, (b) a documentation lapse — charge on key machinery not registered with the RoC in time, making the security legally weak, (c) ineffective follow-up — RM noted a sales drop from GST returns but never raised it with the borrower.

    Technology in post-sanction monitoring

    • Centralised credit monitoring system — real-time tracking, integrating borrower account data, credit bureau, stock statements; auto-flags SMA-1 at 30 days overdue.
    • Big data & analytics — bank account data + GST returns for a real-time view of sales/purchases/cash flow; a sudden drop in GST filings = early warning.
    • Automated verification — drones for large construction projects; satellite imagery for agricultural produce/agri loans.
    • Blockchain for supply chain finance — transparent, immutable transaction record; verify invoice authenticity and goods movement in real time.
    • API integration with the borrower's ERP/accounting software — real-time financials, inventory levels; removes manual data submission.
    • Examples: Swift Logistics — GPS/telematics on financed trucks verifies commercial use; extended downtime or unusual location triggers an alert. Artisan Crafts — API-linked working capital; payment initiated in the accounting software, verified against sanctioned purpose, disbursed directly to the supplier. Weave Tech — ERP API shows raw-material inventory spiking without a matching rise in finished-goods sales → alert → export order was cancelled → bank arranges a contingency plan early.
    • Bonus benefit: this visibility improves MSME access to credit, because the bank sees day-to-day operations it could never get from financial statements.

    1.9Collateral, Charges and Documentation1

    Types of collateral

    Class Examples Notes
    Tangible Real estate (residential, commercial, land, agri), inventory, gold, vehicles, machinery & equipment Gold is favoured — easy to value and liquidate
    Financial Fixed deposit, shares/bonds/mutual funds, life insurance policy FD with the same bank ≈ risk-free (bank already holds the money)
    Intangible Book debt / accounts receivable, intellectual property (patents, copyrights, trademarks), corporate guarantee IP is hard to value/liquidate → not mainstream

    Margin & margin call (worked example): Loan against shares, 50% margin. Collateral ₹2 L → loan ₹1 L. Share value falls to ₹1.5 L → eligible loan is only ₹75,000, but ₹1 L is outstanding. Bank issues a margin call; borrower must either bring ₹50,000 of extra collateral (making collateral ₹2 L against ₹1 L outstanding) or repay ₹25,000.

    Life insurance as collateral: must be an endowment or money-back policy with a surrender value — not a pure term policy (term pays only on death, has no cash value). Endowment accumulates cash value and pays a lump sum at maturity or on death; money-back returns a % of the sum assured at intervals. Surrender value = amount the insurer pays if the policy is terminated early. The policy is assigned to the bank.

    Corporate guarantee: the guarantor promises to pay if the borrower defaults. Common when lending to a subsidiary/group company of a strong parent. Not a traditional security — it's a contractual obligation; the bank is effectively taking a call on the guarantor's financial strength and reputation.

    Fixed vs floating charge

    Fixed charge Floating charge
    Created on A specific, identifiable asset that doesn't change A class of assets that changes over time (inventory, receivables)
    Can borrower deal with it? No — cannot sell/dispose without the bank's permission Yes — can buy and sell in the normal course of business
    Example Mortgage on a house under a home loan Charge on a company's current assets
    Key event — Crystallises into a fixed charge on default or liquidation

    Modes of creating a charge — the classic MCQ table

    Mode Asset type Possession Example
    Pledge Movable Transferred to the bank Gold jewellery kept in the bank's vault
    Hypothecation Movable Stays with the borrower Car loan (bank named on RC book); company inventory
    Mortgage Immovable only (land, building) Stays with the borrower Home loan
    Lien Something of the customer's already in the bank's custody Bank retains possession Banker's lien on an FD against an overdue loan
    Set-off Combining the customer's accounts — Adjust an overdue loan against a positive savings/current balance; can be contractual or statutory
    Assignment Transfer of a right from assignor to assignee — Contractor assigns project receivables; life insurance policy assigned to the bank

    Two types of mortgage in India: - Simple mortgage — borrower transfers a legal interest in the property; bank gets the right to sell on default; borrower retains possession and use. - Equitable mortgage (mortgage by deposit of title deed) — borrower simply hands over the original title documents; no formal mortgage deed. Simple, quick, cost-effective — the majority practice in India.

    Charge filing (legally mandatory, not optional)

    • Charge must be registered with the Registrar of Companies (RoC).
    • Why: (a) creates a public record preventing double financing of the same asset; (b) establishes priority — the bank that filed first has the first claim on the sale proceeds.
    • Forms: CHG-1 to create a charge; CHG-4 to modify. Must be filed within 30 days of charge creation; beyond that a more complex extension process applies.

    Legal documentation — why it matters

    • Legal record of agreed terms; the only evidence in court on dispute/default. Without documentation there is no lender-borrower relationship and no recovery.
    • Regulatory compliance (RBI and other statutory bodies).
    • Risk management — checks done, collateral properly charged, identity verified.

    Key documents: 1. Loan / facility agreement — the core contract: parties, amount, purpose, rate (fixed/floating), repayment schedule, penalties, prepayment options, events of default. 2. Security documents — create the charge: mortgage deed (registered mortgage only; not needed for equitable mortgage), deed of hypothecation, deed of pledge, assignment agreement, deed of corporate guarantee. 3. DPN — Demand Promissory Note — a simple, unconditional promise to pay a specific sum on a specific date or on demand. An "IOU"; key instrument for debt recovery. 4. Corporate documents — Memorandum of Association, Articles of Association, board resolution authorising the loan. If the borrowing isn't authorised or the signatory isn't properly authorised, the loan can be held ultra vires (beyond powers → unenforceable). 5. Personal guarantee — deed of guarantee from promoters in their personal capacity.

    The three pillars of a safe loan: (1) security, (2) a properly created charge on that security, (3) meticulous, defect-free documentation.

    1.10Management Quality Assessment

    "The quality and integrity of the management team and promoters is the single most important factor in lending." A company with great financials but a shoddy management team will ultimately fail; average financials with a strong, honest, experienced team usually turns out fine.

    Six evaluation factors: 1. Reputation for integrity — red flag: routinely defaulting on supplier payments, changing business address to avoid creditors. 2. Experience across business cycles — has the promoter lived through a boom and a bust? (Survived 2008 > only ever operated in a boom.) 3. Aggressiveness — unrealistic growth targets, rapid inorganic expansion (M&A) into unrelated markets without a plan. 4. Management stability — frequent senior departures (e.g. CFO and COO leaving within months of each other) = huge red flag. 5. Regulatory history — tax raids, SEBI penalties, pending litigation = poor corporate governance = high credit risk. 6. Transparency in disclosures and accounting — numbers are only as good as the accounting policies and internal controls. Frequently changing accounting policies, cagey disclosure, or adverse auditor comments/qualifications = serious doubt.

    1.11MSME Landscape in India

    Numbers to memorise

    • MSMEs ≈ 29% of India's GDP.
    • ≈ 46% of India's total exports (FY 2024).
    • Huge employment generator, especially non-agricultural.
    • Credit gap ≈ ₹28 lakh crore — credit gap = credit demand − credit supply from formal channels.
    • Udyam Portal registration is mandatory to avail benefits; ~7 crore registrations to date.

    International comparison

    • Germany: SMEs = >99% of all firms, >50% of economic output, ~two-thirds of exports.
    • South Korea: MSMEs employ ~80% of the workforce.
    • Japan: SMEs employ >70% of the workforce; supply parts/components to large corporations.

    MSME classification (as of April 2025) — composite criterion

    Based on (a) investment in plant, equipment & machinery, net of depreciation (excludes land and building) and (b) annual turnover (excluding exports).

    Category Investment up to Turnover up to
    Micro ₹2.5 crore ₹10 crore
    Small ₹25 crore ₹100 crore
    Medium ₹125 crore ₹500 crore

    MSME-dominant sectors

    • Textile & apparel — ~45% of registered MSMEs; 70–80% of textile production; ~90% of handloom/handicraft. Clusters: Tiruppur (TN), Surat (Gujarat), Panipat (Haryana). ~one-third of workers are women.
    • Agro-processing — dairy, fruits, vegetables.
    • Auto components — ~80% of registered units are micro or small.
    • Leather — Kanpur, Agra; big export/forex contribution.
    • Gems & jewellery — ~90% of units micro or small.
    • IT services — software development, digital marketing.

    Challenges in MSME finance

    • Lack of formal records — informal operation, no proper financials or credit history.
    • Limited collateral — no land/large factory; banks reluctant to lend unsecured.
    • Liquidity issues — MSMEs supply large corporates; delayed payments cause cash crunches.
    • Inadequate financial literacy — can't navigate complex loan processes or pick the right product.
    • Result: rejection rates of 50–60%; treated as high-risk → higher interest rates.

    The mindset shift and adapted credit assessment

    • Ask "How?" instead of saying "No."
    • Look beyond the balance sheet — focus on cash flow.
    • Adaptations of the 5 Cs for MSMEs: 1. Focus on Character — formal data is thin, so local reputation, past (even informal) repayment history and honesty matter more. 2. Embrace alternative data — bank account statements (daily cash flow), GST returns (sales/purchases), utility bills (financial discipline proxy), merchant/payment-gateway data (Paytm, PhonePe daily sales for a kirana store). 3. Use digital tools — AI-based credit scoring on alternative data, no extensive paperwork. 4. Adopt cash-flow-based lending — shift away from balance-sheet/collateral-based; use bank statements, GST returns, Udyam registration data. 5. Use government guarantees — see CGTMSE below.

    MSME loan products

    • Working capital: CC, OD — borrow up to a limit against inventory and receivables.
    • Invoice / bill discounting — MSME sells unpaid invoices to a bank for immediate cash at a discount. Great when selling to large corporates with long payment cycles.
    • TReDS — Trade Receivables Discounting System — online platform to finance MSME trade receivables; banks/NBFCs bid competitively.
    • Term loans — machinery, equipment.
    • Unsecured business loans — smaller amounts, collateral-free but higher interest.

    Government schemes — learn the numbers

    Scheme Full form What it does
    CGTMSE Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises Government guarantee enabling collateral-free loans up to ₹10 crore. Owned by Government of India + SIDBI. Guarantee covers 75–90% of the loan. Reduces (but doesn't eliminate) the need for due diligence
    PMMY Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana Loans up to ₹10 lakh to non-corporate, non-farm micro enterprises. Three tiers: Shishu (up to ₹50,000), Kishor (₹50,000–₹5 lakh), Tarun (₹5–10 lakh)
    Stand Up India — Loans of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore for women and SC/ST entrepreneurs, for greenfield (new) projects
    PSB Loans in 59 Minutes Public Sector Bank loans in 59 minutes Government-backed digital platform; algorithmic analysis with no human intervention; integrated with the GST portal and Income Tax department; gives an in-principle approval in under an hour. Requires GST details, ITR, and 6 months' bank statements. Integrated with CGTMSE. Actual disbursement still takes 7–8 working days after the borrower picks from 20+ partner banks/NBFCs who do final due diligence

    MCQ trap: "59 minutes" is only in-principle approval, not disbursement. MCQ trap: Shishu/Kishor/Tarun slab boundaries.

    1.12Supply Chain Financing (SCF)

    Core idea: get the supplier paid early while the buyer pays later, funded by a third-party financier (bank/fintech).

    Fundamental difference from traditional lending:

    Traditional lending Supply chain financing
    Whose creditworthiness is assessed? The borrower's (financials, history, collateral) The corporate anchor's + genuineness of the transaction
    Basis Balance sheet funding Cash-flow / transaction-based funding

    Result for the MSME: cheaper, faster, collateral-free credit by leveraging the anchor's financial strength.

    Types of SCF — know which party initiates

    Product Who initiates / who is financed Example
    Invoice discounting MSME supplier takes its invoice to a bank Pune IT firm, ₹10 L invoice on 60-day terms; bank pays ₹9.8 L now; ₹20 k is the bank's fee; corporate pays the bank ₹10 L at maturity
    Factoring Supplier sells the invoice to a factoring company, which then collects from the buyer Tiruppur garment exporter selling to a reputed European buyer
    Reverse factoring The BUYER sets up the programme for its suppliers Car manufacturer with 90–120 day terms partners with a bank; suppliers get paid in days at a competitive rate; the manufacturer pays the bank on the due date. TReDS is India's reverse-factoring platform
    PO (Purchase Order) financing Financing against the strength of a purchase order, before production Noida manufacturer with a ₹50 L PO from a reputed retailer, no cash for raw material
    Inventory financing Existing inventory used as collateral for a short-term loan Electronics wholesaler stocking up for the festive season; very popular with automobile dealers
    Channel finance Anchor manufacturer arranges a line of credit for its dealer network Car maker ensures dealers can hold stock → boosts the manufacturer's own sales

    MCQ distinction to nail: Factoring = supplier-driven (supplier sells its invoice). Reverse factoring = buyer-driven (buyer sets up the programme for its suppliers). Channel finance = anchor funds its downstream dealers; reverse factoring/invoice discounting = funds upstream suppliers.

    Benefits — a win-win

    For the MSME/supplier: improved cash flow (paid in days, not 60–90); lower cost of capital (priced off the anchor, not its own balance sheet); reduced risk of buyer payment delay/default. For the large corporate/buyer: extended payment terms → holds cash longer → better working capital; stronger supplier/dealer relationships → higher sales; supply chain stability (suppliers stay liquid and fulfil orders).

    Credit appraisal in SCF — what gets appraised

    Product Primary appraisal focus
    Inventory financing The inventory itself — resale value, liquidity, shelf life, obsolescence. (Rice < risk than fashion apparel.) Not the dealer's financials
    Invoice discounting The corporate buyer's creditworthiness + authenticity of the invoice + no disputes over delivered goods
    PO financing The buyer's creditworthiness, strength of the PO (non-cancellable, clear profit margin), and how recurring the relationship is. Common in autos — component suppliers financing against OEM POs (Maruti, Honda)
    Channel finance The anchor's credit profile + vintage of the anchor-dealer relationship; limits based on historical business volume with the anchor. The anchor typically nominates which dealers get limits and ensures repayment, because it won't let 1–2 defaults kill the programme. Track record with Tata Steel, Tata Motors, GAIL, SAIL has been excellent despite looking like unsecured MSME exposure on paper

    Technology in SCF

    Fintech platforms automate onboarding → invoice verification → disbursement. - Speed & efficiency — digital onboarding, quick KYC/GST/bank checks; weeks → days. - AI-powered credit assessment — GST filings, bank statements, ERP data → granular risk profiles and automated scoring; enables lending to thin-file businesses. - Reduced costs — automation makes even small-ticket loans viable.

    Blockchain / distributed ledger - Secure, tamper-proof, shared record of every transaction → transparency, fraud reduction, trust. - Smart contracts — self-executing contracts with terms written in code; automatically release payment when goods are confirmed delivered/accepted. No manual approval.

    Trade finance as the flagship use case - 80–90% of global trade relies on trade/supply chain financing in some form. - Problem: paper-based, many intermediaries (financial institutions, credit insurers, export credit agencies, logistics providers, government agencies, regulators) across different languages, time zones, currencies, accounting systems, regulatory and legal regimes → duplication across ledgers, repeated due diligence, time, cost, reconciliation errors. Worst for MSMEs. - Blockchain covers order, shipment, insurance, logistics, financing, customs, delivery in one mechanism. - Landmark examples (memorise): - 2016 — Barclays issued the world's first blockchain-based Letter of Credit: process cut from 7–10 days to under 4 hours. - 2018 — HSBC and ING executed a live trade finance transaction for Cargill on the Corda platform: LC issued in 24 hours vs the usual 5–10 days.

    SCF case studies

    1. Commercial vehicle manufacturer + bank → channel finance for dealers. Problem: dealers needed working capital for vehicle inventory, had poor financials, relied on high-interest loans. Solution: loans sanctioned on the anchor's credit profile, not individual dealer assessment; platform gave real-time visibility of dealership inventory for dynamic risk assessment. Result: cheaper/faster working capital, better liquidity, more trucks bought → higher sales for the anchor.
    2. E-commerce company + fintech → AI-driven SCF for thousands of small suppliers. Problem: 60–90 day payment cycles choking supplier cash flow. Solution: early payment on invoices, credit risk assessed in real time from sales data on the e-commerce platform itself. Result: suppliers paid in 2–3 days, 50% faster loan approval, higher order volumes.

    1.13Digital Lending in India

    Definition: loan origination, underwriting, disbursement and servicing all done through digital channels (mobile app, website, API) with minimal or no physical/in-branch paperwork.

    Three phases of evolution

    Phase Period What happened
    1. Early fintech adoption mid-2010s Startups targeted unmet demand from young salaried people and informal workers. Enablers: Aadhaar, eKYC, smartphone proliferation, collapse in mobile data prices after 2016
    2. Scale & product diversification 2018–2022 Instant personal loans, merchant lending, gig-worker credit, BNPL at checkout. Fintechs partnered with NBFCs/banks: fintech does origination + UX; NBFC carries the credit risk. Digital disbursements ≈ ₹21 trillion in FY22, forecast to more than double by FY27
    3. Regulatory consolidation 2023 onwards Predatory practices (hidden charges, coercive recovery) → RBI rulebook, culminating in the Digital Lending Directions, 2025 (dated 8 May 2025)

    The ecosystem — 9 participant categories

    Participant Who Role
    Borrowers Salaried, self-employed, gig workers (Swiggy/Zomato/Uber/Ola), MSMEs Want quick, flexible, small-ticket loans without paperwork. Their diversity shapes product design
    Traditional lenders SBI, HDFC, ICICI; SFBs (Ujjivan, AU); large NBFCs (Bajaj Finance, Tata Capital) Provide the actual loan capital, carry the risk, own RBI compliance. Needed because fintechs can't always lend directly (capital + regulatory barriers)
    Fintech lenders / LSPs (Lending Service Providers) CreditBee, CASHe, Slice, ZestMoney, Navi; platforms like Paytm, PhonePe Build the customer-facing app/UX, AI-driven underwriting, alternative data analytics; intermediary between bank/NBFC and borrower
    Technology providers Perfios, CreditVidya, HyperVerge APIs for KYC, fraud detection, credit scoring; video KYC, biometric onboarding; secure cloud processing
    Payment system players NPCI (UPI, AePS), Razorpay, PayU Instant disbursement; auto EMI collection via UPI AutoPay, NACH, e-mandate — the "payment rails"
    Data providers / credit bureaus CIBIL, Experian, Equifax Credit history and scores; detect over-leverage. The risk management layer
    Regulators RBI (lending), TRAI (spam calls), MeitY (data privacy, IT rules) Set rules, protect consumers, maintain the app registry
    Collection partners Licensed collection agencies, digital collection platforms Recover overdues via legal means, digital nudges (SMS, WhatsApp); must comply with RBI's Fair Practices Code
    Consumer protection bodies / industry associations DLAI (Digital Lenders Association of India), FACE (Fintech Association for Consumer Empowerment) Represent industry, draft codes of conduct, educate consumers. FACE's April 2025 report stressed ethical use of alternative data

    End-to-end flow (Ravi, a gig worker): downloads app (LSP) → bank statement analysed by Perfios (tech provider) → score checked at CIBIL (bureau) → loan disbursed by an NBFC partner → EMI collected via UPI AutoPay (payment player) → collection partner if he defaults → RBI monitors → FACE ensures borrower rights.

    Automated underwriting

    What it is: programmed rules + machine learning models evaluate creditworthiness and set sanction terms without human underwriters in most cases.

    Inputs: credit bureau scores, bank transaction history, account statement analysis, payroll credits, UPI inflows, GST filings (for MSMEs), device and behavioural signals (app usage, OS metadata), alternative data.

    Output decision: approve / reject / flag for manual review.

    Advantages: - Speed and scale — thousands of decisions daily, in seconds. - Inclusion — can score thin-file borrowers with no long credit track record. - Consistency — removes human bias and subjectivity/friction.

    Risks and limitations (know all four): 1. Model bias and explainability — models can reflect and amplify biases in training data (e.g. penalising rural users with less digital activity). Regulators want explainable decisions and audit trails so a customer knows why they were declined. 2. Model drift — models trained on past data underperform in new macro conditions (pandemic, sectoral shock). 3. Data quality — incorrect/incomplete inputs (e.g. mismapped UPI IDs) → wrong decisions. 4. Privacy — large-scale data collection raises consent and surveillance concerns.

    Alternative data

    Definition: non-traditional credit signals, useful when bureau history is thin or absent.

    Sources: UPI transaction patterns; telecom data and recharge frequency; utility bill payments; GST and ITR filings; e-commerce purchase behaviour; device metadata; social profile signals (with borrower consent).

    How it becomes a credit signal: feature engineering — frequency of inflows, size volatility, recurring bill payments, merchant mix are fed into predictive models as proxies for income stability and repayment intent.

    Benefits: expands inclusion (young consumers, gig workers, small merchants); real-time behavioural insight; early detection of stress. Safeguards required: standardised definitions, audits for bias, privacy controls, consent, data minimisation, explainability — otherwise misclassification and exclusion of underrepresented groups.

    BNPL vs credit cards

    BNPL (Buy Now Pay Later) Credit card
    Origination At checkout, by fintech/merchant Issued by banks
    Underwriting Requires lower formal credit history Stricter underwriting
    Structure Short tenure, fixed instalments, often merchant-subsidised / 0% cost for short tenures Revolving credit with interest beyond a grace period
    Customer base First-time borrowers, millennials without cards Established credit users

    Regulatory angle: RBI's 2025 guidelines mandate clearer disclosures and inclusion of BNPL in credit bureau reporting where appropriate. Reason: BNPL improved access for thin-file borrowers but created hidden indebtedness — multiple BNPL loans accumulating with no bureau visibility.

    RBI Digital Lending Directions, 2025 (dated 8 May 2025)

    Key requirements: - Registration of DLAs (Digital Lending Apps). - Standardised disclosure — the Key Fact Statement (KFS): a one-page standardised document given to every borrower before disbursement, stating rate of interest, amount, repayment schedule, and all fees and charges (processing fee, platform fee, late payment penalty). Also requires APR (Annual Percentage Rate) disclosure. - Restrictions on intrusive app permissions. - Clear allocation of responsibility between the LSP and the Regulated Entity (bank/NBFC). - CIMS — Centralised Information Management System: RBI-operationalised system where DLAs must be reported.

    Why each element matters: registration → enforceability; KFS → less mis-selling; CIMS + mandatory bureau reporting → less loan stacking; data-collection limits → privacy.

    Risks and mitigations (likely "match the pair" MCQ)

    Risk Mitigation
    Consumer protection — hidden charges, coercive recovery KFS, disclosure rules, grievance channels
    Credit risk / over-indebtedness — loans stacking across apps Bureau reporting, dual reporting in co-lending so exposures are system-visible
    Operational & cyber — fake apps, data breaches, API failures App registry on CIMS, cyber audits, stronger merchant and code controls
    Model risk and bias — unfair ML outcomes Model governance, explainability, periodic backtesting, human override points
    Systemic risk — small NBFCs concentrated in digital unsecured lending Capital adequacy norms, prudent risk sharing by regulated entities

    Global comparison

    • China — Ant Group: vast lending ecosystem tied to e-commerce and payments; the 2020 regulatory tightening showed unchecked scale can create systemic risk.
    • US — Affirm, Klarna (BNPL): consumer convenience but concerns about default dynamics and the need to integrate BNPL into credit reporting.
    • India's uniqueness: UPI — a real-time payment network that is a strong foundation for data-driven underwriting; India is choosing to balance innovation with tighter consumer protection and registry mechanisms.

    Way forward by stakeholder

    • Banks/NBFCs: strengthen model risk management; clear contractual governance with LSPs; periodic independent model validation.
    • Fintechs/LSPs: standardised KFS templates; limit intrusive app permissions; prompt bureau reporting; grievance redressal.
    • Regulators: monitor CIMS and DLA registrations; publish dashboards (sector volumes, delinquencies); coordinate with data protection authorities.
    • Consumer groups: financial literacy on APR, EMI stacking, grievance escalation.
    • Investors: due diligence on model governance and compliance — not just growth metrics.

    Quick-fire revision — numbers from this course

    Item Value
    NPA threshold Overdue > 90 days
    SMA-0 / SMA-1 / SMA-2 1–30 / 31–60 / >60 days
    CRILC reporting threshold ₹5 crore and above
    Charge filing with RoC CHG-1 (create) / CHG-4 (modify), within 30 days
    DSCR covenant threshold 1.25×
    Current ratio covenant threshold 1.33× (India)
    Quality of earnings (CFO/PAT) ≥ 1 is good
    MSME share of GDP / exports 29% / 46%
    MSME credit gap ₹28 lakh crore
    Micro / Small / Medium investment ₹2.5 cr / ₹25 cr / ₹125 cr
    Micro / Small / Medium turnover ₹10 cr / ₹100 cr / ₹500 cr
    CGTMSE collateral-free limit / cover ₹10 crore / 75–90%
    Mudra: Shishu / Kishor / Tarun ≤₹50k / ₹50k–5L / ₹5L–10L

    Global trade reliant on trade finance 80–90%
    Barclays blockchain LC (2016) 7–10 days → <4 hours
    HSBC–ING / Cargill on Corda (2018) 5–10 days → 24 hours
    Digital disbursements FY22 ₹21 trillion

    Wealth Management

    Wealth Management

    (Instructors: Dr. L. Ravindran, N. Gopalakrishnan, Kalpana Chauhan, K. R. Aravind — Modules 0–4)

    Course map — Module 1: foundations, goals, asset allocation. Module 2: practice management, taxation, alternative investments. Module 3: regulation & technology. Module 4: estate planning & fiduciary duty.

    2.1Global Perspective and India's Growth Story

    Why wealth management matters in India now: demographic change — ~55% of the population is young (new corporate employees, business owners, startup entrepreneurs) who have amassed wealth and need long-term goal planning and risk management.

    Three client archetypes: - Young professionals (22–30) — digital-first, systematic monthly investing into mutual funds (SIPs). - Business owners / startup entrepreneurs — graduated beyond mutual funds into Portfolio Management Services (PMS), regulated by SEBI; need estate planning. - HNWIs — diversified across financial assets and real assets; private equity and alternative investments.

    50-year GDP comparison (1975 → 2025)

    Country 1975 2025 Growth
    USA $1.6 tn $27 tn ~17×
    UK $0.3 tn $3 tn ~10×
    Canada $0.1 tn $2 tn ~20×
    India $0.1 tn $4.5 tn ~45×

    Forecast to 2050: India $4.5 tn → ~$30 tn (the largest growth of the 20 economies surveyed); USA $27 tn → ~$40 tn. India 2025 → 2035: conservative $4.19 tn → $6.6 tn; optimistic $10.3 tn; average ~$8.87 tn.

    What changed: USA went manufacturing-led (1975) → dot-com/tech boom (2000) → AI, digital innovation, fintech, cloud (2025). India went agrarian with high poverty and low industrialisation (1975) → economic reforms of 1992–93 → by 2025 the hub for startups, Global Capability Centres, and the world's back office. 2015–2025 saw the startup boom and 100+ unicorns, supported by Atmanirbhar Bharat.

    Millionaires vs billionaires

    Country Millionaires Billionaires
    USA ~25 million 850
    UK ~3 million —
    Canada ~1.5 million —
    India ~1.2 million 358

    UHNWI population growth forecast: India ~+50% (highest), China ~+47%, rest ~27% or lower.

    2.2Investor Segments and the Wealth Management Ecosystem

    Investor categories

    1. Individuals — salaried, business, professionals (lawyers, CAs), retired; resident or non-resident.
    2. Institutions — public/private sector banks, financial institutions, mutual funds, pension funds, provident funds, government and private organisations.
    3. Others — charitable organisations, hedge funds, venture capitalists, private equity investors; plus foreign hedge fund and portfolio investors.

    Wealth tiers — memorise the thresholds

    Tier Investable liquid assets
    HNWI (High Net Worth Individual) ≥ $1 million
    VHNWI (Very High Net Worth) $5 million – $30 million
    UHNWI (Ultra High Net Worth) > $30 million

    (Note: thresholds can vary by institution and region.)

    UHNWIs hold only ~13% of global wealth and are ~0.003% of the world's ~8 billion population.

    HNWI vs UHNWI — service needs

    HNWI UHNWI
    Special wealth management services; asset accumulation focus Complex portfolios, expansive needs
    Tax management a pivotal reason to choose a manager Access to global private equity
    Estate planning Offshore banking incl. GIFT City funds; large-scale real estate
    Relies on a finance professional, boutique firm or private bank Employs a family office (financial, legal, lifestyle, even concierge services)
    Access to hedge funds and PE funds Sophisticated tax structuring; succession planning; trusts and private foundations
    Active in capital markets; buys luxury goods Extremely risk-sensitive; large-scale philanthropy

    Players in wealth management (excluding banks)

    Brokerage houses · product specialists · fintech and robo-advisory firms · independent advisors · family offices. Boutique firms/product specialists give higher-touch service; brokerage houses serve the mass market; fintech/robo-advisory is still evolving.

    2.3Asset Classes and the Indian Investment Landscape1

    AUM by asset class (as of 30 May 2025 / 31 Mar 2025) — likely MCQ on rank order

    Asset class Size
    Bank deposits ₹231.70 lakh crore (largest)
    Mutual funds ₹75.61 lakh crore (~⅓ of bank deposits; roughly doubled in ~3 years)
    Life insurance ₹62 lakh crore
    EPFO ₹23 lakh crore
    AIFs (~1,700 players) ₹15.05 lakh crore
    NPS ~₹14 lakh crore
    PMS (495 SEBI-registered) ₹8.37 lakh crore

    Trend: money is steadily migrating away from bank deposits into mutual funds, PMS and other asset classes ("financialisation of savings").

    Four product tiers in wealth management

    1. Traditional products — mutual funds (mass market + specialist).
    2. PMS — customised portfolios; minimum threshold ₹50 lakh.
    3. AIFs — private equity and venture capital funds; riskier than mutual funds and PMS.
    4. Other/distribution products — insurance (term = pure life cover only; pension plans; whole life = benefits up to age 100; endowment = money returns sooner), EPFO (mandatory savings on basic + DA, withdrawable at retirement or earlier for loan/education/marriage), NPS (retirement saving with much greater flexibility than EPFO).
    5. Advanced solutions — venture capital, structured products, private equity (direct company investments through entities), hedge funds (absolute return strategies).
    6. Digital innovation — robo-advisory platforms, digital wealth management, digital assets and cryptocurrency (adopted by youngsters comfortable with risk).

    2.4Financial Goals and the Three Phases of Life

    Standard human financial goals

    Maintaining/upgrading standard of living (Indian household expenses rising 4–8% p.a.) · travel and holidays · pursuing special interests, philanthropy · medical exigencies · transferring wealth to the next generation.

    Three phases

    Phase Age Character
    Accumulation 22–45 Start investing and saving in the right asset class
    Transition between accumulation and distribution Retirement becomes imminent; rebalance risk
    Distribution 55 onwards (retirement may be 60 or 65) Risk appetite is very low; need withdrawable income; still keep some growth assets to fight inflation

    Asset allocation matters most between the accumulation and transition phases. You only create wealth when your return on investment exceeds inflation.

    Wealth destroyers: spending heavily at a young age; large credit card debt; living beyond one's means; wrong investment choices; lack of clarity on objectives; speculative investments.

    2.5Savings, Investing and the Rules of Thumb1

    Ramit Sethi on frugality: "choosing the things you love enough to spend extravagantly on, but cutting costs mercilessly on the things you don't love."

    Budgeting rules — know all of them and don't mix them up

    Rule Split Applies to
    50 / 30 / 20 (salary split taught here) 50% household expenses (incl. rent) · 30% savings · 20% into a secondary account = "happy to spend" money Monthly salary
    50 / 30 / 20 (budgeting) 50% needs · 30% wants · 20% goals Spending categories
    Rule of 110 Equity % = 110 − age; rest in debt. (Age 40 → 70% equity, 30% debt) Asset allocation
    5-5-R framework (Arun Kumar) First 5% of monthly income → emergency fund + term insurance + health insurance; next 5–10% → short-term goals; Remainder → long-term bucket, split equity/debt using the Rule of 110 Monthly savings
    50 / 40 / 10 rule For one-time/lump-sum money: 50% spend now (so you don't feel deprived) · 40% long-term bucket · 10% short-term bucket Windfalls

    Emergency corpus: 3 to 12 months of household expenses.

    Savings vs Investing

    Savings Investing
    Safety; withdrawable even in the middle of the night (bank deposit) Not instantly accessible
    Doesn't beat inflation → not ideal for wealth creation Long-term wealth creation
    Principal secure Volatility; principal not always returned
    — Involves measured risk to enhance returns

    Key investment considerations

    Safety (get your money back) → Liquidity (get it back when you want) → Convenience (easy to invest/disinvest) → and above all, post-tax returns. Trade-off: for the same liquidity, higher safety means lower returns; for the same safety, higher liquidity means lower returns.

    Four major investment risks — classic MCQ

    Risk Meaning
    Solvency / credit risk Will the principal be repaid? (Governments cannot go bankrupt)
    Liquidity risk Cannot disinvest on the day you want to
    Reinvestment risk On maturity of a 1-year FD, you cannot get the same rate again
    Interest rate risk Bonds/debentures: market price moves inversely to interest rates

    The power of starting early

    Early vs late starter — both invest ₹10,000/month at 10% for 30 years (₹36 lakh invested): - Early starter (begins at 20) → ₹2.26 crore at 60 - Late starter (begins at 30) → ₹1.13 crore at 60 → Same return, same amount invested, double the outcome. Start now.

    Three brothers (Amar, Shyam, Rajesh) — ₹1 lakh at 8% compounded to age 58. A 5-year difference in start age means the youngest earns 47% less than the eldest (a gap of ~₹4.04 lakh).

    The 8-4-3-2 rule of compounding

    Arun invests ₹30,000/month at an average 12%: - First ₹50 lakh → 8 years - Second ₹50 lakh → 4 more years (year 12) - Third ₹50 lakh → 3 more years (year 15) - Fourth ₹50 lakh → 2 more years (year 17) - By year 20, roughly ₹50 lakh is added every year.

    Compounding kicks in hard only after the first ~8 years. Note "average 12%" means some years 6%, some 18%.

    Savings rate matters: Arun earning ₹1 lakh/month with a 5% annual hike, over 30 years at 9% return — - Saving 5% → invests ₹40 lakh → ₹1.5 crore - Saving 15% → invests ₹1.2 crore → ₹4.5 crore (₹3 crore more)

    2.6The Investment Pyramid and Goal-Horizon Matching

    Investment pyramid: as you ascend, return ↑, risk ↑, investment period ↑. - Base (capital protection) — money market funds, short-term deposits, government papers. - Middle (medium term, 1–3 years) — income funds, company fixed deposits. - Top (medium-to-high risk, 3–5 years+) — equity stocks, equity growth funds.

    Horizon definitions: short-term ≤ 1 year; medium-term 1–5 years; long-term > 5 years.

    Goal Horizon Approach
    Retirement (5 yrs away) Long-term view Safety matters but return drives growth
    Children's education/marriage (1–5 yrs) Medium Mix liquidity and returns; tactical shift into safe options after 3 years
    Buying a car in 3–4 months Short Maximum liquidity, ignore returns → bank deposits

    2.7Asset Allocation and Portfolio Rebalancing1

    Asset allocation = splitting money across equity, debt, gold, and other liquid asset classes.

    Research shows 80–90% of long-term return outcomes trace back to this single decision. highly likely MCQ Crises referenced: mid-90s Asian crisis · dot-com boom and bust · 2008–09 subprime/global financial crisis · COVID-19 (2020). These are bubble markets preceding black swan events. A bubble can run for years — frustrating for a long-term investor who is out of the market — and even the best experts cannot consistently predict the peak or the crash.

    Rebalancing mechanics

    Arun starts 50 equity / 50 debt. Equity rallies → allocation drifts to 57/43 → sell some equity, move to debt. Markets fall → skewed toward debt → book profit on debt, move into equity. This is counter-cyclical by construction.

    The 1999–2011 rebalancing study (12 years, ₹1 lakh, 50:50)

    Strategy Overall CAGR Capital gains booked
    No rebalancing (buy & hold) 11.44% Nil
    Annual rebalancing 13.06% ₹2.63 lakh
    Threshold rebalancing (back to 50:50) 13.01% ₹2.36 lakh

    Details from the study: 1999 equity return +24.4%, debt +9.5%, portfolio value ₹1.17 lakh (≈17% annual return). 2000–01 equity fell −13.4% then −15%, wiping out 1999's equity gains; debt slid 9.5% → 8.5%; portfolio fell to ₹1.108 lakh, annualised return −2.6%. Debt bottomed at 5.3% in 2003. Portfolio ended at ₹3.67 lakh, below its 2010 peak of ₹4.285 lakh.

    Takeaway: rebalancing added ~1.5% CAGR. Booking profits and paying taxes is of paramount importance — otherwise you risk capital deprivation or slower wealth growth.

    Cross-country 5-year rolling CAGR (2015–2024): USA consistently produced the best returns; Indian mid-caps sometimes beat the US; gold caught up notably from 2020 onwards; but USA still rules the roost.

    2.8Budgeting, Cash Flow and Life Goal Planning

    Cash flow components

    Income: fixed (salary, business income) · variable (speculative gains, lottery, bonus, incentive) · passive (dividends, rent, interest — "comes silently"). Expenses: essential (household, school fees, conveyance, travel) · discretionary (sudden vacation, new TV). Net cash flow must be a surplus — income > expenses. Track at least yearly, ideally monthly.

    Cash flow optimisation

    • Reduce debt as you progress.
    • Restructure obligations — refinance a 10% loan when rates fall to 8%; or prepay ahead of term to free up surplus for higher-return long-term goals.
    • Budget 50 needs / 30 wants / 20 goals.
    • Build the emergency corpus (3–12 months) before everything else, for a COVID-type situation.
    • Align budget with risk tolerance and financial goals.

    Monitoring tools: an Excel income & expenditure statement built from bank statements plus cash withdrawals; budgeting apps on smartphones; monthly review of plan vs actual; build in flexibility for lifestyle changes; integrate with financial plan updates.

    Human life cycle

    • Phase 1: birth → graduation, first 21–22 years.
    • Phase 2: earning years, 22/25 → 60. Marriage, children, home loan, children's higher education, children's marriage.
    • Phase 3: retirement, potentially 25–30+ years (many now reach 100). No productive income — living on the wealth built in Phase 2.

    Inflation maths — memorise the worked examples

    Item Today Inflation Future
    Monthly household expense ₹30,000 (2025) 6% ₹96,214 by 2045
    Child's degree ₹10 lakh (2025) 7% ₹27 lakh by 2040
    Child's graduation (Arun's 7-yr-old, 11 yrs away) ₹20 lakh — ~₹42 lakh
    Food & snacks basket ₹1,000/month 8–10% ₹21,700 in 35 years

    Arun's retirement corpus: age 40, 20 years to retirement, ₹30,000/month expenses at 6% inflation → ₹96,214/month at 60 → retirement corpus needed ≈ ₹1.6 crore. - At 12% return → save ≈ ₹16,200/month - At 15% return → save ≈ ₹10,600/month

    Child's education: ₹42 lakh needed in 11 years → at 15% ≈ ₹12,500/month; at 12% ≈ ₹15,000/month.

    Second retirement example: age 35, retire at 60, yearly expense ₹2.5 lakh, inflation 5%, return 12% pre-retirement and 8% post-retirement → corpus needed at retirement = ₹1.05 crore → must save ≈ ₹76,000 per year for 25 years.

    2.9Retirement Planning

    Retirement myths (survey findings): "I have enough" · "family/children will stand by me" · "my needs are limited" · "my health is sound and will stay sound" · "time will take care of itself". Reality: headwinds you're not prepared for.

    Longevity assumptions: female ~87, male ~83 — females live longer. Cost rise: generally 8–10%; food grain prices rose ~500% in 25 years and climate volatility may repeat this.

    Ways retirees cope (not all good): manage current savings and investments; work post-retirement to 85–90 (Japan model); become more aggressive in investing (risky); borrow from friends and relatives; or use a reverse mortgage.

    Reverse mortgage: an aged person mortgages a property that is free of lien and mortgage to a bank/FI and draws surplus cash to the extent of 60–80% of market value, repaid as interest for as long as the person lives; thereafter the property passes to the bank/FI.

    2.10Compounding, Insurance and Diversification

    Compounding illustration: ₹10,000/month at an average 12.64% → ₹24 lakh in 10 years; the same continued for 30 years → ₹4.07 crore.

    Life insurance need calculation (the "expense method") — learn the formula

    Cover = (Annual household expenses × Remaining working years)
      + Outstanding loans
      + Major future expenses
      − Existing investments

    Arun, 40, married, 2 children: (₹10 L × 20 years) + ₹40 L loans + ₹50 L future expenses − ₹10 L savings = ₹2.8 crore cover needed. Rationale: life insurance answers "what if I don't exist tomorrow?" — the family's income stream is at stake.

    Real estate yield

    Real estate yield = (Monthly rental income × 12) ÷ Capital invested in the property

    Examples cited: Kolkata 9.77%, Bengaluru 10.3%. Tier-II and tier-III cities can also give high yields.

    Real return — the foundation of wealth creation

    Real return = Nominal return − Inflation

    10% nominal − 6% inflation = 4% real. Indian inflation has historically fluctuated 4–8% annually; 2000–2025 price rise ≈ 250%, i.e. ~6.5% annual inflation.

    Evaluate performance on real returns, not nominal figures. Money in low-interest savings accounts loses real wealth.

    Diversification

    "Don't put all your eggs in one basket" — if the basket falls, all eggs break. Spread across equities, debt securities, real estate, gold, and alternatives.

    Crisis evidence: - 2008 GFC (US subprime mortgage crisis, housing bubble burst): Indian equity markets fell as much as ~35% in a single day. Anyone diversified beyond equities survived the systemic shock better. - 2020 COVID-19: economies paralysed, jobs lost, digitisation accelerated. On recovery, technology and healthcare held up, while hospitality and aviation were grounded.

    Key takeaway: diversification does not prevent losses in a downturn — it significantly reduces the impact and positions you better in the recovery. It requires patience and discipline, not jumping out.

    Risk–return trade-off: higher risk correlates with higher potential return and a higher probability of capital erosion. Diversification across equity, gold, debt (and for affluent investors PE, alternatives, PMS), aligned with a 3–5 year+ horizon, lower liquidity needs and higher risk tolerance, is the cornerstone of prudent wealth management.

    2.11Practice Management — Ethics, Behaviour, Client Relationships

    The 8 principles of the code of ethics (Financial Planning Standards Board, Denver, USA) — memorise all eight

    Principle Meaning
    Professionalism Conduct that reflects positively on the profession at all times
    Competence Continuous skill enhancement, knowledge upgradation, expertise
    Confidentiality Protect client privacy; safeguard sensitive data
    Diligence Timely, meticulous, thorough, detailed service
    Client First Prioritise the client's interest above all other considerations
    Integrity Unwavering honesty, transparency, ethical conduct
    Fairness Openly disclose all conflicts of interest; equal treatment
    Objectivity Unbiased advice free from personal prejudice or external influence

    Investment discipline principles

    • Diversified asset allocation across domestic and foreign equities, fixed income, real estate, gold.
    • Chasing past top performers doesn't work — winners keep rotating across asset classes, funds and sectors.
    • Don't invest purely to save tax — identify good investments, pay taxes, maintain your risk profile.
    • Don't rely on friends/relatives — do your own due diligence.

    Things beyond your control

    Earnings potential can change (unemployment, health issues, job loss, gig work) · household expenses can exceed means · loans and liabilities can arise suddenly · life is not predictable · black swan events (COVID-19) · lure of quick money leading to bad choices.

    Do's and Don'ts

    Do's: have a plan · invest for the long haul (at least 5 years) · go for growth · keep an emergency fund · hold a mix of assets.

    Probability evidence (1979–2025): returns of 12–15% are achievable; the probability of loss when invested for under 15 years is high. Using 15-year moving averages, 15 out of 15 times there was a 100% probability of positive returns.

    Don'ts: don't buckle in the short term · don't chase past performance · don't be reckless · never ignore insurance.

    The asymmetry of loss: ₹100 that falls 50% becomes ₹50; getting back to ₹100 requires a 100% gain. That's a tall task.

    Making an equity corpus shockproof: avoid borrowing to invest in equity · don't speculate · invest with a long-term view · invest only if you understand the business · beware of letting your broker trade on your behalf · don't follow anyone blindly · avoid investing on rumours · maintain a strict stop loss on momentum stocks at higher levels.

    Words of wisdom on equity: A good company is not necessarily a good stock. Buy stocks with high return on equity, a solid brand and management, low debt gearing, capital efficiency. Avoid me-too business models, companies with huge debt and heavy capital requirements. Warren Buffett's two rules: (1) Never lose money. (2) Never forget rule number 1. Also: "The time to get interested in a stock is when no one else does." · "Owning stocks is like having children — don't get involved with more than you can handle."

    Investor mistakes (6)

    1. Not knowing where to spend. 2. "I saw it, I liked it, I shopped." 3. Living on credit cards / plastic money. 4. Postponing an investment decision when it is due. 5. Taking on risky projects/stocks without the risk appetite. 6. "My uncle bought one, so I'll buy one too, to save tax."

    Behavioural finance — the emotion cycle and biases

    Emotion cycle: 2019–20 fear → 2020–23 recovery, returns surpass prior decade → greed and belief the world will stay this way → 2024–25 market slides → hope of returning to old levels.

    Client emotions: regret (lost opportunity) · impatience ("I missed that IPO") · confusion (buy or not buy) · overconfidence (belief markets only go up) · herd mentality (following family friends) · emotional anxiety (worry when markets fall) · distrust (of the advisor and everyone).

    Client psychology / biases: herd mentality · overconfidence · familiarity bias · return chasing · confusing horizons — short-term is under 3–5 years, long-term is over 10 years; you cannot flip one into the other · loss aversion, which shows up two ways: (a) exiting an investment just because it is temporarily down, and (b) holding on to a losing stock hoping it returns to past glory. Both should be avoided — cut losses when due, and don't hold for eternity. Risk perception varies from person to person.

    The advisor–client relationship

    Build long-term trust · understand goals · keep the risk profile stable unless a review reveals a genuine need to change · proactive, consistent service without reminders · offer a wide spectrum of services — not just financial instruments but concierge, legal, tax and accounting, succession planning, philanthropy · handle emotions with care, never let conflict become personal · personalise every client experience.

    Client communication

    Explain in lucid, simple, jargon-free language · set expectations upfront on both sides · active listening + maintain a paper trail · general updates via email, calls, reports · personalised messages · transparent disclosure of risks and fees at the beginning. Crisis communication: in a COVID-type crisis, calibrate carefully — simply parroting what's published elsewhere creates unnecessary anxiety and conflict. Technology support: electronic dashboard showing investments vs capital invested · portfolio insights with commentary · AI-driven profiling on risk appetite and goals · portfolio restructuring backed by a research team.

    2.12Practice Management — Acquisition, Retention, Ethics, Documentation

    (N. Gopalakrishnan)

    Practice management = the process of managing a practice effectively so that maximum value is delivered to the client. Components: client relationship (acquisition, retention), professional ethics, reporting and documentation.

    Client acquisition funnel

    Population → data analytics filters to leads → nurture the lead → convert to client. - Need a healthy pipeline of leads. - Initial engagement to understand the lead's requirements and check alignment with the practice's service deliveries — a mismatch is fatal. - Filtration narrows to the focus population; conversion nurtures prospects and demonstrates value to build initial trust. - Smooth onboarding: virtual rooms (AI/VR), helplines, an escalation matrix so the client can escalate grievances, and online (not physical) documentation — preferred especially by younger clients post-COVID.

    Retention

    "A client retained is much more than a client earned." - Generates word-of-mouth referrals, which empirical study shows are more loyal and more satisfied. - Reduces cost of acquisition → optimal profit for the practice. - Three key retention strategies: (1) relationship management (periodic portfolio reviews, personalised touch points), (2) proactive service (reach out to the client rather than waiting — market intelligence alerts/reports, regular portfolio reviews), (3) feedback mechanism giving the client an independent voice. The relationship begins at the point of acquisition — it doesn't end there.

    Professional ethics and governance

    • Ethical standards set by the practice may go beyond regulatory compliance requirements.
    • Benefits: systematic, transparent process; minimises legal and reputational risk (acts as "armour" when a client is aggrieved); promotes a sustainable ethical business culture.
    • Key components: governance framework · confidentiality (breach only with regulatory requirement or client consent) · conflict of interest management · ethical selling (transparency + suitability; the client's requirement at the top of the value chain).
    • Client protection standards: disclosures, consent for documentation, grievance redressal mechanisms, safeguarding of data.

    Reporting and documentation

    Two purposes: (1) regulators may mandate independent verification/inspection of records; (2) demonstrate to the client that their interests were kept topmost. Key components: mandatory records (KYC, financial background, proof of identity — these are only the minimum) and reporting protocols (periodic statements + regulatory formats).

    Risk profiling is not static — it evolves as the client progresses along the wealth-creation path, so it must be undertaken periodically and documented.

    2.13Taxation Planning2

    (Dr. Ravindran)

    Basics

    • Financial year (FY) = year 1; Assessment year (AY) = year 1 + 1 (the following year).
    • Old regime: deductions available (EPF, PPF, life insurance savings, post office deposits, housing loan interest, etc.).
    • New regime: those deductions do not exist — practically everything is taxable. Once you switch over, coming back may not be permitted.

    Residential status under the Income Tax Act (individuals only)

    Basic conditions (Criteria): - Criterion 1: stays in India ≥ 182 days during the FY (1 April – 31 March) → Resident. - Criterion 2: stays ≥ 60 days in the FY AND ≥ 365 days in the preceding 4 years → Resident.

    Relaxations to the 60-day rule:

    Situation 60 days replaced by
    Person leaving India for employment abroad or as a member of the merchant navy 182 days
