    Indian citizen / PIO visiting India with Indian income > ₹15 lakh 120 days
    Indian citizen / PIO visiting India with Indian income ≤ ₹15 lakh 182 days

    RNOR (Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident) — a resident who ALSO satisfies any of: - Was a non-resident in 9 out of the 10 preceding FYs, OR - Stayed in India ≤ 729 days during the preceding 7 years, OR - Is an Indian citizen / PIO outside India who visits India for more than 120 but less than 182 days with total Indian income exceeding ₹15 lakh.

    Tax incidence by residential status — guaranteed MCQ

    Status Income earned in India Income received in India Foreign income
    ROR (Resident & Ordinarily Resident) Taxable Taxable Taxable
    RNOR Taxable Taxable Not taxable (except if derived from India / a business controlled from India)
    NR (Non-Resident) Taxable Taxable Not taxable

    Only ROR is taxed on global income.

    Asset classes and income types

    Class Instruments Income type Risk
    Equities Equity shares, preference shares, mutual funds, ETFs Dividends + capital gains Higher / can be aggressive
    Fixed income (bonds) Government bonds, G-secs, debt mutual funds, FDs Interest + capital gains Lower risk, lower return
    Cash & equivalents Savings account, FD, liquid funds Interest Extremely low risk
    Real estate Residential property, agricultural land, REITs / InvITs Rental income + capital gain Highly illiquid, capital-heavy, high maintenance cost
    Commodities Gold, silver, crude oil, commodity ETFs Capital gain only Highly volatile — supply/demand mismatches (e.g. Red Sea shipping disruption)
    Alternative investments VC, cryptocurrencies, private equity Capital gains Extremely complex; possible total loss of capital

    Accredited investors: typically $1 million or more; must take the necessary SEBI approvals; once permitted they can invest smaller sums across asset classes.

    Capital gains

    Definition: Capital gain = Sale proceeds − Cost of acquisition (purchase price + modifications). Modifications example: fencing, gardening, employing a gardener on land purchased. - Applies to movable or immovable assets. - The profit must be realised — unrealised profits are not capital gains. - Capital loss = the reverse.

    Holding period thresholds:

    Asset Long-term if held
    Listed securities — listed equity/preference shares, UTI/mutual fund units, zero coupon bonds > 12 months
    All other assets > 24 months
    Debt mutual funds acquired on/after 1 April 2023 and market-linked debentures Always short-term under Section 50AA, regardless of holding period

    Zero coupon bond = carries no interest; e.g. issued at ₹85 for 15 years, redeemed at ₹100 — the differential is the growth. Why the 2023 change: debt mutual funds previously enjoyed indexation, so investors and companies shifted from bank deposits into debt MFs. That arbitrage was removed.

    Indexation and the Cost Inflation Index (CII): indexation adjusts the purchase price for inflation. Base year 2001-02 = 100. Notified annually by the central government.

    Year CII
    2022-23 331
    2023-24 348
    2024-25 363
    Current 376

    (≈7–8% growth per year.)

    Taxability of capital gains — the numbers to memorise

    Short-term Long-term
    Equity shares / equity-oriented MF units (STT paid) 20% 12.5%, after an exemption of ₹1,25,000
    All other capital assets Slab rate (0% up to ~30% + cess) 12.5%

    Grandfathering on land and building: if acquired before 23 July 2024, you may choose either 20% with indexation or 12.5% without indexation. After 23 July 2024, no indexation benefit is allowed on any long-term capital asset other than the grandfathered land/building option.

    Why 23 July 2024? That is the date the Finance Bill was presented in Parliament after the new government took office in May 2024. The government rolled back the pure-12.5% approach for property after representations, since Indians hold land bought in the 1980s–90s that has appreciated enormously.

    Exemptions from long-term capital gains (Sections 54 to 54GB)

    The important ones for individuals: Section 54, Section 54EC, Section 54F.

    Asset sold Reinvest in Maximum exemption
    Residential house (Sec 54) New house property, or park in a Capital Gain Account Scheme with SBI/other nationalised banks Lower of: the LTCG, ₹10 crore, or the amount invested in the new house
    Land / building / both (Sec 54EC) Capital gain bonds: NHAI, REC (Rural Electrification Corporation), HUDCO — within 6 months of sale and in the FY before tax filing ₹50 lakh per PAN. If property is jointly held, each holder gets ₹50 lakh
    Any LTC asset other than a residential house (Sec 54F) Purchase/construct a new residential house — 1 year before or 2 years after the sale date —

    Set-off and carry-forward of capital losses — very likely MCQ

    Loss type Can be set off against
    Short-term capital loss Both short-term and long-term capital gains
    Long-term capital loss Only long-term capital gains

    Carry forward: unabsorbed losses carry forward to 8 subsequent assessment years.

    Worked example — Mr Arun, aged 40

    Step 1: Income heads

    Head Computation Amount
    Salary Gross ₹12,00,000 − standard deduction ₹75,000 ₹11,25,000
    House property Annual rent ₹5,00,000 − 30% standard deduction (₹1,50,000) ₹3,50,000
    Other sources Dividend ₹50,000 + FD interest ₹80,000 ₹1,30,000
    Gross Total Income ₹16,05,000

    Step 2: Capital gains — WITHOUT indexation

    Item Buy Sell Result
    A. Debt mutual funds ₹1,00,000 ₹75,000 Short-term capital LOSS ₹25,000
    B. Shares + equity MF ₹10,00,000 ₹12,00,000 Long-term GAIN ₹2,00,000
    C. House property ₹40,00,000 ₹38,00,000 Long-term LOSS ₹2,00,000

    Net LTCG = B − C = ₹2,00,000 − ₹2,00,000 = Nil. Carry forward STCL of ₹25,000.

    Step 3: Capital gains — WITH indexation on the house Indexed cost of acquisition = ₹40,00,000 × 376 / 331 = ₹45,43,807. Long-term capital loss on house = ₹38,00,000 − ₹45,43,807 = ₹7,43,807 (i). Less LTCG on shares/equity MF ₹2,00,000 (ii). Carry forward LTCL to the next 8 years = ₹5,43,807. The short-term loss on debt MF remains ₹25,000 — indexation has no effect on it.

    These are reported in ITR-2 or ITR-3.

    Tax-efficient investing

    Definition: maximise returns by minimising taxes. Two account types: - Taxable accounts — savings account, regular mutual fund (taxed via TDS and otherwise). - Tax-advantaged accounts — PPF, NPS, ELSS. Three sub-types: (a) tax-deferred, (b) tax-exempt, (c) hybrid (a combination).

    The E/T notation — at three points: contribution → earnings → withdrawal. E = exempt, T = taxed. - PPF = EEE — exempt on contribution, exempt on interest, exempt on withdrawal after 15 years. (The course also mentions EET as a category.)

    Trade-off: instruments that are taxed tend to have higher liquidity; instruments that are not taxed usually carry a lock-in.

    Tax-smart withdrawals — the bucket approach: withdraw systematically from different products at different times to spread the tax burden across multiple years instead of paying it all in one. Key strategies: - Multi-bucket portfolio — FDs laddered across 1, 2, 3 and 5 years; 3- and 5-year FD rates are usually higher, so you capture rate momentum. - Systematic Withdrawal Plans (SWP) — after years of SIP, withdraw a mix of principal and income so capital stays intact for decades. - Mix tax-free and taxable sources. - Senior citizen benefits — post office deposits, bank FDs (subject to limits). - Long-term equity-oriented mutual fund withdrawals attract only ~12.5% capital gains tax instead of ~30% on FD interest. ← the single most quotable tax-efficiency point. - NPS — postpone withdrawal to retirement (now possible up to age 75). - Insurance pension plans — sustained cash flows for life, then benefits to the nominee.

    2.14Alternative Investments

    Private Equity (PE)

    What: investment where HNWIs support bootstrapped companies (started with the founder's own money or from family/friends) that need growth capital to reach the next stage.

    Key characteristics: - Valuation is critical because there is no underlying benchmark. Methods: listed peer comparables, discounted cash flow (DCF), multiples of asset/book value. - Long lock-ins — growth capital takes time to fructify; not a short-term play; illiquid. Clients need alternative liquid holdings for sudden needs. - Capital is drawn down by the business as and when needed.

    Deal sourcing: industry bodies · mentor groups (a small world where PE players meet each other) · networking · investment bankers · cold calls and outreach. Goal: early access to attractive opportunities.

    Due diligence — three types:

    Type What it examines
    Commercial DD Business/operational aspects — market, TAM (Total Addressable Market), competitive position, who the competitors are, where each is in its lifecycle
    Financial DD Quality of earnings, quality/timing/quantum of cash flows, working capital cycle, whether the capital structure is optimum (growth equity may not be ideal — debt could raise the IRR)
    Legal DD Constitution documents, employee appointment letters, rental agreements, business support service contracts. Critical because bootstrapped companies make decisions informally without documentation

    Return metric: IRR (Internal Rate of Return) guides most PE decision-making. Exit clauses are essential — a PE fund makes money only when it exits.

    Exit routes (4): 1. Strategic sale — sell the stake to a strategic partner in the same industry/geography. 2. Secondary buyout — PE investor B buys out PE investor A. 3. IPO — most prominent recently; excellent returns, business visibility, and further growth capital. 4. Recapitalisation.

    Risks: illiquidity · no comparable valuation → valuation risk · long holding period · concentration risk if the portfolio is heavy in PE · exit uncertainty (the fundamental PE risk).

    Venture Capital (VC)

    Institutionalised form of private equity, investing at the early stage. - Funding rounds: Series A → B → C → D, each typically at a higher valuation because the prior round funded growth. Write-downs do happen when the industry or business turns. - Early-stage failure rates are very high — VCs expect several investments to be written off. A few big winners generate multiple returns that even out the portfolio. - Don't over-diversify at the VC level — you need to be able to monitor and assess the portfolio properly.

    Hedge Funds

    What: funds that hedge a price differential in one market/instrument against another market or similar product. - Positions: go long (bullish, buying undervalued instruments) or short (bearish, selling in anticipation of a fall). - Strategy: essentially arbitrage — on price differentials or market inefficiencies. Arbitrage extends beyond price to corporate actions — mergers, demergers, or a new listing in an industry not previously listed (price discovery creates arbitrage opportunities). - Fee structure — dual: a fixed fee on AUM (effort basis) plus a performance fee on returns generated beyond the benchmark. AUM = total assets managed by the fund manager. - Risk profile — three dimensions: leverage (borrowed money magnifies risk) · transparency (traditionally much lower than conventional investments) · liquidity (hedge funds usually confine themselves to highly liquid instruments to meet investor redemptions).

    Structured Products

    What: customised investments designed for a particular investor's need, built on an underlying (a commodity, an investment, a business). Example: Sovereign Gold Bond — benchmarked to the market value of gold.

    Components: (1) the underlying asset to be benchmarked (gold, silver, coffee, soya bean…), (2) the payoff formula and relationship, (3) safeguards protecting the downside.

    Common types: - Capital-protected products — the core capital goes into a debt instrument, and only a small component goes into a risk investment. - Yield-enhancing products — return linked to price movement of a benchmarked product. - Market-linked notes.

    Risks: complexity (customised → far more complex than an off-the-shelf product) · issuer credit risk (default by the issuer) · liquidity risk.

    ESG Investing

    ESG = Environmental, Social, Governance. SEBI, as the listing regulator, has already framed ESG reporting guidelines for listed companies. - ESG reporting goes beyond conventional financial reporting: what the entity took from the environment and what it contributed to it — water, air, CO₂, oxygen. - Environmental metrics: carbon emission norms, energy efficiency, recycling of processed water, waste management, effluent treatment. - Social: relationships with employees, suppliers, customers and other stakeholders (bond investors, equity investors), reported on a sustainable basis. - Framework objectives: standardisation so results are comparable across industries and companies; scoring and rating of ESG initiatives used as an evaluation matrix. - Screening: negative screening excludes companies harming nature/society or extracting more than they return; positive engagement favours those greening the environment, including indirect contributors. - Criticisms/challenges: greenwashing — over-reporting ESG effort while ground-level initiatives are limited; inconsistent standards — there are no standardised ESG reporting formats.

    Impact Investing

    For investors driven by passion for a cause rather than returns alone — themes such as equal opportunity, support for the physically or mentally challenged. Objective: not just return, but control over the objective the investment supports. Vehicles: thematic funds · green bonds · social enterprises (not-for-profits supporting a cause). Aligned with Sustainable Development Goals, with regular standardised tracking and reporting.

    2.15Regulatory Landscape1

    (Kalpana Chauhan)

    The five regulators — learn Act, year, and scope

    Regulator Act & year Governs Objective
    RBI RBI Act, 1934 Whole financial system — currency, forex, banks, financial institutions, NBFCs Financial stability, consumer protection, sound banking practices
    SEBI SEBI Act, 1992 Capital and securities markets — exchanges, brokers, mutual funds, intermediaries Investor protection, market integrity, fair transparent trading
    IRDAI IRDAI Act, 1999 Insurance sector Market growth, stability, transparency, consumer protection and trust
    PFRDA PFRDA Act, 2013 Pension instruments, pension funds, related intermediaries Safe management of retirement savings, transparency, risk control, subscriber protection
    IFSCA IFSCA Act, 2019 Unified regulator for IFSC entities like GIFT City — powers of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA relating to IFSCs are transferred to IFSCA Strong global connection; international financial platform

    SEBI

    Scope: licensing norms for intermediaries · investor safety mechanisms · tech risk management (cybersecurity, cyber resilience protocols) · market integrity (algo trading, system risk controls) · fair distribution of mutual funds and securities · KYC-KRA framework for onboarding · oversight of digital advice and robo-advisory · accountability of finfluencers and platforms.

    Finfluencer enforcement: SEBI has banned unregistered financial influencers, penalised them, and in a recent case impounded over ₹500 crore made through unregistered investment advisory (online stock tips and live trading calls).

    Market intermediaries = entities registered with SEBI acting as a bridge between investors and the securities market (buy, sell, invest, clear, settle; manage and safeguard securities). Four buckets:

    Bucket Members
    Trading & investment Stockbrokers, research analysts, investment advisors, portfolio managers
    Issue management Merchant bankers, Registrar & Transfer Agents (RTAs), credit rating agencies
    Market infrastructure Depositories and depository participants, clearing corporations, custodians
    Fund management Mutual funds, AMCs, AIFs, venture capital funds, collective investment schemes

    Obligations of all intermediaries: mandatory SEBI registration · maintain prescribed net worth · report changes in shareholding, KMPs, infrastructure · immediately inform SEBI of material events, frauds, cyber incidents, major outages, regulatory breaches, disciplinary actions, litigation or change in control · file quarterly/half-yearly/annual financials · submit to surprise inspections and internal/external audits · disclose risk factors, fee structures, conflicts of interest, performance reports, grievance mechanisms, investor complaint status, plus cybersecurity incidents, system vulnerabilities and technology audit reports. Purpose: a continuous flow of data enabling early detection of red flags and misconduct.

    Investment Advisors — SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013

    • Anyone giving investment advice for a fee — individual, firm, company or online platform — must register with SEBI as an Investment Adviser (IA).
    • Must meet minimum educational norms and hold the NISM (or other SEBI-prescribed) investment adviser certification.
    • IAs act in a FIDUCIARY capacity — always put the client's interest first, avoid mis-selling, maintain high integrity and fairness.
    • Must clearly separate advisory from distribution to avoid conflict of interest.
    • Must assess the client's risk profile, financial goals, investment horizon and capacity to take risk before advising.
    • Fees within SEBI-prescribed limits: either a fixed fee or an AUA (Assets Under Advice) fee.
    • Must disclose conflicts of interest, product risks, compensation details, past disciplinary actions.
    • Records preserved for SEBI inspection for at least 5 years (risk profiling forms, agreements, advice reports, communications).
    • Annual compliance audit mandatory.
    • Enforcement example: SEBI imposed a ₹7 lakh penalty on the proprietor of an IA firm for failing to comply with regulations and to adhere to high standards of service.

    Mutual Fund Distributors (MFDs) — contrast with IAs, this is a classic MCQ

    Investment Adviser (IA) Mutual Fund Distributor (MFD)
    SEBI-registered; advises for a fee Bound by the AMFI code of conduct
    Fiduciary — client's interest first Product expert who recommends and sells based on risk profile and suitability
    Can use "advisor" in the name Cannot use the word "advisor" in their name
    Deals in direct plans Prohibited from dealing in direct plans
    Paid by the client Paid commissions by AMCs; must disclose commissions on all recommended products
    — Strict norms on advertising and social media; cannot induce clients with freebies, including free advice or free portfolio review
    — Can only suggest — the client's decision is final

    RBI framework

    Empowering statutes beyond the RBI Act 1934: - Banking Regulation Act, 1949 — regulating banks; powers to inspect banks and issue binding directions. - FEMA, 1999 (Foreign Exchange Management Act) — governs all forex transactions; rules, directions, circulars, approvals for FDI and ECBs (External Commercial Borrowings). - Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 (PSS) — regulates and supervises RTGS, NEFT, UPI; designates RBI as the regulating authority.

    RBI preamble/mandate: regulate the issue of banknotes and keeping of reserves to secure monetary stability; operate the currency and credit systems to the country's advantage; a modern monetary policy framework to maintain price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth.

    KYC — RBI Master Directions, Know Your Customer Directions 2016

    KYC = the process by which a regulated entity obtains and verifies information on a customer's identity, address, nature of business and financial status, so the financial system is not misused for money laundering or terrorist financing.

    Four key elements of a board-approved KYC policy — memorise all four: 1. Customer Acceptance Policy (CAP) — explicit criteria for onboarding; precludes anonymous, fictitious or benami accounts. 2. Customer Identification Procedures (CIP) — identification and verification using reliable, independent documentary sources. 3. Monitoring of Transactions — ongoing surveillance for consistency with the customer's risk profile. 4. Risk Management — risk categorisation of customers and commensurate due diligence.

    Ongoing due diligence requires: regular transaction review · investigation of unusual/suspicious activity · periodic customer profile updates · documentation of CDD review · risk assessment across clients, countries, geographies, products, services and delivery channels.

    FATCA — Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act

    • A US law of 2010 to prevent US taxpayers hiding income and assets in offshore accounts.
    • Requires financial institutions worldwide to report to the US IRS information on accounts held by US taxpayers or by foreign entities in which US taxpayers hold a substantial ownership interest.
    • India signed an Inter-Governmental Agreement (IGA) with the US in 2015 — Indian banks, mutual funds, NBFCs, insurance companies must identify and report US persons.
    • Collected via a self-declaration form. Two general types of certification: one for pre-existing accounts, one for periodic certification of compliance.
    • Reportable accounts are reported annually to the CBDT (Central Board of Direct Taxes), which transmits to the US IRS under the Automatic Exchange of Information arrangement.
    • Non-compliance → regulatory risk and, globally, a possible 30% withholding tax on certain US-source payments.

    CRS — Common Reporting Standard

    • Developed by the OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development).
    • Enables automatic exchange of information between countries to curb tax evasion and ensure accurate reporting of offshore assets/income.
    • Financial institutions determine the tax residency of account holders; if resident in another participating country, they collect and report annually to their own authorities, who then exchange with the other jurisdiction.
    • Done via self-certification (usually combined with the FATCA form), KYC checks, and review of account indicators — year-end balances, dividends, income, interest.

    FATCA vs CRS — the distinction: FATCA is US law, unilateral, US persons only, reports to the IRS. CRS is OECD, multilateral, all participating jurisdictions.

    AML — Anti-Money Laundering

    Source law: Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) + guidelines from the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU-India).

    Definition of money laundering: whoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge in, knowingly assists, or is a party to any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime — including its concealment, possession, acquisition or use, or projecting/claiming it as untainted property — is guilty of money laundering.

    Obligations on regulated entities (banks, financial institutions, intermediaries): - Maintain records of all transactions in a manner enabling reconstruction of individual transactions. - Maintain records of documents evidencing identity of clients and beneficial owners, account files and business correspondence. - File reports when thresholds are crossed: CTR (Cash Transaction Report), STR (Suspicious Transaction Report), NTR (Non-Profit Organisation Transaction Report), Cross-Border Wire Transfer Reports. - Retain identity and KYC documents for 5 years after the business relationship ends.

    IRDAI — the consolidated 2024 regulations

    In 2024, IRDAI consolidated its scattered rules into new consolidated regulations.

    1. IRDAI (Registration, Capital Structure, Transfer of Shares and Amalgamation of Insurers) Regulations, 2024 - Mandatory registration of all insurance business — life, general, health, reinsurance. - Maintain minimum prescribed capital. - Promoters and investors must meet "fit and proper" standards and are subject to a lock-in period during which they cannot alienate stakes. - No transfer of shares, merger or amalgamation without prior authority approval.

    2. IRDAI (Corporate Governance for Insurers) Regulations, 2024 - Board of competent, qualified individuals independent of management and promoters, meeting fit and proper criteria, with experience commensurate with scale/nature/complexity/size. - Mandatory board committees: Risk Management · Policyholder Protection · Grievance Redressal · Claims Monitoring · Investment · With Profit Committee. - Systems/policies to address conflicts of interest; actuaries appointed to continually monitor solvency and investment risk. - Board approves policies on product development, risk, investments, remuneration (incl. intermediary commission structures). - ESG framework reviewed by the board annually. - Minimum of 2 auditors as joint statutory auditors, with no conflict of interest.

    3. IRDAI (Insurance Products) Regulations, 2024 - Products must cover genuine insurable risks, address evolving customer needs, follow sound pricing and actuarial principles, have proper categorisation, and be reviewed by an appointed actuary. - Products must be clear, simple, standardised wherever possible. - Board must constitute a Product Management Committee and an Advertisement Committee. - Suitability checks and robust disclosures for investment-linked and retail products.

    4. IRDAI (Payment of Commission to Agents/Intermediaries) Regulations, 2024 + expense regulations - Board-approved annual policy for Expenses of Management (EoM) and commissions, aimed at increasing penetration and density throughout the country. - Board approves an annual business plan with projected capital, solvency margin and EoM quarterly. - EoM and commissions are capped by IRDAI, linked to insurance type and product premium. - Periodic review and strict reporting in financial statements.

    5. Protection of Policyholders' Interests regulations and Master Circulars, 2024 - Board-approved policies for e-policies, claim settlement turnaround times, outsourcing pricing with related parties, policyholder protection. - Policy documents in simple, clear terms; avoid coercive, unfair, one-sided clauses. - Mandatory Customer Information Sheet with every policy document; data privacy safeguards. - Standardised claim settlement in reasonable time, with all documents called for in one go. - Advertising: must not mislead; must give a fair and true view reflecting potential risk; distribution-channel advertising under adequate control and oversight. - Free look period: 15 to 30 days after purchase to review or cancel with refund.

    Case law/ombudsman examples: - Complainant paid a first premium of ₹25,000, then learned she must pay for 10 years; the agent claimed only 5 years with a ₹1,80,000 maturity in year 6. She cancelled within the free look period, the insurer refused, the ombudsman ordered a refund. (Had she complained after the free look period, she might not have succeeded.) - The Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission ruled that an insurance contract procured by fraudulent inducement is voidable, and the insurer cannot deny a premium refund by citing expiry of the 15-day free look period. It found deficiency of service for mis-selling to a farmer with false promises and ordered full refund and compensation even after the free look period expired.

    PFRDA and NPS

    NPS = National Pension System — a defined contribution pension system introduced by the Government of India in 2004; replaced the old pension scheme for government employees; extended in 2009 to private sector employees, self-employed and NRIs. It is market-linked — the corpus depends on investment performance, and there is no assured pension amount.

    At retirement (age 60): 40% of the corpus must be used to buy an annuity; 60% can be withdrawn tax-free. - Every subscriber gets an individual pension account with a PRAN (Permanent Retirement Account Number). - Partial withdrawals up to 25% of contributions are permitted, subject to conditions. - A subscriber may invest up to 100% in government securities; those seeking minimum assured returns may opt for notified schemes. - Exit not allowed except as specified; at exit an annuity must be purchased from a life insurance company.

    Accounts and asset classes: - Tier 1 = long-term retirement account; Tier 2 = voluntary savings account. - Four asset classes — "E C G A": E = Equity and related investments · C = Corporate debt / credit risk fixed income · G = Government securities and government-backed fixed income · A = Alternate assets (AIFs and permitted non-traditional instruments). - Allocation choice: Active Choice (subscriber decides) or Auto Choice (system-driven).

    NPS ecosystem entities — know the roles:

    Entity Role
    CRA (Central Recordkeeping Agency) Digital backbone — subscriber records, PRAN generation, transaction logs, data flow between intermediaries
    Pension Fund Managers (PFMs) Licensed by PFRDA with fit-and-proper criteria; manage funds across approved asset classes; publish daily NAV; adhere to performance benchmarks
    Trustee Bank Currently SBI; manages cash flow — contributions routed to PFMs, redemption proceeds back to CRAs
    Points of Presence (PoPs) Banks, NBFCs and others registered to onboard subscribers, complete KYC, handle service requests, customer interface
    Custodians Hold NPS assets (equity, corporate bonds, G-secs) in demat form for safety and settlement efficiency

    Grievance redressal — escalation matrix by regulator

    Regulator First level Escalation
    RBI Grievance system of the regulated entity If no resolution in 30 days → RBI Ombudsman, or the Jurisdictional Consumer Commission
    SEBI SCORES (SEBI Complaints Redressal System) Request a SEBI review
    IRDAI IGMS (Integrated Grievance Management System) Insurance Ombudsman, or Consumer Commission
    PFRDA CGMS (Central Grievance Management System) Ombudsman
    IFSCA The entity itself IFSCA via its portal

    First approach in every case: raise a complaint with the grievance cell of the entity that caused the grievance.

    2.16Technology in Wealth Management3

    (K. R. Aravind)

    "Technology has changed wealth management more in the last 10 years than in the previous 50."

    Three major trends: (1) automated advisory via robo-advisory, (2) self-service digital portfolio management tools, (3) AI-driven personalisation and risk monitoring.

    Robo-advisory

    Definition: automated investment platforms that create and manage portfolios with minimal human intervention, helping people invest toward goals (retirement, education, wealth accumulation).

    Risk profiling — three steps: 1. Questionnaire — short structured questions. 2. Analysis — the system analyses answers; removes emotion, ensures consistency and fairness. 3. Risk profile assignment — becomes the foundation of portfolio construction.

    Sample questions: investment goal (safety vs growth priority) · reaction to a market fall (emotional response to volatility) · time horizon (longer reduces risk). There are no right or wrong answers.

    Three risk categories:

    Profile Risk Who it suits
    Conservative Low Near retirement; cannot tolerate losses; wants stable income
    Moderate Medium Mid-career professionals; medium-term goals (buying a house); can handle some ups and downs
    Aggressive High Young investors; 10–12 year horizons; high risk tolerance

    Why risk profiling matters: investors aren't pushed into risky products; portfolios match personality and goals; regulations and suitability rules are followed; protects both investor and platform.

    "Your investment style should match your life stage, not your emotions."

    Life stages and fintech logic — a likely match-the-pair MCQ

    Stage Age Objective Key goals Focus Fintech logic
    Foundation / early accumulation early 20s Financial stability, habit formation Emergency fund, first investments, skill development, basic purchases (laptop, phone, two-wheeler) Capital protection, discipline Low-ticket investments, simple products, high liquidity
    Accumulation mid-20s to late 30s Wealth creation Aggressive SIPs, vehicle, marriage/family, home down payment, insurance & tax planning Long-term growth, asset building Higher equity allocation, goal-based portfolios, automated rebalancing
    Asset building & responsibility 30s–40s Managing multiple goals simultaneously House purchase, renovation, children's education (India/overseas), loan management Growth with risk control Balanced portfolios, education goal buckets, AI-based personalisation
    Consolidation 40s–early 50s Optimisation and stability Portfolio review & consolidation, loan closure, tax efficiency, increasing retirement contributions Optimising what has been built Advanced analytics, portfolio dashboards, tax optimisation tools
    Pre-retirement 50s Capital protection and income planning Finalise retirement corpus, health planning, reduce volatility exposure, predictable cash flows Risk reduction, income visibility Automated de-risking, glide path models, income projections
    Distribution & legacy 60+ Income stability and legacy Regular retirement income, medical/lifestyle expenses, estate & succession planning, capital preservation Income safety and legacy Withdrawal planning, document vaults, nominee and estate tools

    Algorithmic portfolio construction — four steps

    1. Risk profiling → convert responses into a numerical risk score → conservative / moderate / aggressive.
    2. Strategic asset allocation → e.g. conservative 20% equity / 80% debt; aggressive 80% equity / 20% debt.
    3. Fund selection → low-cost funds matching the allocation; diversified across sectors, geographies, investment styles.
    4. Automated rebalancing → market drift moves actual weights away from target; the robo-advisor pulls them back. Maintains discipline and reduces emotional decision-making.

    Gold appears at 5–10% in ALL three risk profiles — because gold acts as a hedge, stabiliser and protection during market stress. Expected volatility in a normal market: 5–10%. likely MCQ Rebalancing impact (same figures as the Module 1 study): not rebalanced → CAGR 11.44%; rebalanced → CAGR 13% — a ~1.5% gap that grew portfolio value by ₹2.36 lakh over the period.

    Tax loss harvesting

    Scenario 1 — no harvesting: Investment A has a ₹4,000 loss; Investment B has a ₹4,000 gain. The gain is taxed; the loss is unused. The investor pays tax despite a net-neutral portfolio. Scenario 2 — with harvesting: the ₹4,000 loss is set off against the ₹4,000 gain. Net taxable = 0; tax payable = 0.

    Long-term impact illustration: without harvesting, total tax liability over time ≈ ₹15 lakh; with harvesting ≈ ₹5 lakh → net tax saving ≈ ₹10 lakh.

    Core message: tax loss harvesting does NOT improve market returns — it improves AFTER-TAX returns. Lower tax → more money stays invested → compounding works better. Robo-advisors automate harvesting; AI optimises loss-booking opportunities; digital platforms make it systematic and emotion-free. (Available only in advanced platforms.)

    Robo-advisory — advantages vs limitations

    Advantages Limitations
    Low cost — automation cuts human effort and advisory fees Limited personalisation for complex financial situations
    Consistency — algorithms apply rules without bias or emotion Cannot fully understand needs like inheritance planning or business cash flows
    Accessibility — even small amounts get structured advice; available 24×7 During volatility, clients still need human reassurance
    Real-time monitoring — continuous portfolio tracking Tax planning, inheritance, estate decisions and sudden life events need human guidance
    Heavily dependent on the quality of the underlying algorithms and data
    User profiling may not capture behaviour under stress

    Summary: robo-advisors work best for standardised, goal-based investing; human advisors remain essential for complex decisions. Robo works best when the user is disciplined and goals are straightforward.

    Digital portfolio management tools

    Purpose: consolidate all investments into one dashboard for both clients and advisors. Key features: dashboard (total net worth, asset allocation, performance) · analytics (return breakdown, risk measures, diversification) · alerts (market events, deviations, deadlines) · consolidation across mutual funds, equities, bonds, insurance · document vaults (compliance and tax reporting).

    Types of tools globally: broker applications (direct trading and tracking) · robo-advisory platforms · aggregators (accounts, loans, investments for a 360° view) · wealth platforms used by banks and AMCs (advisory support, portfolio rebuilding, research-driven recommendations).

    Dashboard concepts to know: - Net worth = what you own − what you owe. "More important than salary." - Assets: investments (MFs, stocks, bonds, ETFs) = long-term wealth · bank balance = liquid money for expenses and emergencies · insurance = "doesn't make you rich, but prevents you from becoming poor". - Liabilities: home, vehicle, credit card dues, personal loans. "Loans are not bad, but they must stay under control." - Debt-to-asset ratio — how much of your assets is funded by debt. Lower is better; generally below 40% is healthy, beyond that is risky. Tells you whether your lifestyle is asset-driven or debt-driven. likely MCQ number - Alerts — the app actively watches your money, not just displays it.

    Three big dashboard lessons: wealth is net worth, not income · investments and loans must be seen together · goals, alerts and protection matter as much as returns.

    Goal-based tracking: goals shown with target year, amount saved, % completion, status indicator (green = on track, orange = attention needed). Debt payoff treated as a goal, not a burden. Emergency fund completion matters because it prevents forced liquidation of investments. The focus shifts from "how much did I earn?" to "am I on track for what matters?"

    Four alert types: 1. Portfolio drift detected — stock allocation moved 5% above target → rebalancing alert (classic robo function: automated, rule-based, emotion-free). 2. Sector allocation threshold exceeded — e.g. technology crossed a predefined 25% threshold → concentration risk; suggests diversification. 3. Market correction / buying opportunity — informational; combines market data with behavioural nudges, encouraging disciplined investing instead of panic selling. 4. Goal update / retirement milestone — e.g. 85% of the retirement goal achieved → positive reinforcement, increases confidence and engagement.

    Performance analytics — the metrics

    Metric Meaning Example given
    Absolute return Total gain since you invested +2.83%
    Annualised return Return converted to a per-year number 11.46%
    Benchmark What the market did +2.49% → the portfolio beat the market
    Volatility How much the value moves up and down 12.3%
    Beta Portfolio movement vs the market. 1.0 = moves with the market; >1 = more aggressive; <1 = more conservative 1.05 → slightly riskier than the market, normal for young investors

    Performance attribution — which part of my portfolio actually made money? Example: equity +1.46%, fixed income +0.52%, technology +0.73%, financials −0.28%, healthcare +0.17%. Three lessons: return and risk must be seen together · ups and downs are normal, long-term trends matter · diversification means not all parts move the same way.

    Digital vaults

    Definition: a secure online locker for all important financial and personal documents. Contents: bank statements, investment statements, tax reports and ITR acknowledgements, KYC documents (Aadhaar, PAN, passport), insurance policies, loan documents. DigiLocker = the Government of India initiative — an official digital wallet for documents; documents are legally valid at many Indian institutions, removing the need for physical copies. Benefits in wealth management: faster account opening · seamless KYC · easy tax filing · faster loan and insurance processing · smoother onboarding with advisors/robo-advisors · fewer manual errors · ISO-certified security, encryption, controlled and audited access · one-click sharing instead of repeated uploads.

    Client benefits of digital tools (3): transparency (see exactly what you own, how it performs, why you own it) · real-time monitoring · simplified decision-making (clear visuals without deep financial expertise). Plus portfolio aggregation and behavioural nudges. For wealth managers, they cut administrative work and free time for client engagement.

    "Digital tools empower clients rather than overwhelm them."

    AI and Big Data in client servicing

    • Predictive analytics — anticipate client behaviour; churn prediction (who may withdraw assets), studying transaction history, spending patterns and market reactions. Identify future financial needs from spending, investing habits and life-stage indicators → proactive rather than reactive service.
    • Personalisation engines — tailored recommendations instead of the same advice for everyone; smart nudges ("increase SIP by 5% to meet your retirement goal") delivered at the right time through the right channel; customised product suggestions (funds, insurance, loans).
    • AI chatbots — handle balances, NAV updates, transaction status; assist onboarding through KYC documents and forms; speed up workflows; let wealth managers scale client bases without losing service quality.

    Chatbot pipeline — six steps (memorise the order): 1. User input (typed or spoken) — e.g. "show my portfolio returns" 2. NLP (Natural Language Processing) — understand words, identify intent, ignore irrelevant detail 3. AI reasoning / response generation — decide what data is needed and how to frame the answer 4. Backend processing — securely fetch real data from investment databases, bank records, portfolio systems (the chatbot does not guess) 5. Response delivered — numbers, charts, simple explanations 6. Continuous learning — improves with use

    "A chatbot listens, understands, thinks, fetches data, replies, and learns."

    RPA — Robotic Process Automation

    Definition: software that acts like a human and performs repetitive computer tasks automatically.

    Six steps: 1. Identify the process — repetitive, rule-based, done the same way every time (downloading bank statements, updating customer records, processing KYC forms). 2. Capture the workflow — record exact human steps (open site, log in, copy, paste, save, log out). 3. Build the bot — configure it to click, enter data, read screens, follow rules. No emotions, no guessing. 4. Run the bot — faster, no breaks, no mistakes, 24×7, large volumes. 5. Monitor and optimise — is it saving time, reducing errors, can steps improve? 6. Orchestration and scaling — manage many bots, assign tasks automatically, scale up at peak workload.

    Finance uses: account opening, KYC verification, report generation, compliance checks, back-office operations.

    "RPA teaches software to do boring, repetitive work so humans can focus on smarter tasks."

    Risk monitoring and compliance with AI

    • Anomaly detection — identifies suspicious trading patterns or unusual cash flows.
    • AML compliance — analyse large data volumes in real time.
    • Suitability engines — ensure recommendations match the client's profile, reducing regulatory risk; clients aren't sold products exceeding their risk profile (a regulatory requirement).

    Quotes cited: Satya Nadella (Microsoft Ignite, 2023): "AI is perhaps the most transformational technology of our time." JPMorgan: its wealth management arm's use of AI boosted sales to wealthy clients and added new clients even during market turbulence.

    2.17Estate Planning and Inheritance3

    (Module 4 — Ravindran & Gopalakrishnan)

    Definitions — guaranteed MCQ material

    Term Definition
    Testator The person who has made a will or given a legacy
    Beneficiary A person who derives advantage from something cast upon them through a will
    Settlor A person who makes a settlement, especially of property
    Administrator / Executor Person or institution appointed by the will-writer to carry out the terms of the will
    Legatee A person who receives a legacy out of the will
    Will A legal document declaring how assets are distributed, appointing guardians for minors and naming an executor; prevents family disputes. Must be signed and witnessed to be valid
    Witness A mentally competent adult who is NOT a beneficiary, who observes the will-maker signing, then signs to attest the signing was voluntary, not coerced, and the will-maker was of sound mind. Serves as an independent verifier if the will is contested
    Trust An arrangement whereby a trustee holds property as its nominal owner for the good of one or more beneficiaries
    Probate The process of getting a will certified by the court after death
    Succession certificate Issued by a civil court to the legal heir when a person dies without a will

    Estate planning (definition): the process of creation, accumulation and disposition of wealth to one or more chosen beneficiaries in a systematic and predetermined manner.

    Tools: either a will or a trust — it can't be both. - A will can be challenged after the death of the maker. - A trust is preferable, manned by trustees. Preferably one-third of trustees should be unrelated to each other so the transfer process is unbiased and neutral.

    The estate planning process — 6 steps

    1. Establish the objectives behind creating the estate plan
    2. Gather relevant data
    3. Analyse the data
    4. Recommend the estate plan
    5. Implement the plan
    6. Monitor and review the plan

    Deep dive on the steps: (a) determine net worth — list all assets (fixed and current), liabilities, and income across phases of life; (b) establish goals and plan in advance for both assets and liabilities; (c) select the appropriate estate planning tool (how); (d) set a time frame (when); (e) execute (who — the team of professionals).

    The estate planning team: accountants, attorneys (legal specialists), and financial advisors. They help develop and review estate goals and provide direction on strategies. Because of the number of professionals and the quantum of assets, a planned approach with the best professionals yields better results and lower disputes.

    Succession laws in India — classic MCQ grid

    Situation Hindu / Jain / Sikh / Buddhist Christian / Parsi / Jewish Muslim
    Dies WITHOUT a valid will (intestate) Hindu Succession Act Indian Succession Act Shariat (Muslim law)
    Dies WITH a valid will Indian Succession Act Indian Succession Act Shariat

    Mnemonic: For Muslims it's always Shariat. For everyone else, a valid will → Indian Succession Act. Without a will, Hindus/Jains/Sikhs/Buddhists → Hindu Succession Act; Christians/Parsis/Jews → Indian Succession Act.

    Intestate — defined in Section 30 of the Indian Succession Act: a person is deemed to die intestate in respect of all property for which he has not made a testamentary disposition capable of taking effect. Examples: bequeathing property for an illegal purpose, or where the subject of the bequest does not exist. Intestacy is of 2 types: total or partial. Property devolves upon the spouse or those related by blood or marriage, per the personal law applicable to the deceased.

    Per stirpes vs per capita — very likely MCQ

    Family: one daughter, one son; the son has 2 children.

    Per stirpes (by family lines) Per capita (equal shares of surviving members)
    Daughter 50% 25%
    Son 50% shared down his line 25%
    Son's 2 children 25% each (splitting the son's 50%) 25% each

    Costs associated with death and distribution

    • Final expenses — funeral costs, personal debts owed, illness expenses.
    • Administrative expenses — attorney fees, executor's fees, appraisal fees, court costs, probate costs.
    • Taxes — capital gains tax, income tax obligations of the person inheriting on transfer.

    Hindu Succession Act 1956 — classes of heirs for a male dying intestate

    (Sections 8–13 and the Schedule.) Order of preference: Class 1 → Class 2 → Agnates (Sec 12) → Cognates (Sec 13).

    Class 1 heirs — closest relatives, first right. If any Class 1 heir exists, they take the entire property simultaneously, to the exclusion of all others. Distribution: they inherit equally — the widow takes 1 share, the mother takes 1 share, each child takes 1 share. Key relatives: mother, widow, son, daughter; extended to son/daughter of a predeceased son, son/daughter of a predeceased daughter, widow of a predeceased son, and son/daughter of a predeceased son of a predeceased son.

    Class 2 heirs — apply only if no Class 1 heir exists. Organised in entries; a higher entry is preferred over a lower one. - Entry 1: Father - Entry 2: son's daughter's son, son's daughter's daughter, brother, sister - Entry 3: daughter's son's son, daughter's son's daughter, daughter's daughter's son, daughter's daughter's daughter - Entries 4–9: brother's son/daughter, sister's son/daughter, father's parents, father's widow, brother's widow, father's brother/sister, mother's parents, mother's brother/sister

    Class 3 — AGNATES (Sec 12): related to the deceased wholly through males. Example: father's brother's son. Class 4 — COGNATES (Sec 13): related by blood or adoption but NOT wholly through males — at least one female ancestor in the chain. Example: sister's son.

    Agnate vs cognate is a classic MCQ. Agnate = all-male chain. Cognate = at least one female in the chain.

    How to write a will

    • Can be written yourself or with a lawyer.
    • Registration is NOT mandatory, but better.
    • Two witnesses, ideally including one doctor and one lawyer.
    • The beneficiary must not be a witness.
    • Appoint an executor — responsible for distributing wealth after death.
    • Choose an executor younger than yourself; more than one executor can be appointed.

    The 10 mistakes to avoid in a will: 1. Improper execution; ambiguous wording 2. Gifting property to an attesting witness 3. Using nicknames or incomplete names 4. Unclear description of property 5. Passing property to unborn persons 6. Having no residuary legatee 7. Not updating the will 8. Incorrect conditions for inheritance 9. Violating the rule against perpetuity 10. Creating a will where no probate is possible

    Succession certificate

    • Issued by a civil court to the legal heir when a person dies without a will, to realise the debts and securities of the deceased.
    • Establishes the authenticity of heirs and authorises transfer of securities and other assets into their names, as well as inheriting debts.
    • Necessary but not always sufficient to release assets — also need a death certificate, letter of administration, and no-objection certificates.
    • Court fee paid in judicial stamp papers; then the certificate is typed, signed and delivered. Add lawyer's fees.
    • Timeline (uncontested): about 5 to 7 months.
    • Process: the court issues a newspaper notice for about 45 days; if uncontested at expiry, the court orders issuance. The court levies a fixed percentage fee based on the value of the estate.

    Probate

    • Probating = registration of a deceased person's will by the court. Can be done only in a High Court or a District Court.
    • Granted to the executor named in the will. If there is no executor, the court grants probate on the beneficiary's demand and appoints an executor.
    • Cannot be granted to: a minor, a person of unsound mind, or a corporate entity.

    Process (6 steps): 1. Executor files a petition in a District Court or High Court 2. Court issues notice to legal heirs 3. Public notices published in newspapers inviting objections for a period 4. Heirs agree and submit consent affidavits / NOCs 5. Probate granted to the executor 6. Executor has legal authority to distribute the assets

    Documents to submit: proof of death of the testator, proof the will was validly executed, and that it is the last will and testament. Timeline: minimum ~5 months, up to 12 months or more if heirs object → higher court and lawyer fees.

    Court fee example — Maharashtra:

    Estate value Fee
    < ₹50,000 ₹25
    ₹50,000 – ₹2,00,000 4%
    > ₹2,00,000 7.5%
    Ceiling ₹75,000 (Bombay High Court upper limit)

    Overall cost typically 2–8% of asset value.

    Where probate WAS compulsory (before the amendment): - For Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains — if the will was made in West Bengal, Bihar, Jharkhand, Orissa, Assam, Bombay and Madras (Chennai). - Also for Parsis if immovable property is within the limits of the High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras. - It is the LOCATION OF THE PROPERTY that matters, not where the will was executed. - Regulations differ by state; probate is not compulsory in all states.

    December 2025 amendment — the most recent, most testable fact

    Before After (December 2025)
    Probate mandatory for wills covering property in Mumbai, Chennai or Kolkata Probate no longer compulsory in those cases
    Mandatory for Hindus, Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists and Parsis Heirs can act on a valid will if there is no dispute
    Even undisputed estates had to go to court Probate becomes an OPTIONAL safeguard

    Probate is still recommended when: assets are spread across states · NRI heirs or foreign assets are involved · high-value property or investments · family members raise disputes · the will excludes close family members.

    Why banks and financial institutions may still ask for probate: internal risk and audit policies · protection against future claims by heirs · high-value or unclear wills · court-backed proof still required in some sectors, e.g. housing societies in Bombay/Pune/Maharashtra.

    Trusts

    Benefits of a trust: protection of assets from creditors · avoids probate for faster, private asset transfer · controlled distribution to beneficiaries such as minors or those with special needs, over time · ensures assets are used as intended (e.g. education) · potential tax efficiency · family planning for diverse/blended families.

    Three main uses of a trust: 1. In jurisdictions with estate tax, to freeze the value of an estate — once transferred to a trust, the asset's value doesn't grow in the settlor's hands, so estate tax on death doesn't grow either. 2. To hold and protect assets for minor or incapacitated dependents. 3. To protect assets in the event of insolvency — creditors cannot claim money held in a trust.

    Types of trust — by PURPOSE: - Public — public charitable trust (non-profit for the public good: poverty relief, education, healthcare, environment; managed by trustees for community benefit, not private gain; strict transparency/accountability regulations) · public religious trust (manages assets for religious purposes — preserving heritage, supporting worship, religious education; usually tax-exempt; governed by e.g. India's Charitable and Religious Trust Act, 1920 and state regulations; holds property in perpetuity). - Private — private specific (non-discretionary) trust vs private discretionary trust.

    Types of trust — by INTENTION:

    Type Definition
    Express trust The settlor transfers assets to a trustee who manages them according to the settlor's specific instructions
    Implied trust A trust exists based on a person's actions, relationships or property ownership, even without a formal written document, to prevent unjust enrichment
    Constructive trust Imposed where the legal owner is treated as a trustee for the beneficial owner because keeping the property would be unfair or fraudulent — even if no formal trust was intended
    Resulting trust Property reverts to the original owner because the intended trust failed or did not dispose of all property; or where someone pays for property but title is in another's name
    Precatory trust Property given with words of wish, hope or desire — creates a moral obligation, not a legally binding trust. Flexible (instructions can sit in a separate, easily changed document) but the recipient is not strictly bound

    Private specific (non-discretionary) vs private discretionary — key contrast:

    Private specific / non-discretionary Private discretionary
    Trust deed explicitly defines who gets what share and when Trustees decide who, how much and when at their own discretion
    Trustee has no choice but to follow fixed instructions Offers flexibility and asset protection
    Creator retains control by predetermining all distribution — a fixed / non-flexible trust Beneficiaries have no automatic right to specific shares; ideal for complex family wealth planning

    The estate planning "to-do list" (checklist)

    1. Always make nominations wherever applicable — bank accounts, deposits, demat, life insurance policy, commodities account, mutual fund holdings.
    2. When making a will, specify and earmark the beneficiaries of each asset.
    3. Ensure the beneficiaries in the will are the same as the nominees wherever possible.
    4. If you want assets to transfer to children only on attaining a certain age or on an event (higher education, marriage), create a trust.
    5. If you want to leave an asset you're not using (e.g. a house) to your children, gift it while you're alive.

    2.18Fiduciary Responsibilities1

    (Gopalakrishnan)

    When a practice unit decides on a client's asset allocation, it has a FIDUCIARY relationship with the client. This is onerous — due process and care are mandatory.

    Components: conflict of interest management · due diligence · ongoing oversight.

    Three core fiduciary duties: 1. Duty of loyalty — loyalty to the client's objectives, which drove and continue to drive the relationship. 2. Duty of prudence — decisions taken with care and skill, based on objective analysis of past data rather than subjective judgement; informed judgements with clear client communication. 3. Duty to act in the client's best interest — prioritise the client's goals, needs and well-being; unbiased, well-informed guidance. Builds sustainable trust and professional credibility.

    Managing conflicts of interest — the hierarchy matters for MCQs

    1. AVOID the conflict in the first place — the best option.
    2. If unavoidable, DISCLOSE it to the client upfront and take CONSENT.
    3. Recusal — the individual steps back from the assignment ("I am not going to handle this relationship because of an inherent conflict"), and another professional takes over that segment.

    Conflicts arise, for example, when the person recommending a product has a relationship with the product provider; also from financial interests and personal relationships.

    Due diligence and suitability

    Periodic due diligence covers product research, risk alignment, documentation.

    • Product research: product features · performance history (may not be freely available; may need adjustment to be comparable) · liquidity · regulatory oversight — not all products carry the same regulatory oversight; some are highly regulated, some are not bound by regulatory constraints.
    • Risk alignment: the client's risk profile must be clearly understood by everyone in the practice unit involved in the relationship; asset allocation must match the agreed risk profile; ensure appropriate diversification. Product-specific risks: equity → market risk · debt → credit risk and interest rate risk · foreign exchange products → exchange risk · illiquid products → valuation risk, lack of control, no benchmarking.
    • Documentation: detailed prospectuses for each product conveyed to the client; the client understands each product's unique features and consents in writing; aligned with the risk profile. Goes beyond regulator-mandated KYC — includes risk profiling and important developments in the client's family.

    Ongoing oversight

    • Monitor portfolios regularly — performance tracking benchmarked against underlying assets; risk management; check diversification (a highly concentrated portfolio carries much higher risk); benchmark against the market to ensure the portfolio is current.
    • Periodic reviews → identify implementation gaps that have crept in → correct them, not just identify them. Reviews lead to either rebalancing or a strategic revaluation (e.g. rapid price moves in equity and gold have drastically changed the intended equity/gold/debt mix).
    • After every review, hold a detailed client meeting; reporting must be as transparent as possible; implement review gaps on a timely basis — time is of the essence.

    Key takeaways: keep the client's interest in mind and align the portfolio to it · document well to remove miscommunication gaps · review periodically, address gaps promptly and communicate them to the client on time.
