    Explorations in Entrepreneurship

    Explorations in Entrepreneurship

    (Prof. Suresh Bhagavatula; FinTech Entrepreneurship section by Akarsh Naidu, Head of FinTech & Startups, Reserve Bank Innovation Hub)

    3.1What is Entrepreneurship? — History of the Idea

    Silent trade — the earliest form of commerce: Europeans left goods at a location in Africa; locals came, examined them and left gold or something valuable; either side could walk away by simply not picking up the offer. People were trading before they even conversed — hence homo economicus preceded homo sapiens as a trading being.

    The intellectual lineage — memorise the three names, dates and contributions

    Thinker Period Contribution
    Richard Cantillon ~1700 (risk noticed as far back as the 1600s) Coined the term "entrepreneur": people willing to take a risk. Buying spices in one land, sailing for months, not knowing what price the spice will fetch on arrival — inherent uncertainty
    Jean-Baptiste Say early 1800s (~1789 referenced) Separated the provider of capital from the person undertaking the venture. This is the intellectual origin of banks and VCs — capital provider ≠ operator
    Joseph Schumpeter ~100 years later Creative destruction — young, nimble ventures overtake and destroy large incumbents. This drives economic transformation

    Creative destruction examples: Kodak, Nokia ceased to exist because someone nimbler, better at technology, disrupted them. Amazon put millions of books online — local bookstores that only stocked high-probability-of-sale titles went out of business. Sam Altman/ChatGPT — AI research had existed in labs for decades; the disruption came from someone outside Microsoft, Google, Facebook, Intel or IBM taking it into the public domain. Facebook would have been displaced (like Orkut, MySpace) had it not bought WhatsApp and Instagram.

    Creative destruction happens incessantly and continuously.

    Human progress framing: Wright Brothers' first heavier-than-air flight ~1903; a man on the moon by the late 1960s. For all of history until ~120 years ago we could not fly. Life for most of the world was not materially different from evolution until the late 1800s — the take-off came with the ability to invest in companies and receive benefits from them.

    3.2Entrepreneurship in India — the historical arc

    Are Indians entrepreneurial or risk-averse? Both are true. We weight a secure job higher than starting a business, but historically India was highly entrepreneurial.

    By 1850, roughly a quarter of world GDP was in India. Two engines:

    1. Spices — India sat on the spice and silk routes (spices also routed from Indonesia, Malaysia, Sri Lanka through India). In cold European climates with barren winters and bland food, spices were transformative; only nobility could afford pepper, cinnamon. "Food was something we were not controlling, but what we were controlling was the taste part of food." Arabia prospered because it had access to the west coast of India and east coast of Africa.

    2. Textiles — the decisive advantage. Europe had coarse fabrics (flax, jute, linen). India had: - Unmatched weaving — ikat (tie-and-dye weaving), extra weft weaving; Banaras, Kanchipuram, Pochampally, Patola, Sambalpuri. - Unmatched dyeing — vibrant natural colours (maroons, yellows, indigo, block printing) that Europe could not replicate until chemical dyes arrived. Roman nobility wore purple silk precisely because it was so rare. - Muslin — so fine it was called "woven air".

    Encountering Indian cotton for the first time was, for a European, comparable to the joy of an iPhone.

    Key ports: Muziris (Kerala — known only from Roman texts, located archaeologically only decades ago), Machilipatnam / Bandar (Andhra, the Coromandel Coast block-print hub), Tranquebar/Tharangambadi (Danish). Trade route: block prints from Machilipatnam → sold in Indonesia → buy spices → sell in Amsterdam/Venice → more money.

    Why India lost it: - Taking things for granted — abundance made us complacent. - The French, English, Dutch and Portuguese came to control the source. They mechanised — the early Industrial Revolution was built on cotton. - Tariffs and taxes raised the price of Indian fabric in Europe; when people still bought it, social pressure ("we will tear your Indian fabric off you in the street") killed the market. - Europeans documented Indian textile patterns — to study Indian textile design documents today you must go to Scotland. They industrialised coarse fabric and sold it back to India. - By ~1900 India became a net consumer of Western textiles, though handloom survived — partly because men switched to trousers and shirts while women continued wearing traditional clothes.

    Post-independence phases:

    Period Character
    Post-independence industrialisation Jamsetji Tata, Walchand, Godrej — steel, cement, roads, ships, dams, airports. "The fight has moved on: it's no longer about making things by hand, it's making things by industry"
    1950s–70s/80s: License Raj Entrepreneurship not seen as positive; bureaucratic controls suppressed entrepreneurial behaviour. 14-year waits for a phone; years for a scooter or a mixie
    1990s Infosys — the breakthrough: founders not from a business background, trained engineers who built a multi-billion-dollar company and made employees wealthy. ICT changed how enterprises are created
    Late 1990s–2000s Wipro, Infosys, TCS plus Western firms set up in India to solve world problems using cheap, talented engineers + improved communications
    2007 onwards Flipkart — taking money from the West to build companies in India, solving India's problems. Blinkit, BigBasket, FabIndia, online medicine and hospitals

    The framing: entrepreneurship is a vehicle to solve problems. The locus of economic control is moving east.

    3.3The Entrepreneurial Mindset — three great debates

    Debate 1: Entrepreneur vs businessman

    Schumpeter's problem: are all entrepreneurs innovators? No. This created a hierarchy — "entrepreneurs bring innovation, businessmen just sell pizza/panipuri." Modern, inclusive resolution: entrepreneurship is defined around UNCERTAINTY.

    If you are taking judgement calls about a future you cannot know, you are an entrepreneur — innovation or not. An employee knows their salary arrives on the 21st; a panipuri seller can be wiped out by one complaint. This debate has been laid to rest. ← highly testable.

    Debate 2: Are entrepreneurs born or made?

    The 1960s–70s "entrepreneurial gene" search looked for personality traits: - Risk-taking propensity - Tolerance for ambiguity (decision-making under uncertainty) - Need for achievement - Internal locus of control (I control my future, the world doesn't tell me)

    Why it failed: questionnaires showed not everybody with a high risk tolerance was an entrepreneur, and not everybody with a low tolerance for ambiguity was an employee. Entrepreneurs had these traits, but so did non-entrepreneurs — and some entrepreneurs lacked them entirely. The trait approach became muddled and was abandoned, though popular journalism still talks about "hustle" and personality.

    Debate 3: Is entrepreneurship teachable?

    Yes. The argument: if creativity can be taught — artists do MFA/BFA, architects do B.Arch/M.Arch, people study product design and interaction design — then entrepreneurship can be taught too. There is an entrepreneurial method, like the scientific method or an educational method.

    Requirements: commitment, some level of intelligence, and reflexivity. The goal of the course is not that you must become an entrepreneur but that you become entrepreneurial — able to take ownership whether you are an employee in a large corporation, in a startup, in a family business, or on your own.

    Socio-cultural influences

    Certain regions (Silicon Valley, Israel, Bengaluru) and communities are more entrepreneurial. Why? 1. Learning resided in those communities — at the dinner table, at meetings, at events. Children are "baptised into entrepreneurship" very early. 2. Control of resources — they could decide who participates. Example: the diamond industry, long controlled by close-knit communities like Hasidic Jews and Palanpuri Jains (with De Beers as the largest diamond company). 3. Enforcement without contracts — high-value goods are handed over on credit and money comes much later. Written contracts take time and need courts to enforce; a close community enforces by ostracism — misbehave and nobody does business with you again.

    Displacement theory: immigrants in a strange land, displaced by events at home, set up enterprises at high rates — even when people from the same home country were not entrepreneurial at home.

    The trend: these advantages are diminishing rapidly. Entrepreneurial knowledge is now ubiquitous (YouTube, events, government support), so barriers to participating in business are now very low. Community and region mattered in the past; their role in future will keep shrinking.

    3.4Necessity-Based Entrepreneurship

    Source: the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) — a UK-based consortium studying entrepreneurial activity across economies. GEM did not expect India to be entrepreneurial, but found a high prevalence of entrepreneurship — and the same in other emerging economies. This led to formally categorising two kinds of entrepreneurship.

    Definition: people start ventures not to pursue an opportunity, not to scale, not from passion or calling — but because there is nothing else to do and no resources.

    Canonical example: a small farmer sells his land to service loans taken for seeds/pesticides after a failed crop → becomes landless → migrates to a town → starts a street food stall, sells vegetables, or takes up repair work.

    Characteristics: - Informal — not registered entities. - Cannot go to a bank for a loan; no PF; no formal hiring. - Just pick a street corner and start small. - Heavy mimetism/replication — they work in an existing establishment first (learning the trade, suppliers, raw material sourcing), then set up something similar in a new area. This is not lack of innovation — it is a survival strategy built on knowing what actually sells at a profit. - Also triggered by job loss.

    Microfinance — the biggest source of resources for necessity entrepreneurship. Invented by Professor Muhammad Yunus, Bangladesh, who started Grameen Bank. Mechanism: loans given to a group, and the community acts as the collateral — members hold each other accountable. Repayment rates are very high despite borrowers having very low means.

    Prof. Bhagavatula's field experiments (the papad/energy bar story) — why the lesson matters

    He set up an Enterprise Research and Marketing Unit, funded ~₹2–3 lakh raised by AID (Association for India's Development) volunteers in the US. (AID was the inspiration for the film Swades.) Ventures attempted: papad, pickles, coir rope, energy bars, handmade paper/greeting cards, screen printing.

    What went wrong — the concrete failures are the teaching points: - Papad: rolling was hard (South Indians weren't chapati-rolling households); papad dough is elastic so you must roll past its elastic point; excess rice powder to prevent sticking darkened the frying oil; the product wasn't hollow/crisp; the single village flour mill left residues of whatever was milled before (chilli, turmeric) so quality could not be controlled. Customers compared it unfavourably with Lijjat Papad. Hack attempted: heavily spice it and sell to bars with low lighting. - Energy bars: a home-science college produced a good recipe (jaggery, peanuts, chana dal, til — nutritious, locally available, inexpensive), but in the village they cooked on wood stoves and could not reach the heat needed for jaggery to caramelise, so the bars crumbled. Villagers suggested making laddus instead — refused, because that would collapse into a lower price category rather than creating a new premium category. Sold at a heavy loss to schools. - Screen printing was the most successful venture. Key insight: craft beats food for necessity ventures — if you don't sell today you can sell tomorrow or next year; food expires. - People problem: they trained young unmarried girls who then married and moved to other villages → switched to training women who had married into the village so the skill stayed put.

    Conclusion: necessity entrepreneurship is just as hard as opportunity entrepreneurship.

    What he would do differently: not start by teaching someone to make papad. Instead go to a woman already making 1 kg of papad and work on efficiencies, bulk buying for economies of scale, better-graded raw material, rebranding — scale her from 1 kg to more, from 1 kg of pickle to 5 kg. "You don't have to tell her what it takes to roll 1 kilo — she's already rolling 1 kilo."

    Why Indian necessity ventures often don't scale (vs the West)

    • No access to capital or cheap finance — no collateral to pledge; cost of money can be 24–36%, so servicing the loan eats a third of your time. Rational to be cautious.
    • The venture supports a whole family — started by the elder brother, funding the younger brother's marriage and education. It is used as a catapult into the formal economy, not as an inherently scalable business. "I'm doing this because there was nothing else. You do something else — get into the formal system."
    • Lack of access to high-quality education, unlike Western counterparts where schooling is free and good.
    • Not lack of intelligence — people in Dharavi show immense intelligence. If they aren't doing something, it's usually because they or others already tried it and it didn't work.
    • Standardisation is genuinely hard — a juice stall has many moving parts.

      Trend: this is changing — internet publicity gives models to emulate (Rameshwaram Cafe, the Bengaluru darshini format), so more necessity entrepreneurs should scale.

    Success stories cited: Adyar Ananda Bhavan, Naturals Ice Cream, Saravana Bhavan; Subbamma in Basavanagudi; Vasena Poli in Vizag (millet idlis sold in tendu-leaf pouches stitched with coconut twigs, sourced from tribal communities, given space by the Girijan Corporation — nostalgia + experience as the value proposition; grew from a pushcart to a formal kiosk and is imminently franchisable).

    The cycle-repair widow story — the key structural lesson: husband died leaving a cycle shop; she had only ever watched him work. "When your back is to the wall and you have three children to feed, you'll just do anything." Neighbours brought business; someone told her to move closer to the main road for a larger market; someone said if you can do cycles you can do scooters; then bikes; then spark plugs; then the SEZ's large vehicles.

    This is the "corridors" principle: you move into one corridor and start to notice other corridors that are available. It is why business plans don't work out — what eventually works is only discovered by engaging. Milk not selling? Convert it to koya — then you sell 5 kg instead of 54 litres.

    How necessity entrepreneurs help each other: the Dharavi story — arrive from Bihar with a distant contact, start at the absolute basic level (picking up waste cloth), learn over 7–8 years, and then the employer says "here's ₹50,000, start on your own." Often the venture they work for gives them the resources to start — which is also good business sense (outsourcing to a contractor).

    The fieldwork exercise (method matters for exam questions)

    • Talk to necessity entrepreneurs around you. Be curious, genuine.
    • Ask about what happened WHEN THEY STARTED — the difficulties and how they were overcome — not what is happening now.
    • Go during lean periods, not when customers are queuing. Ring ahead.
    • Develop trust first, then probe deeper. You may need multiple meetings.
    • Their first answers will not be the true story — that's the version they tell city officials and policemen. Stay longer to unearth the real one.
    • Note everything down; record only with prior permission.
    • Don't take your family along the first time.

    Field data example: a chaat vendor serves ~100 customers/day, ~200 at weekends → ~1,000 plates/week × ₹40 = ₹40,000/week ≈ ₹1.6 lakh/month, COGS ~40% → but also business operating costs including payments to hold the location.

    3.5Opportunity-Based Entrepreneurship

    Definition: starting a venture although you have a definite career/vocational trajectory in front of you — you chose to be an entrepreneur.

    Important corrective: for a long time it was assumed only opportunity-based entrepreneurs create wealth and jobs. Data shows necessity-based entrepreneurs have similar importance in providing livelihoods, especially in difficult and distant situations.

    The definition of entrepreneurship used in this course — memorise verbatim

    "Entrepreneurship is the pursuit of opportunities, although you don't have all the resources with you."

    The macho version is Reid Hoffman's "jump off a plane and build a parachute on the way down", which the professor deliberately avoids. What this definition deliberately excludes: personality, extroversion, "fire in the belly", undying motivation, need for achievement, "I will disrupt". What it is instead: "It is a cognitive game. It's not a fire-in-the-belly passion game. It's a clever game." You notice a faint signal, put attention on it, analyse whether it's real, and try to amplify it.

    Illustration 1 — the caricaturist who cycled to Sweden (1975)

    A young painter in Delhi (from Odisha) drawing caricatures fell in love with a Swedish woman who had to return home. His resources: a skill (drawing) and a cycle. Everybody said it was a stupid idea. He pedalled. He needed no foreign currency — at each marketplace he sketched and was paid in local currency; the compelling story earned him free food and lodging. He reached Sweden, married her, and lives there.

    The point: pursuing an opportunity with the resources at hand, disregarding what you lack.

    Illustration 2 — Mango Technologies vs Qualcomm (2007–08)

    A startup on Bannerghatta Road, Bengaluru — "back and beyond" (autos charged double/triple meter). Thesis: while everyone chased smartphones, the world was full of feature phones — build an operating system with a much smaller footprint so feature phones could do more for resource-constrained users (carpenters, plumbers). - Nobody would fund "global innovation from India" then, so they funded the product by selling IT services. - At a Bombay conference they weren't interested in, a chance corridor conversation with someone from a large company led to a demo video. The other company's engineers found it solved problems they had. - The large company's legal team refused to hand proprietary chips to "a no-name entity based out of Bangalore" — so they organised a quarter-million dollars for the startup to make the relationship contractual. - The large company was Qualcomm — a Fortune 500 firm. Mango Technologies was eventually acquired by Qualcomm.

    The exam-worthy question: How can Qualcomm, with virtually unlimited resources — able to hire any MIT or Stanford engineer — have a product not as good as a startup on Bannerghatta Road? The lesson: "In entrepreneurship you are likely to die of indigestion rather than of hunger." Too many resources can be counterproductive; some resource crunch drives creativity and out-of-the-box thinking. They played the game with their legs tied — and still coded better.

    3.6Social Entrepreneurship

    Why the construct exists: normal entrepreneurship pursues an opportunity that should pay you money. But some problems are social or cultural — poverty, health, education. Social entrepreneurs address these while not primarily making money.

    Models of social enterprise — know each with its example

    Model How it works Examples
    Grant-funded Survives on grants from government, wealthy individuals, banks, multilateral agencies like the UN, development offices of advanced economies. Founders take a minimum salary; motivated by a calling Guardians of Dreams (orphanages), Bridges of Sport, Mantra4Change (teacher training), Anthill — all incubated at NSRCEL's not-for-profit incubator ("Social Orbit"), some supported by MSDF (Michael & Susan Dell Foundation)
    Enabling technology for local for-profit ventures The social venture sells enabling tech; the local buyer runs a for-profit business with it SELCO — solar energy for remote hills: home electricity, pump sets; a villager buys a solar-powered flour mill (previously they travelled 10–12 km to grind atta). For SELCO it is a social venture; for the local entrepreneur it is for-profit
    For-profit social venture Solve a social/sustainability problem and make money Rescript — bamboo paper. Bamboo is highly regenerative; the historic problem was smudging, solved with a paper mill partner; now smudge-proof, whiter, doesn't jam laser/inkjet printers, so bamboo is the main ingredient, not a filler. IIMB is a customer. Also Good Gum — most chewing gum contains plastic (it began plant-based, moved to fossil fuel); Good Gum returns to tree-derived gum. The Indian chewing gum market is $100 million and had no competition in this niche
    Cross-subsidy / differential pricing Those who can afford pay more; that offsets the cost for those who cannot. Both get the same top-quality service Sankara Nethralaya — state-of-the-art equipment, best doctors, differential prices. OLPC (One Laptop Per Child) — buy one rugged laptop and one is sent to a child in Africa or elsewhere. OLPC was ultimately not successful, but the construct is valid
    Cooperatives Legal entities where ownership is spread across everybody — farmers own a farmers' co-op, weavers own a weavers' co-op. If it does well, everyone does well Amul (below); Lijjat Papad (below)
    NGOs / not-for-profits Take no profits — all surplus is repurposed into the mission (clean water, child education, social justice). Increasingly some earn income Craft/handloom NGOs: buy from skilled rural craftsmen, sell in urban areas, use the margin to retrain, educate and insure them. Toys from Channapatna, Etikoppaka, Varanasi — lead-free dyes, well designed, an alternative to Lego
    Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) Farmer-owned, moving up the value chain Farmveda — started by IIMB's Prof. Trilochan Sastry; began with groundnut, now thousands of farmers and crores of rupees. Also GoCoop

    Amul — the flagship cooperative

    Started by Dr Verghese Kurien when India was totally milk-deficient. Mechanism: farmers with 1–2 cows bring morning and evening milk to village collection centres, where it is measured on two parameters — quantity and fat content (higher fat = higher price). Farmers are paid every 15 days. Milk goes to chilling plants, then to dairy cooperatives in larger cities, where it becomes cheese, buttermilk, curd, flavoured milk, whey — "one milk gives rise to lots and lots of different products" — and profits go back to the farmers. Beyond milk: successful cooperatives also provide insurance for farmers, hospitals, vets, and animal insurance — taking care of the whole community, collectively owned. Kurien's achievement: kept it out of politicisation despite tens of thousands of farmers being an obvious vote bank; transformed India from milk-deficient to one of the largest milk producers in the world; Amul now competes in milk-surplus countries — Australia, New Zealand, UK, US. Replicas across states: Vijaya (Andhra), Nandini (Karnataka), Aavin (Tamil Nadu), Visakha Dairy, Mother Dairy — all owe their origin to the Amul model.

    Why you don't hear about them: "They're not creating wealth for people who already have wealth. They're creating wealth for people who don't have any."

    Lijjat Papad — the decentralised production model

    7 or 8 women in the 1950s started rolling papads on a balcony. Today tens of thousands of women roll papads daily. Mechanism: women go to a local Lijjat centre where one person who knows the recipe makes the dough in the morning; women take dough home, roll while watching TV or talking to neighbours, and return the papads for payment. Heuristic: X number of dried papads per kilo of dough (with a small tolerance) — too thin and they break in transport, too thick and customers won't like them. Why quality is consistent (contrast with the professor's failed venture): - They use a specific variety of black gram, seed obtained from an agricultural research centre, given to their own farmers, and the entire produce is bought back. - Cleaned and sent to mills that mill only Lijjat dal. - Different crushing methods for different spices — pepper uses a hammer mill, not a rolling mill.

    Result: decentralised production, decentralised sales, extremely difficult to replicate — the system grew organically over years with all parts working together.

    Network effects (introduced here): on a music site, a song played 200 times attracts your click over one played 15 times; you make it 201, five friends make it 207 — the popular node keeps accumulating while others get nothing. Amul and Lijjat have built exactly this kind of self-reinforcing system.

    3.7Deliberate vs Accidental Entrepreneurship

    Critical framing: deliberate vs accidental is ONLY about the PLUNGE DECISION — "are you jumping off a cliff because you wanted to, or did you slip and fall off?" It says nothing about what you do afterwards, and nothing about scalability or size.

    Deliberate Accidental
    Definition You decide to stop what you're doing and pursue this opportunity You had no plan to be an entrepreneur; something in the environment changed or you observed something
    Examples Amagi, Zoojoo.be, GoDESi, Mango Technologies (Sunil and Lake both had jobs; a random conversation led them to quit) redBus, Instant Pot

    redBus — the canonical accidental venture

    Phanindra and friends went to Silk Board to travel to Hyderabad for Diwali. Buses were leaving empty but every travel agent said tickets were sold out — because bus owners parcelled out inventory to travel agents (an agent with 5 seats sells 5, then says "no tickets"), and even the bus owner couldn't tell you availability without calling every agent. The hard part came after: bus operators had no pain point — their system worked, they were cushy; occasionally unsold inventory, but that was fine. They spoke to ~3,000 bus owners to build the first platform. The pivot: they originally wanted to sell a bus operating system, and nobody would migrate from the traditional travel-agent model. Someone advised: become an agent yourself — that's a role the industry already understands. So they took inventory as a "new agent" and put it on redBus. It took off because young people in IT parks in Bengaluru and Hyderabad had credit cards (unlike Flipkart's early customers, which is why Flipkart needed cash on delivery). The punchline: students later asked Phani how redBus survives now that KSRTC and VRL have their own websites. His answer: "On which platform do you think they're selling tickets?" — the bus operating system he originally wanted to build is what he ended up owning.

    They had no burning desire to disrupt bus ticketing. They just couldn't get tickets and found the system inefficient.

    Instant Pot — accidental, from job loss, creating a huge market

    A young engineer lost his job, had young kids to care for, and built the electric pressure cooker. Before it, Indians in the US tracked whistle counts to manage heat, pressure and cooking. The technology was not rocket science — pressure sensors, temperature sensors, timers all existed and simply needed to be put together and coordinated. Neither TTK nor the existing pressure-cooker companies did it. It is now a hundreds-of-millions-of-dollars market.

    The wheeled suitcase — the definitive "obvious in hindsight" example

    We put a man on the moon in the late 1960s. We put wheels on a suitcase in the 1970s. The wheel was invented thousands of years ago; suitcases had existed for hundreds of years; nobody put the two together. "We really don't know the universe of solutions that could have come but aren't there, because people just didn't put their minds together."

    Necessity + accidental combinations: an immigrant mathematics professor without recognised credentials might end up doing tuition, baking cakes, or ethnic food. Opportunity-based ventures still require legitimacy — certificates. Where legitimacy is demanded, immigrants are pushed into something completely different.

    iD Fresh Food — a software engineer with an IIMB MBA starting an idli-dosa batter business in "the Silicon Valley of India" was a family joke. The market turned out to be seriously large, expanding into parathas, coffee, bread. Bengaluru was a good place to start because it is cold enough that batter doesn't ferment easily — so well-fermented batter sold itself.

    Scalability has nothing to do with your starting point or with the industry. It is a choice. Some owners of a beloved Pune bakery deliberately don't want to grow.

    3.8Entrepreneurial Resources

    1. Equity as a resource

    "There is only 100% equity, but you could give a bit of equity."

    Mango Technologies' resource story: - Sunil asked his friend Ram for his office, engineers and computers, in exchange for 2% of the venture. At the time it was "2% of a zero-billion-dollar venture" — it sounded absurd. When Qualcomm acquired Mango, that 2% was a significantly large amount. - When Ram moved to Jaipur, they moved to NSRCEL inside IIM Bangalore — 6 seats, 6 computers, internet, power for a ridiculously low rent (~₹4,500). They then leveraged the address: telling engineering applicants "we are inside IIM" gave them enormous legitimacy, letting them recruit good engineers who would otherwise never join an unknown startup. They had a 10×10 cubicle; applicants imagined the whole campus.

    Licious: two founders wanting to "disrupt the meat industry" knew they weren't from the food industry. They pitched five-star chefs ("how would you change the meat industry?") until one agreed to join as a co-founder for roughly a third of the equity and no salary. Getting a chef worth ₹50–60 lakh a year onto the founding team was a powerful signal to investors.

    So equity was used twice: to buy the resource, and to signal quality to investors.

    2. Bootstrapping

    Bootstrapping is not itself a resource — it is a SET OF TECHNIQUES for bringing slack resources and customers' money into your venture.

    The idli podi story: a 12th-standard girl from a family unwilling to fund her degree started making idli podi from a family recipe and selling it in the neighbourhood. Customers then asked for curry leaf powder → she asked her grandmother → made it. A neighbour's son returning from the US wanted 2–2.5 kg instead of 200 g to carry abroad → bulk deals emerged. Then bachelors asked for payasam and sakkarai pongal mixes. She took a neighbourhood garage and started selling with idlis. She used customers' money to buy more inventory each cycle, and paid for her education.

    Slack resources — look around for them: - You don't need to build a factory to use one for two days. - Someone may lend a garage for free; an aunt may lend a motorcycle lying unused because her son has left India; a landlord may drop rent from ₹40,000 to ₹5,000–10,000 for something interesting; people may even come and help because they're bored.

    Why bootstrapping is attractive: you take no outside money early, so you don't dilute your stake or lose control — 100% or 90% stays yours. If you take money and the company gets big, you hold only a small slice.

    3. Debt

    Bank loans; loans from parents. MyCaptain: while in engineering college, they took ₹60,000 from parents promising repayment with interest (Zeeshan says he paid it back with interest); the venture was otherwise extremely bootstrapped. Weavers post-12th standard use Prime Minister loan schemes with subsidy.

    4. Grants

    The best deal of all: you don't give equity and you don't pay it back. Government grants (e.g. Karnataka's Elevate 100) and CSR funds — corporates want to address social problems.

    5. Venture capital

    • VCs raise money from pension funds, HNIs and wealthy individuals and deploy it for equity.
    • The VC currency is dollars everywhere in the world, regardless of local currency.
    • The maths: give you $1 million and they want $10–30 million back. That requires the company to become 20–30× larger → hyperscale / hockey-stick growth.
    • Hence the question: is the problem/market large enough? "You can't have a billion-dollar venture in a $100 million market." This is where TAM matters.
    • VCs are not in it for charity — you cannot demand money because they have it.
    • Risk profile: equity financing means if your venture goes down, they go down with it. With debt, you may still have to pay back even if the venture fails.
    • Other instruments exist — e.g. convertible equity.

    3.9Seven Ways to Start a Venture — likely list MCQ1

    1. "Put a dent in the universe" (Steve Jobs) — disrupt an industry, a moonshot. Vocabulary: blitzscaling, network effects, Series A → G (Series A is small; Series H can be hundreds of millions). Examples: Flipkart (legitimised India as a market, made e-commerce and Indian investment take off — "there is life before Flipkart and after Flipkart"), Ather (created the electric vehicle category), Amagi, Zoojoo.be, Bisho, Zeto.
    2. "Scratch your own itch" — solve your own problem, assume others share it. Mansi (IIMB PGP) became a mother, found no processed food safe for 4–5-year-olds (too many additives), and started Troovy sauces.
    3. Moonlighting — keep the job, build in the evening. Apple: Steve Wozniak was at HP when they built the first machine. HP passed on it — but note Wozniak had signed a fine-print clause that anything built in spare time also belonged to HP. "Read your fine print."

      Why it's recommended: it's a sandbox. Wait until you have customers, then paying customers, then enough paying customers, before letting go of what's in your hand. Harder because you're doing two things — but far safer.

    4. Start small and bootstrap.
    5. For-profit social venture — solve a social problem and make money (Rescript, Good Gum).
    6. Not-for-profit social venture — leverage grants and CSR money (Guardians of Dreams, Bridges of Sport, Mantra4Change, Anthill).
    7. Accidental / necessity — after a job loss or after retirement.

      The age data: entrepreneurship is bimodal. One bump is young people (no encumbrances, high energy, willing to give 2 years). A second bump starts after 40 — kids grown, 20 years of experience. The most successful time to start is early-to-mid 40s (~44) — you have experience, connections, networks, capabilities, industry understanding, and still 20–25 years to run the venture. At 60 people are high on energy and experience with 10–12 productive years left.

    3.10Idea Generation

    Brainstorming — three principles

    1. Go for quantity — a long list raises the likelihood of finding a radical, effective idea. Quantity breeds quality.
    2. Withhold criticism — take off the evaluation hat. Don't feel good about a good idea or bad about a bad one.
    3. Combine and improve ideas — "associative thinking": how can 1 + 1 = 3? Example: a software engineer in the professor's Social Network Analysis course was migrating servers, with no method to decide which server to start with (they picked randomly). He applied node centrality from social network analysis to servers — built a spider to map program-server dependencies, identified central vs peripheral servers, and started migration from the periphery, moving to the most central server last. He patented it.

    Painstorming

    Over 3–4 days after brainstorming, set aside 30–45 minutes a day to talk to people and observe life, collecting problems worth solving — youngsters, elderly, your child, yourself. Example: a Stanford student whose grandmother had Alzheimer's sat with her daily and noticed patterns among dementia patients under care — they dropped food, ate too little, were frustrated, and caretakers were unhappy about the mess. As a designer she created a table set the elderly could use themselves without spilling or frustration.

    Wacky ideas — seriously

    "Stupid ideas that made their owners wealthy." Examples: the pet rock, goggles for dogs, plastic wishbones. It's not just smart people who made money.

    Hobby / passion as an idea

    An IIMB graduate ran a consulting agency Monday to Thursday; on Friday she ran her baking hobby as a venture — subscribers received a mystery box every Friday evening (cupcake, muffin, banana waffle cake — whatever she felt like baking), which felt like a prize at the end of the week.

    Antecedents / sources of opportunity — the three drivers

    Context — the shrinking corporate lifespan: average lifespan of a Fortune 500 company fell from ~75 years to ~15 years. Only 61 of the 1955 Fortune 500 still existed in 2004 — about 12%. ← memorise these figures. This is Schumpeter's creative destruction. "Your ability to threaten a very large company is higher now than at any point of time."

    Source Explanation and examples
    Technological change Incumbents run on older technology; new technology makes previously impossible things possible. In India and other emerging economies many people experience the internet first through mobile phones, not desktops → serve them in one of India's ~15 official languages and you can threaten large commerce companies
    Political and regulatory change Government can enable or curtail an opportunity space. Demonetisation enabled a wave of digital payments companies — the space had existed for years but the policy change unlocked it. Track regulatory changes to find new opportunities
    Social and demographic change Japan is getting older; India is getting younger. The shift from joint families to nuclear families means both spouses work → opportunities in restaurants, food delivery, childcare, domestic help. Youngsters working in other cities/countries → products and services for the elderly

    Indian challengers cited: Flipkart (and the e-commerce logistics infrastructure others now ride on), CaratLane (diamonds online), Amagi, Zoho (Chennai), Just Books, Cradle, Cloud 9.

    Jobs To Be Done (Clayton Christensen, Harvard)

    The milkshake study: a large fast-food chain wanted to grow milkshake sales. Observers found a huge sales spike around 6:30 a.m. Who buys a large thick milkshake at 6:30 a.m.? Long-distance truck drivers. They weren't drinking it for pleasure or hunger — it kept them occupied; the shake is so thick it takes about 25 minutes to finish. They don't need different flavours or consistencies.

    The "job" the milkshake was hired to do was to keep a trucker engaged for a stretch of the drive.

    Theodore Levitt's formulation: "Customers don't buy drills; customers want holes." Therefore adding features to the drill makes no sense unless they change the hole, make it easier to make, or make it more efficient.

    3.11Idea Evaluation

    "Ideas don't mean anything. Ideas are probably 1% of the venture or even less. It's all about execution." Expect 10+ ideas coming into evaluation week; come out with no more than two.

    Filter 1: Yourself

    Which ideas excite you? Which are close to who you are? (If you love travelling, do you have travel ideas on the list?)

    Filter 2: The 2×2 matrix — rows: Market / Personal; columns: Feasibility / Value

    Quadrant Question
    Technological feasibility Is it overall possible? (A washing machine that also irons: market feasible, technologically not)
    Market feasibility Would enough people want a product like this?
    Value Even if feasible and wanted — is it worth doing? Is there enough money in it? Is it financially feasible?
    Personal / values Do I really want to do this? Is my heart in it?

    TAM / SAM / SOM

    Construct Meaning Smartphone example
    TAM — Total Addressable Market The overall market Total number of smartphone users
    SAM — Segmented (Serviceable) Addressable Market The segment you address How many of them play games on mobile phones
    SOM — Share of the Market Your realistic share of that segment Realistically 2–5%, not 70%

    The logic: these are indicative, not promises. If the segment is very large, even a small share yields a large venture. Conversely, this is why VCs care about market size.

    3.12The Lean Canvas and the Lean Startup

    Provenance — know who did what

    • Alex Osterwalder and colleagues created the Business Model Canvas — a one-page canvas with 9 modules defining any venture's business model.
    • Eric Ries created the Lean Startup.
    • Ash Maurya merged the Business Model Canvas with lean startup thinking to create the Lean Canvas.

    Lean startup's founding assumption: every starting business has two aspects — a CUSTOMER and a PROBLEM — and before you start, both are only a hypothesis.

    Worked example: the "clinic at home" venture

    • Problem: the elderly have health issues; getting to a hospital/clinic is hard, especially in a large metro with traffic, and especially when alone.
    • Solution: send a doctor home.
    • Customer segments: (a) the elderly themselves; (b) children living abroad, who may feel guilty they can't take their parents to hospital — a second paying segment.
    • Channels: television advertising, starting in the US to reach NRI children.
    • Revenue streams: pay-per-house-visit, or a subscription paid monthly/yearly by NRI children.
    • Cost structure: doctor's charges + transportation.
    • Unfair advantage: things that cannot be copied — here perhaps first-mover brand plus clever advertising, and once people sign into a service they tend to stay.
    • Key metrics (thumb rules before you bring in an accountant): website visitors, sign-ups, and referrals (a satisfied customer in New Jersey tells a friend whose father in India needs the service).

    Lean Canvas vs Business Model Canvas: the Lean Canvas replaces Customer Relationships with Unfair Advantage.

    The five principles of the Lean Startup (Eric Ries) — memorise all five

    # Principle Meaning
    1 Entrepreneurs are everywhere Anybody can become an entrepreneur — entrepreneurs are made, not born
    2 Entrepreneurship is management You can systematically work on and develop your idea; it just needs discipline
    3 Validated learning Take decisions based on hypotheses, then go out and test whether they are valid. If valid, proceed. If not, change the hypothesis or pivot completely. Get data from customers
    4 Build – Measure – Learn Don't build every bell and whistle. Start very small, see whether it works, learn, come back and add a feature. A wireframe or shell is enough to gather feedback
    5 Innovation accounting Account for all the innovations you're building in; use measures to see whether the venture is growing and the innovation makes sense

    Lean startup in practice — the failure it prevents

    Entrepreneurs fall in love with their product and build feature after feature; by the time they reach the market, nobody wants those features. All it would have taken was stepping out to ask.

    Failure case: around 2006 in Bengaluru, several ventures built hyperlocal mobile search — painstakingly documenting and mapping every establishment in the city, assuming people would search for "Chinese restaurant nearby" while out. People had internet-capable phones but no data plans, because data was very expensive. The ventures were too early to market.

    Success cases — starting lean without inventory: - The online bookstore (Amazon): put up a website with images and descriptions of books but no books. When an order came in, go to the local bookstore, pick up the book, wrap it, post it. Only after volume justified it did they build inventory and publisher relationships. And they were not the first — many tried and failed; they needed data to convince publishers. - The online grocer (BigBasket): a well-designed website, no inventory. Collate the whole day's orders, go to the hypermarket in the evening, buy, deliver next day. No inventory carried, no money raised until the model was proven.

    The downside was tiny: a website with pictures and a payment gateway costs a few thousand rupees and a few weeks — not millions and not years.

    Ash Maurya's Lean Canvas walkthrough — the details worth knowing

    Why 20 minutes? "The perfect plan is a myth." Successful companies (Groupon, PayPal, Flickr) drastically changed their original plans. What separates winners is finding a plan that works before running out of resources — through empirical testing, not whiteboard reasoning. Time is the scarcest resource in a startup, so time-box the canvas to avoid analysis paralysis. The goal is a snapshot of current thinking, not perfection.

    Order and blocks — Maurya's preferred flow: 1. Problem + Customer Segments quadrant (the foundation) 2. Solution + Unique Value Proposition + Revenue Streams (together these define your offer / MVP) 3. Channels → Key Metrics → Cost Structure → Unfair Advantage

    Customer Segments: - Name the canvas by the customer segment — it drives everything else. - Split broad segments into narrower verticals; each vertical potentially needs its own canvas. "When you try to market to everyone, especially as a startup, you end up marketing to no one." - Don't go too broad or too narrow (shrinking market size). - Distinguish customers from users: customers pay you, users do not. In SaaS you attract users and convert some to customers. In a multi-sided business like Google Search, advertisers are the customers and searchers are the users — keep both on one canvas. For marketplaces (eBay, Airbnb) where two or more parties simultaneously create value and each has different incentives and channels, create a separate canvas for each party. - Early adopters: those who need your product most. Even Facebook started with a very specific early adopter: a college student — and not just any, one on the Harvard campus. - CloudFire example: customer = parents; users/viewers = family and friends; early adopters = parents with younger kids.

    Problem box: - List the top 3 problems — fewer is fine, not more than 3. - The "5 Whys" — start from the surface problem/symptom and ask why five times to reach deeper problems. - Jobs-to-be-done — customers hire your product to get a job done. - Also list EXISTING ALTERNATIVES — how do early adopters solve this today? "Doing nothing" is also an alternative. This is invaluable for positioning and pricing.

    Solution box: "The solution is the one we entrepreneurs are most in love with, but it usually isn't what's riskiest on the canvas." - MVP (Minimum Viable Product) = the smallest solution you can build that still delivers customer value — solves a specific problem and ideally captures some of that value (i.e. gets you paid). - Outline one solution per listed problem, constrained to the top 3.

    Unique Value Proposition — "one of the hardest things to get right, and the most critical initially." - The initial battle is getting noticed and earning a chance at a meaningful dialogue with a prospect. - Derive it from the intersection of your problem and your solution; craft it around your number one problem. - Think in terms of the "finished story benefit" — the value the customer derives after using the product. A job board's UVP isn't the cool resume builder; it's helping job seekers find their dream job. - Avoid empty words — simple, fast, easy. "Yes, Apple uses these all the time, but you are not Apple." - Dane Maxwell's 3-fragment formula: (1) the end result the customer wants, (2) a specific period of time in which they'll see it, (3) address their objections. Use (2) and (3) only if they don't sound salesy. - High-concept pitch — the Hollywood device: "It's Jaws in space" (Aliens); YouTube = "Flickr for videos." This is NOT the UVP and doesn't go on your landing page, but it spreads the meme by word of mouth.

    Revenue Streams / Pricing: - Price is part of the product. Two bottles of water, $1 and $3 — indistinguishable in a blind taste test, but price alone defines the product in your mind and determines which customers you attract. - Value-based, not cost-based pricing. Customers compare against existing alternatives, not your costs — those alternatives are price anchors. - Keep pricing simple at first; resist multiple plans. Pick a price aimed at your early adopters. - For multi-sided models, you're building an asset that is worth nothing until you pass a tipping point; find the tipping point and ballpark the asset value from comparable advertising rates and/or acquisitions. - CloudFire example: alternatives anchored from $0 (Facebook) to $99 (Apple MobileMe) → starting price $49/year.

    Channels (path to customers): - One of the riskier items on the canvas. You can find a real problem, build a solution, get a small group to love it — and none of it matters if you can't get in front of enough customers. - Don't defer channels — start building and testing from day one. - You don't need scalable channels from day one: start with a handful of outbound channels to jumpstart learning, but also identify where scalable (inbound) channels might come from, since those take time.

    Key Metrics — identify exactly two: 1. The key customer action that drives value — the activity that measures your value proposition. Blogging platform → publishing a post. Twitter → posting a tweet. CloudFire → sharing: if a parent doesn't routinely share photos/videos, they'll lose interest and stop paying. 2. Your success metric — a revenue target, an impact on the world, or something else. CloudFire: a $5 million business ≈ 100,000 paying customers.

    "A startup is inherently chaotic, but at any given time only a few key actions or metrics matter" — and they change as the product moves through stages.

    Cost Structure: outline fixed and variable costs (people, servers, resources). Accuracy is impossible; the point is ballpark sizing. Use a short horizon like break-even: how many customers to break even, and how many to hit your success metric. This establishes whether you have a problem worth solving.

    Unfair Advantage — "something that cannot be easily copied or bought" (definition from Jason Cohen, founder of WP Engine, author of the A Smart Bear blog). - NOT an unfair advantage: being first to market. Many giants were fast followers, not first movers. One could argue being first is a disadvantage — the burden of learning and educating the market falls entirely on the first mover. - Even Facebook had no unfair advantage at the start — it was roughly the 11th or 12th social network. The network it built became its unfair advantage. - If you don't have one, leave the box BLANK rather than writing something weak. A blank box is a constant reminder to keep looking. Some unfair advantages are revealed over time (Zappos). - What matters most early is having an unfair advantage story. Unlike other boxes, you can't decide to test it one day — it gets tested by competitors and copycats when you gain traction. - CloudFire's: a specific, emotional niche → build differentiation over time by fostering a strong community.

    3.13Effectuation (Prof. Saras Sarasvathy)1

    The three-jars thought experiment — know which jar maps to which concept

    Jar Setup Concept
    Jar 1 — transparent You can see the chocolates, call a colour, and pick it Perfect information
    Jar 2 — opaque, contains chocolates of a fixed set of colours Each failed guess reveals a colour; over many turns you learn the distribution. With 4 colours, the 25th person has ~¼ chance RISK — outcomes are knowable; probabilities can be estimated
    Jar 3 — opaque, contains arbitrary objects You get a knife, then a spoon, then a pencil, an eraser, a keychain. No number of attempts tells you what comes next UNCERTAINTY — unknowable

    Most entrepreneurship lives in Jar 3. That is where effectuation is useful.

    The definitional chain — a favourite MCQ

    Idea + Action = Opportunity Opportunity + Commitment = Viable Opportunity

    "Action" means talking to customers, developing a product, finding co-founders, raising money. "Commitment" means committing time, resources and attention.

    The five principles of effectuation

    # Principle Content
    1 Bird-in-hand ("means-driven") Start from who you are, what you know, and whom you know — your kind of person, your knowledge, your network
    2 Affordable loss Start with whatever you are willing to lose — "6 months of my time and ₹50,000". This takes risk entirely out of the equation because you've already decided what you'll spend. At the end you take a call on whether to commit more
    3 Crazy quilt Learn from interactions with stakeholders and move to a better opportunity. Entrepreneurship is not a jigsaw puzzle (one right solution, and a missing piece means no solution) — it is a quilt: stitch together whatever fabric comes; if you wanted a square and get a round piece, put the round piece in
    4 Lemonade Leverage surprises, positive or negative. Don't ask how to circumvent or prevent them — ask how you can bring them into your venture
    5 Pilot in the plane Do not try to predict — control. "To the extent that you can control things, do not try to predict them." You can control the resources in your hand, your interactions with others, the contingencies you leverage, and how much you're willing to lose

    Causal vs Effectual decision-making — the cooking metaphor

    CAUSAL EFFECTUAL
    Metaphor "I want to make blue cheese pasta." Fixed goal → look up the recipe → list what you have vs what's needed → go buy blue cheese, half-and-half, parmesan → but you only have ₹500 and the neighbourhood store doesn't stock them, so you must travel to a store with international products "I'll cook a healthy meal." Open the fridge — spring onions, tomatoes, capsicum, onions, olive oil, salt, pepper, butter, soy sauce, chilli sauce, spaghetti → make pasta with a fresh vegetable sauce right away, and save the ₹500
    Starting point The goal is fixed first The means at hand are the starting point
    Business analogue The business plan — describe the profitable venture, list needed resources, spend a lot of time convincing others to fund the gap (promising 10× returns) Action bias — start with what you have, who you are, what you can do; leverage your network for expertise
    Outcome space Binary: either you make blue cheese pasta or you don't Many possible outcomes from the same ingredients
    Cost Extremely time-consuming Start cooking right away

    The expert-chef demonstration: given the same four vegetables, professional chefs generated main courses, multiple salads, tangy tomato sauce, stuffed capsicum starters, hara pyaz masala, tomato-onion-chilli salad. That is the difference between a novice following a recipe with a specific outcome, and experts who combine, cut, deep-fry and recombine.

    Effectuation is needed not just at the start of a venture but throughout it.

    3.14FinTech Entrepreneurship in India1

    (Akarsh Naidu, Head of FinTech & Startups, Reserve Bank Innovation Hub (RBIH) — a subsidiary of the RBI created to promote and accelerate innovation in financial services)

    The opportunity — numbers to memorise

    Metric Value
    India's rank as a fintech ecosystem Third largest in the world
    FinTech unicorns 20+ (a unicorn = a startup valued over $1 billion)
    Soonicorns (soon to be unicorns) 30+
    FinTech startups 10,000+
    UPI transactions ~18 billion per month ≈ 600 million per day

    Why the sector is thriving: a digitally native young population · deep smartphone penetration · among the lowest data rates in the world · and above all the Digital Public Infrastructure (India Stack).

    The evolution of banking channels: branches → ATMs → online banking → smartphone transactions. Why financial inclusion matters economically: someone in the formal system gets credit from banks at lower interest rates; someone outside it goes to a moneylender at much higher rates. Inclusion spans payments, credit and investments.

    The India Stack — the five layers — learn the order and what each unlocks

    Think of DPI as digital highways built by government for public good, the way roads and buildings are.

    Layer Components What it does
    1. Identity Aadhaar — biometric identity for over a billion Indians Verify an individual to a financial institution without physically visiting a branch
    2. Verification eKYC, eSign, DigiLocker Verify documentation beyond identity; sign documents digitally; store submitted documents. Replaces photocopies and 100 documents at a branch — a bank account or credit card now verifies in minutes
    3. Payments UPI; AePS (Aadhaar enabled Payment System) for offline payments in rural areas via micro-ATMs Only possible because layers 1 and 2 exist. Also generates the digital footprint that cash transactions never left — essential for getting a loan
    4. Consent Account Aggregator framework A consent mechanism to share your data with a financial institution. Also gives you a single snapshot of finances held across banks A, B, C and SIPs elsewhere
    5. Lending ULI — Unified Lending Interface (built by RBIH under RBI's guidance) Unlocks financial and non-financial/alternative data to lenders on a consent basis, so loans can be verified and disbursed digitally in minutes

    Why DPI is decisive: this is infrastructure a startup would otherwise have had to build itself. Being given it saves enormous cost and time and provides access at population scale unavailable in any other country.

    Regulators of the Indian financial sector

    Regulator Covers
    RBI Banking, NBFCs, payments, digital lending / lending at large
    SEBI Stock/capital markets, mutual funds, investments
    IRDAI Insurance — life, vehicle, etc.
    PFRDA Pensions — NPS; how pension money is utilised and invested
    IFSCA Set up in GIFT City as a global launchpad — for foreign fintechs entering India and Indian fintechs exploring global markets

    Why regulators matter: financial services deal with customers' money, so trust must be embedded. The regulator ensures stability plus consumer protection — no untoward or unregulated practice, no extremely high interest rates, transparent terms and conditions.

    Bank–FinTech collaboration — the symbiotic relationship

    The rule: in India you are either a regulated entity or you must work with one, because you are dealing with people's money.

    Banks FinTechs
    Built for scale, stability and compliance Built for speed, agility and user-centric innovation
    Hold regulatory licences, manage risk and profitability, have access to low-cost capital Focus on innovation, customer experience, accessibility through digital channels
    Slower to innovate alone Alone, lack trust, compliance and funds

    Together they deliver innovation at scale in a regulatory-compliant manner. Example: PhonePe/Google Pay give you the customer-friendly interface and QR codes; the bank processes the transaction at the back end. The result is finance that is frictionless, inclusive, accessible, affordable and intuitive.

    The five FinTech sub-sectors and their value chains — the most likely MCQ structure

    BFSI = Banking, Financial Services and Insurance.

    Sub-sector Value chain Startups cited
    1. Payments Tech Initiation (QR code, POS machine, NFC, app-based) → Processing (authentication, back-and-forth at the back end) → Settlement (funds move from account A to account/merchant B) B2B: Razorpay, Cashfree, Juspay, PayU. Consumer: PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm, CRED
    2. Lending Tech Origination (the need + application) → Underwriting (assessing creditworthiness; credit score / credit bureau data, collateral, consent via Account Aggregator) → Disbursement → Collections (EMIs, prepayment, NACH e-mandate) KreditBee (small-ticket unsecured personal loans), Lendingkart (MSME/small business), BNPL as embedded finance, B2B debt marketplaces
    3. WealthTech & Savings Initiation (KYC, goal setting, user/risk profiling) → Advisory/Planning (incl. robo-advisors; when to pause or double down on SIPs) → Execution (buying mutual funds/stocks) → Monitoring & Rebalancing Zerodha, Upstox, Groww; goal-based apps Jar, Smallcase, INDmoney. Historically instruments were held on paper, then demat accounts, now apps
    4. InsurTech Discovery (understand the products before deciding) → Underwriting (risk-based premium — older applicants pay more; younger and healthier pay less) → Policy issuance (a checkbox at checkout for travel insurance; policy in your inbox in minutes) → Premium collection (auto-debit, UPI, recurring) → Claims assessment (credibility, management, frictionless experience) Acko (vehicle), Digit, Policybazaar (discovery), Plum (business insurance)
    5. TechFin (the infrastructure layer) KYC & compliance (video KYC, fraud checks, AML) · APIs and banking infrastructure (two softwares talking to each other, bridging core banking systems to the India Stack) · Risk analytics (bureaus, alternative data scoring) · RegTech (automatic reporting of transactions, compliance) Perfios (financial data aggregation, analytics), Setu (API bridges between banks/FIs and fintechs), Signzy and IDfy (KYC, onboarding, fraud detection)

    "What you see at the front end is the exciting part; what you see at the back end is the trust layer or infrastructure layer powering all these transactions."

    AI-based credit underwriting is called out specifically: conventional underwriting assumes the customer already has a credit score — but you only get a score after your first loan. Customers without a digital trail have no score by default. AI startups underwrite with limited data to predict behaviour so thin-file customers can get small-ticket, collateral-free loans.

    Digital Financial Inclusion — the underserved segments and their specific frictions

    Segment The problem and the fintech opportunity
    Women ~50% of the population, but most products are gender-neutral rather than tailored; women's needs and repayment behaviour differ. SHGs (Self-Help Groups) — collectives of women who pool savings and lend to each other — kept books on pen and paper, so banks could not lend to them. RBI digitised the SHG onboarding process, so SHGs now open bank accounts, transactions and repayments are tracked digitally, and they get better interest rates than informal channels
    Farmers The Kisan Credit Card — a working capital loan of up to ₹1.6 lakh for fertilisers and inputs — used to take 4–6 weeks, hundreds of papers and several bank visits. RBIH digitised land record data and made it available through the ULI, so a farmer sharing a land record number is verified digitally and the digital KCC is disbursed in minutes. Startups now use satellite data, soil health, and for dairy farmers, cattle health, as the basis for lending
    People with disabilities Can a visually impaired person use a UPI app? Can a deaf person transact at an ATM? ~2–3% of the population has some form of disability → voice-based solutions and accessible banking apps
    Gig workers Income is inconsistent and unpredictable — it depends on jobs undertaken, orders delivered, rides completed, and they choose when to work. Banks therefore can't extend credit. The opportunity: showcase their credit behaviour to banks
    Daily wage labourers Paid in cash, so no digital trail to establish
    Gen Z Will undertake the next set of major financial transactions; their financial behaviour and goals differ sharply from millennials or older cohorts
    Elderly and feature-phone users IVR or helpline-based transactions — even a helpline to check a balance is an innovation for feature-phone users

    RBIH's support mechanisms for entrepreneurs — know these by name

    • Hackathons, incubation and acceleration programmes for early-stage through growth-stage founders.
    • Finteract — RBI sits with fintech entrepreneurs to understand white spaces and opportunities and enable more proactive policy formulation.
    • FinTech Repository — a one-stop digital platform where fintechs register, connect with banks, financial institutions, investors and incubators, and showcase their profile. A key RBIH initiative.
    • Bank–FinTech Demo Day — the flagship fix for a real bottleneck: bank–fintech collaboration used to take 18–24 months, partly because a fintech doesn't know the right stakeholder inside the bank and finding them takes months. The Demo Day puts 20+ banks/FIs and 20+ startups into a matchmaking exercise in a single day producing 100+ one-on-one meetings, which lead to pilots and proofs of concept.

    Six white-space opportunities in Indian fintech — a likely list question

    1. AI-powered RegTech — help fintechs make sense of, stay updated with, and actually implement evolving regulations and circulars (KYC, onboarding, transparent disclosure of terms). Liked by regulators, banks and fintechs alike because trust depends on how well regulations are implemented in delivery.
    2. Hyper-personalised finance — two 18-year-olds in the same college can have completely different financial behaviour. Most products are built on demographics or hard criteria that may not hold. Includes AI-native personal finance advisors (regulation still to be created), and unlocking better options within a stated preference — e.g. a conservative FD investor could be shown higher-interest FDs or government-backed bonds.
    3. Financial inclusion for the underserved — women, gig workers, farmers, Gen Z, people with disabilities, the elderly, feature-phone users (IVR/helpline transactions).
    4. Voice and vernacular tech — local language banking. For lower/mid-income customers, walking into a bank is intimidating; people ask strangers for help filling a deposit slip or using an ATM. Opportunity: local language interfaces, customer support in one's own language, voice-based services for the "Bharat" segment beyond cities and towns.
    5. CBDC — Central Bank Digital Currency — think of it as digital cash in a digital wallet, versus physical cash in a physical wallet. Built on blockchain and, critically, programmable: if the government gives a farmer a grant for fertiliser via Direct Benefit Transfer, CBDC can program the money so it can only be used to buy fertiliser, and trace it. Also enables goal-based saving. Programmable money, tokenisation and a cashless economy are the direction of travel.
    6. The MSME credit gap — the difference between the number of MSMEs that need loans and those actually getting them. Requires solving for documentation and cash-flow-based assessment — is the business actually making revenues on which a loan can be given? "Which in turn will accelerate the growth engine for India's economy."

    International Trade Finance

    International Trade Finance

    (Instructor: Mithun Raj — Modules 1–4)

    This is the most jargon-dense course of the set. Almost every MCQ will hinge on a precise definition, an acronym expansion, a party's role, or which rulebook governs which instrument. Learn the tables.

    4.1What is Trade? Domestic vs International

    Trade = exchange of goods or services between two parties for a value. Started as the barter system (goods/services exchanged directly for other goods/services).

    Domestic trade International / cross-border trade
    Scope Within a nation's geographical borders Across borders of countries
    Currency Invoiced in the same currency as the country Invoiced and settled in a freely convertible / major currency — USD, EUR, GBP, JPY
    Importance Boosts consumption and economic growth Lets countries (especially developing ones) compete globally and build strategically important foreign exchange reserves

    Why nations/companies trade: - Market expansion — the primary reason; a significant lever in growth strategy. - Abundant resources vs scarcity — classic case is oil: Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, US, Russia have huge reserves and sell to countries that don't. This is competitive advantage from natural resources. - Tangible vs intangible — tangible = physical goods you can see/hold/weigh; intangible = services, e.g. India's software and services exports.

    Consolidated reasons companies engage in international trade (list-type MCQ): excess production capacity or surplus resources · saturated home market → overseas market expansion · opportunities in foreign markets · change in skill sets and demographics of the population, allowing those skills to be monetised globally.

    4.2Patterns in Trade

    Patterns change as countries' economic or political conditions change — movements can be slow or sudden (an economic or political crisis can change export/import patterns dramatically).

    The general rule: as a country progresses, it pays workers more and the general cost of production rises. Companies staying in the same industry with the same process become uncompetitive → they must constantly improve productivity and lower manufacturing cost. - Example: manufacturing moved from the US and Europe to China because China supplied the same goods far cheaper. - As literacy and skill levels rise, manufacturing moves away from cheap-labour products toward high-value manufacturing (high-tech products) and professional services. - A developing country can attract high-tech manufacturers by improving education and literacy at a low cost base, and its trade pattern shifts from agricultural produce and raw materials to finished high-tech goods. - Blue-collar → white-collar transition within one generation — visible in India, where educated rural youth move to urban areas into IT and Global Capability Centre jobs.

    4.3Factors Influencing International Trade

    Beyond natural competitive advantage, protectionist policies shape trade — to protect local industry, support favoured partners, or punish enemy countries. Three tools: tariffs, trade blocs/FTAs, sanctions.

    Tariffs

    Definition: a tax or duty imposed on imports (occasionally exports) of certain goods.

    Three objectives — memorise: 1. Protect domestic industries — e.g. India taxing cheap Chinese steel so it costs more than domestic steel. 2. Raise government revenue — tariffs go to the government's pocket; before income taxes were widespread, tariffs were often the primary way governments funded budgets. 3. Control the flow of certain goods — prevent the local market being flooded.

    Export tariffs are imposed when there is a shortage in the country — typically on goods critical to the economy: food grains, vegetables, and infrastructure-critical materials like steel and cement.

    Worked example: a 100% import duty on a German luxury car into India doubles its price by the time it reaches the consumer.

    Trade-offs: protects local jobs, but raises consumer prices; for manufacturers relying on imported raw materials, tariffs raise production costs so even local produce becomes costly; and retaliation leads to a trade war where everyone is worse off.

    Real examples: the US–China trade war from 2018 — US tariffs on hundreds of billions of Chinese goods citing unfair trade practices and IP theft; China retaliated on soybeans and automobiles. "What began as a tax tool became a diplomatic weapon." India keeps high import duties on milk and dairy (butter, cheese) to protect local dairy farmers, but reduced tariffs on electronics components to boost Make in India.

    Trade blocs vs Free Trade Agreements — the comparison table is highly testable

    Dimension Trade Bloc Free Trade Agreement (FTA)
    What it is A formal group of countries with common trade policies A treaty between two or more countries to reduce trade barriers
    Scope Broad — may include common tariff, customs union, even shared governance Focused on reducing tariffs and quotas
    Geography Usually regional — EU, ASEAN Bilateral (two countries) or multilateral (more than two/three)
    Integration Much higher — may include political and economic alignment (EU) Much lower — limited to trade in goods/services
    Benefits Deep economic integration, common market access Faster negotiation, flexible, improves ease of export/import
    Drawbacks Complex governance, potential loss of sovereignty Very limited scope; no economic/political integration issues

    Trade bloc examples: EU — allows free trade and free movement of people among member states. ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) — economic integration, less flexible than the EU, many FTAs among members. SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation) — India is a member; considered a trade bloc but not as strong or fully integrated as the EU or ASEAN.

    FTA examples: India–UAE CEPA (eliminates duties on many products); NAFTA (US, Canada, Mexico).

    Brexit is the sovereignty-loss illustration: Britain walked out of the EU partly because people from the rest of Europe were coming in and working, affecting the local population.

    Sanctions

    Definition: prohibitions or restrictions imposed by one country or group of countries on another country, group or individual to influence their behaviour. Imposed for: political, security or human rights reasons. Forms: trade bans, asset freezes, travel restrictions, export/import restrictions.

    Unilateral vs multilateral: - Unilateral — imposed by one country. The key example is OFAC — Office of Foreign Assets Control, a division of the US Department of the Treasury, which administers and enforces economic and trade sanctions based on US foreign policy and national security goals.

    Why OFAC matters globally: the majority of global trade is invoiced in US dollars, so any USD-invoiced trade transaction is automatically subject to OFAC sanctions policies. - Multilateral — imposed by international bodies like the United Nations.

    Examples: US sanctions on Iran (comprehensive — prohibits dealings of any kind; aimed at the nuclear programme); EU sanctions on Russia after the Ukraine invasion; UN and US sanctions on North Korea.

    4.4Key Multilateral Agencies

    Agency Established / HQ Role
    WTO — World Trade Organization 1995 The principal international body regulating global trade between nations. Provides frameworks so trade flows smoothly, predictably and freely. Facilitates trade negotiations, monitors trade policies, and settles disputes through its Dispute Settlement Body
    World Bank — Global financial institution providing funding, knowledge and technical assistance to developing countries to reduce poverty and promote sustainable development. Focus: large-scale infrastructure, education, healthcare, governance reforms. Uses concessional loans, grants, advisory services
    IFC — International Finance Corporation Member of the World Bank Group The private sector arm. Invests in profitable, sustainable private enterprises in developing countries. Provides trade finance, risk mitigation and advisory services, especially to SMEs. Its trade and supply chain finance programmes bridge financing gaps in emerging markets
    ADB — Asian Development Bank HQ Manila, Philippines Regional multilateral development bank for Asia-Pacific. Loans, technical assistance, grants, equity investments for infrastructure, regional connectivity, competitiveness. Its trade and supply chain finance programme supports commercial banks and exporters via guarantees and loans
    ICC — International Chamber of Commerce HQ Paris, France; members from 170+ countries The world business organisation. Makes the rules governing cross-border business conduct and harmonises trade finance products. Runs the ICC International Court of Arbitration to resolve international commercial disputes

    The ICC rulebooks — you must know all of these by number

    Rulebook Full name Governs
    UCP 600 Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits, publication 600 Letters of Credit
    URC 522 Uniform Rules for Collections, publication 522 Documentary collections
    URDG 758 Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees Bank guarantees
    ISP 98 International Standby Practices Standby LCs (alternative to UCP 600)

    These frameworks provide predictability, trust and legal clarity in cross-border trade.

    4.5Parties in an International Trade Transaction

    "International trade is not just a transaction between a buyer and a seller."

    Main parties: exporter/seller · importer/buyer · banks (exporter's bank, importer's bank, and banks clearing funds in foreign currency). Other critical parties: shipping and logistics providers · insurance companies · customs authorities · inspection agencies · chambers of commerce · credit insurers.

    Exporter (seller) — sources or manufactures the product (need not be the manufacturer; often just a trader sourcing from domestic manufacturers), prepares trade documents (commercial invoice, packing list, transport documents), may handle insurance and freight depending on the agreed commercial terms, complies with export regulations, coordinates with banks, logistics partners, inspection agencies.

    Importer (buyer) — places the purchase order, obtains an import licence if required, ensures goods meet regulatory and quality standards, arranges customs clearance at the discharge port, ensures timely payment. Also need not be the end user — often a trading company supplying local companies. Note: many intermediaries between manufacturer and end user add to cost.

    Banks — "it is banks, financial institutions and intermediaries who fuel and accelerate global trade." - Exporter's bank: receives trade instruments like LCs, verifies documentation, may offer pre-shipment or post-shipment credit. - Importer's bank: issues trade instruments such as LCs on the importer's behalf, ensures payment against required documents. - Both act as trusted intermediaries, reducing payment and performance risk.

    Shipping and logistics providers — memorise the modal split:

    Mode Share and character
    Sea ~80% of global trade by volume, ~70% by value. The backbone. Cheaper but slower → ideal for bulk, non-perishable items. Nearly all commodities (oil, gas, food grains) move by sea. Major lines: CMA CGM, Hapag-Lloyd, Maersk, Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC)
    Air Volume far lower, but value share substantial because of the nature of goods — perishables, pharmaceuticals, time-sensitive and high-value goods
    Road Significant in domestic and regional trade; connects inland areas to ports and airports. Less dominant globally due to distance and capacity limits

    They issue bills of lading / airway bills — evidence of shipment, often required for payment processing. Customs brokers secure regulatory clearances and manage duties/taxes. Timely logistics prevents demurrage.

    Chambers of commerce — recognised independent bodies that validate and authenticate trade documents. Most common role: issue or certify the Certificate of Origin (indicating where goods were manufactured, needed for tariff assessment or trade agreement eligibility).
