May also verify commercial invoices and offer dispute resolution, trade promotion and arbitration.

    Credit insurers — Export Credit Agencies (ECAs), development banks (IFC, ADB), and private credit insurers. Provide insurance and guarantees protecting exporters and banks against commercial and political risk; may also offer funding support, risk-sharing structures, technical assistance. Their involvement increases private players' confidence to extend credit or enter new markets.

    4.6Risks in International Trade

    Problem areas for exporters (the underlying causes): - Distance between buyer and seller — transportation takes time and money; mistakes are expensive to correct → prevent misunderstandings while negotiating the contract itself. - Assessing the buyer — both honesty and financial standing. Specific risks: goods retained but not paid for; buyer slow to pay; buyer cannot or will not pay. → the exporter must assess both the ability and the intention to pay. - Efficient resolution of disputes — misunderstandings arise from differences in language, local customs, business practices; disputes must be resolved at a distance, and legal action in the buyer's country is expensive. - Restrictions imposed by overseas governments — country-specific labelling and packaging rules, documentary evidence of compliance with local safety legislation; and shortage of foreign exchange in the buyer's country meaning FX may simply not be available, or payment restrictions are imposed.

    The 10 risk categories — learn the list and the distinctions

    Risk Definition Mitigation
    Commercial risk One party (normally the buyer) fails to meet its contractual obligation, particularly payment — via insolvency, illiquidity or wilful default. Biggest in open account Letters of credit, trade credit insurance, advance payment or secured terms
    Sovereign risk (country/political) Adverse political, economic or regulatory developments in the buyer's country: policy change, expropriation, civil unrest, foreign exchange controls, sanctions, war. Even a willing and able buyer may be unable to pay. Recent examples: Sri Lanka, Argentina restricting foreign payments Political risk insurance, support from ECAs
    Credit risk Broader than commercial risk — the general creditworthiness of the counterparty; probability of default on a financial obligation. Commercial risk is transaction-specific; credit risk is assessed on the buyer's overall financial health, credit history and market reputation Bank assessment before issuing instruments; reflected in pricing and payment terms
    Foreign exchange (FX) risk Exchange rate moves between contract signing and payment Forward contracts, currency options, invoicing in domestic currency (rarely practical)
    Transportation & logistics risk Goods damaged, lost, stolen or delayed — accidents, weather, strikes, port congestion, piracy (Somali pirates) Marine and cargo insurance, careful selection of shipping lines, strong contractual terms
    Legal & regulatory risk Diverse legal systems, differing laws, dispute resolution procedures and interpretations; jurisdiction, contract terms, customs rules, sanctions, AML UCP 600 and Incoterms provide a common language; seek legal counsel
    TBML / fraud risk Using legitimate trade channels to launder illicit money, finance terrorism or commit fraud Robust due diligence, sanctions screening, document verification
    Sanctions risk Knowingly or unknowingly trading with sanctioned individuals, entities, vessels, countries or sectors. Complicated by secondary sanctions and sectoral sanctions Real-time sanctions screening of parties, vessels, goods and documents against global watchlists
    Force majeure / natural disaster Earthquakes, floods, pandemics, geopolitical conflicts — beyond the control of either party; also called "act of God" clauses. They protect parties from liability but do not eliminate the financial impact Contingency planning, risk-sharing mechanisms in contracts
    Technology & cyber risk Hacking, phishing, document tampering, system outages as trade finance digitises Secure IT infrastructure, encryption, multi-layered access control, cyber insurance

    FX worked example — learn the direction of the effect: Indian garment export to Dubai worth USD 1,000. At contract signing USD/INR = 85 → goods worth ₹85,000. One month later the rupee has appreciated to 80 → payment received is worth only ₹80,000 → exporter loses ₹5,000. The reverse benefits an Indian importer, who needs fewer rupees when the rupee appreciates.

    Ever Given (Suez Canal) — one of the world's largest container ships became stuck diagonally across a single-lane section of the Suez Canal after strong winds, halting traffic for hundreds of ships. A 6-day salvage operation with tugboats, dredging vessels and a king tide was needed to refloat it, causing significant delays to global supply chains. COVID-19 is the force majeure example — oil and many commodity prices fell drastically because there was no demand and no means to ship.

    4.7International Trade Documents

    The foundational principle: for banks, regulators and insurers, DOCUMENTS — not the goods themselves — form the basis of decision-making.

    Draft / Bill of Exchange

    Definition: a written unconditional order issued by one party (the DRAWER, typically the exporter) directing another party (the DRAWEE, usually the importer or their bank) to pay a specified sum either on demand or at a fixed future date. A negotiable financial instrument, governed in many jurisdictions by local negotiable instruments laws.

    Party Who Role
    Drawer Exporter Demands the payment
    Drawee Importer or importer's bank Obliged to make the payment

    Two types: - Sight draft — payable immediately upon presentation. - Usance / time / term draft — payable after a specified credit period, e.g. 30 or 60 days after sight, or 30 days after the invoice date or bill of lading date. Gives the buyer an extended credit period; they provide acceptance to pay on a future predetermined date.

    Key features: once accepted by the drawee, it becomes legal evidence of debt and can be discounted by banks if the exporter needs liquidity before maturity. So the bill of exchange functions as a payment instrument, a tool for extending credit, a trade finance instrument, and a means of enforcing obligations.

    Commercial Invoice

    The foundational document. Issued by the exporter, presented to the importer. Acts as the official claim for payment, and encapsulates the full commercial terms.

    Contains: names and addresses of both parties · detailed product description · unit price, quantity · currency of trade · payment terms and where payment should be made (bank account details) · vessel name · port of loading, port of discharge · country of origin · HS code (Harmonized System code).

    Used by: customs to assess duties and taxes (a percentage of invoice value) · banks for documentary compliance and regulatory checks · buyers for accounting and goods reconciliation.

    In an LC transaction, the commercial invoice must match the LC EXACTLY — any discrepancy can result in non-payment. An accepted invoice can also be used by the seller to obtain receivable financing (bank discounts it and pays the seller).

    Packing List

    Invoice = what is being sold and at what price. Packing list = how it is packed. Details: how goods are distributed across shipping units (boxes, pallets, containers, bulk) · type of packaging (wood, cardboard, sacks) · gross weight, net weight, volume · package count · marks and numbers for identification. Unlike the invoice, it normally contains NO pricing details. Used by logistics providers and customs officers to verify physical cargo against declared quantities; on physical inspection at a port it is usually the first document checked; warehouse operators use it to store goods accurately.

    Bill of Lading (B/L) — the most important sea document

    Issued by the shipping line or their agent. Three essential legal functions — memorise: 1. A receipt for the goods shipped 2. A contract of carriage 3. In its negotiable form, a DOCUMENT OF TITLE — whoever holds it can take delivery of / has rightful claim over the goods

    Contains: shipper (the party shipping), consignee (the party goods are consigned to), port of loading, port of discharge, vessel name, voyage number, container numbers, package details, nature and quantity of goods.

    Types: a CLEAN bill of lading confirms cargo was received in apparent good order and condition; a CLAUSED (dirty) bill of lading indicates visible damage or shortfall. In LC transactions, a negotiable B/L lets the bank control the goods until payment is made — the consignee cannot take delivery until the bank releases the original B/L. Misuse or misrepresentation leads to cargo fraud.

    Air Waybill (AWB) — the key contrast with the B/L

    Bill of Lading Air Waybill
    Mode Sea Air
    Negotiability NEGOTIABLE NON-NEGOTIABLE
    Document of title? Yes — represents title to goods No — does NOT represent title
    Release of goods Requires the original B/L Airline releases to the named consignee without requiring the original AWB
    Control over goods Strong Weaker — riskier in terms of control, but much faster

    AWB includes flight numbers, departure/arrival airports, cargo weight, volume, goods details, consignor and consignee. Many LCs still require an AWB. Errors (mismatched weights, wrong consignee) cause customs delays or disputes.

    Certificate of Origin (CO)

    Declares the country in which goods were manufactured, processed or substantially transformed. Usually issued and attested by a chamber of commerce or authorised government body, but not mandatorily so — can be issued by a third party, the manufacturer or the exporter. Why it matters: determines eligibility for preferential tariffs under bilateral/multilateral trade agreements — e.g. under SAFTA, ASEAN or EU GSP schemes, goods with a valid CO may attract lower or zero import duties. Customs use it to verify compliance and impose import restrictions or anti-dumping duties. Two types: PREFERENTIAL (tied to trade agreements) and GENERAL (all other cases). Also used for origin-based restrictions — goods from a sanctioned country may be blocked.

    Insurance document

    Evidence that goods in transit are covered by a valid policy. Covers container losses at sea, fire, piracy, theft, handling damage. Includes: insured party's name · coverage amount · nature of coverage (e.g. all risk, ICC Clauses A / B / C) · voyage details · name of the insurance company and underwriter.

    Under Incoterms CIF or CIP, it is the EXPORTER'S obligation to obtain insurance and submit the insurance document as part of the shipping documents. In LC-backed trade it must comply with UCP 600 — correct beneficiary named, type of coverage shown, appropriately dated.

    Inspection Certificate

    Usually issued by a third-party inspection agency — SGS, Bureau Veritas, Cotecna — confirming goods meet contract specifications. Covers quantity, quality, packaging, labelling, safety compliance. In some jurisdictions pre-shipment inspection is mandatory for high-value or sensitive commodities. Buyers may demand it as a condition of payment, especially with a new or unknown seller. Can be issued by the manufacturer or exporter, but third-party issuance adds validity — it acts as a neutral verification tool.

    Proforma Invoice

    A preliminary document resembling a quotation but with more structure and detail, issued before the formal commercial transaction begins. Outlines product description, quantity, unit price, shipping method, delivery time, Incoterms, validity of the offer, payment terms.

    It is NOT a request for payment and creates NO legal obligation by itself. It lets the buyer begin internal processing — arranging financing, applying for an import licence, seeking approvals. Once accepted it leads to a formal purchase order and sets the baseline for the commercial invoice.

    Customs Declaration

    Required by customs in both the exporting and importing countries before goods cross borders. Includes description of goods, HS codes, invoice value, country of origin, country of destination, tax ID of the importer, applicable duties. Essential for trade data collection, valuation, duty computation, and anti-fraud enforcement.

    Specialised certificates

    Certificate Issued by Purpose
    Phytosanitary certificate The exporting country's authorities Certifies agricultural products (seeds, grains, foods, vegetables) are free from pests, diseases and contaminants. Ensures compliance with international plant health standards; protects the importing country's ecosystems. Without it: delays, rejection or destruction at the port of entry
    Fumigation certificate A licensed pest control agency Confirms goods (agricultural products, wooden packaging, containerised cargo) have been treated with fumigants. Specifies the type of fumigant (e.g. methyl bromide), dosage, exposure time, treatment temperature, date and place. Mandatory for countries with strict quarantine regulations; addresses biosecurity risk
    Health certificate A government-approved health or food safety authority Certifies a food or animal-origin product is safe, hygienically processed and fit for human consumption. For meat, dairy, seafood, processed foods. Includes product, origin, producer, date of inspection, compliance confirmation
    Halal certificate — A variation of the health certificate — certifies compliance with Islamic dietary laws. Important for exports to the Middle East and Southeast Asia
    Export licence (strategic export control) Designated regulatory bodies — in India DGFT, DRDO Government authorisation for goods, technologies or software with potential military applications or DUAL-USE functionality (both civilian and military). Covers advanced electronics, radar, surveillance equipment, aerospace components, nuclear materials, encrypted communications, many chemicals. Needed for compliance with arms control agreements, non-proliferation treaties, national security regulations. Applicants provide details of end use, end user and destination. Failure → penalties, shipment seizures, reputational damage

    Other transport documents

    Document Mode
    CMR consignment note Road transport in Europe under the CMR Convention — outlines carrier liability and cargo details
    Railway consignment note Rail, particularly domestic/regional corridors (widely used in India)
    Multimodal / combined transport document When goods move by more than one mode — e.g. rail from interior India to the port, then by vessel
    Truck receipt Road shipment

    4.8SWIFT

    SWIFT = Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication.

    The single most important point: SWIFT is NOT a payment system. SWIFT does not move money — it gives instructions to move money. Think of it as "the email service of the global banking world", except every message is heavily standardised, encrypted and verified.

    Governance and scale: - Owned and governed by its member institutions — no single owner. Over 11,000 financial institutions across 200+ countries. - Headquartered in Belgium, overseen by the National Bank of Belgium along with other central banks — the US Federal Reserve, ECB, Bank of England, Bank of Japan, Swiss National Bank. A cooperative, but heavily influenced by leading central banks → neutrality and credibility. - Founded in 1973 by a group of major banks. Before SWIFT, banks used TELEX — no standard format, no verification tools, high risk of errors and fraud. Goals: security, reliability, standardisation. - Today SWIFT sends over 45 million messages every day.

    Five key roles: secure communication (encrypted and authenticated) · standardisation (a message type means the same in India as in Italy) · speed and reliability (delivered in seconds) · audit trail (every transaction logged and traceable — who initiated, who received, when) · global reach.

    BIC / SWIFT address structure — exam-critical

    BIC = Bank Identifier Code. "The international email address for a bank." 8 or 11 characters, in four parts:

    Part Length Content Mandatory?
    1. Bank code 4 letters Abbreviation of the bank's name — ICIC (ICICI), HDFC, CITI Mandatory
    2. Country code 2 letters ISO country code — IN (India), SG (Singapore), US Mandatory
    3. Location code 2 alphanumeric City/location of the head office — NY (Citibank New York), BB (ICICI Mumbai) Mandatory
    4. Branch code 3 alphanumeric Branch OPTIONAL — this is why a BIC is 8 or 11 characters

    A small typo in a BIC can delay or misroute a payment, just like a wrong email address.

    SWIFT message types (MTs) — memorise these

    MT Purpose
    MT 700 Issuance of a documentary credit (LC) — issuing bank → advising bank
    MT 707 Amendment to a documentary credit
    MT 734 Advice of refusal — sent by the issuing bank to the negotiating bank when documents contain discrepancies
    MT 400 Advice of payment in collections
    MT 410 Acknowledgement of collection
    MT 103 Customer credit transfer — a corporate-to-corporate payment (buyer's account → seller's account). Used in advance payment and open account trade, but used across all of banking, not just trade
    MT 202 Bank-to-bank fund transfer — no corporate involved
    MT 760 Issuing a guarantee or standby LC

    Message families: MT 7xx = documentary credits · MT 4xx = collections · MT 1xx = customer transfers · MT 2xx = financial institution transfers. MT 103 vs MT 202 is the classic trap: 103 = customer/corporate credit transfer; 202 = bank-to-bank.

    Alternatives to SWIFT

    • Bank proprietary networks — secure but very limited reach.
    • CIPS — China's Cross-border Interbank Payment System, a SWIFT-like platform launched by China for RMB (renminbi) transactions, often used by Belt and Road countries.
    • SPFS — Russia's financial messaging system, developed after Russia faced SWIFT sanctions in 2014.
    • APIs and fintech messaging platforms.

      None have matched SWIFT's standardisation, neutrality and global scale.

    SWIFT's own evolution: SWIFT gpi (Global Payments Innovation) and the transition to ISO 20022 message formats for richer, more structured data.

    4.9Payment Methods — the Risk Spectrum1

    Four settlement methods: open account · advance payment · documentary collections · letters of credit.

    The risk spectrum (know both ends): Open account = MOST risky for the EXPORTER, most favourable for the IMPORTER. Advance payment = MOST secure for the EXPORTER, least attractive/most risky for the IMPORTER. Documentary collections = moderate control but NO payment guarantee. Letters of credit = balanced structure backed by banks, but higher cost and documentation.

    Open Account

    Definition: the importer receives the goods first and pays at a later date — commonly 30, 60 or 90 days as per contract.

    Flow: sign contract → exporter ships goods → exporter sends documents DIRECTLY to the importer (NO bank involvement) → importer uses documents to clear goods from the discharge port → importer pays (immediately or after the agreed credit period).

    The biggest risk is at the final stage — delayed or no payment.

    Advantages for the importer: no advance payment or bank guarantee upfront · payment deferred, so they can receive, inspect and even resell the goods before paying · optimises working capital, manages inventory, reduces reliance on external finance. In competitive markets (electronics, garments, commodity exports) buyers often demand open account terms as a condition of doing business.

    Risk for the exporter: bears the entire credit and political risk; no guarantee of payment; buyer insolvency, currency restrictions or political upheaval can cause severe loss; without a third-party bank holding the shipping documents, the exporter has NO control over the goods once shipped.

    Why exporters still accept it: to stay competitive and retain key clients; for long-term relationships with reputable buyers (large retailers) the commercial upside outweighs the risk; it expedites shipping and documentation, reduces bank fees and improves transaction speed.

    General principle stated here: the more intermediaries (banks) you add, the higher the transaction cost and the slower the transaction. Open account has the maximum transaction speed.

    Risk mitigation in open account: trade credit insurance (from agencies like ECGC or private insurers) covering both commercial risk (buyer default) and political risk · a standby letter of credit as a payment guarantee · factoring (selling receivables to a bank at a discount) · credit checks, financial due diligence, setting credit limits per buyer.

    Global trend: open account is growing in popularity with integrated, digitally-enabled supply chains; fintechs and banks offer automated credit checks, digital invoice financing, and blockchain-based settlement layers.

    Advance Payment

    Definition: the importer pays first (in full or in part), and only after receiving the funds does the exporter manufacture, assemble or ship the goods. No bank or third party holds documents or funds during the transaction — the entire trust rests on the exporter's ability and willingness to perform.

    Exporter benefits: immediate liquidity · eliminates payment default risk · funds production, raw materials, logistics without tapping a credit line · reduced administrative complexity (no banks managing documents).

    Importer's position: least desirable — ties up working capital before receiving goods, with no assurance goods will be delivered on time or as agreed; risk of fraud or non-performance, especially with unverified suppliers; recovery is difficult or impossible across borders.

    Importer's mitigations: supplier due diligence · requesting trade references · escrow services · partial payments tied to project milestones · performance guarantees · export credit insurance · certifications from export promotion agencies. These are not always sufficient in regions with weak legal enforcement.

    Typical use cases: customised / made-to-order / high-demand goods where the seller holds a strategic advantage — the example given is NVIDIA chips (a seller's market) · certain commodity trades · government-to-government contracts · project-based exports · first-time buyer relationships · cross-border e-commerce for low-value shipments where LCs or collections are impractical.

    Digital shift: platforms like Alibaba, Amazon, eBay, PayPal facilitate advance payments in global retail trade — but this convenience doesn't eliminate risk; digital payments are now subject to KYC checks, fraud monitoring and dispute resolution protocols.

    Documentary Collections

    Definition: the exporter ships goods and entrusts their bank to forward the trade documents to the buyer's bank, instructing that bank to release documents to the buyer only against payment or acceptance of a draft.

    Critical distinction from an LC: the banks involved undertake NO PAYMENT OBLIGATION. They act only as intermediaries handling documents and instructions.

    The four parties — memorise the terminology:

    Party Who Role
    Drawer Exporter Ships goods, prepares documents, draws the bill of exchange on the drawee, initiates the collection through their bank
    Drawee Importer The party on whom the bill of exchange is drawn; must pay or accept to gain access to the shipping documents
    Remitting bank Exporter's bank Receives documents and collection instructions from the exporter; sends them to the presenting bank; follows up for payment. Acts purely on the exporter's instructions
    Presenting bank Importer's bank Receives documents from the remitting bank and presents them to the drawee. Acts purely on the remitting bank's instructions; releases documents only against payment or acceptance

    Governing rules: URC 522 (Uniform Rules for Collections, ICC). It sets international best practice for how remitting and presenting banks operate; clarifies that banks act only as intermediaries with NO obligation to inspect the goods, verify document content, or guarantee payment; defines the responsibilities of drawer and drawee; defines DP and DA; specifies timelines and the procedure in case of dishonour (the drawee refuses to pay or accept). URC does not override national laws — it provides a globally accepted standard reducing ambiguity.

    Process: exporter ships and gathers documents (invoice, packing list, B/L, certificate of origin, and the bill of exchange — the bill of exchange is not mandatory in collections but has a role depending on terms) → submits them with collection instructions to the remitting bank → remitting bank does preliminary checks (sanctioned entities, money laundering risk — mandated by local regulators) → forwards documents to the presenting bank on its own letterhead with a collection order / collection schedule stating all conditions → presenting bank contacts the drawee and presents documents → drawee pays (DP) or accepts (DA) → only then does the presenting bank release the shipping documents → payment or acceptance advice flows back to the remitting bank → exporter.

    DP vs DA — guaranteed MCQ

    DP — Documents against Payment (delivery against payment) DA — Documents against Acceptance (delivery against acceptance)
    What the importer must do Make full payment Accept a time (usance) draft — sign it, creating a legal obligation to pay on the due date
    When goods are released After payment After acceptance, before payment
    Timing Immediate 30/60/90 days after sight, B/L date or invoice date
    Exporter's position More favourable — maintains constructive control over the goods until funds are secured Riskier — the importer gets control of the shipment without paying upfront; if they default at maturity, recovery is difficult cross-border
    Importer's position Must fund immediately More flexible — gets a credit period
    Suitable when Moderate risk; goods not easily perishable or custom-made Higher trust; established relationships

    If the importer refuses to pay under DP, the exporter bears the cost and hassle of redirecting, storing or reselling the shipment.

    Why exporters use collections: moderate trust in the buyer but still want leverage over release of goods; cost-effective versus LCs; useful in established relationships, low-risk jurisdictions, or medium-sized deals that don't justify the cost of an LC. Why importers prefer them: flexibility, lower cost, no need to reserve funds or secure a credit facility as with LCs; they see the documents before paying or accepting. Key limitation: no payment assurance; banks are under no obligation to verify authenticity of documents or goods; disputes depend on slow, costly jurisdictional legal processes.

    4.10Letters of Credit

    Definition: an IRREVOCABLE commitment by a bank on behalf of a buyer (the APPLICANT) to pay the seller (the BENEFICIARY), provided the seller presents documents that strictly comply with the LC conditions.

    The fundamental principle: BANKS DEAL IN DOCUMENTS, NOT GOODS. The bank pays based solely on documentation, not on the trust or the actual condition of the goods.

    Irrevocability: once issued, an LC cannot be amended or cancelled without the explicit agreement of ALL parties — the issuing bank, the beneficiary and the applicant. This eliminates the risk of unilateral change or withdrawal by the buyer.

    Under UCP 600, ALL letters of credit are deemed IRREVOCABLE unless clearly stated otherwise.

    The parties to an LC — learn every role

    Party Who Role
    Applicant Buyer / importer Initiates the LC; requests their bank to issue it; defines the terms and conditions under which they will pay. Legally obliged to reimburse the issuing bank once terms are fulfilled. Does not pay the exporter directly
    Beneficiary Seller / exporter Receives payment provided documents are fully compliant — every term, condition and timeline precisely followed, within the stipulated timelines
    Issuing bank Applicant's bank Issues the LC; undertakes the obligation to pay the exporter on the importer's behalf; checks the documents on receipt; pays the exporter's bank; releases documents to the importer. Its commitment is valid only if documents comply
    Advising bank Usually in the exporter's country Receives the LC from the issuing bank and authenticates it — its primary responsibility is to ensure the LC is GENUINE and not fraudulent. Takes no payment obligation
    Nominated / negotiating bank Exporter's bank, designated in the LC Examines documents and, in case of negotiation, advances funds to the exporter. Often the same as the advising bank, but not necessarily. Forwards documents to the issuing bank and claims reimbursement. Under UCP 600 it MAY advance funds to the beneficiary BEFORE receiving funds from the issuing bank
    Confirming bank Usually in the beneficiary's country Adds its OWN irrevocable payment guarantee on top of the issuing bank's — based on authorisation from the issuing bank

    Why confirmation matters: used when the exporter is unsure of the issuing bank's standing — a bank from a country with low credit ratings or political turmoil. A confirmed LC gives the exporter DUAL security from both the issuing and confirming banks. Confirming banks charge a fee based on the risk profile of the issuing bank and country.

    UCP 600

    Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits, issued by the ICC — the de facto rulebook for letters of credit. It: - Standardises terminology, procedures and obligations across jurisdictions. - Defines terms like honour, negotiation, complying presentation. - Stipulates 5 banking days for examination of documents. ← memorise this number. - Emphasises that banks are not responsible for the goods, only for verifying documentation. - Sets rules for discrepancies, partial shipments, expiry dates and place of presentation.

    The LC process — step by step

    1. Buyer and seller agree on an LC as the mode of payment in the contract.
    2. Buyer requests the issuing bank to issue the LC in favour of the seller.
    3. LC transmitted via SWIFT (MT 700) to the advising bank, which authenticates and forwards it to the exporter.
    4. Exporter reviews the LC terms; if acceptable, ships the goods and prepares required documents.
    5. Exporter presents documents to the nominated/negotiating bank, which checks compliance and pays or commits to pay at a future date.
    6. Documents forwarded to the issuing bank for final examination and payment.
    7. Issuing bank delivers documents to the importer, who clears the goods at the destination port.
    8. Importer pays the issuing bank per LC terms — immediately or on a future date; or the importer can request the issuing bank to finance the documents, giving them a credit period.

    The LC terms and conditions should ideally be a SUBSET of the sales contract between buyer and seller.

    The four LC availability types — the single most important table in this course

    Available by PAYMENT (sight LC) Available by NEGOTIATION Available by ACCEPTANCE Available by DEFERRED PAYMENT
    When paid Immediately at sight — usually within 1–2 working days of compliant presentation On or BEFORE the due date On the maturity of the accepted draft On the due date
    Bill of exchange Usually none — beneficiary is not required to draw one OPTIONAL — may or may not be present MANDATORY — a time/usance draft drawn on and accepted by the nominated or issuing bank NONE
    Bank's undertaking Definite obligation to pay The bank MAY negotiate — it has DISCRETION and is NOT obliged unless it has added its confirmation The bank ACCEPTS the bill of exchange, creating a legally binding obligation to pay at maturity The bank issues a DPU — Deferred Payment Undertaking, an irrevocable promise to pay on the agreed date
    Recourse on the nominated bank's payment — Normally WITH RECOURSE, unless the negotiating bank is also the confirming bank or there is an explicit agreement WITHOUT recourse once the draft is accepted WITHOUT recourse
    Early liquidity for exporter Immediate by definition Yes — by negotiation, subject to the negotiating bank's approval Yes — discount the accepted draft (primary or secondary market) Yes — discount the deferred payment undertaking
    When used Exporter needs prompt funds; new buyer-seller relationships, high-risk markets, time-sensitive goods Exporter wants early payment and flexibility to choose among banks Buyer wants deferred terms and a bill of exchange is preferred or required by local law Buyer wants deferred terms with simplicity — no bill of exchange, and avoids stamp duty

    Document compliance is mandatory in all four.

    Negotiation, defined under UCP 600 Article 2: the purchase by the nominated bank of drafts drawn on a bank other than the nominated bank, and/or documents under a complying presentation, by advancing or agreeing to advance funds to the beneficiary.

    With recourse vs without recourse — memorise: - WITH recourse: if the issuing bank doesn't pay for any reason, the negotiating bank can go back to the beneficiary and reclaim the money. - WITHOUT recourse: once paid, the negotiating bank cannot reclaim the money from the beneficiary, whatever happens. Banks negotiating without recourse must rely entirely on the issuing bank's creditworthiness and their own accuracy of document examination.

    The risk: if a nominated bank negotiates and the documents turn out to be discrepant, the issuing bank may refuse to reimburse.

    Payment LC advantages: for the exporter — immediate payment, better liquidity, no draft to handle, reduced reliance on the importer's creditworthiness (payment guaranteed by the issuing bank). For the importer — payment only after shipment with clean documents, establishes credibility with new suppliers, and can negotiate a price discount in return for prompt payment.

    Acceptance LC considerations: (a) the accepted draft can be discounted before maturity for early liquidity, at a cost (discount interest); (b) STAMP DUTY — in many jurisdictions a draft must be stamped to be legally valid in a dispute, and the duty is usually calculated on the face value of the draft, so a higher draft value means higher duty. This is a key reason to prefer a deferred payment LC over an acceptance LC.

    Deferred payment LC — key exporter risks: the exporter bears the BANK credit risk during the deferred period; if confirmation is not added, the exporter must trust the issuing bank's ability to pay and be mindful of country risk; and not all banks are willing to discount a deferred payment undertaking, limiting the ability to get funds early.

    Worked examples: Indian exporter selling rubber to a Japanese buyer under an LC available by acceptance, draft drawn on the issuing bank at 90 days after B/L. Indian machinery manufacturer exporting to an Egyptian construction firm under a 90-day deferred payment LC advised through a major Indian bank. Bengaluru textile exporter with an LC from a French buyer available by negotiation with ANY bank — so their own (unnamed) bank can negotiate and pay upfront.

    4.11Guarantees and Standby LCs1

    Bank Guarantee

    Definition: a written promise, usually by a bank, on behalf of a customer, that "if my customer doesn't do what they promised, I will step in and pay you." - Only triggered if something goes wrong — a breach of contract or failure to perform. Not to be used casually. - Crucially: a guarantee is a SEPARATE, INDEPENDENT undertaking from the underlying contract. Even though it refers to the contract, it stands on its own — the guarantor will pay the beneficiary on a valid claim EVEN IF a dispute is ongoing between the two parties.

    Three parties:

    Party Also called Role
    Applicant Principal Requests the guarantee; usually the buyer, contractor or supplier — the party whose performance or payment is being guaranteed
    Issuing bank Guarantor Issues the guarantee and takes on the financial obligation. Assesses the applicant's financial strength, usually requires collateral or a credit limit, and charges a fee based on the guarantee amount and tenure
    Beneficiary — The party in whose favour it is issued — the party who stands to lose if the applicant does not perform

    Standby Letter of Credit (SBLC)

    A promise from a bank to pay, very similar to a guarantee but structured like an LC, governed by UCP 600 or ISP 98.

    "A standby LC is like a safety parachute." It is not meant to be used unless something goes wrong. Documented and handled more formally than a guarantee — standard clauses, presentation period, expiry dates, documentary terms. Popular in cross-border trade because internationally accepted frameworks make them legally enforceable and easier to rely on across different legal systems.

    Guarantee vs SBLC — the comparison table

    Dimension Bank Guarantee Standby LC
    Purpose Financial assurance for performance or payment Backup commitment — same purpose
    Trigger Applicant defaults / fails to perform Same
    Governing rules URDG 758 or local law UCP 600 or ISP 98 or local law
    Structure Simple letter format, varies by bank and country Structured like a letter of credit — MT 700 or MT 760
    Typical types Performance guarantee, bid bond, advance payment guarantee Payment standby, performance standby, financial standby
    Acceptance Well accepted in Europe, Asia, Middle East Globally accepted, especially in the United States
    US law May NOT be recognised under US banking law Preferred and enforceable under US law
    Invocation Written demand, sometimes with proof of default Written demand plus presentation of documents — e.g. an unpaid invoice or bill of lading
    Formality More text-driven, less formal More standardised format and rules
    Bank's role Independent obligation Independent obligation

    Both are SECONDARY instruments — they let the beneficiary claim money directly from the bank without chasing the applicant or going through lengthy legal dispute. (Note: guarantees need not be issued by a bank — even individuals can issue them — but commercially, corporates normally accept bank guarantees.)

    Financial vs Performance guarantees — the classification MCQ

    The simple test: what is the underlying event that triggers the claim? If the applicant DIDN'T PAY what they owed → FINANCIAL standby. If the applicant DIDN'T DO what they said → PERFORMANCE standby.

    Financial guarantee / standby Performance guarantee / standby
    Guarantees A monetary payment obligation Doing — completing a task/project, meeting quality, time or technical commitments
    Trigger examples Non-payment of an invoice · failure to repay a loan · missed lease or rental payments Failure to complete a project on time (a bridge 3 months late → delay penalties) · defective goods (3 of the transformers faulty on testing) · non-delivery or partial fulfilment (100 units promised, 50 delivered)
    Keywords in the wording payment obligation, invoice default, repayment, monetary value completion of works, delivery deadlines, technical specs
    Credit risk to the bank Higher — the bank is likely to pay the full amount Lower — more discretion; claims are often smaller or more conditional
    Regulatory/capital treatment Under Basel norms, closer to credit substitutes → may require higher capital provisioning May remain off balance sheet until triggered

    Direct vs Indirect guarantees

    Direct guarantee Indirect guarantee
    Structure Issued directly by the applicant's bank in favour of the beneficiary — one-to-one, no bank in between The applicant's bank issues a COUNTER-GUARANTEE to a local bank in the beneficiary's country, and that local bank issues the actual guarantee to the beneficiary — TWO independent instruments
    Example Indian construction company contracting with the Government of India; SBI issues a direct performance guarantee to the GoI German engineering firm supplying an Indian defence manufacturer that will only accept a guarantee from an Indian bank; Commerzbank issues a counter-guarantee favouring SBI, and SBI issues the local guarantee to the Indian buyer
    Typical use Most domestic/inland guarantees, where applicant, issuing bank and beneficiary are all in the same country. Also covers the case where the issuing bank sends the guarantee to the beneficiary's bank as advising bank (which takes no obligation) When the beneficiary insists on a local guarantor for legal, regulatory or risk-based reasons
    Beneficiary comfort Must be comfortable dealing with a foreign bank Gets a document from a domestic, familiar bank, in their own language and legal format
    Legal jurisdiction Disputes may fall under foreign jurisdiction The final guarantee is issued under local law, making enforcement easier
    Cost and complexity Simpler and cheaper More expensive and complex — one more bank means more fees
    Risk for the final issuer — The local issuing bank takes ZERO applicant risk — it relies fully on the counter-guarantee; its only concern is whether the applicant's bank will honour it

    Commercial LC vs Guarantee/SBLC — the three-way comparison

    Dimension Commercial LC Guarantee / Standby LC
    Function A PRIMARY payment mechanism — meant to facilitate the actual trade payment A SECONDARY instrument — a backup, only used if something goes wrong
    Trigger The seller ships the goods and presents complying documents The applicant FAILS to pay, deliver or perform
    Documents required Draft, invoice, transport document, packing list, certificate of origin, insurance document A simple statement of default or non-performance, sometimes with supporting proof (unpaid invoice, bill of lading)
    Governing rules UCP 600 Guarantees: URDG 758 or local law. SBLC: UCP 600 or ISP 98 or local law
    Legal nature Primary undertaking Secondary obligation
    Geography Widely used across all geographies Guarantees common in Europe, Middle East, Asia; in the US, standby LCs are preferred
    Risk covered Payment risk Broader — non-payment, non-performance, default on advance payment, breach of contract
    Typical setting Trade transactions Contractual performance scenarios — construction, infrastructure projects, financial undertakings

    Types of guarantees — know the trigger and typical percentage

    Type Also called What it covers Typical size
    Bid bond Tender guarantee Used at the very beginning when companies submit bids for large projects. If the bidder is awarded the contract but backs out, the tendering authority claims. Acts as a deterrent against frivolous bidding 2–5% of the bid value
    Performance guarantee — Once the project is awarded — ensures the contractor delivers on time and to specification. Covers failure to meet milestones, abandoning the site, faulty installation. Siemens installing wind turbines for an Indian power project ~10% of contract value (₹10 mn on a $100 mn contract)
    Advance payment guarantee — Protects the buyer who has paid an upfront mobilisation amount (e.g. 20% of project value). If the contractor takes the money and doesn't start work, the advance is refunded. Ensures public money is protected until work actually starts Tied to the advance
    Retention money guarantee — Contracts normally hold back 5–10% of total payment as retention money, released only after final inspection and the defect liability period. A retention money guarantee is given in lieu of the cash holdback so the contractor gets full payment early. (Indian firm building a highway in Kenya avoids waiting 6 months) 5–10%
    Payment guarantee — The most straightforward financial guarantee — ensures the seller is paid even if the buyer defaults. Common in bulk commodity trades, capital equipment supply, leasing contracts Contract value
    Lease guarantee — Bank pays the landlord if the tenant defaults on rent or other lease obligations. Used in commercial office leasing, equipment/aircraft leasing, retail and warehouse rentals. Replaces a massive security deposit — landlord gets peace of mind, tenant preserves cash flow. From the bank's view it is contingent, but exposure runs over several years, so it is carefully underwritten with margin/collateral e.g. 6 months of rent
    Bond repayment guarantee — A bank or multilateral agency promises to pay bondholders if the issuer fails to pay interest or principal. Improves the credit rating of the bond, lowers the interest rate, and makes the issue attractive to institutional investors. An Indian state raising a 10-year infrastructure bond for a water treatment plant secures a credit guarantee from the ADB covering 80% of interest and principal; the bond gets a higher rating and becomes attractive to pension funds and insurance companies Partial (e.g. 80%)

    4.12Supply Chain Finance (SCF)

    A supply chain = the entire network of individuals, companies, resources and activities involved in producing and delivering a product from raw material to final customer. "Like a relay race." Example chain: supplier (textile mill) → manufacturer (garments) → distributor → retailer → end customer. Each step involves procurement, production/assembly, transportation and logistics, warehousing, inventory management, sales, after-sale service. It applies to services too (software, consulting) — just without trucks and warehouses.

    Why financing is needed: goods move quickly, payments don't. Large buyers (MNCs) negotiate longer payment terms to improve their own working capital while expecting uninterrupted supply.

    The core tension: the SUPPLIER wants funds as early as possible; the BUYER wants to delay payment as long as possible. That gap is the financing gap. Example: Maruti sources axles, brakes, wheels, nuts and bolts from small SME suppliers who lack bargaining power and must accept 30/60/90-day terms. Distributors need loans to buy stock in bulk; retailers need credit to keep shelves full; manufacturers need funding to bridge the production cycle. Cross-border shipments, customs procedures and currency fluctuations add further delay and uncertainty.

    Payables vs receivables: - Payables = amounts a business owes to others, usually suppliers, for goods/services received. - Receivables = amounts a business is entitled to receive, usually from customers who bought on credit.

    Definition of SCF: a set of technology-driven financing solutions that optimise working capital for BOTH buyers and suppliers. Suppliers receive early payment, often at a lower cost of credit; buyers extend payment terms without damaging supplier relationships.

    KEY: SCF is NOT a loan in the traditional sense. It is a collaborative financing model that leverages the BUYER'S STRONGER CREDIT RATING to help the supplier access cheaper liquidity. SCF is also called reverse factoring.

    Payables finance (reverse factoring) vs Receivables finance

    Dimension Payables finance Receivables finance
    Initiated by The BUYER (a large corporate) The SUPPLIER
    Buyer participation Always required Optional
    Credit risk sits on The BUYER Primarily the buyer, but can also be on the supplier depending on the programme structure
    Cost of financing Lower — the financier takes exposure on the large corporate Higher — the risk is mostly on the supplier, a smaller entity with a lower credit rating
    Who benefits most Both — buyer gets a higher DPO, supplier gets liquidity Mostly the supplier (immediate payment); the buyer benefits indirectly
    Best for Strategic long-term supplier relationships — one large buyer funding many small suppliers Fragmented supply base or unstructured buyers
    Payment flow Buyer pays the financier directly Buyer may or may not pay the financier; often pays the supplier

    Payables finance flow: supplier ships goods → submits invoice to buyer → buyer APPROVES the invoice → the financing partner offers the supplier early payment at a preferential rate based on the BUYER'S creditworthiness.

    Types of payables finance: 1. Standard payables financing / reverse factoring — the classic structure. 2. Dynamic discounting — the BUYER, not a bank, pays early directly to the supplier in return for a discount. NO third-party financing involved. ← a favourite distinction question. 3. Approved payables finance via fintech platforms — e.g. Taulia, PrimeRevenue, linking multiple suppliers and banks in a tech-enabled ecosystem.

    Parties in payables finance: the buyer / ANCHOR CLIENT (the large corporate who initiates the programme and approves invoices) · the supplier · the financier (bank or fintech, taking credit risk on the buyer) · the platform provider (optional — hosts the interface and connects the parties).

    Benefits of payables finance: - Buyer: extends payment terms without harming supplier relationships; improves DPO; strengthens supply chain resilience and supplier loyalty. - Supplier: faster liquidity at lower cost; improves DSO; avoids taking debt onto their own books — no debt on the balance sheet. - Bank: low-risk lending tied to the buyer's credit profile, and recurring flow-based business.

    DPO and DSO — memorise the formulas and directions

    Metric Formula High means Good for whom
    DPO — Days Payable Outstanding: how long a company takes to pay its suppliers (Accounts Payable ÷ COGS) × 365 Taking longer to pay — improves cash flow but may strain supplier relationships A high DPO is GOOD for the BUYER
    DSO — Days Sales Outstanding (days receivable outstanding): how long it takes to collect from customers (Accounts Receivable ÷ Total Credit Sales) × 365 Taking longer to collect — indicates poor cash flow or lenient credit terms A high DSO is BAD for the SUPPLIER

    Worked examples: AP ₹3 crore, COGS ₹36 crore → DPO = 3/36 × 365 = 30.4 days. AR ₹5 crore, credit sales ₹60 crore → DSO = 5/60 × 365 = 30 days.

    Payables finance case study — Walmart / Indian garment supplier / Citibank

    • Indian supplier ships shirts and invoices Walmart for $500,000.
    • Walmart approves the invoice within 5 days; payment due after 60 days.
    • Citibank, the SCF financier, offers early payment at 1.2%.
    • Supplier opts in and receives $494,000 — the $6,000 is Citibank's interest.
    • Walmart repays $500,000 to Citibank on the due date. Outcome: supplier meets cash obligations without waiting; Walmart still holds its cash to the due date; Citibank earns $6,000 by taking exposure on Walmart, not on the small Indian supplier.

    Types of receivables finance

    Type Mechanism
    Invoice discounting Supplier gets a loan/advance secured against outstanding invoices. The supplier remains responsible for collecting payment
    Factoring (with or without recourse) The financier PURCHASES the receivables and assumes responsibility for collection — the financier goes to the buyer to collect. In NON-RECOURSE factoring the financier also assumes the CREDIT RISK, taking exposure on the buyer
    Export factoring Designed for international trade; may involve credit insurance and cross-border risk sharing

    Parties in receivables finance: supplier (initiates; sells or pledges receivables) · financier / factor · buyer / debtor (obliged to pay the invoice) · credit insurer (optional) — involved in international or non-recourse factoring. Benefits: supplier improves liquidity without increasing debt, supports operational continuity, offloads credit and collection risk in some cases. Buyers continue normal terms without pressure for early payment. Financiers get risk-priced lending collateralised by trade receivables and can build SME/export-focused portfolios.

    Receivables finance case study — Vietnamese furniture exporter / Walmart No SCF programme exists from Walmart's side; the exporter needs working capital within 10 days of shipment to pay wages and local suppliers. - Exporter ships and invoices Walmart for $75,000. - Approaches a local Vietnamese bank with the invoice plus Walmart's payment history. - Bank finances 85% of invoice value = $63,750. (Note: in receivables financing, banks typically fund only 85–90%, not the full amount.) - On day 90 Walmart pays the bank directly; the bank then pays the supplier the balance less interest and fees.

    Why SCF is displacing traditional instruments

    Modern trade has speed, scale and complexity: sourcing from many countries, thousands of suppliers, razor-thin margins. - LCs: strict rules, significant paperwork, long processing cycles (more intermediaries = more delay); for SMEs too slow, complex and costly; for buyers they lock up credit lines and working capital. - Documentary collections: simpler but still involve banks as intermediaries, require document verification, and offer limited protection if the buyer refuses to pay.

    SCF instead is: digitally driven (real-time visibility of invoices, payment statuses, transaction flows) · credit efficient (buyers support suppliers without tying up their own cash) · scalable (onboard hundreds of suppliers across countries into one ecosystem) · inclusive (small suppliers get cheaper credit even with weak balance sheets, because financing is backed by the large buyer's credit profile).

    The verdict: "faster than a letter of credit, safer than an open account, and more adaptive than documentary collections." It is not replacing traditional tools but complementing them, especially for recurring, high-volume transactions between trusted partners.

    The future of SCF: digitisation (integration with ERP systems, e-invoicing tools, blockchain-based trade networks) · regulatory and institutional support (ICC and multilateral development banks like ADB backing SCF for SMEs) · new models (risk scoring, tokenised receivables, dynamic discounting engines) · sustainability — ESG-linked SCF, with financing rates potentially linked to carbon footprints, labour practices, circular economy metrics · greater platformisation with embedded finance in procurement and trade systems · more non-bank financiers and institutional investors · enhanced cross-border interoperability.

    4.13Structured Trade Finance (STF)

    Also called Structured Trade and Commodity Finance — for commodities: oil, metals, minerals, iron ore, and agricultural produce such as coffee, cocoa, soybean, corn.

    Core distinction: unlike traditional trade finance which relies on the buyer's or seller's balance sheet strength, STF focuses on the TRANSACTION ITSELF — the bank asks "will this deal produce enough revenue to repay the loan?" and structures the financing around those cash flows, secured with collateral. Layers of protection may include export credit agencies, insurance policies, and hedging tools against currency swings, price volatility and political risk.

    STF is about enabling trade that might not happen otherwise — widely used in emerging markets where financing options are limited and risks are higher.

    The six STF products — learn each with its example

    Product How it works Example
    1. Pre-export financing Funds provided BEFORE the goods are shipped, structured around the confirmed export contract and secured against the future sale proceeds. The buyer's payment is often routed directly to the financier Ghanaian cocoa exporter with a contract to deliver 10,000 tons to a Swiss chocolate manufacturer needs capital to pay local farmers, arrange logistics and cover port fees. In oil, crude exporters use pre-export facilities with repayments from oil sale proceeds deposited into offshore accounts controlled by the lenders
    2. Prepayment finance The BUYER advances funds to the seller before delivery (or arranges a bank to finance it). The seller uses the funds to produce/source goods and commits to deliver over an extended period, often multiple years Energy trading — large oil companies prepay national oil companies billions of dollars to secure multi-year crude supplies. Buyers secure critical supply and may negotiate discounts; sellers gain liquidity
    3. Borrowing base facilities Revolving credit where the amount borrowable depends on the value of eligible assets — inventory in storage, goods in transit, receivables. Banks regularly monitor and RECALCULATE the borrowing base: if oil prices rise the company can borrow more; if they fall, capacity shrinks Global trading houses like Glencore or Trafigura
    4. Warehouse / inventory financing The stored goods themselves are the collateral. The bank secures the loan against WAREHOUSE RECEIPTS — documents proving ownership of stored goods. Control over the warehouse may be handed to a trusted third party, the COLLATERAL MANAGER, to ensure goods aren't moved without lender consent Ukrainian grain trader with wheat in a bonded warehouse near the Black Sea awaiting shipping instructions
    5. Tolling finance A producer without processing capability sends raw material to a processor under a TOLLING AGREEMENT (the processor charges a fee and returns the refined product). The bank funds the processing cost, secured against the final product, and may take an assignment over the sales proceeds from end buyers Zambian mining company with copper ore but no refining capability sends it to a smelter in China. In gold, artisanal miners use tolling with refineries, financed by trade lenders, to turn raw ore into bullion bars
    6. Receivables-backed finance The exporter has shipped and invoiced with 60–90 day terms; instead of waiting, sells the receivable to a bank at a discount. The bank is repaid when the buyer pays. The bank may seek credit insurance or guarantees if the buyer is in a risky jurisdiction Indian textile exporter shipping garments to a European retailer

    The Qingdao warehousing fraud (2014) — the STF case study

    • Location: the port city of Qingdao, China's east coast — a hub for copper and aluminium, with giant bonded warehouses.
    • Perpetrator: a Chinese trading company, Decheng Resources, which looked respectable on paper.
    • The scheme: they stored metals in Qingdao's warehouses and issued DUPLICATE warehouse receipts, giving the same receipts to multiple banks and traders as collateral to raise loans again and again on the same pile of metal.
    • Discovery: mid-2014, when Chinese authorities investigating an unrelated corruption case inspected the warehouses. Banks and traders rushed to check their stocks and found the same metal had already been pledged to others — or in some cases wasn't there at all.
    • Losers: Citigroup, Standard Chartered, Standard Bank — hundreds of millions of dollars each; trading house Mercuria was also caught up and ended in a legal battle with Citigroup over who bore the loss for aluminium that wasn't there. Total estimated losses: over $3 billion.
    • Outcome: the owner was arrested and sentenced to 23 years in prison; company assets seized.
    • Industry impact: banks became far more cautious about lending against warehouse receipts, demanded real-time tracking of goods, and started using digital tools like LME Shield to prevent forged or duplicated receipts.

      "Even something as simple as a warehouse receipt, just a piece of paper, can be at the centre of a multi-billion-dollar fraud."

    4.14Regulatory Compliance — Sanctions

    Definition: restrictive measures imposed by governments or international bodies to achieve foreign policy or national security objectives — blocking movement of money, goods or services to pressure individuals, entities or countries. "Tools used to influence behaviour without resorting to military action."

    Who imposes sanctions

    Body Country/scope
    OFAC — Office of Foreign Assets Control United States (Dept of the Treasury)
    OFSI — Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation United Kingdom
    Global Affairs Canada Canada
    UNSC — United Nations Security Council Global, multilateral
    European Union Imposes its own sanctions independent of the UN

    US, EU and UN sanctions have the widest global impact because of their legal reach and financial influence — mainly because most global trade happens in USD or EUR.

    Why countries impose sanctions: prevent terrorism and organised crime · punish human rights abusers or genocide · prevent nuclear proliferation · respond to military aggression or cyberattacks · curb funding to rogue states or criminal regimes.

    The five types of sanctions

    Type Meaning Example
    Comprehensive Total ban on trade and financial dealings with a country North Korea, Iran (UN and OFAC)
    Sectoral Target specific industries Russia's energy or defence sectors
    Targeted Freeze assets and restrict travel of specific individuals or companies —
    Export-import bans Prohibit shipment of specific goods or technology —
    Embargoes Ban all commercial transactions with a country or territory —

    OFAC's SDN list — Specially Designated Nationals: individuals and companies whose assets are blocked and with whom US persons are generally prohibited from dealing unless they obtain permits.

    Why sanctions matter in trade finance

    Trade finance inherently involves cross-border flows of goods and money — a high-risk area for violations. Banks must ensure none of the parties in the trade chain — buyers, sellers, ships, shipping lines, insurance providers, third-party intermediaries — are sanctioned. Even the origin, transit or destination country can trigger exposure. Consequences of failure: massive regulatory penalties, reputational damage, and in extreme cases loss of access to the international banking system, especially USD clearing. Banks have lost their licences over this.

    How banks screen: transactions screened against the OFAC SDN list, EU Consolidated Sanctions List, UN sanctions list, and lists from local regulators (UK, Canada, Australia; in India, the DGFT — Directorate General of Foreign Trade). Methods: name matching against restricted parties · real-time alerts on hits · document examination for dual-use or military items, prohibited destinations, red-flag terms (e.g. Syria, Pyongyang, shell companies) · automated systems scanning commodity codes and product restrictions.

    Major sanctions fines — memorise bank, year and amount

    Bank Year Fine For
    BNP Paribas (French) 2014 $8.9 billion Violating sanctions related to Sudan, Cuba and Iran
    Standard Chartered 2019 $1.1 billion Processing transactions violating US sanctions on Iran and others
    Commerzbank (German) 2015 $1.45 billion Sanctions violations and AML control failures

    4.15Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML)

    Money laundering = making illegally obtained money appear legitimate. TBML = using international trade transactions (imports/exports) as a COVER to move or clean illicit money. "They are not hiding suitcases of cash. They are hiding illegal value inside invoices, shipping documents and goods descriptions." Trade is an ideal playground because of the massive volume of transactions, documents, goods and jurisdictions.

    The five TBML methods — know each mechanism

    Method How it works
    Over-invoicing Machinery actually worth $100,000 invoiced at $200,000 — the extra $100,000 is illegal money moved across borders disguised as a genuine trade payment
    Under-invoicing Invoice for $50,000 when goods are worth $100,000 — the importer gets value but pays only half on record, settling the rest through informal channels. Also used to evade customs duty and taxes
    Quantity or quality mismatch 1,000 mobile phones documented but only 500 shipped; or low-grade electronics billed at premium rates. Value is shifted without price manipulation
    Phantom shipments No goods at all — just documents. A fake export is recorded, the bank processes payment, nothing is ever shipped. Creates a paper trail to justify large illegal fund movements
    Multiple invoicing A single shipment invoiced 2–3 times to different banks in different countries — a $100,000 shipment brings in $300,000. Layering that is very hard to trace
    Mislabelling / misclassification Military-purpose chemicals labelled as cleaning agents; expensive diamond jewellery declared as costume accessories. Masks illicit goods and hides massive value discrepancies

    TBML is considered one of the HARDEST forms of money laundering to detect — which is exactly why it's dangerous. A bank that unknowingly processes a TBML transaction can face huge penalties even if unaware. It undermines global trade, destabilises economies, and can fund criminal or terrorist groups.

    Five detection methods

    1. Trade data and price checks — compare invoice values against global pricing databases. Exporting pencils at $20 each when the global average is 50 cents is a red flag. Sources: S&P Global, UN Comtrade, customs data.
    2. Dual-use goods screening — goods usable for both civilian and military purposes. Example: ammonium nitrate — a fertiliser and an explosive. Banks must scan for military applications, especially to sensitive jurisdictions.
    3. Vessel tracking and maritime intelligence — an unusual route or high-risk port may indicate TRANSSHIPMENT (goods moved from one ship to another to avoid detection). Platforms: Lloyd's List Intelligence, S&P Global.
    4. AI and machine learning — detect patterns humans miss: repeated trade between the same two parties, unusual payment terms, links to shell companies.
    5. Manual document review and red-flag alerts — do goods, quantities and invoices align? Does the port of loading match the shipping route?

    4.16Fraud in Trade Finance1

    Why trade finance is vulnerable: multiple parties (banks, buyers, sellers, shipping companies, insurers, freight forwarders) across jurisdictions, cultures and time zones · documents move with no real-time verification · information asymmetry · heavy reliance on paper documents and manual checks · sometimes purely trust-based interactions.

    This creates what we call a TRUST GAP — and that's exactly where fraud thrives. Per the ICC and enforcement agencies, billions of dollars are lost globally every year to trade-related fraud. Trade fraud is often organised, cross-border and highly sophisticated, with multiple colluding entities.

    The eight fraud types

    Fraud Mechanism
    Invoice fraud A fake invoice for goods never shipped, or over-invoiced. Presented for financing under receivables finance, documentary collection, LC or open account. Sometimes buyer and seller collude. "The documents match. There is a real invoice, a real bill of lading — but the entire transaction is fabricated."
    Duplicate financing The same invoice or shipment financed by multiple banks. Company A presents a $500,000 invoice to Bank X and Bank Y (or a fintech lender); each thinks it's a unique deal. Especially common in open account trade where documentation isn't tightly controlled
    Phantom shipments Seller claims to have shipped, submits documents, gets paid — but goods never existed or never left port. Relies on forged or manipulated shipping documents. Sometimes a real container is shipped filled with worthless goods — scrap instead of steel, sandbags instead of electronics
    Falsified / forged bills of lading Shows goods loaded when they weren't; fake vessel names, ports or cargo descriptions. Used to secure payment under an LC. "If the B/L looks real, the bank pays. If it turns out to be fake, the bank is left holding just the bill."
    Sanctions evasion as fraud Hiding the real origin of goods or routing through third countries. Examples: Iranian oil shipped via the UAE and relabelled "Middle East origin"; a Russian shipping company using a flag of convenience to disguise its identity
    Advance fee / prepayment scams The fraudster poses as a supplier, demands advance payment, then vanishes or ships something not per contract. Common in emerging markets with new counterparties met online or via intermediaries. Hits small businesses hardest — once funds are wired, recovery is nearly impossible
    Identity and documentation fraud Stolen or fake company identities; forged company seals, look-alike email domains, forged invoices, certificates of origin or inspection certificates. Supported by social engineering — convincing emails, phone calls, fraudulent websites
    Fraudulent guarantees and SBLCs Forging a guarantee document, or claiming a real guarantee was issued when it wasn't — attractive because they can be used to extract credit or performance assurances from third parties

    Case study 1 — Hin Leong Trading (Singapore, 2020)

    • Founded 1963 by OK Lim; grew into one of Asia's largest independent oil trading companies, supplying bunker fuel to ships, with ties to nearly two dozen international banks including HSBC, ABN AMRO, Deutsche Bank and Standard Chartered.
    • The speculation: Hin Leong placed speculative bets on oil prices using derivatives, especially crude oil futures.
    • The trigger: COVID-19 in 2020 — global lockdowns crushed oil demand and US crude futures briefly turned NEGATIVE. Their positions, betting on a rebound, bled money — losses estimated at over $800 million.
    • The concealment: instead of reporting losses, they instructed the finance team to hide them, showing profits where there were none.
    • The trade finance fraud: they had borrowed billions using trade finance facilities — LCs and invoice financing backed by physical cargoes, presenting bills of lading, invoices and warehouse receipts. Investigations revealed many documents were duplicate (multiple financing), fictitious (phantom shipments), or backed by non-existent cargo. Hin Leong claimed to hold millions of barrels of oil in storage — the oil simply wasn't there.
    • The collapse: by April 2020 the company owed over $3.5 billion to 23 banks and could not repay any of them. OK Lim was charged with forgery, cheating and false financial statements.
    • The aftermath: banks tightened trade finance operations, demanding greater transparency, independent verification of cargoes, stricter due diligence. Previously banks financed purely on the strength of the paper — a bill of lading or invoice — never verifying the cargo existed. Singapore introduced reforms to restore market confidence.

      The lesson: fraud happens when relationships override controls and risk management is ignored in pursuit of profit.

    Case study 2 — Standard Chartered (2019 sanctions violations)

    • A UK-based multinational with deep roots in Asia, Africa and the Middle East, known for its trade finance presence.
    • April 2019: agreed to pay over $1.1 billion in fines to US and UK regulators for violating US sanctions relating to Iran, Cuba, Sudan, Syria and Myanmar.
    • What happened: between 2007 and 2011 (and in some instances after 2012), it processed thousands of transactions through the US financial system involving sanctioned countries, especially Iran, moving through New York-based correspondent banks — but with critical details like the origin or identity of the sanctioned entity deliberately stripped from payment messages.
    • The technique: WIRE STRIPPING — removing or hiding information that would trigger a sanctions red flag. OFAC found bank staff were instructed how to format payment messages to avoid sanctions filters.
    • The aggravating factor: Standard Chartered had already been penalised in 2012 for similar violations, and had entered a deferred prosecution agreement committing to strengthen compliance — yet misconduct continued after the settlement.
    • Regulators involved: OFAC, the US Department of Justice, the Federal Reserve, and the UK's FCA.

      Lessons: accurate payment screening, robust internal controls, employee training, and a CULTURE OF COMPLIANCE FROM THE TOP DOWN. Poor communication between frontline staff and compliance teams leads to systemic failures.

    Case study 3 — Greensill Capital (2021, supply chain finance)

    • Founded by Australian financier Lex Greensill; hailed as revolutionary in SCF.
    • The basic model: when a supplier issued an invoice, Greensill paid the supplier almost immediately minus a small discount, funded by big investors; the buyer paid Greensill later.
    • The escalation: Greensill bundled these invoices into financial products and sold them to investors, notably Credit Suisse's asset management arm, marketed as low-risk, short-term instruments backed by real trade flows. "Greensill turned supply chain financing into an investment product."
    • The concentration: a biggest client was GFG Alliance, owned by Sanjeev Gupta, to which Greensill extended billions, often based on PROSPECTIVE / FUTURE RECEIVABLES — money lent against invoices that didn't even exist yet, based on predicted future sales.
    • The collapse: the receivables were backed by credit insurance. When insurance coverage was withdrawn in early 2021, Greensill lost the ability to fund its programmes. Credit Suisse froze $10 billion of SCF funds tied to Greensill. In March 2021 Greensill filed for insolvency; Credit Suisse, SoftBank and corporate clients scrambled to recover funds.
    • What went wrong: blurred lines between legitimate invoice finance and aggressive financial engineering · reliance on a few high-risk clients · poor transparency · excessive use of future receivables financing · a dangerous mismatch between what investors believed they were buying (low risk) and reality.

      The instructor compares it to the Lehman Brothers collapse. "When finance becomes opaque, even well-intentioned tools can be used recklessly."

    Red flags — the list is a likely MCQ

    1. Repeated trade between the same two parties, especially high values with limited documentation.
    2. Inconsistencies in shipping details — container listed as loaded at one port but the vessel's GPS shows it elsewhere; the vessel is unusually small for the listed cargo; a bill of lading issued BEFORE the shipment date.
    3. Abnormal pricing — significantly above or below market rates without explanation (over/under-invoicing).
    4. Round dollar values — clean numbers like 100,000 / 200,000 / 500,000, which are uncommon in real trade where taxes, duties and miscellaneous fees produce odd amounts.
    5. Shell companies or recently established entities — no credible digital footprint, no website, recently incorporated in a high-risk country or tax haven (St Kitts, Mauritius, Cayman Islands).
    6. Rapid change in trade volume — a small exporter suddenly shipping millions monthly with no change in staffing or infrastructure.
    7. Mismatches across documents — invoice says "steel coils", packing list says "aluminium scrap".
    8. Transshipment through high-risk or sanctions-prone jurisdictions — routed through countries with weak compliance or near embargoed zones, to conceal the true origin.

    Detection mechanisms

    1. Document examination — the first line of defence. Trained staff ask: do the goods on the invoice match the packing list? Is the vessel name on the B/L consistent across documents? Are certificate dates in the correct sequence? Was insurance issued before the shipment date? Any signs of tampering or image manipulation? These checks are manual, time-consuming and prone to human error — practitioners handle hundreds of pages daily.
    2. Data cross-validation and third-party integration — cross-check a vessel named "Ocean Star" against Lloyd's List Intelligence and find it has been docked in Shanghai for 45 days with no voyage recorded. Also customs databases for port entry/exit, and US Department of Commerce / EU data for dual-use goods classification.
    3. AI and machine learning — models trained on thousands of historic transactions including fraud cases assign a fraud risk score; high-risk transactions flagged for human review, low-risk fast-tracked. Notably, AI can detect document duplication across banks by scanning for identical invoice numbers, quantities, descriptions and dates even across different formats.
    4. KYC / KYG / KYT — the three K's: - KYC — Know Your Customer: company structure, beneficial ownership, nature of business, reputation. - KYG — Know Your Goods: what the client trades. Is it dual-use? Subject to export control? Meant for military use? Are there price anomalies? - KYT — Know Your Transaction: the specific transaction — where is the money going, who are the counterparties, which countries are involved, does the trade make commercial sense?

      KYC and KYG look at the customer and their line of business as a whole; KYT looks at the specific transaction.

    5. Network analysis and relationship mapping — two companies look unrelated on paper but share the same warehouse address, use the same freight forwarder, and transfer funds to the same offshore account — a classic collusion indicator. Uncovers front companies, shell companies and collusive trading structures.
    6. Vessel and route monitoring — AIS (Automatic Identification System) data from MarineTraffic, IHS Markit, Lloyd's List Intelligence. Detects when a vessel "goes dark" by switching off transponders near high-risk areas (Iran, Syria, North Korea) — a strong sign of sanctions evasion.

    Who does what inside the bank

    Role Responsibility
    Relationship Managers (RMs) First line of commercial and customer awareness. Know the client's trade patterns, counterparties, goods and ownership structure. Example: a long-time machinery client suddenly importing seafood from a high-risk country — even with clean documents, this business inconsistency is a red flag. Also vital during onboarding — KYC/KYG checks, flagging front companies, shell entities, sudden ownership changes
    Trade operations team Gatekeepers of document validation. Examine invoices, B/Ls, certificates, LC terms, guarantees for discrepancies, inconsistencies in descriptions/quantities/weights, unusual issuers of certificates, altered or forged signatures and stamps. A second filter where AI isn't trained for the nuance
    Compliance and sanctions teams The risk detectors. Ensure compliance with sanctions, AML regulations and internal controls; check whether parties, ships, goods or countries are sanctioned; whether dual-use goods are involved; whether repeated transactions look like layering. Review escalations and decide whether to proceed, reject or file an STR with the Financial Intelligence Unit
    Credit and risk teams Final gatekeepers. Evaluate financial implications: what is the bank's exposure? Can we stop the payment or hold the financing? Do we adjust credit limits? Should we escalate to regulators or external legal advisors? Also conduct periodic risk reviews

    All of this only works if the bank invests in regular staff training — identifying trade-specific red flags, using tools correctly, reporting through the right channels, and staying updated on evolving fraud methods.

    Escalation process

    1. Internal escalation from frontline to compliance — a trade ops analyst who notices the vessel name doesn't match the shipping database raises a red flag alert / internal suspicious activity notification up the chain to the team lead, compliance, and if needed risk or legal. "This ensures no single person bears the full responsibility — a vital safeguard against both mistakes and cover-ups."
    2.
