Cross-functional collaboration — banks set up fraud risk committees or financial crime panels with representatives from trade finance ops and product, compliance/AML, legal, IT and digital risk, relationship/coverage, and credit risk. They decide to hold payment, freeze accounts, or file an STR, and assign ownership.
    3. Documentation and record keeping — detailed audit trails: what was flagged, by whom, when, what actions were taken, final resolution. Needed for internal accountability and regulatory reporting — the bank must prove it acted promptly and responsibly.
    4. Reporting to regulators and FIUs — for cross-border, large-value, potential money laundering, terrorism financing or sanctions breaches. India: FIU-India. United States: FinCEN. UK: National Crime Agency. The bank files an STR (Suspicious Transaction Report) or SAR (Suspicious Activity Report).
    5. Industry-level collaboration — The Wolfsberg Group, the ICC, and SWIFT's Financial Crime Compliance encourage banks to share anonymised case data, emerging red flags and typologies. Some countries run shared registries of high-risk entities, fraudulent documents or blacklisted exporters/importers. "In trade finance, no bank is an island. Fraudsters often hit multiple institutions at once."

    Preventive controls (7)

    1. Strong KYC and onboarding — verify ownership structures and beneficial owners, business legitimacy (years of operation, office location, website, tax filings), adverse media checks, screening against sanctions and PEP (politically exposed person) lists, confirming trade references and banking history. Plus KYG: does the product match the company's known operations? (A textile company suddenly exporting high-end electronics is worth digging into.)
    2. Standardised documentation and controls — template LCs and guarantee formats, restricting presentation to originals only, not photocopies, requiring third-party validation for inspection/insurance/shipping, and MAKER-CHECKER controls so no one person can approve a full transaction.
    3. Transaction pattern monitoring — unusual spikes in trade volume, frequent use of high-risk countries, price discrepancies vs market, sudden changes in trade corridors. A client normally shipping $200,000 of electronics monthly suddenly requesting a $5 million LC for scrap metal is a red flag.
    4. Digital document authentication — electronic bills of lading (eBLs), blockchain-based trade platforms, secure PDF/XML with digital signatures — with audit trails and tamper-proof history.
    5. Trade compliance automation tools — AI-driven platforms scanning for sanctions breaches, dual-use/military goods, vessel tracking anomalies, unusual country routes; can automatically flag, hold or block transactions.
    6. Regular staff training and red flag awareness — internal red flag libraries, e-learning modules, simulation exercises.
    7. Client education — SMEs can be victims themselves. Banks run outreach on how to verify trade partners, what a legitimate LC or guarantee looks like, how to spot phishing or fake email fraud, and why documentation matters. "An informed client is less likely to fall for trade scams and less likely to be used as a front."

    4.17Banks, DFIs and ECAs

    Commercial banks DFIs — Development Finance Institutions ECAs — Export Credit Agencies
    Primary objective Profit and serving clients Development and market support Promote national exports
    Risk appetite Moderate Higher — very large institutions backed by the World Bank or major countries Higher — backed by government mandates
    What they offer LCs, guarantees, loans, supply chain financing; processing and settlement; pre-shipment finance (packing credit), invoice discounting, post-shipment finance; FX management (forwards, options); compliance and due diligence (sanctions screening, AML, KYC) Long-term project and trade finance — infrastructure, energy, logistics (ports, roads, railways, supply chains); support SME exporters who can't meet commercial bank credit standards; de-risk investments via guarantees, insurance, first-loss coverage to attract private capital; act as catalysts by co-financing or syndicating large deals Export credit insurance, loan guarantees, and direct financing to FOREIGN BUYERS. Protect exporters against buyer default, political risk, non-payment; support banks in providing trade finance in high-risk markets
    Target customers Corporates, SMEs, MSMEs Emerging markets, countries, large businesses Domestic exporters and foreign buyers
    Government backing No (unless a government entity) Yes Yes
    Examples HSBC, Citibank, ICICI, HDFC IFC (World Bank Group), African Development Bank, ADB, US DFC (International Development Finance Corporation) US EXIM (Export-Import Bank of the US), UKEF (UK Export Finance), ECGC (Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India)

    Why ECAs exist: global trade is competitive, and buyers often choose the supplier who offers financing or better payment terms. ECAs make that possible. The combined power: a commercial bank lending under a DFI guarantee, or an ECA insuring a bank's LC, creates a powerful ecosystem for safe, scalable global trade. DFIs don't always directly finance trade — they create the conditions that allow trade to flourish.

    4.18Digitalisation of Trade

    What digitalisation means: the shift from physical to electronic workflows — electronic bills of lading, automated compliance checks, blockchain for document exchange, AI to detect red flags. Benefits: businesses get reduced cost and faster transaction cycles (shorter working capital cycle); banks get better risk management and streamlined operations; regulators get better monitoring and compliance enforcement; and it levels the playing field for small exporters.

    "It's no longer about moving just goods or money. It's about moving data, trust and value in a frictionless way."

    Paperless trade is NOT just scanning documents or switching to email. Four requirements: 1. Legal modernisation — governments legally recognising electronic documents. Without legal backing, a digital bill of lading is just a nice-looking PDF. This is where MLETR comes in. 2. Technology — platforms like Bolero and CargoX using blockchain and digital signature infrastructure to securely issue, transfer and store trade documents, connecting banks, customs, ports and corporates. 3. Government and trade bloc push — Singapore's TradeTrust, the EU's e-Customs initiatives. 4. Standardised data formats and APIs — developed by bodies like the ICC and WCO (World Customs Organization) so different systems can talk to each other.

    TradeTrust (Singapore)

    • A blockchain-enabled framework developed by Singapore's IMDA (Infocomm Media Development Authority) in collaboration with the MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore — the central bank) and international trade partners.
    • Not a single platform but an OPEN FRAMEWORK — a set of digital tools, legal standards and governance structures. Establishes trust without centralised control.
    • How it works: when a shipping line issues a B/L electronically through a TradeTrust-compatible system, the document is digitally signed and recorded on the blockchain, creating a verifiable, tamper-proof record. A buyer or bank can instantly verify authenticity using TradeTrust's verification tool — without logging in, registering or relying on a third party. The document can be securely transferred just as a physical B/L is endorsed and handed over.
    • Legal alignment: aligned with MLETR. Singapore amended its Electronic Transactions Act to incorporate MLETR principles, becoming one of the first countries to give full legal backing to digital trade documents.
    • Scope: already piloted in cross-border trade with Australia and the Netherlands.
    • Impact: what took several days of couriering and manual verification now takes minutes; enhances transparency, reduces document fraud, supports sustainability (no paper, less carbon-intensive courier logistics).

    Electronic Bills of Lading (eBL)

    Why the B/L is the crux: it plays three roles — receipt of goods, evidence of the contract of carriage, and DOCUMENT OF TITLE. Whoever physically holds the original controls the cargo. Delays or loss of this one document holds up millions of dollars of goods.

    An eBL is a digitally issued and managed version — created, transmitted and endorsed through a secure digital platform, accessible in real time by shipping companies, exporters, importers, freight forwarders and banks.

    Critical: an eBL is NOT just a scanned version of a paper document. It is built on a legal and technological framework ensuring it carries the same legal weight as its physical counterpart. Platforms like Bolero and CargoX use blockchain, digital signatures and smart contracts so that once transferred, it cannot be tampered with or duplicated — solving the age-old problem of multiple parties claiming ownership of the same goods.

    Case study — Hyundai Merchant Marine + CargoX (2021): partnered to issue eBLs for cargo destined for Egypt, because Egypt's customs authority began mandating digital document submission including eBLs for faster clearance. What took 5–7 days to transfer title and release goods could be done in a few hours. A physical B/L from China to Egypt takes 4–5 days through multiple intermediaries; an eBL is sent instantaneously "just like an email." Benefit for importers: avoids demurrage, storage fees and missed deadlines.

    Adoption barriers: many countries still don't recognise digital documents of title; not all stakeholders (smaller freight forwarders, banks) have integrated with eBL platforms. But the UK's Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 and MLETR's momentum are opening the door.

    MLETR — Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records

    • Developed by UNCITRAL — the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law. Released in 2017.
    • A MODEL LAW — countries are encouraged to adapt and adopt it into their national legal systems.
    • Purpose: allow electronic transferable documents to be treated the same as paper counterparts — particularly instruments involving ownership or title: bills of lading, promissory notes, bills of exchange, warehouse receipts.

    The three capabilities MLETR provides — memorise: 1. Functional equivalence — if it's legal in paper form, MLETR makes it legal in digital form (subject to conditions). 2. Control — introduces exclusive control over a digital document. Just as possession of a paper B/L proves ownership, MLETR ensures there is only ONE true digital owner. 3. Integrity — the electronic record must be reliable and tamper-proof: no duplicates, no edits after issuance, and a clear transfer trail.

    Adoption timeline — testable:

    Country Development
    Singapore FIRST country to adopt MLETR, in 2021 — legislation recognising eBLs and other trade documents
    Bahrain Followed with its own MLETR-based version
    United Kingdom Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023, aligned with MLETR principles

    Why it matters: without legal acceptance, a buyer, bank or shipping line might still demand a paper document to be safe, slowing the whole ecosystem. MLETR provides trust, enforceability and cross-border recognition. Promoted by the ICC, UN, ADB and development finance institutions. Scenario: a Vietnamese exporter ships to a German buyer using a digital B/L on CargoX; thanks to MLETR-aligned laws in both Vietnam and Germany, the buyer's right to the cargo at the Port of Hamburg is fully recognised, and if the buyer defaults the financing bank can enforce its rights based on the electronic promissory note.

    4.19FinTech Disruptors in Trade Finance

    Context: for decades trade finance was dominated by a few large banks, piles of paper and siloed systems. Traditional SCF served only top-tier corporates, displacing SMEs and MSMEs — because of complex onboarding, bank-driven structures and legacy platforms.

    The questions fintechs asked: Why does it take weeks to onboard a small supplier? Why can't financing be embedded inside an ERP system? Why should access to capital depend on who your bank is?

    Three things fintechs did differently: 1. Democratisation of access — open digital platforms where even a small seller with $10,000 in monthly invoices can upload documents, get real-time risk scoring, and receive early payment offers. Examples: Drip Capital and Incomlend globally; Cashinvoice/Credable in India connecting buyers, suppliers and financiers with automated onboarding. 2. Technology-first approach — cloud-native, API-enabled, integrating directly with corporate ERP systems (SAP, Oracle, Tally) and government platforms (India's GST system), e-invoicing systems and customs portals. Reduces manual errors, enables real-time data validation, speeds funding decisions. 3. Alternative credit assessment — traditional banks use credit ratings, balance sheets and historical financials; fintechs use invoice payment history, digital buyer confirmation, real-time trade and tax filings, port logistics and shipment confirmations. "This allows fintechs to underwrite even thin files or non-rated entities — a game changer for MSMEs."

    Traditional vs FinTech-driven SCF

    Dimension Traditional (bank-led) SCF FinTech-driven SCF
    Platform access Bank-led, restricted to a limited few Cloud-based, open access — anyone who signs up can connect
    Onboarding Manual, paper-intensive, can take months Instant — digital KYC, API-based, data pulled from various systems
    Credit risk Buyer-driven / corporate-led Multi-party and alternative-data based
    Financing trigger Buyer confirmation via email or a portal connecting only buyer, bank and suppliers ERP integration via APIs with real-time data
    Scalability Difficult to onboard beyond tier-1 suppliers Designed for large volume, high client counts, cross-border and long programmes

    Forces reshaping the landscape: - Digital infrastructure and regulation — governments mandating e-invoicing, digital tax reporting, online customs declarations. In India, B2B invoices above a threshold must be registered through the Invoice Registration Portal and linked to GST, creating an authoritative digital trail that fintechs like Vayana Trade Exchange can tap for real-time risk scoring. In the EU, PEPPOL-compliant structured invoices for public procurement. "Providers no longer have to ask 'is this invoice real?' — they can check instantly against tax systems and customs records." - Inclusivity and SME participation — with nearshoring, buyers work with a longer tail of suppliers, many small, digitally inexperienced and in emerging markets. Fintechs build mobile-first, multilingual, intuitive interfaces, some partnering with governments and development banks to fund otherwise unbankable suppliers. - ESG-linked trade finance — sustainability scores assigned to suppliers, with preferential financing rates for those meeting environmental and social benchmarks. - Technology evolution — AI in credit underwriting, blockchain for traceability, APIs for integration. Financing embedded not just in ERPs but in shipping portals, procurement tools, even messaging platforms. "Imagine a supplier confirming a purchase order on WhatsApp and receiving a financing offer a few minutes later." - Changing global trade — geopolitical tensions, sanctions, port disruptions, supply chain fragmentation → demand for resilience and visibility. Fintech platforms offer end-to-end data tracking: finance the invoice and track delivery, customs clearance and buyer payment in one view.

    4.20ESG-Linked Supply Chain Finance

    The shift in question: from "how quickly can we finance an invoice?" to "can we finance the RIGHT KIND OF BEHAVIOUR in the supply chain?"

    ESG = Environmental, Social, Governance: - Environmental — impact on the planet: pollution, carbon emissions, energy usage, water consumption, waste management. - Social — how the company treats people and communities: employees, suppliers, customers, communities; labour rights, diversity, health and safety, human rights. - Governance — how the business is run: leadership, ethics, transparency, board composition, anti-corruption policies.

    Why supply chains are the ESG battleground: "A large multinational might claim to be sustainable, but if its suppliers are dumping toxic waste, underpaying workers or engaging in deforestation, that sustainability badge means little." If suppliers violate labour laws (child labour) or pollute rivers, it's not just reputational — it leads to regulatory penalties and disrupted operations.

    The mechanism — how ESG links to SCF: - Better financing terms for suppliers with high ESG scores — faster payments or lower discount rates. - Restricted access for those failing minimum ESG standards. - Tiered incentives — ESG improvements over time unlock better liquidity access.

    "This approach doesn't just encourage ESG compliance — it REWARDS it."

    Four drivers of momentum: 1. Regulatory pressure — the EU's CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive) and supply chain due diligence laws require corporates to track and disclose ESG risks in their supply chains. 2. Investor expectation — ESG is embedded in institutional investment mandates; corporates that can't demonstrate ESG compliance get lower ESG ratings, impacting valuation and financing cost. 3. Procurement and brand risk — consumers and advocacy groups hold brands accountable for their suppliers' practices. SCF becomes a strategic tool to influence behaviour without force, by linking money to values. 4. Economic incentive — for SMEs/MSMEs in emerging markets, cheaper and faster liquidity is a major motivator to improve sustainability practices.

    The Starbucks illustration: Starbucks sources coffee from hundreds of farms across Latin America, Africa and Southeast Asia. It works with a fintech partner to collect ESG data from suppliers — a Colombian farm shares water usage, soil preservation methods, worker treatment policies. Farms using organic compost, efficient irrigation, paying fair wages, investing in community healthcare get a higher ESG rating and are offered early payment at a discounted rate through a digital SCF platform. Lower-scoring farms face stricter payment terms. Outcome: farmers get quicker liquidity; Starbucks safeguards its brand by sourcing responsibly; consumers know their coffee supports ethical practices.

    Where it's heading: most ESG-linked SCF programmes today are voluntary, offered by large buyers. In coming years ESG scoring will likely become a standard input in credit risk models for SCF, and we may see green supply chain finance funds — a new asset class where investors specifically allocate capital to sustainable trade practices. FinTechs will be essential to scaling this.

    4.21Cloud Computing in Trade Finance

    Definition: accessing software, data and storage over the internet instead of installing and managing them on your own physical computer/server. "Renting computing power and storage space instead of buying and maintaining it." Everyday analogues: Google Drive/iCloud, email from any device, OTT platforms.

    Why it matters for trade finance — traditionally documents were printed, signed, stamped and couriered across countries: time-consuming, costly, and full of risk (delays, fraud, document loss, human error).

    Six benefits: 1. Shared secure environment — an exporter in Mumbai uploads documents; within seconds a bank in Singapore, a freight agent in Rotterdam and a customs authority in Dubai can all view and verify the same set. No couriers, no waiting, no duplicated data entry. 2. Automation — cloud-based platforms use AI to automatically check trade documents for errors or discrepancies. Instead of a human spending hours validating whether the invoice matches the LC, the system flags mismatches in seconds. 3. Scalability — a bank processing 1,000 LCs a day would need a major IT upgrade to handle 2,000 more on traditional infrastructure; with cloud you scale instantly and pay only for what you use. 4. Security — enterprise-grade protection: encryption, data backups, access controls. "For many organisations, cloud storage is MORE secure than physical files or local servers." 5. Anytime, anywhere access — trade spans time zones; 24×7 access from any device with an internet connection. 6. Integration — connects easily with ERP software, customs systems, shipping platforms and blockchain networks.

    Without cloud infrastructure, many recent advances — electronic bills of lading, AI-powered compliance checks, digital LCs — would not be feasible at scale.

    4.22Data Service Providers

    Platforms: S&P Global, Lloyd's List Intelligence, Moody's Orbis, and others. Five check types:

    Check What it looks for Providers
    1. Maritime intelligence Vessel ownership and registration screening (ships owned/managed by sanctioned individuals or countries — Iran and Cuba own vessels) · voyage irregularities (unusual port calls, ship-to-ship transfers, routing via blacklisted jurisdictions) · FLAG HOPPING (frequent changes in the ship's country of registration) · DARK VESSEL ACTIVITY (transponders switched off, ship disappears for 3–4 days then reappears) · high-risk zones (ports in embargoed countries). Uses AIS plus ownership databases, port call histories, transshipment activity Lloyd's List Intelligence, S&P Global
    2. Fair value checks / price benchmarking Verifies declared invoice prices against global pricing databases and trade data. Detects over-invoicing (disguising illicit transfer of money abroad) and under-invoicing (evading customs duties) S&P Global, TradeMo, Kpler
    3. Negative / adverse media checks Scans global news databases, regulatory announcements and watchlists for financial fraud or money laundering charges, sanctions or export control breaches, ties to PEPs, corruption/bribery, and ESG controversies Dow Jones Risk & Compliance, World-Check, LexisNexis
    4. Military / dual-use goods and export control Are the "radio components" civilian-grade or usable in weapon systems? Dual-use items: drone parts, chemicals, encryption technology, navigation systems. Uses HS code-based classification, screening against export control lists, validation of end-use and end-user statements, flagging goods linked to arms embargoes or restricted defence sectors. Governed by the Wassenaar Arrangement, EU export control rules, and the US Export Administration Regulations Export control tools
    5. Shell company checks Shell companies hide the real owners — a clean-looking exporter in country A may be a front for a sanctioned entity in country B. Traces corporate hierarchies and ownership chains, identifies incorporation in tax havens, detects circular ownership patterns, and checks whether the Ultimate Beneficial Owner (UBO) is on a sanctions or PEP list. Essential for TBML detection and often required under FATF (Financial Action Task Force) guidelines Moody's Orbis

    Quick recap of providers: S&P Global — maritime risk intelligence, financial and country risk assessments, credit risk ratings, pricing benchmarks. Lloyd's List Intelligence — vessel tracking, dark shipping, transshipment alerts, maritime risk profiles. Orbis by Moody's — legal ownership, shell company detection, corporate linkages, financial health, UBO data. World-Check / Dow Jones / LexisNexis — sanctions and reputational/regulatory red flags. Export control tools — military and dual-use goods classification.

    New Age Business Models

    New Age Business Models (NABM)

    (Instructor: Ganesh K)

    5.1What is a Business Model?

    Definition: how a company plans to create and capture value in the ecosystem. It's a conceptual structure supporting the viability of a business — explaining how it operates, makes money and achieves its goals. It encapsulates the value proposition — the unique cocktail of products, services and experiences that make a business stand out.

    The three formal definitions — memorise author + year

    Author Year Definition
    Teece 2010 "A conceptual model of the business. It describes the organisational and financial architecture of a business."
    Magretta 2002 "A business model is a story that explains why and how a business works."
    Osterwalder & Pigneur 2010 "A business model describes the rationale of how a business creates, delivers and captures value."

    The opening stories

    Story The business model innovation
    Netflix (1997) Reed Hastings, a software entrepreneur, borrowed Apollo 13 from a video rental and was fined $40 — more than the cost of the DVD. He started Netflix as DVD-by-mail with NO LATE FEES, later transforming into subscription streaming. The change: from per-day/per-week rental per DVD to a FIXED MONTHLY SUBSCRIPTION — as many DVDs as you want, as long as you return the earlier one
    Arunachalam Muruganantham / Jayashree Industries Affordable sanitary pads. Business model built around empowering rural women — supplied semi-automatic machines to women-led self-help groups who produced and sold the pads. Turned a societal challenge into an entrepreneurial opportunity, creating micro-entrepreneurs while solving a rural healthcare issue
    Ford Motor Company (early 20th c.) Not just the assembly line — a business model of mass production and standardisation that drastically cut the cost of a car. Henry Ford's vision of "a car for the great multitude." A model based on cost efficiency and economies of scale. (Also: Ford cut cost by offering only one colour)

    Key statistic: each year more than HALF of the Fortune 500 companies have to innovate their business model to stay on that list. Business models are not set in stone — they are dynamic and must evolve. Firms that fail to innovate get left behind — Kodak.

    5.2The Three Pillars of a Business Model1

    Pillar The question it answers Examples
    1. Value Proposition What important, pervasive customer problem or need is the business solving? How is the solution superior to the alternatives? The reason customers turn to one company over another Flipkart — the biggest challenge in Indian e-commerce was low credit card penetration and distrust of online sites. Flipkart offered CASH ON DELIVERY — a game changer, done nowhere else in the world — addressing the trust issue. Swiggy — food delivered to your doorstep; differentiators: wide variety of restaurants in your locality, user-friendly app, rapid AND PREDICTABLE delivery times (you can see the order being picked up and where it is)
    2. Value Delivery What capabilities must the business build to deliver a great customer experience? Who are the actors in the value network? Everything from production to delivery Maruti Suzuki — widespread dealership and service centre network across India (support even in the remotest part), efficient supply chain, effective after-sales service. Reliance Jio — robust 4G coverage including rural India, affordable plans, user-friendly payment app
    3. Value Appropriation How does the company capture value in monetary terms — revenue models, pricing strategies, cost structures, profit margins? Zomato — restaurant advertising, online food delivery commission (% of order value) from restaurants, Zomato Pro subscription, delivery fees from customers. Credit cards — three sources: (1) interest when people roll over payments, (2) fees charged to cardholders, (3) transaction fees paid by businesses that accept cards

    These pillars must be clearly defined, aligned with each other, and flexible enough to evolve.

    Business Model vs Strategy — a likely comparison MCQ

    Strategy Business Model
    A set of choices the organisation makes vis-à-vis its competition A blueprint to achieve that strategic position
    High-level plan to achieve objectives and gain competitive advantage Describes how the company creates, delivers and captures value
    Choices: what business to be in, how to position, where to compete, what unique value, how to use resources Outlines processes, resources, structure; value proposition, target customer, delivery mechanism, revenue generation, cost management
    Deals with competition and achieving competitive advantage in the broader market Concerns the system of operations WITHIN the company
    Includes market positioning, differentiation, growth direction, response to trends and competitor action The business model is, in essence, the IMPLEMENTATION of a strategy

    Linkage: a differentiation strategy leads to a business model emphasising premium products and high-quality service; a cost leadership strategy leads to one prioritising efficiency and scale. Multiple business models can achieve the same strategic position. Both must be aligned.

    5.3The Business Model Canvas — the 9 elements

    (Illustrated with Swiggy and BigBasket.)

    # Element Question Swiggy BigBasket
    1 Customer relationships How does the business interact with customers? Dedicated customer support team, in-app chat, social media, email Website, app, call centre, email, chat, Tata Neu app
    2 Customer segments Who are the primary customers? People wanting convenience and wide food variety — urban dwellers with smartphone and internet Monthly grocery shoppers (main service), top-up purchases via bb now, unplanned purchases via bb instant, daily milk/fresh needs via bb daily
    3 Value propositions What unique value is offered? Fast, convenient food delivery from a wide variety of local restaurants Fresh fruits and vegetables at your doorstep — convenience, quality and price
    4 Channels Through what means does the business reach customers? Mobile app and website (Contrast: Uber is accessible through the app only; Lenskart has app, website, and physical stores both company-owned and franchised)
    5 Key activities Most important activities to meet the value proposition Maintaining a user-friendly app, managing logistics, marketing, customer support Sourcing from farmers, quality control, merchandising, daily pricing decisions (prices fluctuate daily), warehousing, storage, delivery logistics
    6 Key partnerships Who does the business rely on? Restaurants, delivery personnel, payment gateways, cloud kitchen partners Major FMCG companies — Unilever, Procter & Gamble
    7 Key resources What unique resources set it apart? The delivery network, technology (app and website), large repeat customer base Pickers and packers, warehouses, city delivery staff, technology teams running the app 24×7
    8 Revenue streams How does it make money? Delivery fees, restaurant commissions, advertisements Margins on products sold, margins on own brands, delivery fees, promotion fees from brands
    9 Cost structure Major costs of running the business Technology development and maintenance (friction-free app), logistics, customer support, marketing, partnerships Manpower (warehousing, sourcing, technology, delivery), warehouse rentals, delivery vehicles

    5.4Traditional Business Models

    They are NOT mutually exclusive — organisations often use a COMBINATION. Example: a company may use contract manufacturing to make the product (like Apple with Foxconn), then franchising to go to market, and bundling to attract customers. Some models optimise GO-TO-MARKET (how to reach the market and stimulate demand); others focus on efficiently USING EXISTING STRENGTHS (the brand, the IP).

    The oldest model: the BARTER model — began with the tribes of Mesopotamia around 6,000 BC; the Phoenicians adopted it. Used to obtain food, weapons and spices.

    Manufacturer model

    Creating products from raw materials or components; sold directly or through intermediaries. Examples: Tata Motors (designs and manufactures vehicles sold via dealers); Reliance Industries — the Jamnagar Refinery is the world's largest refining hub (control over quality + economies of scale made Reliance a global petrochemical leader); Hindustan Unilever (80+ years in India, products touch two-thirds of Indians daily).

    Strengths Weaknesses
    Control over production, quality and pricing Very high capital expenditure to set up a plant
    Economies of scale — higher volumes drive down cost, raising profitability Continuous maintenance and upgrading expenses
    Potential supply chain complexities
    Inflexibility — large upfront investments make it very hard to change established infrastructure as market dynamics and preferences evolve

    Failures: HMT Watches — once the leader, couldn't keep up with changing market dynamics, more advanced manufacturing and newer designs (Titan) → steady decline → shutdown. Moser Baer India — leading manufacturer of optical storage media (CDs, DVDs) with the latest technology at the time; the digital era and cloud storage collapsed demand; diversification into solar energy failed; bankruptcy — the entire manufacturing investment wasted.

    Distributor model

    An intermediary acquires products from the manufacturer and sells to retailers or consumers. Examples: Redington India (IT and mobility products), Ingram Micro (global technology distributor operating in over 100 countries).

    Five roles of a distributor: (1) storage and transportation (managing inventory, moving goods from manufacturer to retailer/customer) · (2) market knowledge — deep local knowledge and retailer relationships providing critical feedback and market intelligence to manufacturers who may be in another country · (3) sales and marketing support — promote the product, create demand, generate local sales · (4) financing · (5) RISK ABSORPTION — "if a product doesn't sell, the distributor is often the one left with the unsold inventory" — the manufacturer transfers risk and gets money upfront.

    Five success factors: relationships (strong ties with both manufacturers and retailers give preferential access; many top Indian brands have generational relationships with distributors) · market knowledge · efficient operations (inventory management, quick turnaround, efficient transport; perishables need a cold chain) · financial management (very thin margins — manage credit terms with both sides, cash flow; "what they give up in margin they make up in turnover") · customer service.

    Challenges: low margins · high investment in inventory · disruption from online B2B marketplaces · changing supply chain dynamics — D2C and third-party logistics models enable direct dealing between retailer/consumer and the brand. Disruption examples: independent pharmaceutical distributors squeezed as large organised pharmacy chains and e-pharmacies procure directly from pharma companies; small book distributors disrupted by Amazon and Flipkart (wider range, heavy discounts, home delivery). Strong Indian distribution networks: Pidilite (Fevicol), Marico (Parachute, Saffola), ITC (deep rural and urban penetration, cigarettes to FMCG).

    Retailer model

    Purchase from manufacturers/distributors and sell to end consumers via brick-and-mortar or e-commerce. Omnichannel retailing = a combination of both. Examples: Reliance Retail (JioMart, Reliance Jewels, Fresh Signature, Reliance Trends), Walmart (world's largest retailer).

    Four roles: customer interface (the final link in the supply chain, the face of the product) · demand fulfilment (holding inventory from different manufacturers) · marketing and sales (in-store promotions, online marketing, product information) · market feedback to manufacturers and distributors on preferences, product performance, competitors.

    Five success factors: customer service (including after-sales) · product selection ("if you don't have a product, it forces your customer to go to your competitor") · location (convenient and accessible; or an easy-to-use online platform) · pricing · effective marketing (including hyper-local promotion often sponsored by the brand or distributor).

    Four challenges: inventory management (over/understocking, especially perishables) · intense competition from physical and online (competitors open similar stores in the same locality when they see one doing well) · operational cost (high rentals in prime areas and high streets are a severe dampener, salaries, utilities) · changing consumer trends.

    Strengths: direct interaction building relationships and loyalty · control over product selection · potential for higher margins on high-demand items.

    Successes: DMart — legendary strategy of everyday low prices, efficient supply chain; a unique thing: they OWN the premises and avoid the high rental costs that are the bane of retail. Reliance Retail. Failures: Subhiksha — venture funded, raised a lot of capital, rapid expansion, but failed from lack of operational efficiency, financial mismanagement, very low margins, and write-offs from wastage and unsold inventory. Future Group / Big Bazaar — one of the oldest and largest hypermarket chains, brought down by heavy debt, aggressive expansion, and the failed deal with Amazon.

    Franchise model

    The franchisor (owner of the business concept/brand) grants the franchisee the licensed right to operate under the franchisor's name and system for a fee or percentage of profit.

    The three acronyms — memorise who owns and who operates:

    Model Who owns the assets Who operates Payment
    COFO — Company Owned, Franchise Operated The franchisor (company) owns store, machinery etc. The franchisee Franchisee pays a % of revenue as royalty
    FOCO — Franchisee Owned, Company Operated The franchisee invests the capital The franchisor (company) runs day-to-day operations Profit shared between franchisor and franchisee
    FOFO — Franchisee Owned, Franchise Operated The franchisee The franchisee Franchisor provides brand, products/services and the business model

    Examples: Café Coffee Day — FOFO. Dr Batra's Homeopathy (200+ clinics worldwide). McDonald's — primarily FOFO with a few company-owned stores. Marriott Hotels — operates under various models globally (COFO and FOCO). Domino's Pizza India — 1,000+ outlets under FOCO. Tanishq (Tata Group). BlueStone (online jewellery, 150+ franchise stores). Raymond — FOFO. Struggles: Subway (high operational costs, location issues, competition — moderately successful); Quiznos (high cost, lack of localisation to the Indian palate, stiff competition); Cartridge World (Australian printing solutions — lack of consumer awareness about refilling cartridges and local alternatives).

    Franchisee Franchisor (company)
    Advantages Brand recognition — leverage an established name · training and ongoing support · lower risk — a proven business model already working elsewhere Rapid expansion without significant capital investment (the franchisee puts up capital) · regular income from fees and royalties · reduced financial risk
    Disadvantages Limited control — must follow the franchisor's rules or lose franchise rights · fees and royalties hit profitability · dependence on the franchisor — e.g. when Café Coffee Day faced financial challenges and the founder's death, franchisees were affected. You are not master of your own destiny Loss of day-to-day control → quality control issues (franchisees may cut corners) · brand reputation risk — one poor franchisee can damage the brand globally · profit sharing — less money to be made

    Contract manufacturing

    Outsourcing production to a third-party contract manufacturer. The hiring firm provides specifications and design; the contract manufacturer produces the goods. Examples: Apple → Foxconn (Apple focuses on design, marketing, branding, consumer experience). Flextronics. Nike owns NO factories — contracts manufacturers in Vietnam, China, Indonesia.

    Perspective Pros Cons
    The brand/company Cost efficiency — scale and lower labour/operational costs in low-cost geographies · focus on core competency (R&D, marketing, pricing, design) · reduced capital investment Quality control difficult, especially overseas · Dependency — disruptions at the contract manufacturer hit your supply chain (China's pandemic issues; geopolitical issues) · INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RISK — you must share designs, often well before public launch, and the manufacturer's country may lack strong IP laws
    The contract manufacturer Stable orders — long-term contracts give predictable revenue · large-scale production for multiple clients → multi-shift operation and economies of scale · technological upgrades / technology transfer from large international clients Dependence on few clients — if Apple decides to move country or manufacturer, the entire plant investment is at risk · very low profit margins (you don't own the brand or the IP — you need large scale) · high capital investment in facilities, equipment, skilled labour

    Licensing model

    The licensor allows the licensee to use its intellectual property — brand name, patents, copyrights, technology, product design — for a fee or royalty. Examples: Disney (Mickey Mouse licensed to toys, clothing, food, video games); Marvel; Star Wars; Microsoft (licenses software to PC manufacturers who pre-install it); Qualcomm (licenses advanced wireless technology to smartphone manufacturers worldwide — the design and IP are Qualcomm's but all commercial exploitation is by the manufacturers).

    Licensor pros Licensor cons
    Monetise IP that would otherwise remain unused (Disney's theme parks are capital-intensive; licensing characters earns extra from the same IP) · expansion into new markets/industries without establishing operations · lower risk — the licensee assumes operational risk and cost Quality control — the brand's reputation is at risk · dependency on the licensee's success if licensing is a large share of revenue · IP protection — risk of misuse or infringement
    Licensee pros Licensee cons
    Access to established IP and immediate brand recognition (launching a video game with Mickey Mouse beats a new character) · cost saving versus developing your own IP · competitive advantage Licensing fees can be substantial · limited control — must adhere to terms on how and where the brand is used · dependency — if the agreement is terminated, the licensee is in trouble

    Licensing failures: Kodak — virtually invented digital camera photography but failed to effectively license the technology — a missed opportunity. Pierre Cardin — over-licensed its brand to anybody and everybody, losing its exclusivity and luxury status. Blockbuster — had the opportunity to license its brand and technology for online video streaming and failed to do so.

    Razor Blade model (bait and hook)

    Definition: a pricing strategy where a dependent good is sold at a loss or given away free to stimulate demand for a paired CONSUMABLE good. First implemented by King C. Gillette — sold razors at affordable prices while the blades customers repurchase generate the profit. Purpose: create a LOCK-IN EFFECT through compatibility or quality assurance.

    Strengths: recurring revenue · customer loyalty (they cannot buy the consumable elsewhere) · competitive advantage — a switching cost: to change brands you must replace the primary product, and a new competitor must first sell you their razor. Weaknesses: initial losses or low margins on the primary product · dependence on consumables — if the customer stops using it or finds an alternative consumable, the model breaks · potential backlash if consumables are priced too high relative to value.

    Successes: Gillette · Hewlett-Packard (printers priced competitively; profits come from replacement ink cartridges) · Nespresso (affordable machine, pods only from Nespresso — you buy the machine once but buy pods every week for life). Failures: Kodak — tried it with digital cameras and printers, but couldn't compete with cheap THIRD-PARTY cartridges — customers bought the cheap Kodak hardware and third-party ink. Sony PS Vita — proprietary memory cards priced significantly higher than other cards; consumers were turned off, contributing to lacklustre console sales.

    Leasing model

    The company retains ownership of an asset (equipment, vehicles, property) and rents it out for a set duration and fee. Often includes terms for maintenance, repair and eventual return. Examples: CAT Financial (Caterpillar's financial arm — operating leases on construction and mining equipment); automotive manufacturers leasing vehicles; aircraft leasing — AerCap, Air Lease Corporation (airlines operate without the capital cost of a fleet, so they can have more planes on lease than they could buy); WeWork (leases office space from landlords and subleases smaller spaces — per seat, per day, per week, per meeting); GE Healthcare (medical equipment on lease so hospitals access up-to-date technology without upfront investment).

    When to USE leasing: high-value assets essential for operations (mining, earth-moving, construction) · assets requiring regular upgrades (customers get the latest technology without depreciation costs) · markets with financial constraints where customers cannot afford outright purchase. When NOT to use: low-cost assets (when leasing you also pay finance costs indirectly — customers prefer to buy) · high-maintenance assets prone to breakdown · unpredictable market conditions where resale/residual value may depreciate significantly.

    Failures: Xerox — tried a leasing model for copiers in the late 1990s but the cost of maintaining and repairing the machines far exceeded leasing revenues. WeWork — over-committed to LONG-TERM leases without securing enough SHORT-TERM subleases → substantial losses and a highly publicised failed IPO.

    Bundling model

    Selling multiple products or services together as a package, often at a lower price than buying individually. Purposes: increase average order value · encourage engagement · move unsold inventory · cross-sell ancillary products. Forms: pure bundling, mixed bundling, leader bundling.

    Examples: Tata Sky (channel packages/bouquets), Reliance Jio (data + calls + app access in one plan), MakeMyTrip (flights + hotels + car rentals), Microsoft Office (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook), Adobe Creative Cloud (Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro), McDonald's bundled meals (burger + fries + Coke cheaper than separately).

    When to USE: product complementarity (burger → fries → Coke) · diverse product portfolio — introduce customers to new products or move slow sellers (Amul butter is very popular, Amul cheese less so — bundle them) · competitive markets — differentiate and provide better value. When NOT to use: lack of product strategy — if products don't complement each other or appeal to the same target market, bundling can harm the brand · risk of lower perceived value — if the bundle looks much cheaper than the sum of parts, customers may think the quality is poor · unwanted products in the bundle discourage purchase.

    Failures: Microsoft Windows 8 + Surface RT (2012) — the poor reception of Windows 8's drastic interface change dragged down the Surface RT tablet, which was already struggling. Amazon Fire Phone (2014) — bundled a one-year Amazon Prime subscription, but the phone lacked features competitors had and the focus on driving Amazon purchases was off-putting. Even though Amazon Prime was very successful, the Fire Phone failed.

    5.5New Age Business Models

    Context: the Digital Revolution, hailed as the FOURTH Industrial Revolution. Some new models are fleeting and hyped (NFTs, airdrops); others have become part of everyday life (Uber/Ola, BigBasket, Swiggy).

    The three forces of disruption

    1. Technology disruption — AI, machine learning, generative AI, blockchain, internet, smartphone, data analytics.
    2. Changing customer expectations — convenience, personalisation, on-demand services; unwillingness to wait.
    3. Geopolitical factors — China Plus One strategy, growing nationalism, COVID impact and supply chain disruption, the Russia–Ukraine war.

    After a boom of surging valuations followed by a steep downturn in unicorn valuations, questions are being raised about resilience and sustainability — but the dominance of new age models across every sector is here to stay.

    Platform business model

    The Uber story (summer 2007): the traditional taxi industry — a company owns a fleet, employs drivers, services vehicles, and the customer pays per day or per trip — created and controlled value in a linear, unidirectional way for decades. Uber owned no cars and hired no drivers as employees. It built a digital marketplace.

    Uber's genius: it didn't need to create value by itself. It FACILITATED the creation of value by connecting people who HAD something of value (a car, free time) with people who NEEDED that value.

    Definition: a digital platform acting as an intermediary between independent parties — typically consumers and producers. The operator does NOT own the asset being traded but profits from facilitating the interactions/transactions.

    Examples: Flipkart (commissions, fees, advertising, fulfilment services), Ola (commission per ride), Zomato (restaurant commission + Zomato Pro), Uber, Airbnb (connects hosts with guests, earns commission per booking).

    Strengths: scalability (once set up, accommodates large numbers) · NETWORK EFFECTS — the value of the platform increases as more people use it, creating a virtuous cycle · low asset intensity — no investment in the assets traded → lower capital requirement, potentially high margins. Weaknesses: 1. Significant initial investment and effort to get the flywheel moving to critical mass. If you're the first rider and no cars are available, the model fails — so Ola/Uber must ensure enough cars exist before the first ride, paying drivers to be there; equally, the first driver with no customers will walk away, so riders must be incentivised with discounts and free rides. 2. Regulatory risk — platforms disrupt existing models; protests against Uber continue (e.g. in Goa); some countries don't permit them. 3. Dependence on user loyalty — all participants must derive value. Too much surge pricing upsets customers; too little pay and drivers won't drive at 2 a.m. Platforms must constantly BALANCE THE NEEDS OF BOTH SIDES.

    Critical success factor: achieving a BALANCED, VIBRANT ECOSYSTEM of users on BOTH sides. Failures: PepperTap — a leading grocery app, well funded across multiple cities, failed due to poor unit economics, poor customer experience, unreliable hyper-local delivery. Homejoy (global) — connected cleaners with homeowners, well funded, but shut down over worker misclassification lawsuits (contractors vs employees).

    Aggregator business model

    Definition: consolidating specific services or products and offering them under a SINGLE BRAND. The aggregator does not provide the service or product itself — it acts as a connecting point. Examples: Urban Company (formerly UrbanClap) — beauty, cleaning, appliance repair, carpentry, plumbing; Ola Cabs (doesn't own the cabs); Policybazaar (compare and purchase insurance); Booking.com (owns no properties); Just Eat.

    Benefits: asset-light (no vehicles, hotels or goods owned → low capex) · scalable · variety — consumers access a range of services under one roof. Disadvantages: 1. A large user base is required to be profitable — the aggregator takes a very small fee, and attracting both service providers and consumers is challenging. 2. Quality control — the aggregator doesn't own the service. A bad plumber experience via Urban Company means the customer blames Urban Company and may never return. "That's not fair, but that's how life is." 3. DISINTERMEDIATION RISK — once a direct relationship forms between customer and service provider, they may bypass the aggregator, losing revenue on future or even the current transaction.

    Failures: TinyOwl (Indian food delivery aggregator — logistical challenges, high cash burn, insufficient funds, lack of profitability); Homejoy. The Homejoy challenge: if a contractor damages a home, who bears the insurance — Homejoy or the individual contractor?

    On-demand business model

    Definition: companies using technology to fulfil customer needs immediately or with minimal waiting, leveraging ubiquitous internet access, mobile technology and real-time location. Examples: Swiggy (food within 30 minutes), Urban Company, Practo (connects patients with doctors, diagnostic centres, pharmacies on demand), Instacart (personal shoppers pick up groceries and deliver within a promised window).

    Strengths: customer convenience → satisfaction and loyalty · scalability — "who likes to wait when you can get it instantly?" · cost efficiency — typically app-based with no physical infrastructure. Weaknesses: - Logistical nightmare — demand near office complexes between 1–2 p.m. can be multiple times the daily average. - Fluctuating demand — during an IPL match or Wimbledon, food demand far outstrips the supply of delivery riders. - Quality control given the immediate nature of the service. - Substantial real-time infrastructure requirement — the app must be highly robust. - Supply chain — managing inventory for instantaneous demand (Diwali sweets or gold). - Service provider availability during holidays and long weekends.

    Failures: TinyOwl (excessive cash burn, negative unit economics — "for an on-demand business to make money is very tough because people use it once in a while when there is an urgent need"); TaskRabbit (trouble scaling and acquiring customers profitably).

    Subscription-based model

    Definition: charging a recurring fee, typically monthly or yearly, to access a product or service. Originally for traditional media (newspapers, magazines). Traditional examples: Times of India, India Today, Vogue India, Tata Sky / Dish TV. Digital examples: OTT — Netflix, Amazon Prime, Disney+ Hotstar · SaaS — Zoho, Freshworks (subscription rather than a one-time perpetual licence) · Music streaming — Spotify, Gaana.

    Strengths: predictable revenue — a steady income stream that makes financial forecasting easy · customer retention and higher lifetime value · inventory management — predictable demand reduces storage costs and helps production scheduling (a daily milk subscription tells you exactly how much to procure, so wastage is minimal). Weaknesses: customer acquisition is hard — convincing customers to commit to recurring payment, especially where the model isn't common · customer churn — retention is difficult without continuous value addition or against competing services · price sensitivity — customers won't continue if they don't see value.

    Successes: Amazon Prime, Zomato Pro, Netflix (vast library, personalised recommendations, consistent value addition). Failures: HOOQ (couldn't compete with Netflix or Prime, shut down in India); MoviePass (unlimited cinema tickets for a monthly fee — the model was not financially sustainable).

    D2C — Direct to Consumer

    Definition: selling directly to end customers without traditional retail channels or intermediaries (distributors, wholesalers, retailers). Full control over manufacturing, marketing, selling and distribution. Indian examples: Lenskart (website, app, physical stores; controls everything from manufacturing to customer service and the entire supply chain), Zivame (online lingerie — a breadth of sizes and styles traditional retailers can't match), Bewakoof (online fashion, popular with younger consumers, effective social media marketing), boAt (trendy affordable headphones and speakers). Global examples: Warby Parker (stylish glasses direct at lower prices), Casper (mattresses, 100-night risk-free trial — unheard of in the industry), Dollar Shave Club (razors and grooming on subscription).

    Strengths: better margins — the distributor/wholesaler/retailer margin is captured by the brand · control over customer and brand — they get the data: customer experience, direct feedback, repeat purchase rate · flexibility — implement changes quickly on customer feedback (vs coordinating multiple intermediaries). Weaknesses: logistics and supply chain complexity and expense (previously outsourced to distributors/retailers) · customer acquisition — you must acquire customers digitally and spend heavily on marketing (vs a neighbourhood store where people simply walk in) · scaling challenges in maintaining product quality and customer service. Failure: Juicero — sold a juicer plus proprietary juice packs; shut down after criticism of high prices and the discovery that the juice packs could simply be squeezed by hand — you didn't need the juicer at all.

    Creator economy

    Definition: creators — individuals or small groups — produce, share and monetise their original content or products, often via social media or specialised platforms, building businesses around their PERSONAL BRAND and ability to attract and engage audiences. Monetisation: physical goods, digital goods, affiliate marketing, brand sponsorships, subscriptions from followers.

    Indian examples: Bhuvan Bam (BB Ki Vines) — YouTube ad share, sponsorships, merchandise; Kusha Kapila — sponsored posts and brand collaborations; Moj (short video platform). Global: MrBeast (Jimmy Donaldson) — ad share, brand partnerships, merchandise; Charli D'Amelio (TikTok) — sponsorships, product promotions, merchandise; Twitch streamers — subscriptions, donations, sponsorships.

    Strengths: democratisation of value creation — monetise talent WITHOUT GATEKEEPERS · flexibility — work on your own terms, choose your content, engage directly with the audience · diverse revenue streams. Weaknesses: intense competition — the barrier to entry is low, so standing out and gathering a substantial audience is hard · PLATFORM DEPENDENCE — heavy reliance on platform policies; any algorithm or monetisation change can significantly impact income · income instability — earnings depend on consistently producing fresh, engaging, on-trend content.

    C2C — Consumer to Consumer

    Definition: transactions directly between two consumers, typically facilitated by a third-party platform, without a business or organisation intervening. Examples: OLX, Quikr, CarTrade; globally eBay, Etsy (handmade and vintage items, craft supplies).

    Strengths: market expansion — no physical storefront; a seller anywhere and a buyer anywhere can transact without geographic constraints · cost reduction — the business holds and manages no inventory · increased variety — access to products unavailable in traditional stores. Challenges: trust and security — "the reason we buy from Amazon, BigBasket or Flipkart is because we trust them to ensure quality is genuine and to give a full refund. Buying from an unknown person is challenging." · quality control — what one person considers a good quality car may differ from another's view · customer service — handling disputes and returns is harder; the platform cannot provide the guarantee.

    "One of the reasons BigBasket, Flipkart and Amazon succeeded in a trust-deficit economy like India is because they managed to BUILD THAT TRUST." Priorities for a C2C platform: trust and security measures, a robust dispute resolution mechanism, and a high-quality user experience.

    Freemium model

    Definition: the product/service is provided free of charge, but money is charged for proprietary or additional features, functionalities, or virtual goods. Freemium = FREE + PREMIUM. Objective: attract large volumes to the free offering, then convert a small portion into paying customers. Premise: once a user is accustomed to the basic version, they'll pay for features that enhance utility.

    When to USE: scalable products — distributable to many users at low cost; suitable for digital products where the marginal cost per additional customer is very low · network effects — the product becomes more valuable as more people use it · a clear, compelling value proposition for the premium features. When NOT to use: high production or maintenance cost per user (significant incremental cost per additional user) · difficulty converting users — if the free version gives too much value there's little incentive to upgrade · too much friction in using the product.

    Successes: Zomato (free discovery app; Zomato Gold → Zomato Pro paid), Gaana (Gaana Plus — ad-free, unlimited downloads), YouTube (ad-free premium), LinkedIn (basic networking free; LinkedIn Premium paid), Zoom (free video conferencing for a limited time, fees for extended usage). Failures: Evernote — "too many features were offered for free, which caused difficulty converting users to premium because users were satisfied and their needs were met." Pandora — pulled out of many international markets due to high costs under its freemium model. Strengths: quickly builds a large user base (no friction — who doesn't like to try something free?) · low customer acquisition cost — converting a small portion of a large free base is cheaper than paid Google/social campaigns. Weaknesses: revenue conversion is very challenging — "people don't like to pay even a small amount; as long as it's free they will use it" · perceived value — if the free version is too good, users see no reason to pay.

    Crowdsourcing model

    Definition: getting work, ideas or funding — typically online — from a CROWD of people. CROWD + OUTSOURCING. Appeal: tap into a diverse, vast talent pool without geographical constraints; give people a platform to contribute to a cause they're passionate about. Mutually beneficial — the business gets input/support, the crowd gets the opportunity to contribute, often for rewards.

    When to USE: need for innovation or new ideas from a diverse group · need for capital — access to many small investors · tasks and services that can be done remotely without a specific skill set (during COVID lockdowns, crowdsourcing provided help in remote areas, especially to the sick and elderly). When NOT to use: tasks involving sensitive or proprietary information (healthcare data) due to security concerns · where quality control is critical — "for healthcare support, mental health support or a suicide helpline, it is better not to crowdsource but to use experts."

    Examples — India: Ketto ("Key To Tomorrow") — online crowdfunding for social, personal and creative causes; its revenue model: a 5% fee on total funds raised plus a 3% payment gateway fee. Topcoder — crowdsourcing platform for designers, developers, data scientists and competitive programmers; now owned by Wipro; pays community members for project work and sells the community's services to corporate and SMB clients. Global: Kickstarter (creators fund projects), Wikipedia (content created and edited by users). Strengths: access to a wide range of talent and ideas, often at very low cost · fosters great engagement by addressing people's passion. Weaknesses: quality control · difficulty managing and coordinating inputs from many contributors.

    SuperApp model

    Definition: a single mobile application offering a wide array of services under one umbrella — a one-stop solution for daily needs from entertainment to shopping to payments. Fundamental characteristic: aggregating various services within one application, reducing the need to switch between apps. Thrives on convenience, ease of use, integrated user experience.

    Three things that make it work: user retention (a holistic solution means no app-switching) · DATA SYNERGY — leverage data collected across services to understand behaviour and personalise · ECONOMIES OF SCOPE — use infrastructure and resources built for one service to support others.

    When to USE: diverse services that can be seamlessly integrated · a large existing user base. When NOT to use: specialised services (a mental health support company is unlikely to belong inside a general healthcare app) · regulatory challenges — in some regions combining certain services may be treated as an anti-competitive practice.

    Successes: Paytm (recharges, bill payments, shopping, banking, investing); Tata Neu (groceries, medicine, electronics, hotel and airline reservations, loyalty points usable across verticals); WeChat (messaging, social media, shopping, payments); Gojek (Indonesia — food delivery, digital payments, ride-hailing, shopping). Failure: Hike Messenger — tried to become a super app by integrating news, payments and messaging, but couldn't retain users and the value proposition was never proven → shut down. Strengths: convenience · data leverage for personalisation. Weaknesses: complex to develop and maintain, requiring huge investment in technology and resources · quality control across a wide range of services.

    5.6SaaS — Software as a Service1

    The bakery story: a small family-owned bakery buried in paper, manually tracking orders, stock and deliveries — mistakes happen, satisfaction declines. He can't afford a computer, an operator, a UPS and all the infrastructure. He discovers a SaaS solution for bakeries: within a few clicks he manages orders, tracks inventory in real time, optimises delivery routes — accessible from mobile anywhere in the world, and customers can see order status from their own phones.

    Definition: a software delivery model where applications are hosted by a provider and made available over the internet, eliminating the need for customers to install, manage and maintain the software. Accessed on a subscription basis (monthly/yearly) with a recurring fee.

    The key shift: responsibility for infrastructure, maintenance and updates moves from the CUSTOMER to the SaaS PROVIDER. In accounting terms, CAPITAL EXPENDITURE on infrastructure becomes OPERATIONAL EXPENDITURE as a monthly subscription fee.

    Why everyone loves SaaS

    Stakeholder Why they love it
    Customers Plug and play — no hardware, backup hardware, multiple software versions or computer-centre operational issues · high uptime and availability — operations don't stop because your computer failed · less upfront cost AND lower total cost of ownership · variable and incremental cost — earlier you had to estimate how many licences you'd need in six months; now you can scale from 10 to 20 to 30 users incrementally
    Developers Easier to develop for one hardware environment and one software version · easier to troubleshoot — recreate the reported problem only in your own environment
    Businesses and investors Subscription revenue = recurring revenue = PREDICTABLE revenue. With 1,000 customers you can predict next month's and next quarter's revenue

    The alternative: legacy on-premise IT infrastructure — high maintenance cost, the need for backups and disaster recovery (what if the office floods or catches fire?), and a lot of trained manpower.

    SaaS challenges

    1. Security — the data is in the cloud somewhere. Is it secure? Can someone else access it? Privacy issues — could a competitor get key data?
    2. Response time — with many people accessing simultaneously, response can be slower than on-premise. Mitigated by today's computing power and SLAs, but technically real. Where microseconds matter — e.g. STOCK EXCHANGE TRADING SOFTWARE — it may make sense to keep enterprise software on-premise, because microseconds can be the difference between profit and loss.
    3. The control perception is a real challenge.

    Evolution: from on-premise installation to cloud, driven by advances in internet connectivity, cloud infrastructure, and the need for scalable, cost-effective solutions. "Internet and cloud are the two drivers of software industry evolution."

    Five key characteristics of the SaaS model — memorise

    1. Multi-tenancy — applications designed to serve multiple customers (tenants) on shared infrastructure → cost efficiency and scalability.
    2. Subscription-based pricing — pay-as-you-go, recurring fees based on usage or a predefined plan.
    3. Centralised management — the provider handles updates, maintenance, security and infrastructure.
    4. Accessibility and connectivity — from anywhere with an internet connection, on laptop, mobile or tablet, enabling remote work and collaboration (SaaS came to the rescue during COVID).
    5. Continuous innovation and upgrades — before SaaS, a developer had to physically install every update at each customer location. Imagine having to install at 25,000 customer premises worldwide. Now you change it once where it's hosted and all 25,000 get it instantaneously.

    Benefits: cost savings · scalability · rapid deployment (no complex installation/configuration) · flexibility and customisation · accessibility and collaboration.

    Horizontal vs Vertical SaaS

    Horizontal SaaS Vertical SaaS
    Definition Usable by any industry across any sector Focused on a specific sector
    Examples Salesforce, Freshworks (CRM), Office 365, Tally, QuickBooks, Slack Textura (construction management), Fleetmatics (logistics/vehicle allocation), Guidewire (insurance), Veeva (pharma), Infor (manufacturing); Zenoti (Hyderabad)

    Newer specialised types that emerged after: developer tools and developer apps.

    The four SaaS company profiles

    Company Business model Key differentiation Strengths Challenges Competitors
    Freshworks (Indian, listed in the US) Suite of customer engagement software — customer support, CRM, marketing automation. Horizontal User-friendly interface, ease of implementation, affordable pricing — accessible to businesses of all sizes Comprehensive suite, seamless integration, excellent customer support Increasing competition; need to continuously innovate to prevent churn; scalability as the base grows Zendesk, Salesforce Service Cloud, Help Scout
    Zoho Suite covering CRM, project management, finance, collaboration A wide range of INTEGRATED business applications covering multiple aspects of operations — one platform instead of many vendors Extensive suite, customisable, affordable, strong support Brand visibility and awareness in a competitive market; enhancing offerings; integration across a wide range of applications Salesforce, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Oracle NetSuite
    Salesforce Cloud-based CRM — the leader and defining company of the SaaS sector Focus on CRM, an extensive ecosystem of third-party integrations, commitment to innovation Robust platform, vast marketplace of add-ons, very strong brand, commitment to customer success. Succeeded through EARLY ENTRY plus continuous innovation Maintaining leadership; scalability; integrating its acquisitions Microsoft Dynamics 365, HubSpot, Oracle CRM
    Zoom Cloud-based video conferencing and communication User-friendly interface, reliable video/audio quality, ease of use Intuitive platform (no learning curve), scalability, cross-platform compatibility, handles both large meetings and one-on-ones. Succeeded through timing of entry, focus on user experience and simplicity, and meeting the COVID-19 surge Security and privacy concerns; competing with established players Microsoft Teams, Cisco Webex, Google Meet

    SaaS pricing models — 8 methods with examples

    Method Description Examples
    Freemium pricing Basic version free, charge for advanced features or additional usage Dropbox (limited free storage), Gmail, Mailchimp (free for limited subscribers)
    Pay-as-you-go Charge based on actual usage or consumption AWS (computing power, storage, data transfer), Twilio (messages, calls, interactions)
    Value-based pricing Prices set on the perceived value or benefit the customer derives Salesforce (users + level of functionality, considering the value it brings to sales and customer management), HubSpot (number of contacts/leads plus advanced features)
    Usage-based pricing Level of usage measured by metrics — active users, data volume, transactions Google Cloud Platform (virtual machines, storage, network traffic, API calls), Twilio
    Tiered pricing Multiple tiers with different feature levels and usage limits for different segments Canva (free, Pro, Enterprise), Zoom (Basic, Pro, Business, Enterprise — varying features, meeting durations and participant limits)
    Feature-based pricing Priced on specific features or modules the customer needs Adobe Creative Cloud (choose specific tools), Atlassian (Jira, Confluence — users + desired feature set)
    Per-user pricing Charge per user accessing the software Slack (active users, tiers for user limits), Microsoft 365
    Contract-based pricing Discounts or customised pricing based on contract duration and terms Adobe Sign (lower prices for longer commitments), Salesforce (discounts for annual vs monthly)

    SaaS metrics — the most testable section

    Metric Definition / formula
    MRR — Monthly Recurring Revenue Predictable revenue from monthly subscriptions
    ARR — Annual Recurring Revenue Current month revenue × 12
    Churn rate % of customers who cancel within a period. 100 customers last month, 90 this month → 10% churn**
    CLV / LTV — Customer Lifetime Value Total revenue expected from a customer over the entire relationship. A function of the churn rate
    CAC — Customer Acquisition Cost Total cost of acquiring customers (marketing, advertising, sales, onboarding expenses) ÷ number of customers acquired
    NPS — Net Promoter Score Customer satisfaction and loyalty

    The revenue evolution chain: Starting revenue + EXPANSION − CONTRACTION − CHURN + RESURRECTION = repeat revenue. - Expansion — more users added, or existing users adding modules. - Contraction — fewer employees at the customer → fewer users; or modules dropped. - Churn — a customer stops using the software entirely (shut down or moved to a competitor). - Resurrection — previously churned customers who come back (they restarted operations, or tried a competitor and didn't like it).

    NDR / Net Revenue Retention — the single most important SaaS metric

    NDR = (Starting MRR + Upgrades − Downgrades − Churn) ÷ Starting MRR

    Worked example: Starting MRR $6,000; downgrade $400 (existing users paying less because they're using fewer modules); churn $500 (customers who left entirely); upgrade $3,000 (existing customers buying more modules). (6,000 + 3,000 − 400 − 500) ÷ 6,000 = 8,100/6,000 = **135%**

    Benchmarks — memorise:

    NDR Verdict
    > 100% Healthy — upgrades outweigh downgrades and churn
    ~107% The average NDR of organisations that have successfully launched IPOs (Crunchbase survey — "just below 107%")
    109% Stated as the "ideal" NDR — customer spending is growing faster than churn
    > 120% Great
    135% Excellent in the SaaS industry

    Capital efficiency: Total cash burned (sales, operations, overheads) ÷ Annual Revenue Run Rate. Closer to 1 is better; ideally below 1 — meaning for every rupee/dollar burned you add a dollar of new ARR.

    The causal chain to remember: poor customer satisfaction → churn → NDR drops → valuation and business attractiveness drop.

    The SaaS customer lifecycle — six stages

    1. Customer acquisition — targeted marketing campaigns (digital advertising, content marketing producing engaging content so people download white papers and articles, generating organic traffic), SEO (rank on the first page), lead generation via webinars, gated content, email marketing, partnerships; conversion optimisation of website, UX and landing pages.

    2. Customer onboarding — "having got the customer to try your product, if the experience has a lot of friction, all the effort of generating the lead is wasted." - User training and documentation — tutorials, videos, knowledge bases, FAQs, interactive guides. - Onboarding emails and guides walking through key features. - Dedicated onboarding support — one-on-one assistance in the initial stages. If support staff are in a lower-cost geography like India, you can provide global support at Indian costs.

    3. Customer success and support — "different from sales, different from onboarding. This comes AFTER, focusing on the customer's desired outcome and how to get there." - Proactive engagement — regular check-ins; if they're struggling with or not using certain features, address it. Don't wait for them to drop off or raise a ticket. - Goal alignment — align the product's capabilities with the customer's specific goals. - Ongoing training and education — webinars and workshops so new joiners at the customer can catch up. - Multi-channel support — email, 24/7 live chat, phone, chatbots · knowledge base and self-service / FAQ · a ticketing system to track and manage enquiries.

    4. Churn management and retention - Churn analysis — analyse behaviour and identify patterns that trigger churn. "It doesn't happen suddenly — they would have stopped engaging with the product." - Intervention and re-engagement with at-risk customers: special offers, targeted offers, personalised communication, discounts. Once churn happens it is much harder to resurrect them.

    The offline analogy: a customer used their credit card regularly for eight months, then stopped for four months just before renewal. That is an at-risk customer — push usage, give promotions and discounts, offer a lower renewal price, before they churn. - Exit surveys and feedback from churned customers to identify improvement areas — product, pricing, functionality, modules, or a competitor. - Retention techniques — regular check-ins, customer success programmes, testimonials, expert panels, loyalty rewards.

    5. Upselling and cross-selling - Upselling — upgrade to higher-tier plans, more licences, or new modules (a Tally accounting customer adding inventory management or payroll). - Feature expansion — when GST was introduced, GST accounting and reconciliation was an additional module = more money and more stickiness. - Value-based selling · targeted upsell campaigns (Amazon Prime users who haven't used Amazon Music) · bundling slow-moving or unused items with what they already use to induce a trial · personalised recommendations — "one of the advantages of SaaS is you know the ENTIRE CUSTOMER JOURNEY — exactly what they're using, where they're struggling, what value they're getting" · education and awareness.

    6. Customer feedback and continuous improvement — surveys and feedback forms · user forums and communities (let them talk among themselves — they will come up with great ideas) · NPS and CSAT · analyse the feedback data to identify trends (if many people talk about price, or people are moving to a cheaper product, that's a trend) · product roadmap alignment · agile development and iterative releases.

    SaaS sales and marketing

    Step 1 — Target market identification and segmentation. Define industries, verticals or customer segments aligned with the value proposition. For vertical SaaS it's easy (built for one segment); for horizontal SaaS you choose which industries are likely early adopters. Then segment by company size, industry, location, specific needs.

    "The sales effort required to sell to a Fortune 50 company or the top 20 companies in India (Reliance, Tatas) is very different from selling to a mid-size company." Example: a project management SaaS targeting SMEs in creative industries (advertising agencies, graphic design studios); a pharmacy SaaS targeting standalone pharmacies of a particular size, not chains.

    Step 2 — Lead generation: content marketing (white papers, articles, blogs — "in order to download those white papers, they must give me their contact information") · SEO · paid advertising (Google Ads, LinkedIn, social).
