    5.8Blockchain and Bitcoin1

    The magic ledger analogy

    Imagine a magic ledger book that everyone in the world can look at. When people trade, they write the details in it. Once written, it can never be erased or changed. And there is not just one copy — everybody has a copy, and every time a new trade is written, all the magic books update.**

    Block + chain: the blockchain is a series of blocks — like pages. Each block contains a list of trades. Once a block/page is full, a new block is created and LINKED to the previous one — forming a chain.

    The puzzle (hash): every page comes with a puzzle whose solution is created from the information on that page. If someone changes the information, the solution no longer matches the original and everyone knows the page has been tampered with.

    The three analogies

    The library analogy:

    Library element Blockchain equivalent
    Books Blocks — each has limited pages; when filled, a new book starts, and each book has a reference to the last book filled — the cryptographic link
    The library's collection The full ledger of all transactions
    A book put on the shelf A block added to the blockchain — it can never be altered. An error requires starting a NEW book with references to the correction
    Librarians NODES or MINERS — volunteers who confirm details before a new book is added; they must agree the information is correct — this is CONSENSUS
    Visitors Transactions — anyone can visit and read; they can start a new book if they have information to add. Once on the shelf it is permanent and visible to everyone
    Thousands of branches worldwide Security — even if one library burns down or is altered, integrity remains, because you would have to alter the MAJORITY of libraries in exactly the same way

    The town square ledger analogy: a large ledger book chained to a table in the town square. Pages = blocks; when a page is filled, a new one starts and the first line of the new page is a SUMMARY OR HASH of the previous page, connecting them. The town committee = nodes/miners — scattered through the town, they must all agree a transaction is legitimate before it's written. They don't erase or change records — they only ADD new verified transactions. Since the ledger is in the square, anyone can read it — full transparency. Trust is established not by trusting an individual but BY TRUSTING THE SYSTEM.

    The three key aspects of blockchain

    1. Immutability — practically unchangeable once data is added.
    2. Trust — data can only be trusted at its entry point; it eliminates reliance on anyone else tampering with the data, intentionally or unintentionally.
    3. Versatility — not just Bitcoin: decentralised finance, non-fungible tokens, smart contracts.

    Decentralised design — the database is scattered across several nodes worldwide, like having many copies of the same ledger. If one node tries to alter data, the network REJECTS it. Transparency with anonymity — anyone can view Bitcoin blockchain transaction activity through personal nodes or online blockchain explorers (contrast: only the bank knows a banking transaction). But encryption ensures anonymity — you can see that A sold something to B, but who A and B are is anonymous. Security — newly added blocks follow a linear chronological pattern; altering data changes the unique identifier (HASH), making unauthorised alteration detectable.

    Blockchain vs Bitcoin — history matters for MCQs

    Year Event
    1991 Blockchain technology first outlined by Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta — two researchers who wanted a system where document timestamps could not be tampered with
    January 2009 Bitcoin launched — blockchain's first real application. In the research paper introducing Bitcoin, Satoshi Nakamoto (the pseudonym of the creator) referred to it as "a new electronic cash system that's fully P2P, peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party."

    The key: Bitcoin USES blockchain as a means to transparently record a ledger of payments or transactions. Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency; blockchain is the technology. Nakamoto introduced blockchain to ensure that THE SAME BITCOIN WAS NEVER SPENT TWICE.

    Blockchain vs Banking

    Dimension Banks Bitcoin / blockchain
    Operational hours Traditional business hours, excluding holidays Round the clock, all year
    Transaction fees and speed Varying fees and timeframes depending on SWIFT/international/domestic and FX; fees can be a substantial portion of a small transfer Fees set by the users; transaction times much faster, influenced only by network congestion; typically a fraction of bank cost
    Regulation Mandated to follow KYC norms Completely open — no mandatory identity verification. Internet connection is enough
    Transfer requirements Government ID, bank account, mobile phone Only internet access and a mobile device
    Privacy and security Reliant on bank server security and user vigilance Depends on the user's anonymity and security measures
    Transaction control and seizure Banks can deny or freeze transactions and accounts; governments can seize assets Anonymously held Bitcoin is much tougher for governments to seize (though the law is still evolving and countries have tried)

    Seven real-world blockchain use cases

    Context: Bitcoin's blockchain stores transactional data, and over 23,000 cryptocurrency systems use blockchain. Companies experimenting: Walmart, Pfizer, AIG, Siemens, Unilever; IBM has a Food Trust blockchain to trace food products.

    1. Banking and finance — "perhaps no industry stands to benefit more." Banks operate 5 days a week — deposit a cheque Friday 6 p.m. and you likely wait until Monday; transactions take 1–3 days to verify. Blockchain never sleeps — transactions in minutes or seconds regardless of day. Also faster and more secure bank-to-bank exchange (given the sums, even a few days of money in transit carries significant cost and risk). Stock settlement and clearing takes up to 3 days, or longer internationally, meaning money and shares are frozen — blockchain could drastically reduce this. Important because if you plan to sell immediately, you can't take possession until the money is credited, and by then the price may have changed.
    2. Currency — the US dollar is controlled by the Federal Reserve; under a central authority, a user's data and currency are at the whim of their bank or government. The Fed can print more dollars → inflation → lower value. Risks: bank hacks exposing private information; bank collapse; unstable government. In 2008 several falling banks were bailed out partially using taxpayer money. Blockchain gives those in countries with unstable currencies a more stable currency and financial system — had they converted to Bitcoin before the devaluation, they would not have lost value — and access to a wider network of counterparties who won't accept a stressed currency. Also profound for those without any state identification who cannot access savings or brokerage accounts and have no safe way to store wealth.
    3. Healthcare — store patient medical records securely; once signed, the record cannot be changed. Records encoded and stored with a private key, accessible only to specific individuals — share the private key with your physician or hospital.
    4. Property records — today a physical deed must be delivered to a government employee at the registrar's office and manually entered into a central database. Costly, time-consuming and prone to human error. Blockchain eliminates scanning documents and tracking physical files; ownership is accurate and permanently recorded. In war-torn areas with no government or financial infrastructure, proving property ownership is nearly impossible — blockchain can establish a transparent, clear timeline of ownership.
    5. Smart contracts — computer code built into a blockchain to facilitate an agreement between two parties. They operate under a set of conditions all users agree to; when those conditions are met, the terms are AUTOMATICALLY carried out — nobody needs to intervene. Example: a tenant leases an apartment; the landlord agrees to give the door code as soon as the security deposit is paid. The smart contract automatically sends the door code when payment is made, and could be programmed to change the code if rent isn't paid.
    6. Supply chain — IBM Food Trust: suppliers record the origins of materials, letting companies verify authenticity of the product and of common labels such as organic, local and fair trade. Forbes noted the food industry is increasingly adopting blockchain to track the path and safety of food from farm to user.
    7. Elections and voting — potential to eliminate election fraud and boost turnout. Tested in November 2018 in the West Virginia midterm elections in the US. Would make votes nearly impossible to tamper with, maintain transparency, reduce the personnel needed, provide nearly instant results and eliminate the need for recounts.

    Two detailed blockchain illustrations

    Coffee supply chain: Without blockchain you'd have to trust supplier claims and certifications — you could never truly know if the "organic" or "fair trade" labels were genuine. With blockchain: Colombian farmers harvest and enter date, location, type of bean → first block. The shipping company logs transportation details, conditions like temperature, expected delivery dates. The Italian roaster logs roasting date, temperature, packaging details. Shipped to a New York coffee store — a QR code on the packaging lets you scan and view the entire journey. Business benefits: builds consumer trust · reduces fraudulent labelling · increases efficiency in spotting bottlenecks (if shipping took too long, or roasting started long after receipt, it's visible and correctable).

    Real estate: Without blockchain the process involves real estate agents, banks, title companies, the registrar, escrow services — each step taking time and involving checks; there is a risk of fraud in title transfers and hidden transaction terms. With blockchain: listing and offer made directly on a blockchain platform · verification — the property's entire history from construction to damages to previous sales is recorded transparently and cannot be tampered with · secure transparent payment via cryptocurrency without traditional banking delays or charges · title transfer executed as a SMART CONTRACT, immediately and transparently. Benefits: fewer middlemen → cost and time savings · speeds up the process with automated smart contracts · increased transparency and security, reducing fraud.

    The 8 benefits of blockchain — memorise the list

    1. Accuracy of the chain — transactions approved by thousands of computers, removing almost all people from verification → less human error. Even if one computer errs, the error affects only one copy and is not accepted by the rest of the network.
    2. Cost reduction — no need for a bank to verify a transaction or a notary to sign a document, eliminating third-party verification costs. Business owners incur a fee when accepting credit cards because a bank or processor handles it; Bitcoin has zero or very small transaction fees.
    3. Decentralisation — no central store; every node updates when a new block is added, making tampering very difficult.
    4. Efficient transactions — no central authority means no operational-hours issues; completed in minutes, especially valuable for cross-border trades across multiple time zones.
    5. Private transactions — many blockchain networks are public databases: anyone can view the transaction history, but cannot identify who made the transaction. It is a MYTH that Bitcoin is fully anonymous — there is a viewable address that can be associated with a user if it gets out, so it is SEMI-ANONYMOUS: the address, not the identity.
    6. Secure transactions — once recorded, the transaction is verified by the network (validation), then added to a block; each block has a unique hash and the unique hash of the block before it, so once confirmed, blocks cannot be altered forever.
    7. Transparency — blockchains are mostly built on open-source software, so anyone can view the code and auditors can review it. No central authority controls the code; anyone can suggest changes or upgrades, but more than 51% of network users must agree — consensus.
    8. Banking the unbanked — "this is really the core of it." Anyone can use it regardless of ethnicity, gender, location, cultural background or income level. Per the World Bank, 1.3 billion adults have no bank account or means of storing their money. Many live in developing countries and depend entirely on cash, which they must store in hidden locations to avoid being robbed. Cryptocurrency is very difficult to steal.

    The 4 drawbacks of blockchain

    1. Technology cost — the technology is not free. Bitcoin's proof-of-work system consumes vast computational power — the energy consumed by the millions of devices on the Bitcoin network is MORE THAN THE COUNTRY OF PAKISTAN CONSUMES ANNUALLY. Some mining farms now use solar power, excess natural gas from fracking sites, or wind energy.
    2. Speed and data inefficiency — Bitcoin's proof of work takes about 10 minutes to add a new block, meaning the network manages only about 3 transactions per second. By comparison, Visa can process 65,000 transactions per second. Some blockchains now boast more than 30,000 TPS, and Ethereum after merging is predicted to reach 100,000 TPS. Block size is also debated, because it directly affects scalability.
    3. Illegal activity — the same anonymity that protects privacy allows illegal trading. Banking has strict AML laws and you can check if a transfer funds terrorism; that isn't possible here. The dark web lets users buy and sell illegal goods using Bitcoin. Law enforcement (the FBI) has shut down some operators. But: illicit activity accounted for only 0.24% in 2022 — the benefits far outweigh this drawback.
    4. Regulation — governments differ on whether and how much to regulate; a decentralised network is tough to regulate, though governments can ban citizens from owning Bitcoin. With widespread adoption this has become less of a concern.

    Cryptocurrency

    Definition: a digital or virtual currency that uses CRYPTOGRAPHY for security, making it difficult to counterfeit. Unlike traditional government-issued currency (USD, EUR, INR), it operates on a decentralised platform based on blockchain technology.

    Three mechanics: blockchain (a decentralised, distributed digital ledger recording transactions across many nodes, ensuring records cannot be altered once entered and validated) · cryptography (secures transactions and controls the creation of new coins) · decentralisation.

    Types — memorise the ticker and the distinguishing feature:

    Cryptocurrency Ticker Distinguishing feature
    Bitcoin BTC The first and biggest; jokingly called "digital gold"
    Ethereum ETH More than a cryptocurrency — it allows SMART CONTRACTS and distributed applications (dApps) to be built and run 24/7 without downtime, fraud, control or third-party interference
    Ripple XRP Known for its digital payment protocol more than for being a cryptocurrency
    Litecoin LTC Created by Charlie Lee; often considered "silver to Bitcoin's gold"
    Bitcoin Cash BCH A FORK of Bitcoin; focuses on larger block size to process more transactions
    Cardano / Polkadot / Chainlink ADA / DOT / LINK Newer coins with unique features around smart contracts and dApps
    Monero / Zcash XMR / ZEC Enhanced PRIVACY features

    Seven uses: transactions (buy goods and services) · investments (hoping the value rises, like gold) · remittances (cross-border payments without high fees, time delays, exchange rate conversion or time zone issues) · fundraising and crowdsourcing — ICOs (Initial Coin Offerings) and STOs (Security Token Offerings) · privacy and anonymity (Monero, Zcash) · smart contracts (conditional self-executing contracts, most notably on Ethereum) · DeFi (Decentralised Finance) — an ecosystem of financial applications built on blockchain, primarily Ethereum, replicating traditional lending and borrowing without any intermediary.

    Five benefits: security against fraud/counterfeiting · decentralisation (no central authority risk, no government interference, no risk of a central agency going bust) · transparency (public ledgers display all transactions) · low fees (important for cross-border and large transactions, and for micropayments where a fixed fee would be a large portion of the amount) · financial inclusion for those who cannot complete KYC or lack documentation to open a bank account.

    Five criticisms and risks: volatility (you may suddenly find you've lost 50%; unlikely with dollars, euros or rupees) · regulatory concerns (governments may ban or regulate because of fears of terrorism, drug dealing, illegal purposes — anonymity and no KYC, outside the well-regulated banking channel) · security issues (cryptocurrency itself is secure but EXCHANGES AND WALLETS are vulnerable to attack) · irreversibility (unlike a credit card where you can appeal to the issuer, stop it, ask for a refund — in cryptocurrency, once done there is absolutely no recourse) · environmental concerns (mining requires significant computational power; a physical note has a one-time printing cost then gets used for years and traded many times).

    Bitcoin deep dive

    Origin: introduced by an unknown person or group under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto in a 2008 white paper titled "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System." Definition: a decentralised digital currency without a central bank or single administrator, sent from one user to another on a peer-to-peer network without intermediaries.

    Four needs it addresses: decentralisation (giving power back to the people, not a central authority) · transparency (all transactions recorded in a public ledger) · financial inclusion (banking the unbankable) · censorship resistance (transactions cannot be blocked or censored by governments or banks).

    Five characteristics — memorise: 1. Decentralised. 2. LIMITED SUPPLY — there will only ever be 21 MILLION Bitcoin. Unlike a government that can print more currency at its discretion, leading to devaluation. This makes it attractive as an asset to hold. 3. Pseudonymous — transactions and addresses are not directly linked to real-world identities. "I know the address; I don't know the person behind it." 4. Immutable — once recorded, a transaction cannot be reversed. 5. Divisibility — the smallest unit is a SATOSHI, named after the creator: one HUNDRED-MILLIONTH of a Bitcoin. This level of divisibility does not exist in physical currencies.

    Advantages: security against fraud · anyone can see the transfer · very low transaction fees, especially international · ease of access — users require only internet access, no bank or ATM · an emerging asset class because of limited supply. Disadvantages: volatility (only savvy investors should get into this; retail investors holding Bitcoin for investment is not advisable) · irreversibility · regulatory and security issues (the network is secure but individual wallets and exchanges may be hacked) · not universally accepted as payment ("can you go to a coffee shop in your local neighbourhood and pay in Bitcoin? Unlikely") · environmental concerns.

    Adoption milestones — memorise: - Japan recognised Bitcoin as legal tender in 2017. - El Salvador in 2021 became the FIRST COUNTRY to adopt it as legal tender. - Microsoft, Starbucks and AT&T accept Bitcoin for certain services. - JPMorgan and other major banks have started offering Bitcoin funds to clients.

    The future — four possibilities: mainstream adoption as a widely accepted payment form · more stringent regulation as adoption increases (which will affect price and usage but be good for the ecosystem) · technical innovation increasing scalability and efficiency · STORE OF VALUE vs CURRENCY — some believe Bitcoin will primarily serve as DIGITAL GOLD (a store of value) rather than an everyday currency.

    The two possible uses: (1) as an everyday currency instead of dollars/euros/rupees; (2) as a store of value — instead of bank fixed deposits, equities or gold, you hold digital gold.

    Is Bitcoin here to stay or a passing fad?

    Here to stay A passing fad
    Strongest brand recognition in the crypto world More efficient, environment-friendly cryptocurrencies will take over — Bitcoin is highly energy inefficient and environmentally damaging
    Continuously growing user base Regulatory crackdown could limit use or appeal
    Institutional interest legitimising it Technological issues like QUANTUM COMPUTING are a threat
    Decentralised and secure

    5.9NFTs — Non-Fungible Tokens

    The problem: You draw a beautiful piece of digital art, share it with friends, and before you know it it's all over the internet — some groups even send the same artwork back to you without realising you created it. How do you prove you are the original artist? How do you maintain value when digital copies look exactly the same as the original? Second example: you unlock a super rare costume in a video game, but in the digital world endless perfect copies can be made and shared — how does your item maintain its rare value?

    Definition — break the term down: - NON-FUNGIBLE = unique and cannot be replaced with something else — irreplaceable. - TOKEN = a digital representation of ownership.

    NFTs represent a way to PROVE OWNERSHIP AND AUTHENTICITY of digital items, irrespective of how many exact look-alike copies exist worldwide.

    Origin: took shape with blockchain technology. Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin proved digital assets could hold value; Ethereum introduced the capability to create more complex tokens, leading to the birth of NFTs. One of the earliest and most famous examples: CryptoKitties — a virtual game where players collected and bred unique digital cats.

    Five applications: digital art (100,000 copies may exist, but ownership traces back to you) · collectibles (digital versions of baseball cards with authenticity assured) · virtual real estate (Decentraland — buy, develop and sell plots of virtual land) · music and entertainment (musicians and filmmakers tokenising works to ensure fair compensation and royalties) · gaming (in-game items tokenised to maintain rarity and value).

    Real-life NFT applications — the five examples, with numbers

    Industry Example
    Digital art / auction houses Beeple's Everydays: The First 5000 Days — a digital collage sold as an NFT for $69.3 million through Christie's. A watershed moment in the acceptance of NFTs in the traditional art world.
    Music Kings of Leon's NFT album — When You See Yourself included a version with exclusive audio-visual art and a "golden ticket" providing special concert perks, letting them monetise directly and interact with fans with no intermediary (three types of NFTs)
    Virtual real estate Decentraland — a virtual reality platform powered by the Ethereum blockchain; users purchase, develop and sell parcels of virtual land; businesses set up virtual shops, casinos and art galleries; land parcels traded as NFTs appreciate based on location and development
    Fashion Gucci virtual sneakers — worn in AR or virtual worlds, sold as NFTs for a fraction of the cost of a real-world Gucci shoe
    Sports memorabilia NBA Top Shot — NBA in partnership with Dapper Labs; users buy, sell and trade officially licensed NBA collectible highlights ("moments"). Some rare moments have sold for hundreds of thousands of dollars

    Indian example: WazirX (Indian cryptocurrency exchange) launched an NFT marketplace where Indian artists and creators can auction digital assets.

    The debate:

    NFTs are here to stay NFTs are a fad
    Digital ownership — as we live more of our lives online, owning unique digital assets becomes more appealing and valuable Over-hype — as more people create NFTs the market may become saturated
    Artist empowerment — more control and better compensation, since commercial users must pay the artist Environmental concerns — NFTs consume a lot of energy to mint
    Diversification for investors — a new asset class for risk capital Regulatory challenges could impact growth

    5.10Web 1.0 / 2.0 / 3.0 — guaranteed comparison MCQ1

    Web 1.0 — the STATIC web Web 2.0 — the SOCIAL web Web 3.0 — the SEMANTIC web
    Also called READ-ONLY web READ-WRITE web READ-WRITE-EXECUTE web
    Characteristics Static HTML pages; information retrieval the primary function; limited basic graphics, mostly text; not optimised for mobile or varying screen sizes; accessed from a computer Users became CONTENT CREATORS and contributors; social media platforms; emphasis on user-generated content; interactive web applications; more vibrant, aesthetically pleasing designs; introduced APIs for software integration AI-driven and semantic technologies; highly DECENTRALISED data networks; various security features; integration of VR and AR; huge personalisation based on user behaviour and data — what you see and what I see will be very different
    Examples LiveJournal (a very early blogging platform), MySpace (precursor to modern social media) Facebook, Twitter, Instagram (user-generated content), Wikipedia (collaborative encyclopedia), YouTube (revolutionised video sharing) Ethereum (blockchain platform for dApps), ChatGPT and Siri (AI-driven tools), Decentraland (decentralised VR platform)
    Business impact Businesses established an online presence, mostly in the form of an ONLINE BROCHURE Businesses could engage directly with customers and gather insights from user-generated data (reviews, ratings); enabled dynamic e-commerce More profound personalised engagement; decentralisation offers a more secure and transparent way of transacting; AI/ML enhances user experience, prediction models and business insights
    Interactivity Minimal interaction Interaction and sharing Intelligent interactions
    Data control Centralised control by big corporations Centralised control by big corporations DECENTRALISATION — giving power back to individual users
    Business model focus Online presence / information User engagement and participation Decentralised business models with focus on security, privacy and enhanced user experience

    Four technological concerns with Web 3.0: 1. Quantum computing — as it advances, it threatens the cryptographic security measures foundational to Web 3.0, especially blockchain; security features could be broken. 2. Environmental impact — blockchain and mining criticised for high energy consumption. 3. Scalability — as decentralised networks grow, can they handle more transactions per second with appropriate response times? 4. Data privacy — decentralisation promises improved user control but demands rigorous security protocols against data breaches.

    Four benefits of embracing Web 3.0: cost efficiency (removing intermediaries) · direct customer engagement with a more personalised experience · enhanced security through decentralised systems and blockchain · fostering innovation.

    Implications for management: better strategic decision-making from comprehensive transparent information · personalised experiences driven by semantic understanding · traceability, transparency and efficiency of supply chains through blockchain · a more global workforce — platforms where professionals offer expertise on demand, breaking geographical boundaries.

    Four challenges: data privacy · uncertain regulatory landscape · learning curve — new skills and continuous upskilling, especially challenging for large companies with an ageing workforce · resource intensity of shifting to decentralised systems and implementing AI.

    Four things this means for students, managers and professionals: stay updated (continuous learning) · innovative mindset (embrace change, experiment) · stakeholder management (with decentralised data, stakeholder trust is crucial — transparent communication and ethical data handling) · collaborative approach (decentralisation leads to more partnerships).

    5.11Artificial Intelligence

    The 50-year framing: the last 50 years of computing was about building faster CALCULATORS — a CPU (hardware) plus software. The next 50 years is about building SUPER-INTELLIGENT SYSTEMS — instead of a CPU you have a GPU, and instead of software you have AI models. "Together, the GPU and AI model combination is literally like creating a NEW BRAIN."

    Value already delivered — memorise the percentages: - GitHub Copilot helps software developers save 55% of their time. - Customer support — AI handling queries/calls can reduce the people required by nearly half. - Creators — video editing and polishing time reduced by almost 90% (an hour becomes about 5 minutes). - Medicine — physicians diagnose with better quality and much faster.

    Three defining features of AI: it mimics human intelligence — simulating human thinking and problem-solving · it improves its performance through experience — it learns over time · it goes beyond simple rules — before AI, programming was completely rule-based: "if this happens, do this." AI handles complex situations without clear, explicit instructions.

    The nested hierarchy — AI ⊃ ML ⊃ Deep Learning ⊃ Generative AI ⊃ LLMs

    Term Definition
    Artificial Intelligence The broader concept of machines mimicking the human brain. Encompasses all intelligent behaviour, includes rule-based systems, focuses on decision making
    Machine Learning A subset of AI focused on DATA-DRIVEN learning. It learns from data (requires training data), improves with experience, and identifies patterns automatically. Uses supervised or unsupervised methods. Example: the Gmail spam folder learns patterns and classifies mail as spam
    Deep Learning A subset of machine learning which uses NEURAL NETWORKS for in-depth data processing and analysis — multiple layers of artificial neural networks extract meaningful inferences like a human brain
    Generative AI A subset of deep learning that GENERATES NEW CONTENT — original text, images, audio, computer code that never existed before. Trained on vast data sets, detects patterns, creates outputs without explicit instruction
    Large Language Models (LLM) Part of Generative AI — an AI model that learns from vast amounts of information (books, articles, websites) and can answer questions, write content, and hold a conversation like a human. Examples: OpenAI 4o, Claude 3.5, Llama

    Generative AI — how it works, in three steps: 1. Massive training — models learn from trillions of examples across the internet and books. 2. Pattern recognition — neural networks identify complex relationships in the training data. 3. Prediction generation — the system predicts what should come next based on learned patterns. "Literally it is predicting the next word and generating the output for you."

    Gen AI examples: ChatGPT (text), DALL·E (artwork), Midjourney (imagery). Gen AI by industry: healthcare — drug discovery and medical imaging/radiology analysis · education — personalised tutoring, generating quizzes, content and adaptive learning material · finance — algorithmic trading systems detecting unusual transaction patterns / fraud detection · media — creating custom content including videos to explain concepts.

    Agentic AI — the new frontier

    Definition: traditional AI (and even Gen AI) waits for instructions and responds to commands — that's PROMPTING. Agentic AI is designed to act like an INDEPENDENT AGENT — it can make its own decisions and perform tasks WITHOUT constant human guidance or prompting. Example: an AI model that not only understands how to book flights, but also finds the best deals, reschedules if there is a delay, and even handles refunds from various websites — all automatically.

    Agentic AI is about creating systems that can LEARN FROM THEIR ENVIRONMENT, MAKE SMART DECISIONS, AND ADJUST THEIR ACTIONS — much like a personal assistant who manages tasks without being told what to do.

    5.12ONDC — Open Network for Digital Commerce

    What it is: a Government of India initiative similar to UPI and other digital public infrastructure. It democratises e-commerce.

    The problem — barriers to SME e-commerce

    For the SELLER, setting up an e-commerce value chain requires: photographing and cataloguing products · a payment gateway · being searchable and reachable by customers · home delivery · a shopping cart for checkout · handling returns and cancellations · order fulfilment. "All of these are too daunting for a small merchant."

    Plus the platform lock-in problem — for BOTH sides: - Buyer: wants a product available at a discount but it's not on Flipkart because the seller sells only on Amazon or BigBasket. The buyer is restricted to the app they are on and misses the options available. To see everything, an individual would need to be on Amazon, Blinkit, Flipkart, BigBasket, Zepto — very cumbersome. - Seller: only gets customers on his app. A seller on Amazon offering a great deal cannot reach a consumer who is on Flipkart. Both sides lose opportunity — one reason for the low penetration of e-commerce in India.

    The e-commerce value chain behind a simple order: physical logistics · ratings and reviews (which the platform relies on to build trust for the next consumer) · warehousing (because customers expect same-day or next-day delivery, so goods must be pre-stocked, not manufactured after the order) · inventory management (right amount, avoiding overstocking especially of perishables) · payments (receipt from buyer, payment to seller, refunds on cancellation/return).

    The resulting challenges for each stakeholder:

    Stakeholder Challenges under the platform model
    Sellers No visibility — one seller among millions on a huge platform; the platform won't promote him · the platform dictates terms — we've seen restaurants complaining that Swiggy and Zomato charge 23–27%, but because it's a duopoly they can't do much · no access to data — the platform owns the buyer, the customer and the data, and won't pass on addresses or details · no data portability — thousands of buyers and 4.8-out-of-5 ratings on one platform cannot be transferred to another; you start from zero
    Buyers Cannot discover new sellers, especially for non-standard items — niche or LONG TAIL categories · must use multiple apps for multiple use cases
    Network participants (logistics) A courier must become a vendor to one or two large centralised platforms, sign a contract, get empanelled (which takes a long time), and is then dependent on the platform's policies, whims and fancies

    The ONDC solution

    An interoperable PROTOCOL, very similar to UPI.

    The UPI parallel: a sender with a sender app connected to the sender's bank initiates a transfer; the UPI layer in between receives it and sends it to the receiver's bank and then the receiver's app. Any sender on the UPI network can send to any receiver on the UPI network even though they don't bank with the same entity. ONDC sits between buyer → buyer app → [ONDC] → seller app → seller.

    Features: decentralised, unbundled, OPEN and INTEROPERABLE network — NOT a platform · population-scale infrastructure · built on the principle of UNBUNDLING of customer and seller acquisition so go-to-market effort is reduced · interoperable between platforms and applications for greater market access — you can be on any platform; if you plug into ONDC you can transact.

    Purpose: promotes fair competition, enhances user convenience, fosters innovation, expands choice, and eliminates the necessity of using multiple delivery apps.

    The illustrative examples: - Ramesh, a handloom weaver in a small Odisha village — for years his intricate sarees sold at a fraction of their worth to middlemen while city consumers paid a premium. With his granddaughter's help he lists directly on an ONDC-enabled platform; Ritu in Delhi buys directly — she gets an authentic high-quality saree at a better price and Ramesh receives the full value of his artistry. - Sunil, a mango farmer in Ratnagiri — a significant chunk of earnings went to dealers, agents and brokers. Through ONDC he gets orders directly from households and restaurants in Mumbai and Pune — he earns more and city customers get the freshest mangoes without transport and storage through multiple hands. - Ananya in Varanasi inherits her grandfather's collection of rare Hindi books; big platforms wouldn't do justice to used old books. She lists on a niche ONDC platform promoting regional literature, and a professor from Bangalore orders some for his course.

    "The aim of ONDC is not just about technology or commerce, but about DEMOCRATISING ACCESS AND EMPOWERING THE SMALLEST STAKEHOLDERS IN INDIA."

    Architecture — platform-centric vs network-centric

    Closed, platform-centric e-marketplace Open, network-centric e-marketplace
    The buyer accesses the platform (Flipkart, Amazon, BigBasket) and the seller accesses the same platform, using PROPRIETARY protocols The buyer interacts with a BUYER APPLICATION (which could be Flipkart, Amazon, MyGate, Paytm — any app); the buyer application exchanges data with a SELLER APPLICATION through OPEN PROTOCOLS created under ONDC, via routing nodes that do the MATCHMAKING; the seller application interacts with the seller

    The participants: buyer-side apps · seller-side apps · logistics providers (sometimes the logistics provider is the seller, sometimes independent) · technology service providers — payment providers, accounting and reconciliation, ratings and reviews, digital cataloguing, inventory management.

    "We have UNBUNDLED all the elements that a proprietary platform like Flipkart or Amazon would have done, broken them into independent steps, and onboarded independent players — so it is democratised." Earlier, when you bought from Amazon, Amazon decided who the logistics provider would be.

    ONDC network services participants: the registry (maintains who the sellers are, what items they sell, who the buyer apps are — which helps in discovery), defines network policies, decides scoring and badging, and determines inter-network interoperability; plus technology providers and payment processors.

    The five pillars of ONDC — memorise

    # Pillar Definition Examples
    1 Buyer-side app Any application interacting with buyers — the DEMAND side where the transaction originates Paytm, WhatsApp
    2 Seller-side app Any application interacting with sellers — the SUPPLY side; publishes the seller's catalogue and fulfils orders Flipkart, BigBasket, Amazon (if they choose to join), or directly kirana stores, brands, or the factory
    3 Adapter interfaces Open APIs developed on the open-source, interoperable specification of the backend protocol —
    4 Gateway Application ensuring discoverability of all sellers by MULTICASTING the search request received from a buyer application, based on location, availability and customer preferences —
    5 Open registries Applications maintaining the list of participants who join ONDC, network policies, what products they sell, what locations, and which logistics providers service which areas —

    The transaction flow — the Atta example (learn this sequence)

    1. Vijay logs into a consumer application and searches for atta.
    2. The GATEWAY checks the multi-domain registry and BROADCASTS the search to retailer seller nodes.
    3. Results displayed: Gupta Kirana Store — ₹50 WITHOUT delivery; BigBasket (fulfilled by a modern kirana store) — ₹150 INCLUDING delivery.
    4. Vijay places the order with Gupta Kirana Store, which doesn't deliver — so he searches ONDC for delivery services.
    5. The gateway again checks the registry and broadcasts to delivery seller nodes.
    6. Results: Dunzo ₹50, Good Box ₹70 in his PIN code. Vijay selects Dunzo.
    7. Payment options offered: UPI or cash on delivery. Vijay pays ₹50 for atta + ₹50 for delivery.

    The four application roles in that flow:

    Role What it allows Who can be it
    Retail buyer application Individual consumers to discover and transact with retailers/kirana stores Paytm, WhatsApp, Google Pay (potentially Flipkart/Amazon too)
    Retail seller application Retailers and kirana stores to offer products and services to consumers BigBasket (a small kirana store can come in through it), or a large kirana store can be a retail seller application DIRECTLY on ONDC
    Logistics buyer application Consumers and retailers to place orders for delivery services WhatsApp, Google, BigBasket, or Gupta Kirana Store itself if it has its own delivery boys
    Logistics seller application Logistics providers to offer services to consumers or retailers Dunzo, Good Box. Earlier they needed a B2B enterprise relationship with Amazon or Flipkart to deliver — now they can be on ONDC and get direct orders from the consumer

    Benefits by stakeholder

    Stakeholder Benefits
    Buyers A single platform to access all domains and all sellers, not restricted to one app · unified experience — choose whom to buy from, who delivers, and the payment mechanism · wider options for price, delivery and add-ons — buy one item from a Flipkart-only seller, one from an Amazon-only seller, one direct from a small merchant, using two different delivery partners, all in a SINGLE ORDER · fast, hyper-local fulfilment
    Sellers Discoverable by the ENTIRE buyer universe across any app on ONDC · one-time single registration, not separate onboarding for each platform · low-cost access to the complete value chain · AUTONOMY over rules and terms — earlier, if 80% of sales came from Flipkart, a dispute could see him removed and 80% of revenue vanish overnight · increased profitability — no single platform taking disproportionate fees (saving a substantial portion of the 23–27% take rate in food delivery goes straight to profit) · PORTABLE NETWORK-WIDE REPUTATION — a restaurant doing half its sales on Swiggy and half on Zomato cannot show one platform's ratings on the other; on ONDC it is a single layer so the same reputation and ratings are available everywhere · no disintermediation risk — Flipkart, Amazon, Swiggy and Zomato have started pushing their OWN brands ahead of other sellers; on an open network that risk is remote
    Technology companies Maximise the value of their technology and innovate on their strengths (payment, logistics, matching), monetising each transaction directly · develop and deploy without long enterprise B2B sales cycles — much faster time to scale and market

    Revenue models and profit pools

    • Buyer-side app: earns commission from seller-side apps and logistics providers on the sale value, when a consumer purchases through it.
    • Seller-side app: earns commission from sellers.
    • Other transaction service providers: commission from sellers and seller apps.
    • ONDC itself is free to start, but the intention is to charge a small fee from all network participants.

      Ultimately the sellers pay a certain commission to all the participants.

    Five challenges

    1. Early stage — initial traction and adoption has been exponential, but there is a long way to go.
    2. Buyer-side incentive to switch is a major challenge.
    3. Digital handholding and onboarding of sellers — Amazon and Flipkart took responsibility for supporting sellers onto digital platforms with huge amounts of support. ONDC is an open protocol — who provides the equivalent support?**
    4. OWNERSHIP OF TRANSACTIONS — one reason BigBasket and Flipkart succeeded is creating trust: they own the transaction end to end — refunds and returns, no questions asked. Under ONDC, if you receive a damaged food item, who is responsible — the restaurant, the logistics provider, or the buyer app (Paytm)? Conflict resolution where there is no single transaction owner is a challenge. Also, a seller theoretically needs multiple seller apps — separate apps for accounting, ERP and banking — whereas Flipkart/Amazon was a single monolithic platform solving all needs**.
    5. Data privacy, security and ownership — who owns the ONDC data: the seller, the buyer or ONDC? "Unless you use the data effectively you cannot cross-sell and upsell. Amazon and Flipkart know so much about consumer behaviour that they increase revenue and profitability BECAUSE THEY OWN THE DATA."

    Four ONDC-leveraged business models

    1. Direct-to-consumer brands bypassing traditional channels — a chocolate maker in Kerala selling all over India without getting empanelled on BigBasket.
    2. Specialised niche platforms — a platform solely for organic products; on ONDC it stands out, whereas on Flipkart/BigBasket/Amazon it would get lost among millions of products.
    3. Aggregator model — a platform bringing together all artisanal coffee producers in one place.
    4. Service providers — payment solutions, logistics, digital cataloguing, offered directly on ONDC without needing to align with a platform.

    What ONDC IS and IS NOT: it IS an open network, an enabler for e-commerce expansion, an enabler for broad-based innovation, a market- and community-led initiative of the Government of India, part of the DPI initiative. It IS NOT an application, a platform, a central intermediary, or a regulator.

    The magicpin case study

    What magicpin is: a hyper-local discovery platform connecting users with local businesses — discovery (search by category, location or keyword), discounts and deals from local businesses, rewards (cashback and points for buying from vendors you'd buy from anyway), and notifications about new businesses, deals and promotions in your area. How magicpin makes money — three ways: commissions (a listing fee from businesses on its platform) · advertising (sells ad space to businesses and brands) · subscriptions (premium plans giving early access to deals and discounts). Scale: raised over $100 million; a network of over 1 million local businesses in India. Strengths: strong local business network · data-driven insights (past purchase behaviour, preferred items, store types, deal responsiveness) · technology-driven, constantly innovating. Challenges: competition (Dunzo, Nearbuy, Zomato) · regulation — the Indian government is considering regulating the hyper-local discovery space · need to raise more funding to continue growing.

    Results after ONDC integration — memorise the numbers: - First month: 20% increase in traffic. - Same month: 15% increase in sales. - Increase in the number of businesses listing their products on the platform. - Positive user feedback on improved user experience. Magicpin acts as a seller app on ONDC — sellers come to ONDC through magicpin. Benefits realised: increased traffic (ONDC created a single market making it easier for users to find local businesses) · increased sales (easier for businesses to list) · improved user experience (access to a wide variety of products and services from local businesses) · increased transparency (access to real-time pricing information).

    Four general benefits of leveraging ONDC: access to a large market (a single market across India) · reduced cost (a common infrastructure — every company doesn't have to create its own) · improved efficiency of the supply chain (a platform for businesses to connect and share information) · increased transparency (a platform to publish prices and terms of trade transparently).

    5.13Business Metrics and Measurement1

    Definition: business metrics — also called KPIs (Key Performance Indicators) — are quantifiable measures used to track and assess the status of specific business processes or the company as a whole, helping monitor progress, understand operational effectiveness and inform strategic planning.

    The five real-world metric shocks — memorise company, year, metric and impact

    Company Year The metric that moved the stock Impact
    Facebook July 2018 Daily Active Users and Monthly Active Users lower than expected (slower-than-expected user growth and revenue) Shares fell nearly 20% in one day, wiping out approximately $120 billion in market value — the largest one-day loss in the history of the American stock market at that time
    Netflix 2019 New subscribers added — added only 2.7 million against an expectation of 5 million; first US subscriber loss since 2011, dropping by 130,000 Share price plummeted nearly 12% in a day
    Bharti Airtel 2020 ARPU — Average Revenue Per User at ₹154 vs ₹123 in the same quarter a year ago and ₹135 the previous quarter Shares surged nearly 6% in a day
    Yes Bank 2019 Net Interest Margin down and Gross NPAs up significantly Shares fell over 10% in a single day
    Maruti Suzuki 2019 Sales volume declined 18% year on year Shares fell nearly 6%

    Why business metrics matter — five reasons

    1. Performance measurement against strategic objectives (year-on-year, quarter-on-quarter).
    2. Guide decision making with quantitative evidence.
    3. Predictive analytics — if your net subscriber base is falling, something is wrong with the product or service; if market share is falling in a geography, competition or changing tastes may be at work.
    4. Identification of problems in operations, functions or geographies.
    5. Improvement over time — tracking CAC: if it is trending upwards, it could indicate marketing strategies need adjusting or the market is becoming more competitive.

    Vanity metrics vs Actionable metrics — a certain MCQ

    Vanity metrics Actionable metrics
    Numbers that look good on paper and make a business feel good, but don't correlate with the health or success of the business Provide insights the business can use to make decisions and drive change
    Examples: total app downloads, page views, number of registered users, social media followers/likes, email open rate Examples: churn rate, retention rate, conversion rate, customer lifetime value, engagement rate, daily active users, monthly revenue
    Sound impressive but offer little insight into profitability or customer behaviour Tied directly to key objectives with a clear line of sight to revenue and profitability

    The four vanity metric case examples: 1. Social media followers — Brand A has 1 million Facebook likes, but only a fraction engage or purchase. Brand B has only 100,000 followers but far higher engagement and conversion. If the marketing manager's metric is "how many Facebook likes," they'll spend all their money going from 1 million to 2, 3, 4 million — without realising it's a vanity metric. 2. Website page views — a startup sees a spike in page views but the bounce rate is extremely high and average time on site very low → many people land but find nothing valuable. Often caused by clickbait. The actionable metrics are bounce rate and average session duration. 3. Email open rate — high open rate (a catchy subject line) but extremely low click-through rate means recipients aren't clicking the content, so the company isn't driving traffic or conversion. The actionable metrics are CTR and conversion rate. 4. App downloads — 100,000 downloads for a new mobile game, so they spend more marketing money to reach 200,000 and 1 million. But only a small portion are active users and in-app purchases are minimal. The actionable metrics are active users, session length and in-app purchases.

    The nuance: "That is not to say the number of downloads is not important — it is important when you launch an app. But remember that's only the FIRST STEP. If it's the ONLY number you track, that's a vanity metric."

    Three common mistakes in choosing and interpreting metrics: 1. Choosing the WRONG metrics — metrics that don't align with strategic objectives. For a telecom company whose real investment is towers and spectrum: is the metric number of users, number of calls made, or number of minutes of talk time? Whichever you choose, the organisation and all its employees will drive towards it. 2. Overemphasis on quantitative data — *"while numbers are important, they don't tell the whole story. Qualitative data provides context and nuance."* 3. Misinterpretation of data — understand the underlying factors; don't draw wrong conclusions from incomplete or biased data**.

    Ensuring metrics are useful: align metrics with business goals · regularly review and adjust as strategies and market conditions change · use a MIX — quantitative and qualitative, input and output metrics, short-term and long-term · context matters (industry, market trends, internal factors).

    How metrics drive strategy — four uses

    Goal setting (Maruti aiming for 20% market share in a segment tracks sales volume and customer acquisition rate) · resource allocation (if Swiggy finds orders falling in a part of Bangalore it can increase advertising and promotion spend there; conversely, analyse why some areas perform well and replicate the practices) · performance improvement (a high churn rate signals a need to invest in retention) · predictive analysis (increasing new user signups indicates future growth, prompting a business to scale up).

    5.14Metrics by Business Model

    Traditional models

    Model Key metrics
    Manufacturer Production volume (indicates operational efficiency and market demand) · COGS (lower COGS = higher gross margin at constant price, or the ability to cut prices to gain share) · operational efficiency metrics — production downtime, machine utilisation rate (an unutilised machine is wasted investment), YIELD RATIO (ratio of good units produced to total units started), scrap rates · profitability — gross profit margin (revenue − COGS), net profit margin, Return on Investment
    Distributor Inventory turnover rate — how often inventory is sold and replaced; high turnover indicates strong sales or effective inventory management · GMROII — Gross Margin Return on Inventory Investment — the gross return for each dollar invested in inventory · order accuracy rate — % of orders delivered without errors; higher accuracy → higher satisfaction and lower costs from returns
    Retail Sales per square foot — critical because retail stores are on high streets or expensive neighbourhoods with very high rental cost · foot traffic / footfalls · average transaction value — raised through successful upselling and cross-selling, a bigger basket, more variety · conversion rate — % of store visitors who make a purchase; raised through merchandising, good display, comfortable environment, and sales assistants who help customers find the right product
    Franchising Number of franchisees (more → increased brand recognition and market share) · sales per franchise (ensures the franchisee makes money, stays loyal, invests more, and may open more stores) · Average Unit Volume · royalty fees — the primary source of income for the franchisor
    Razor Blade CAC — critical because you make a loss or very little margin on the first durable product, so CAC must be low enough to recover over the life of consumable usage · Lifetime Value — the company makes money over a long period; the customer must keep buying for a while before the company makes anything · repeat purchase rate · upsell rate — can you sell a higher-end razor or printer during the long relationship?
    Bundling Average transaction value — one of the purposes of bundling is to raise it · cross-selling rate — % of customers who purchase additional related products · customer satisfaction and retention — tracked via NPS and retention rate
    Leasing Utilisation rate — the proportion of time a leasable asset is rented out. If it's rented only a small fraction of the time the company loses money · Return on Assets · default rate — % of lease contracts where the lessee fails to pay · RESIDUAL VALUE — the estimated value of the asset at the end of the lease period; higher residual value means more profit when the asset is sold post-lease

    New age models

    Model Key metrics
    On-demand CAC — keeping it low is vital because margins are very small · LTV — rule of thumb: LTV should be at least 3× CAC; more is better, but 3 is the golden number · order volume — vital for economies of scale: if Swiggy gets many orders from one area it can station riders there, deliver faster and cut delivery cost; the same order volume from geographically dispersed customers means high delivery cost and low profitability · customer satisfaction rate**
    Aggregator GMV — Gross Merchandise Value (total value of products/services sold through the platform) · TAKE RATE — the commission or fee the aggregator takes; Swiggy and Zomato take typically 23–27% from restaurants. A small change in take rate can mean a substantial increase in profitability · active users (daily or monthly) · customer retention
    Subscription MRR — the revenue reliably expected every month; the predictive number for future business · churn rate · CAC · CLV — essential for determining how much to spend on acquiring a customer
    Platform NETWORK EFFECT — the phenomenon by which each additional user increases the value for all other users; measured through growth rate of new users and increase in transaction volumes · number of active users (daily/monthly) · user engagement — "just having a user is not enough" — time spent on the platform, number of transactions, repeat visits · PLATFORM LEAKAGE — when transactions are initiated on the platform but completed OFF the platform to avoid fees — i.e. disintermediation. Example: a customer comes to Urban Company, the carpenter assesses the job and quotes, and then the two transact directly, so the take rate vanishes. Low leakage indicates users find value in using the platform for the entire transaction
    Marketplace GMV · take rate · BUYER-TO-SELLER RATIO — a healthy ratio ensures adequate liquidity on both sides; buyers keep coming because they find what they want, and sellers stay because they get enough business · LIQUIDITY — the likelihood that an item listed for sale will actually be sold. Higher liquidity makes the marketplace more attractive to both sides

    Note: some metrics are common across models, but many are distinct. Residual value applies to leasing and has no relevance to a marketplace.

    5.15KPIs and the Balanced Scorecard

    KPIs — four reasons they matter

    1. Performance measurement — quantifiable measurements evaluating success in meeting objectives; tracking progress toward targets, market share, revenue, profitability.
    2. Informed decision making — decisions backed by data rather than gut feel or anecdote. Should we cut price and gain share, or raise price and capture more profit?
    3. Strategic focus — KPIs create an operational picture corresponding to organisational strategy.
    4. Boost employee morale and motivation — when employees understand their individual KPIs and the organisation's, they get a clear understanding of their role in the company's success, leading to clear role definition, expectation setting, better performance, and higher job satisfaction.

    How to define KPIs: - Align with strategic goals. For a telecom company, is the KPI number of subscribers, number of calls, or minutes of talk time? It can make a great difference to what the organisation and all employees drive towards. - Industry-specific KPIs — *in retail, sales per square foot; for a subscription service, churn and retention rate.* - Understand the business model's nuances — *in a platform, network effect; in leasing, asset utilisation and return on the capital invested.* - KEEP IT SIMPLE — there should NOT be too many KPIs. "When you have too many, whether it's a company or an employee, they get confused and lose focus." Choose a limited number of relevant ones that matter most.**

    Monitoring and adjusting: regular monitoring (weekly, monthly, quarterly) · dashboard reporting with visual representations so trends and insights surface more readily · comparative analysis against historical data, future forecasts, or across geographies (Maruti sales better in Delhi but lower in Bangalore last quarter → investigate) · adjustment of KPIs — if consistently missing, adjust or re-evaluate the strategy; if consistently meeting them, it may be time to set more challenging targets — maybe your KPIs are too easy**.

    The Balanced Scorecard

    Definition: a strategic planning and management system used to align business activities to the vision and strategy of the organisation, improve internal and external communication, and monitor performance. Created by: Dr Robert Kaplan and Dr David Norton in the EARLY 1990s. ← memorise.

    The four perspectives — each must have objectives, measures/KPIs, targets and initiatives:

    Perspective What it measures Typical metrics
    1. Financial The business's health from the SHAREHOLDER's point of view Net profit, ROI, profitability after tax, operating income, return on capital employed, economic value added, cash flow, revenue growth
    2. Customer The value proposition offered to customers and resultant satisfaction Customer satisfaction scores, market share, retention/churn rate, customer acquisition, NPS, delivery and quality performance
    3. Internal business process Processes that impact customer satisfaction and financial objectives Operational efficiency, quality, innovation, time taken to process an order, productivity, process alignment, level of automation, wastage, absenteeism
    4. Learning and growth Employee learning and growth — the intangible drivers of future success: human capital, organisational capital, information capital Employee satisfaction, employee retention/turnover, training and development, skill levels, specialist knowledge gained, organisational culture

    Why it's popular: it gives a clear prescription of what companies should measure to balance the various perspectives; a concise report encapsulating a wide array of complex measures into a single digestible report; and it aligns key performance measures with strategy at ALL levels of the organisation — not just top management, right down to the lowest employee.

    Balanced Scorecard applications

    Business Financial Customer Internal process Learning & growth
    Retail Sales volume Customer satisfaction scores Average checkout time Staff training hours
    On-demand (new age) Gross margin Customer churn rate Order fulfilment rate Number of new features developed
    Telecom (Airtel/Vodafone) ARPU, reducing churn rate Network quality (dropped calls), customer service Network installation process (number of towers, coverage), error-free and prompt billing process Training programmes, employee satisfaction, reducing employee churn
    E-commerce (Flipkart) GMV, profit margin Website usability, delivery speed (% of orders delivered as promised), easy navigation, relevant search results Inventory management (right level, right item — enough to meet orders without overstocking), logistics (same-day, error-free delivery) Enhance IT skills of staff, improve company culture, upskill on latest technology
    Airline (IndiGo/Air India) Objective: increase shareholder value. Measures: revenue, expenses, net profit Objectives: frequent reliable departures; low ticket prices. Measures: average number of daily departures per route, customer experience survey, ticket price differential vs competition on the same sector Objectives: fast ground turnaround (measure: time at the gate — directly affects aircraft utilisation) · good locations (measure: % of the population served within X miles) · direct routes (measure: % of tickets with direct routes) · fun experience (measure: customer complaints per 100 tickets) · no frills (measure: internal cost per flight — critical for a low-cost airline) —

    Five disadvantages and pitfalls of the Balanced Scorecard: 1. Complex to implement in a large organisation and requires buy-in from ALL parts of the organisation. 2. Not effective if not linked directly to compensation or rewards — "unless we link it to employees' compensation, reward or recognition, employees will not be fully committed." 3. Selection of wrong or ineffective KPIs leads to wrong strategic directions. 4. Time-consuming, and may divert focus from operational performance (normally a company focuses on financial metrics; four perspectives can dilute focus). 5. Its effectiveness depends entirely on how well it is implemented and used.

    5.16Digital Analytics for Online Business Models

    Definition: the practice of measuring, collecting, analysing and interpreting digital data (clicks) to understand and optimise web usage and digital strategy — encompassing online marketing campaigns, user activity on websites and mobile apps, and social media engagement. Goal: improve user experience, enhance marketing campaign effectiveness, and optimise business strategies.

    The six online metrics

    Metric Definition Interpretation
    Website traffic Number of visitors and visits/sessions; can be broken down by source: direct, organic search, paid search (SEM/SEO), social, referral —
    BOUNCE RATE % of visitors who leave after viewing just ONE page High bounce rate indicates poor user experience or irrelevant traffic. Common causes: the CLICKBAIT strategy (an attractive catchy headline that isn't relevant, used to get people to the site — the user gets disillusioned and leaves); or poor technology — slow page loading or page errors
    Conversion rate % of visitors who complete a desired action — a purchase (Flipkart), filling out a form, signing up for a newsletter Key for understanding the effectiveness of the whole website. Improved by quick page load time, nice visuals, a good call to action
    CTR — Click-Through Rate How often people who view your ad or search listing end up clicking on it High CTR indicates the content, copy and images are compelling and relevant — reflects the effectiveness of your advertising or content
    Average time spent on page How long visitors spend on a page Longer times suggest more engaging content and more chance of monetising the viewer
    Page views per visit Average number of pages viewed in a single session More page views indicate deeper engagement and relevant content

    Four roles of digital analytics: 1. Performance assessment — if Facebook advertising isn't giving results while Twitter is, increase spend on Twitter or change the Facebook campaigns. 2. User behaviour understanding — where is the user dropping off, where is the friction? 3. Customer journey mapping — identify friction points and optimise. 4. Resource allocation — this is not always obvious. Google Ads may give a lot of traffic that converts very little; Facebook may give less traffic for the same spend but convert much more, making it far more valuable. By looking at traffic AND conversion AND revenue — not just clicks — you decide where to spend.

    5.17Metric Calculations — work through every one of these

    Zomato — CAC and CLV

    • Spends ₹500 on marketing in an area and acquires 10 new customers → CAC = ₹50.
    • Each customer places 5 orders per year at an average order value of ₹300 → annual revenue per customer = ₹1,500.
    • Customer continues for an average of 3 years → CLV = 3 × 1,500 = ₹4,500.
    • At a 20% take rate, Zomato's profit from this customer = 4,500 × 20% = ₹900 over the lifetime, for a ₹50 acquisition cost.

      The key lesson: keep CAC well below CLV. The rule of thumb is CAC : CLV of at least 1 : 3.

    OYO — occupancy, ADR and RevPAR

    • 100 rooms available in a city, 70 occupied → occupancy rate = 70%.
    • Average amount paid per room per night = ₹2,000 → ADR = ₹2,000.
    • RevPAR (Revenue Per Available Room) = ADR × occupancy rate = ₹2,000 × 70% = ₹1,400.

      Actions: if occupancy is low (20%), run promotions and advertising; if ADR is low, re-evaluate the pricing strategy. Customer satisfaction score matters because a customer stays a short time — OYO becomes valuable when the experience is so good that they choose OYO by default in future.

    Churn rate and Customer Lifetime Value

    Formula: LTV = Monthly revenue per customer ÷ Churn rate

    Problem: an online subscription service charges $15 per month; annual revenue $180,000; average customer lifespan 2.5 years (30 months). Churn is rising from 2% to 3% per month. - At 2% churn: LTV = 15 ÷ 0.02 = **$750** - At 3% churn: LTV = 15 ÷ 0.03 = **$500**

    A 1-percentage-point increase in churn cut lifetime value by $250 — a one-third reduction.

    ROAS — Return on Ad Spend

    Formula: ROAS = Revenue from the campaign ÷ Ad spend

    Problem: spend $100,000 on an online campaign; it produces 500 sales at an average of $250 per sale. - Revenue = 500 × 250 = **$125,000** - ROAS = 125,000 ÷ 100,000 = 1.25 or 125%

    Inventory turnover rate

    Formula: Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ Average inventory, where Average inventory = (Opening + Closing) ÷ 2

    Problem: opening inventory $500,000, closing inventory $400,000, COGS for the year $2,000,000. - Average inventory = (500,000 + 400,000) ÷ 2 = **$450,000** - Turnover = 2,000,000 ÷ 450,000 = 4.44 times — quite efficient.

    Sales conversion rate

    Formula: Conversion rate = (Purchasers ÷ Visitors) × 100

    Problem: 15,000 visitors last month, 300 made a purchase. Target: raise conversion to 5%. - Current conversion = (300 ÷ 15,000) × 100 = **2%** - To reach 5%: 5% × 15,000 = **750 sales** needed → additional sales required = 750 − 300 = 450

    Business of Insurance & InsurTech

    The Business of Insurance and InsurTech

    (Instructors: K. Sriram — life insurance (Modules 0–9) · Sanath Kumar — non life/general insurance and InsurTech)

    How to read this section. The course is two halves stapled together. Sriram's half is technical/actuarial — formulae, tables, risk definitions, solvency numbers. Kumar's half is descriptive — market structure, ecosystem players, product segments, regulation, technology gaps. MCQs from the first half will be definitional and numerical; from the second half they will be "which of these is NOT", counts of players, and match-the-role. Both are covered exhaustively below.

    PART A — LIFE INSURANCE (K. Sriram)

    6.1What insurance actually is — the definition to memorise1

    High-level definition: insurance is a contract for transferring risk. The instructor explicitly says this is inadequate, because it doesn't answer: what risk, whose risk, to whom, and why would anyone accept it.

    The full definition — this is the examinable one:

    Insurance is a FINANCIAL CONTRACT under which one party transfers its financial loss arising from the occurrence of a specified risk event to another party.

    Term Who / what it is
    Policyholder The party that believes it will suffer a financial loss if the risk event happens, and does not have the appetite or the ability to bear that loss
    Insurer / insurance company The party willing to bear the loss. Must be better equipped than the policyholder to deal with that risk event — otherwise it wouldn't be in the business
    Premium The fair compensation paid by the policyholder to the insurer for accepting the risk. "There is no such thing as a free lunch"
    Insured event The jargon for the specified risk event

    The three arrows in the process diagram (a classic diagram-labelling MCQ):

    Arrow Direction What flows
    A Policyholder → Insurer Risk transfer
    B Insurer → Policyholder Financial compensation if the insured event happens (drawn as a dotted line because the event may or may not happen)
    C Policyholder → Insurer Premium payments

    Critical point: if the risk event does not happen, the policyholder gets nothing, and the premiums are NOT refunded.

    The five prerequisites for a life insurance contract guaranteed MCQ| # | Prerequisite | Detail / jargon |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | The insured event must be defined | In life insurance there are exactly TWO insured events: the DEATH of the policyholder and the SURVIVAL of the policyholder | | 2 | A term must be specified | Called the policy term. All life insurance contracts are long-term — typically more than 5 years. There may or may not be a maximum term | | 3 | The financial loss must be quantified | The quantified amount is the SUM ASSURED | | 4 | The premium must be quantified | Called product pricing. Combines three elements: (a) financial quantification of the risks accepted, (b) future expenses of servicing the contract, (c) the insurer's profit margin | | 5 | The policyholder must be selected | Not every applicant is accepted. Screening parameters: age, health condition, financial capacity to pay the premium. The screening process is called UNDERWRITING |

    Terms used interchangeably in this course

    • insurance contract = product = policy
    • insurance = life insurance
    • policyholder = life insured

    6.2Primer I — Time Value of Money

    Why money has time value — three reasons: 1. It can be deployed productively today to generate a real rate of return 2. Inflation — a rupee today ≠ a rupee a year hence 3. People prefer current consumption to future consumption, because the future is uncertain (includes a default risk premium)

    The formula to memorise:

    Nominal rate of interest = Real rate of return + Expected rate of inflation + Risk premium

    Compounding and discounting formulae

    Purpose Notation Formula
    Future value, single cash flow FVIF(i,n) (1 + i)ⁿ
    Future value, annuity in ARREAR FVIFA(i,n) [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1] ÷ i
    Future value, annuity in ADVANCE — FVIFA(i,n) × (1 + i)
    Present value, single cash flow PVIF(i,n) 1 ÷ (1 + i)ⁿ = 1 ÷ FVIF(i,n)
    Present value, annuity in ARREAR PVIFA(i,n) [1 − (1 + i)⁻ⁿ] ÷ i
    Present value, annuity in ADVANCE — PVIFA(i,n) × (1 + i)

    Annuity in arrear = paid at the END of each period → Excel type = 0. Annuity in advance = paid at the BEGINNING of each period → Excel type = 1. FVIFA stands for Future Value Interest Factor Annuity and the base formula presumes annuity in arrear.

    The six worked numbers (all at 8.25% p.a. for 9 years) ← these exact figures could appear

    Example Input Answer
    FV of single cash flow ₹1 million invested ₹20,41,038
    FV of annuity in arrear ₹10 lakh per year ₹1,26,15,546
    FV of annuity in advance ₹10 lakh per year ₹1,36,59,684
    PV — initial investment needed for ₹10 lakh at end of 9 years — ₹4,89,947
    PV of annuity in arrear ₹1 lakh per year ₹6,18,246
    PV of annuity in advance ₹1 lakh per year ₹6,69,252

    Excel functions used: FV(rate, nper, pmt, pv, type), PV(rate, nper, pmt, fv, type), RATE(nper, pmt, fv, type, guess).

    6.3Primer II — Applications of Probability in Life Insurance

    Life insurance is predicated on death and survival, and both are probabilistic events. Only one law of probability is used in this course:

    The multiplicative theorem of probability for INDEPENDENT events: P(AB) = P(A) × P(B)

    Two events are independent if the occurrence of one is not affected by the occurrence of the other. The assumption made throughout: survival in age band (x, x+1) and survival in age band (x+1, x+2) are statistically independent — which is what lets us multiply survival probabilities.

    Notation ← must know cold

    Notation Meaning
    qₓ Probability that a life currently aged x DIES between ages x and x+1
    pₓ Probability that a life aged x SURVIVES from x to x+1 = 1 − qₓ
    ₜpₓ Probability that a life aged x survives from x to x+t
    per mille PER THOUSAND

    Interpretation example: mortality rate at age 60 of 6.3 per mille means out of 1,000 individuals aged 60, 6.3 are expected to die before attaining age 61 → q₆₀ = 6.3/1000 = 0.0063.

    The annuitants' mortality extract used

    Age qₓ Per mille
    60 0.0063 6.3
    61 0.0069 6.9
    65 0.0101 10.1

    The two worked questions

    Q1 — probability that a life aged 60 today survives to age 65: = (1−q₆₀)(1−q₆₁)(1−q₆₂)(1−q₆₃)(1−q₆₄) = 0.96 → a 96% chance

    Q2 — probability that a life aged 62 today survives to 65 but dies before 66: = (1−q₆₂)(1−q₆₃)(1−q₆₄) × q₆₅ = 0.0098 → out of 1,000 individuals aged 62, 9.8 are expected to die between ages 65 and 66

    MCQ trap: Q2 requires three survival probabilities MULTIPLIED BY a DEATH probability — not four survival probabilities.

    6.4Product profiles — the two building blocks and their combinations1

    The two core building blocks ← the single most important idea in Part A

    Abbreviation Product Insured event Payout if the other thing happens
    TA Term Assurance DEATH within the policy term If he survives the term → he gets NOTHING
    PE Pure Endowment SURVIVAL to the end of the policy term If he dies during the term → death benefit is ZERO

    "Using TA and PE as building blocks you can construct ALMOST ALL life insurance contracts offered by life insurance companies."

    The four products, side by side (all: SA ₹10 million, term 10 years, PPT 10 years, annual premium in advance, male aged 30)

    Feature TA PE EA (Endowment Assurance) WL (Whole Life)
    Annual premium ₹12,990 ₹7,09,270 ₹7,22,260 Single premium ₹4,10,241 (or limited pay)
    Insured event(s) Death within 10 yrs Survival to yr 10 BOTH death within term and survival at maturity Death whenever it occurs — no specified term
    Smoking status a screening parameter? YES NO YES YES
    Policyholder's IRR n/a n/a 5.84% 6.88%
    Nature Pure protection Pure savings/survival Protection + savings Pure protection for life

    The identity to memorise

    EA = TA + PE ₹12,990 + ₹7,09,270 = ₹7,22,260 — "Is it by a strange coincidence? The answer is NO." This holds only if the policyholder's age and all policy terms and conditions are identical.

    Extension: if death benefit ≠ survival benefit (e.g. DB ₹20 mn, SB ₹10 mn), then EA premium = TA premium on SA ₹20 mn + PE premium on SA ₹10 mn.

    Key inferences drawn from these examples

    • TA: if the policyholder dies after paying only the first premium of ₹12,990, the insurer must pay ₹10 million — a huge loss. Insurers survive this through RISK POOLING (pooling a group of policies rather than depending on a single policy).
    • PE: if the policyholder dies between year 9 and 10 having paid 9 × ₹7,09,270 ≈ ₹63 lakh, the nominees get nothing and the insurer keeps everything. "It doesn't seem fair, right?" — which motivates the innovative variants.
    • PE premium ≫ TA premium because the likelihood of surviving 10 years is far greater than the likelihood of dying within 10 years.
    • EA is like a recurring bank deposit (₹7,22,260 a year for 10 years → ₹10 million) but protection-proofed, which a bank deposit is not.
    • Comparing EA's 5.84% with a 7% bank deposit is NOT apple-to-apple — because (a) EA carries a significant death benefit and (b) in some tax regimes the maturity benefit is tax-exempt, making 5.84% a tax-free return. Any comparison must convert the bank rate to post-tax terms.
    • Death proceeds are completely tax exempt in the dependents' hands → the WL return of 6.88% is a tax-free return.
    • If the policyholder wants ONLY financial protection, TERM ASSURANCE is the cost-effective approach.

    Premium-related features (TA example)

    Feature Detail
    Premium paying term (PPT) Here PPT = policy term, but this is NOT universal — PPT can be less than the policy term, at the extreme a single premium
