    Premium payment frequency Monthly / quarterly / half-yearly / annual. Changing this example to monthly → 120 monthly premiums instead of 10 annual
    "In advance" Premiums paid at the beginning of the unit time. This is a STATUTORY REQUIREMENT under the Insurance Act — an insurer cannot say premiums are payable at the end of the year; that would violate the Insurance Act
    Issue age The policyholder's age at policy issue (30 in the example)
    Nominees The policyholder's dependents

    The three pricing hypotheses (stated but only validated in the risk module)

    1. Premium at issue age 30 < premium at issue age 40
    2. Premium for a MALE aged 30 > premium for a FEMALE aged 30 (females have lighter mortality)
    3. Premium for a NON-SMOKER < premium for a SMOKER

    Standard vs substandard premium

    Not all 30-year-olds pay the same premium. A policyholder with good health status pays the standard premium (₹12,990). One classified substandard pays more, because of a LOADING built into the premium.

    Why PE has no smoker/non-smoker distinction subtle, likely MCQ

    Applicants for a PURE ENDOWMENT contract are SELF-SELECTED, whereas applicants for a TERM ASSURANCE contract are SELECTED BY THE INSURANCE COMPANY.

    Whole Life Assurance specifics

    • WL = a term assurance with NO SPECIFIED TERM. Pays the SA whenever death occurs after the policy is taken out.
    • PPT cannot equal the policy term (there is no term) — so insurers offer single premium or limited pay (10 / 15 / 20 years).
    • Premiums increase significantly with age; the product becomes much more expensive at higher issue ages because death risk at higher ages is much greater. Hence buy it in the 25–35 age band for a cost-effective lifetime protection solution.
    • A longer PPT means a LOWER annual premium (a 15-year PPT premium < a 10-year PPT premium) — useful when the policyholder cannot afford the 10-year PPT.
    • To compute an IRR you must assume a term → use the expectation of life from a mortality table. Expectation of life at age 30 = 48 years → the SA becomes payable around age 78–80.

    6.5Annuities — products built on the PE building block1

    Products predicated on TA: term assurance, endowment assurance, whole life. Products predicated on PE: ANNUITIES.

    Financial annuity vs LIFE annuity definitional MCQ| Financial annuity | Life annuity |

    |---|---| | A stream of cash flows paid/received over a specified term | Payments CEASE ON THE DEATH of the policyholder | | The survival or death of the recipient is immaterial | Survival is the whole basis of the contract | | — | The recipient is called the ANNUITANT |

    Immediate vs deferred annuity

    Immediate annuity Deferred annuity
    Purpose A steady stream of income starting IMMEDIATELY and continuing as long as the individual survives A pathway for BUILDING the corpus which will later buy the income stream
    Purchase Typically a SINGLE PREMIUM at the start Regular premiums over the deferment period
    Key ages — Vesting age = the age at which the income stream starts; deferment period = from purchase to vesting

    The immediate annuity worked example

    Input Value
    Single premium ₹10 million
    Annuity receivable ₹8,28,000 per annum ≈ ₹69,000 per month
    Expectation of life at age 60 23.5 years (so payouts expected for ~24 years, to about age 84)
    Implied rate of return 7.1%

    Two questions answered: 1. Does the income stop after 24 years? NO — it continues as long as the annuitant lives, even to age 100 or beyond. The risk of the annuitant living longer is LONGEVITY RISK, and it is borne by the LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY. 2. What if there is an early death (say at 61, after one year's annuity)? The annuity CEASES. Dependents get NO death benefit and NOT EVEN A PART REFUND of the ₹10 million premium. "Doesn't seem to be a very fair outcome" → hence the annuity options.

    Contrast to burn in: in TA / EA / WL the MORTALITY (death) risk of the policyholder is borne by the insurer. In an immediate annuity the LONGEVITY risk of the annuitant is borne by the insurer.

    The annuity options offered alongside the plain life annuity

    Option How it works
    Life annuity Always available. Pays only while the annuitant lives
    Life annuity + SPOUSE'S annuity Annuitant gets X p.a. while alive; thereafter the spouse gets a percentage of X while the spouse survives. This is a joint life with LAST SURVIVOR status. Popular with PENSION plans, especially bank pension plans
    Annuity GUARANTEED for a certain period, then life annuity E.g. a 15-year guarantee period: the amount is paid for 15 years even if the annuitant dies (paid to dependents); if the annuitant outlives 15 years, payments continue while he survives
    Immediate life annuity with RETURN OF CAPITAL THE MOST POPULAR OPTION IN INDIA. Annuity paid while alive; on death the purchase price (₹10 million) is returned to the dependents as a death benefit
    IMPAIRED annuity If the annuitant provides medical evidence of poor health/short longevity, the insurer offers the same annuity for a LOWER single premium (or a higher annuity for the same premium). NOT available in the Indian market — available in developed markets such as the UK

    Return-of-capital annuity — the hybrid structure and its cost

    • Structurally: PURE ENDOWMENT (annuity while alive) + WHOLE LIFE ASSURANCE (return of purchase price on death) — "basically a hybrid insurance product."
    • Worked example: single premium ₹10 mn, annuity ₹7,00,000 in advance, expectation of life at 60 = 23.5 yrs → implied return 5.03%.
    • Why lower than 7.1%? Because you pay a premium for the death benefit built into the product, and that premium shows up as a lower annuity payment / lower implied return.

    The deferred annuity worked example

    Input Value
    Current age / vesting age 30 / 60 → 30-year deferment period
    Guaranteed accumulation rate 6% p.a.
    Target corpus ₹10 million
    Annual premium required (in advance) ₹1,19,330

    Equation of value: P × FVIFA(i,n) × (1 + i) = ₹10 million, with n = 30, i = 6%.

    Two questions answered: 1. Death during the deferment period? The death benefit is usually limited to a refund of premiums paid to the date of death, with or without interest — i.e. MINIMAL, unlike EA where the death benefit is very significant. 2. Are the annuity conversion terms guaranteed at the vesting date? NO. Most deferred annuities give no guarantee on future conversion terms; conversion happens at the annuity market conditions 30 years later, dominated by the interest rate environment: - Lower interest rates later → LOWER annuity - Higher interest rates later → HIGHER annuity - Guaranteeing conversion terms can ENDANGER SOLVENCY. ← The example: EQUITABLE LIFE in the UK, which COLLAPSED because of guaranteed conversion terms offered in deferred annuity contracts. After that collapse almost all insurers shied away from the practice.

    Deferred annuity vs Endowment Assurance as a corpus-building vehicle

    Deferred annuity 30-year Endowment Assurance
    Builds the ₹10 mn corpus? Yes Yes — also works
    Death benefit during accumulation Only return of premiums Full ₹10 million
    Cost Cheaper Far more expensive (because of the higher death benefit)

    6.6The four dimensions for classifying life insurance products

    Guaranteed MCQ: "On which of the following dimensions are life insurance products classified?"

    # Dimension Categories
    1 Type of insured event Term assurance (death) vs Pure endowment (survival)
    2 Frequency of premium payment Single premium · Annual premium (PPT = policy term) · Limited pay (PPT < policy term). Sub-annual modes: monthly, quarterly, semi-annual
    3 Retail vs Group Sold to individuals = retail; sold to groups of individuals = group
    4 Transfer of investment risk Non-participating (non-par) · Participating (par) · Unit-linked

    Products offered in practice cut across all four classifications.

    Group insurance — OYRGTA

    In theory all retail products can be sold to groups; in practice the common group product is GROUP TERM ASSURANCE, offered to employer–employee groups, known as:

    OYRGTA = One-Year Renewable Group Term Assurance

    Feature Detail
    Policyholder vs lives insured The EMPLOYER is the policyholder; the EMPLOYEES are the lives insured. (In retail, the two are the same person)
    Example If Infosys buys GTA, Infosys is the policyholder and its 3,23,000-odd employees (as of March 2025) are the lives insured
    Policy term 1 year
    Sum assured Expressed as a multiple of annual salary — e.g. 3 × annual CTC, subject to a monetary minimum (e.g. ₹1 million; if 3×CTC < ₹1 mn, the minimum kicks in)
    Premium Calculated per employee on age and sum assured, then aggregated across employees
    Underwriting NO underwriting — the employer is usually not required to provide any evidence of insurability for its employees
    Renewal Renewable for one more year at a negotiated new premium level
    Market character Extremely competitive and PRICE-SENSITIVE — employers gravitate to the most competitive premium rate

    6.7Non-par vs Par vs Unit-linked — who bears the investment risk

    The single running example: EA with a policyholder's guaranteed return of 5.84%, insurer earning 7%.

    Non-participating (non-par) Participating (par) Unit-linked (ULIP)
    What the policyholder knows upfront Premiums AND sum assured — everything Premiums and basic SA; bonuses are not guaranteed Charges known; fund value is not
    Insurer earns 7%, guarantees 5.84% The 1.16% differential is INVESTMENT PROFIT for the INSURER; the policyholder does NOT share it The policyholder shares the investment profit as a BONUS Not applicable — the whole return goes to the policyholder
    Insurer earns only 3% 100% of the loss is borne by the INSURER; the policyholder's 5.84% does not change Part of the loss can be passed on by REDUCING FUTURE BONUSES Loss borne by the policyholder
    Who bears investment risk ENTIRELY THE INSURER SHARED between insurer and policyholder ENTIRELY THE POLICYHOLDER
    Typical products The numerical examples in this course Savings-oriented: endowment assurance, whole life (they generate substantial investment profit). Annuities — both immediate and deferred — CAN also be structured as par Unit-linked EA etc.

    How bonus is disbursed: invariably ADDED TO THE SUM ASSURED and paid when the insured event occurs — NOT as a cash payout. Death benefit or maturity payout of ₹10 mn is augmented by the bonus. For par annuities, the annuity payouts are augmented by the bonus.

    Limits on cutting bonuses — the insurer's ability to reduce future bonuses is constrained by: 1. What competitors do on similar products 2. Policyholders' Reasonable Expectations (PRE) about the scale of bonuses 3. Regulatory considerations — the regulator can say bonuses must not fall below a predetermined level or below the levels illustrated in the sales illustrations

    How a unit-linked product works — the unbundled structure

    Premium ──┬──► ALLOCATED portion ──► UNIT FUND (the investment fund) ──► maturity benefit
          └──► UNALLOCATED portion ──► NON-UNIT ACCOUNT ──► expenses + the "sum at risk"
    • Typical split: 90% allocated to the unit account, 10% to the unallocated (non-unit) account.
    • Death benefit under a unit-linked EA = HIGHER OF (the unit fund value at death) OR (₹10 million).
    • SUM AT RISK = the difference between the SA and the fund value. Example: death at end of year 2 with only ₹1 mn in the fund → sum at risk = ₹10 mn − ₹1 mn = ₹9 mn, which comes out of the NON-UNIT ACCOUNT.

    The three investment choices offered to a ULIP policyholder

    Choice Composition Risk/return
    Gilt fund State and central government securities Free from default risk → earns the risk-free rate
    Balanced fund E.g. 50% government securities + 50% equities (sometimes corporate bonds too) Middle
    Equity fund Equities and equity-oriented mutual funds Substantial return potential, full equity market risk

    At maturity the market value of the fund is paid. A 20% market rise → the entire unrealised capital gain goes to the policyholder; a 40% fall → the capital loss is also borne by the policyholder. Both the upside AND downside investment risk are entirely the policyholder's.

    What the insurer gets: it merely acts as an investment manager and earns a FUND MANAGEMENT CHARGE (e.g. 3% of the fund). Market up → higher FMC (a SECOND-ORDER benefit); market down → lower FMC (a second-order loss). The insurer is not directly exposed to a significant investment gain or loss.

    6.8IRDAI guidelines on product profiles1

    Part 1 — Principles of product development, pricing and design

    • Risk coverage must take customer needs into account; new products must be developed keeping evolving customer needs in mind
    • The industry slogan: "INSURANCE FOR ALL BY 2047" ← memorise the year
    • Products must be simple and easy to understand, not very complex
    • Transparency and clarity in wordings, policy terms, coverage, exclusions and policy conditions
    • The policyholder's interest is paramount to the regulator

    Part 2 — The Product Management Committee (PMC)

    Every insurer must set up a board-constituted committee called the Product Management and Governance Committee (PMC).

    Functions of the PMC: 1. Adhere to IRDAI's principles of design and pricing 2. Ensure the product design is appropriate to the target market 3. Ensure all product design and pricing regulations are complied with 4. Identify which products go under "FILE AND USE" and which under "USE AND FILE" 5. Periodically review product performance — that the insurer meets its profit target and the policyholder gets a reasonable rate of return 6. Investigate market conduct issues so that policyholder grievances are addressed 7. Take the lead in modifying or withdrawing a product and reissuing it

    The worked withdrawal example: rates are 7% today, so products guarantee 5–6%. If rates fall to 3% five years later, the product is no longer financially viable (offers 5% but earns 3%). The insurer withdraws and modifies it. The insurer then has two variants: the original, whose contractual obligations to existing policyholders must still be honoured, and the modified version sold to new policyholders at a lower rate of return.

    Part 3 — Other regulatory considerations

    Requirement Detail
    Mandatory bucketing Products must be bucketed as non-participating, participating, and LINKED; linked must be further split into UNIT-LINKED and INDEX-LINKED
    Index-linked The fund is linked to a particular index (e.g. the BSE Sensex) so the fund value moves with the index
    Non-par products The policyholder must always get a NON-ZERO POSITIVE rate of return
    Par products The policyholder must get AT LEAST 90% of the investment profits earned on par products classic MCQ number
    Unit-linked products Caps on charges taken out of the premium — e.g. the fund management charge cannot exceed 2.5% of the fund value
    Platforms Products may be offered on an individual OR a group basis; both are allowed

    6.9Risk premium and gross premium

    Risk premium

    RISK PREMIUM = (Likelihood of the insured event happening) × (Sum assured)

    Example Calculation Answer
    1-year TA, age 35, SA ₹10 mn, q₃₅ = 1.2 per mille = 0.0012 10,000,000 × 0.0012 ₹12,000
    1-year PE, same inputs 10,000,000 × (1 − 0.0012) = 10,000,000 × 0.9988 ₹99,88,000

    Why is time value of money ignored here? Because premiums are payable annually IN ADVANCE — the cash flow occurs at time 0.

    This numerically reinforces the module-1 inference: the PE premium is substantially higher than the TA premium.

    The 3-year extension — mortality table used

    Age qₓ pₓ = 1 − qₓ
    35 0.0012 0.9988
    36 0.0013 0.9987
    37 0.0014 0.9986

    Investment return assumed 6% p.a. Additional inputs needed for a multi-year policy: death probabilities in years 1, 2 and 3 and a rate of interest to factor in time value.

    Single premium for a 3-year TA (SA ₹10 mn):

    10mn × q₃₅ × PVIF(6,1) + 10mn × p₃₅ × q₃₆ × PVIF(6,2) + 10mn × p₃₅ × p₃₆ × q₃₇ × PVIF(6,3) = ₹33,338

    Assumption: regardless of when death happens within an age interval, the death benefit is paid at the END of that year.

    Single premium for a 3-year PE (SA ₹10 mn):

    10mn × p₃₅ × p₃₆ × p₃₇ × PVIF(6,3) = ₹83,63,490

    Why the actual premium exceeds the risk premium — three reasons

    1. Acquisition expenses — underwriting expenses and initial commission to the distributor
    2. Maintenance expenses over the policy term for servicing the policy
    3. The insurer's PROFIT MARGIN

    GROSS PREMIUM = Risk premium + Allowance for expenses + Profit margin

    The EQUATION OF VALUE ← memorise this exactly

    EPV(Premiums) = EPV(Insured benefits) + EPV(Expenses) + EPV(Profit margin)

    where EPV = Expected Present Value. "Expected" denotes that the cash flows are contingent on the occurrence of a certain event; the present value accounts for the time value of money.

    The gross premium worked example — a 2-year EA

    Input Value
    Policy term / PPT 2 years / 2 years, annual premiums in advance
    Sum assured ₹10 million
    Initial commission 30% of the FIRST premium
    Renewal commission 5% of the renewal premium
    Initial expense ₹2,000 per policy
    Renewal expense ₹400 per policy
    Investment return 6% p.a.
    Profit margin 10% of the FIRST premium
    ⟹ Annual premium (answer) ₹59,54,375

    The five components of that equation of value: 1. PV of premiums = P + P × p₃₅ × PVIF(6,1) 2. PV of benefits = 10mn·q₃₅·PVIF(6,1) + 10mn·q₃₆·p₃₅·PVIF(6,2) + 10mn·p₃₅·p₃₆·PVIF(6,2) 3. PV of commissions = 0.30P + 0.05P × p₃₅ × PVIF(6,1) 4. PV of expenses = 2,000 + 400 × p₃₅ × PVIF(6,1) 5. PV of profit margin = 0.10P

    6.10Pricing in practice2

    The FOUR pricing assumptions guaranteed MCQ| # | Assumption | Source |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | Mortality and morbidity (survival) rates | A standard mortality table, prepared industry-wide by the MORTALITY AND MORBIDITY INVESTIGATION BUREAU, which is a unit of the INSTITUTE OF ACTUARIES OF INDIA, and approved by IRDAI | | 2 | Expenses (initial and renewal expenses + commissions) | Insurer's own estimates | | 3 | Investment return | Insurer's asset-class views | | 4 | WITHDRAWAL RATES | Not used in the course's numerical examples but used in practice. A withdrawal = the policyholder voluntarily stops paying future premiums and forgoes the benefits |

    What makes real-life pricing different from the contrived examples

    1. Longer terms — real products run more than 5 years (the examples used 2 and 3 years)
    2. Two extra cash flows beyond benefits, expenses and profit margin: - Setting up the POLICYHOLDER LIABILITY — the quantified monetary value of the promise made by the insurer, which must be funded out of the premiums (an explicit cash outflow) - SOLVENCY MARGIN REQUIREMENTS — additional regulatory capital when products are sold, also funded out of the premiums
    3. Consequently the first-year premium is INADEQUATE to cover all first-year outflows → a NEGATIVE cash flow from the shareholders' point of view, possibly continuing into years 2 and 3, followed by positive cash flows.

    Profits start emerging only from the THIRD or FOURTH year of the policy term. Who funds the early negative cash flows? THE SHAREHOLDERS must infuse capital. KEY TAKEAWAY: LIFE INSURANCE PRODUCTS CONSUME CAPITAL.

    Two further real-world pricing considerations

    • Competition — for vanilla products (term assurance, endowment assurance) competitors' rates significantly constrain what you can charge
    • PRE = POLICYHOLDER'S REASONABLE EXPECTATIONS — unique to life insurance. At the point of sale the distributor uses sales illustrations showing the policyholder's IRR. The premium charged must actually generate that illustrated IRR; if premiums are too high, the realised IRR falls below what was illustrated, which is a matter of concern

    Pricing within regulatory boundaries

    Two IRDAI regulations bear on pricing: the PRODUCT REGULATIONS and PROTECTION OF POLICYHOLDERS' INTEREST.

    Element Detail
    FILE AND USE Introduced when the sector opened up in 2000: every product had to be filed with the regulator and cleared BEFORE going to market. As part of the documentation the insurer must demonstrate that (a) the product is financially viable, (b) it generates a non-zero return to the policyholder, (c) the regulator's restrictions on expenses and charges have been incorporated
    USE AND FILE The recent liberalisation: if the product is very similar to one issued in the past, the insurer can issue it first and file it as information. But a product very different from what is in the market must still go through FILE AND USE
    ULIP charging restrictions Charges include mortality charge, fund management charge, surrender charge. The regulator prescribes bands — e.g. the mortality charge must be between 1% and 2% of the account value
    Surrender restrictions Limits on how much surrender value must be offered on non-linked products and how much surrender penalty may be charged on unit-linked products
    Rural and social sector obligation Mandatory for every insurer to offer affordable products to the rural and social sectors. Here the premium will typically EQUAL THE RISK PREMIUM, with the allowance for expenses and profit margins considerably watered down classic MCQ

    6.11The five key product-related risks2

    The definition pattern is identical for all of them: the risk of loss arising when ACTUAL experience diverges from the ASSUMPTION used in pricing. Learn the five definitions verbatim — this is the highest-yield table in Part A.

    Risk Definition Most exposed products Least exposed products
    Mortality risk The risk of loss arising if the ACTUAL number of deaths EXCEEDS the EXPECTED number of deaths — particularly in the EARLY years of the policy term TERM ASSURANCE — "a resounding YES"; the main and ONLY source of risk for TA PURE ENDOWMENT — "a resounding NO" (more deaths is actually good news for a PE portfolio — fewer payouts). EA = "it depends"
    Longevity risk The risk of loss arising from policyholders LIVING LONGER THAN EXPECTED Immediate annuities, pure endowments, and deferred annuities once they enter the PAYOUT phase Term assurance, endowment assurance, whole life
    Investment risk The risk of loss arising when the actual investment return is LESS THAN the expected return — and, more importantly, less than the rate of return GUARANTEED on its products NON-PAR products (highly significant) UNIT-LINKED products (not significant at all); par products in between
    Expense risk The risk of loss arising when ACTUAL expenses incurred EXCEED the EXPENSE LOADINGS built into the premium income Insurers in the START-UP phase Mature insurers
    Withdrawal risk The risk of the actual withdrawal rates being significantly different from what was allowed for in pricing Products with heavy front-loaded cash flows —

    Mortality risk — the worked example

    10,000 one-year TA policies at age 35, q₃₅ = 1.2 per mille. - Expected deaths = 10,000 × 1.2/1000 = 12 - Actual deaths = 26 (say, a pandemic outbreak) → 14 additional deaths - The premium collected from 10,000 policyholders may not be sufficient to meet the additional death benefit outgo.

    Why "particularly in the early years"? Because the product's cash-flow profile is negative early, positive later. More early deaths increase the magnitude of the negative cash flows and can turn a profitable product into a loss-making one.

    Who ultimately bears the mortality loss? ## THE SHAREHOLDERS — in the form of lower profits and lower dividends.

    Longevity risk — why it matters and the natural hedge

    If policyholders live longer, payouts must be made for a longer period or to more annuitants than expected → the premium charged proves inadequate.

    Does longevity risk provide a NATURAL HEDGE against mortality risk? YES. This is one of the reasons an insurer sells both life insurance products and annuity products.

    Scenario Life insurance portfolio (TA/EA/WL) Annuity portfolio
    Pandemic outbreak — more deaths than expected MORTALITY LOSS GAIN (fewer annuitants left to receive payouts)
    Medical breakthroughs — significant longevity improvement MORTALITY GAIN LONGEVITY LOSS

    The two standard mortality tables the most likely single-fact MCQ in Part A| | Insured lives | Annuitants |

    |---|---|---| | Table name | Indian Assured Lives Mortality (IALM) 2012–2014 | Indian Individual Annuitants' Mortality (IIAM) 2012–2015 | | Investigation period | 2012–2014 | 2012–2015 | | qₓ per mille at age 25 | 0.9 | 0.4 | | qₓ per mille at age 35 | 1.2 | — | | qₓ per mille at age 75 | 38.2 | 27.4 | | Gender-differentiated? | NO — the table is GENDER NEUTRAL (even though females genuinely have lighter mortality than males) | — | | Smoker/non-smoker differentiated? | NO — insurers wanting smoker-differentiated products must refine the table using their OWN internal experience (the smoker/non-smoker mortality gap is significant in the 25–60 age band) | — |

    KEY COMPARISON: at EVERY age the annuitants' table shows a LOWER death rate than the insured-lives table — i.e. the ANNUITANTS' TABLE IS "LIGHTER".

    WHY? Because ANNUITANTS ARE SELF-SELECTED, whereas INSURED LIVES ARE SELECTED (UNDERWRITTEN) BY THE INSURER. Someone who believes his health is good buys an annuity; someone who fears early death buys the return-of-premium variant instead. This is a UNIVERSAL phenomenon — most markets maintain separate tables for insured lives and annuitants.

    How a standard table is built: all policyholders alive at the start of 2012 participate, grouped by age; mortality is tracked over 2012–2014; deaths ÷ number of policyholders in that age bracket = the CRUDE DEATH RATE; the crude rate is then SMOOTHED (by the insurer or a central agency like the Mortality Investigation Bureau) to give the published rates.

    How expected investment return is measured — the worked example

    Asset class Allocation Expected return
    Government bonds 70% 6%
    High-quality (AAA-rated) corporate bonds 20% 8%
    Equities / equity mutual funds 10% 10%
    Weighted-average (composite) expected return 6.8% p.a.

    Three constraints on the insurer's investment return: 1. The IRDAI-mandated investment pattern 2. The need to meet guaranteed benefit commitments → pushes the insurer towards default-risk-free assets, mainly central government bonds 3. The need to MATCH LIABILITIES AND ASSETS BY TERM — a 30-year endowment backed by 5-year assets creates significant reinvestment risk

    Historic Indian example of investment risk crystallising: products issued in the 1990s carried guaranteed returns higher than what insurers could earn between 2000 and 2010 (a low interest rate environment) → insurers had to discontinue those products and reissue them with lower guaranteed rates.

    Expense risk — expense loadings and the expense gap

    How expense loadings are determined: 1. Estimate the expenses over the business planning horizon of the next 2 to 3 years 2. Classify into POLICY-RELATED vs NON-POLICY-RELATED (overheads — e.g. rentals, cost of developing the policy administration system) 3. Within policy-related, see what varies with premium: commissions = a % of premium; underwriting expenses (medical examinations) = a % of the SUM ASSURED; some are fixed per policy 4. All non-policy-related expenses are recovered on a PER-POLICY basis

    The worked expense-gap example:

    Step Figure
    Estimated fixed expenses ₹10 million
    Expected policies over 2–3 years 10,000
    Per-policy expense loading ₹10 mn ÷ 10,000 = ₹1,000 per policy
    Policies actually sold 8,000
    Expense loading recovered 8,000 × ₹1,000 = ₹8 million
    Actual expenses incurred ₹10 million
    ⟹ EXPENSE GAP (= expense risk) ₹2 million

    A start-up insurer typically runs a significant expense gap and closes it over a period of about SEVEN YEARS. Start-ups face both substantial fixed expenses with frequent overruns and difficulty achieving projected sales volumes.

    Withdrawal risk — lapse vs surrender

    Four reasons a policyholder withdraws: 1. MIS-SELLING — the distributor sold a product that does not meet the policyholder's financial objectives 2. A change in the policyholder's circumstances — e.g. the employer's group term assurance already meets his protection need 3. Inability to pay future premiums — the most common; typically during a downturn in the economic cycle (job loss) 4. Competitors' rates are lower — he stops and gravitates to a competitor

    LAPSE SURRENDER
    When Withdrawal in the INITIAL years (after 1 or 2 premiums) Withdrawal in the LATER years (e.g. after 8 of 10 premiums)
    Benefit paid NOTHING SURRENDER BENEFIT, also called the CASH VALUE of the policy (so called because the policyholder can take a loan against it)
    Quantum — A % of premiums paid; near the end of the term it can be a % of the MATURITY BENEFIT — e.g. 60% of the sum insured after the 8th of 10 premiums
    Profitable for the insurer? NO — only negative cash flows have been incurred and there are no future positive cash flows to recoup them YES — the policy has already generated enough positive cash flows, and the surrender benefit paid is significantly less than the maturity benefit

    MCQ trap: "Do lapses and surrenders generate profit for an insurer?" — "On the face of it, it appears so… however this statement is only PARTLY TRUE." Lapses = loss. Surrenders = gain.

    Regulatory requirement on surrender value (India): if premiums have been paid for a minimum of 3 years, at least 30% of the premiums paid must be returned to the policyholder. The regulator also prescribes a methodology for later-year surrenders — close to maturity, the benefit mirrors the sum assured/maturity benefit. For unit-linked contracts the insurer deducts a surrender penalty from the fund value, and the regulator caps that penalty.

    The two products on which NO surrender value is offered guaranteed MCQ| Product | Why | The risk it prevents |

    |---|---|---| | TERM ASSURANCE | A surrender benefit would incentivise healthy policyholders to take the cash and rebuy the same cover cheaper elsewhere | ANTI-SELECTION RISK | | IMMEDIATE ANNUITIES | A surrender benefit would be taken by annuitants who believe they are in poor health and won't collect future payouts | ANTI-SELECTION RISK |

    The exception: the annuity with return of premiums variant, where the single premium is returned as a death benefit.

    Estimating withdrawal rates

    There is NO standard table for withdrawal rates (unlike mortality). Instead the Life Insurance Council of India and IRDAI publish periodic LAPSE STUDIES.

    The indicative Indian lapse pattern — memorise:

    Policy year Withdrawal/lapse rate
    Year 1 around 30% or upwards of 30%
    Year 2 15% to 20%
    Year 3 onwards settles to a steady state of 5% to 10% p.a.

    6.12Underwriting — mitigating mortality risk2

    Underwriting = the process of SCREENING applicants using specified criteria. It happens at the PROPOSAL STAGE, i.e. when the applicant fills in the proposal form.

    The two questions underwriting answers: 1. Is the risk acceptable? — can I take this applicant in as a policyholder? 2. If yes, what is the appropriate premium, and what other policy terms and conditions should govern the policy?

    The five objectives of underwriting guaranteed MCQ| # | Objective | Explanation |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | Classify risks into HOMOGENEOUS GROUPS | So that a STANDARD PREMIUM can be set for each group. Example group: male + aged 30 + non-smoker + normal health status | | 2 | Guard against ANTI-SELECTION | Anti-selection arises from INFORMATION ASYMMETRY | | 3 | Offer appropriate SPECIAL TERMS to substandard risks | e.g. a PREMIUM LOADING for ailments; or a loading for a life-endangering hobby, which reverts to the normal rate once the policyholder declares he no longer pursues that hobby | | 4 | Ensure ACTUAL mortality experience does not significantly differ from the ASSUMED experience | Otherwise the product is underpriced. The alternatives are to recall, re-price with a higher mortality assumption and reissue, or to select lives whose experience matches the pricing assumption | | 5 | Protect the insurer from OVER-INSURANCE | There must be a relationship between income-earning capacity and the sum assured — the "10× RULE OF THUMB": in a typical TERM ASSURANCE policy the sum assured should NOT be more than 10 TIMES the annual income |

    The anti-selection illustration (worth understanding, not just memorising)

    • Insurer 1's proposal form is silent on smoking status → it charges one premium for smokers and non-smokers
    • Insurer 2's form asks → it offers a lower premium to non-smokers
    • Result: SMOKERS gravitate to Insurer 1, NON-SMOKERS gravitate to Insurer 2 → Insurer 2 has fewer deaths. The non-smokers have "selected against" Insurer 1 — that is ANTI-SELECTION, and it arose from information asymmetry

    The three types of underwriting

    Type What is examined Notes
    MEDICAL underwriting Health questions on the proposal form → then medical reports from the applicant's general practitioner → then, if still insufficient, a battery of tests Because it is costly, rigorous medical underwriting is applied only above a sum-assured threshold (e.g. above ₹1 million). Above the threshold → MEDICALLY EXAMINED LIVES; below it → NON-MEDICALLY EXAMINED LIVES, who merely answer the proposal-form questions or give a DECLARATION OF GOOD HEALTH
    LIFESTYLE underwriting Geographical location of residence, lifestyle habits, hobbies and pursuits Determines standard vs substandard classification
    FINANCIAL underwriting Income-earning capacity vs sum assured Protects against over-insurance (the 10× rule)

    Classification outcome: standard health risks (normal) vs non-standard health risks = SUBSTANDARD LIVES.

    The three ways to manage LONGEVITY risk distinct from underwriting, likely MCQ

    1. Offer an IMPAIRED LIFE ANNUITY — a higher annuity for the same single premium where the applicant demonstrates impaired health (available in some advanced markets)
    2. Do NOT provide GUARANTEED ANNUITY TERMS, especially under deferred annuity contracts — guaranteeing them exposes the insurer to two risks: (a) earning a return lower than the rate implicit in the guaranteed terms, and (b) paying annuities for longer than expected because of longevity improvements during the deferment period
    3. ADJUST the annuitants' mortality table for FUTURE MORTALITY IMPROVEMENTS — otherwise a table built on 2012–2015 experience becomes out of date and the premium proves inadequate

    Note: annuity applicants are normally NOT required to undergo medical tests — annuitants are self-selected.

    6.13Transferring mortality risk — REINSURANCE (life)4

    Reinsurance = the process of TRANSFERRING mortality risk from the insurer to a THIRD PARTY. Underwriting mitigates/reduces risk; reinsurance transfers it.

    The two legs and the vocabulary

    Policyholder ──(life insurance contract)──► LIFE INSURER ──(reinsurance contract)──► REINSURER ──(retrocession)──► ANOTHER REINSURER
    Term Meaning
    Cedant / ceding company The life insurer, which cedes part of the mortality risk to the reinsurer
    Reinsurance contract The leg between the life insurer and the reinsurer
    RETROCESSION The reinsurer reinsuring with ANOTHER reinsurer guaranteed MCQ

    The worked example — and the critical independence point

    TA policy, age 30, SA ₹10 million, term 10 years; death in year 2; 80% reinsured. - Insurer pays the policyholder ₹10 million; the reinsurer pays the insurer ₹8 million - If the reinsurer retrocedes 80% of its ₹8 mn, the third reinsurer pays ₹6.4 million to the first reinsurer

    If the reinsurer FAILS to pay, is the life insurer still obligated to pay the full ₹10 million to the policyholder? YES. THE TWO LEGS OF THE CONTRACT ARE INDEPENDENT.

    Types of reinsurance the classification MCQ| Category | Type | How it works |

    |---|---|---| | PROPORTIONATE | QUOTA SHARE | A fixed proportion of EVERY contract is reinsured. 80% of the SA reinsured → 80% of the premium on every contract goes to the reinsurer as reinsurance premium. "The easiest reinsurance contract to explain." | | PROPORTIONATE | SURPLUS | The insurer sets a RETENTION LIMIT. It keeps the whole risk up to that limit; only the EXCESS above the limit is reinsured, and only the premium pertaining to the excess is shared | | NON-PROPORTIONATE | (excess-of-loss layers) | Used typically in a GROUP insurance context. The insurer specifies a LOSS AMOUNT, and losses above it are shared in agreed percentages, usually in LAYERS with different reinsurers per layer |

    The surplus worked example — retention limit ₹2,50,000:

    Policy Sum assured Retained Reinsured
    1 ₹10,00,000 ₹2,50,000 ₹7,50,000
    2 ₹6,00,000 ₹2,50,000 ₹3,50,000
    3 ₹2,00,000 ₹2,00,000 (whole) NIL — below the retention limit

    The elegance of the surplus method: as the policy size increases, the REINSURED PERCENTAGE also increases. On smaller policies the insurer keeps the ENTIRE premium; only on larger policies does it share premium with the reinsurer.

    The non-proportionate worked example: a 1-year group term assurance for an employer with 500,000 employees largely in one geographical location; an earthquake causes mass loss of life. The insurer may say "I take 80% of the total sum assured, 20% to the reinsurer"; or, more conservatively, "I bear 40% of the excess over ₹500 million, the reinsurer bears 60%, subject to the reinsurer's cap of ₹1,000 million." Losses above ₹1,000 million require another reinsurer — hence multiple layers.

    The three REASONS FOR reinsurance guaranteed MCQ| # | Reason | Detail |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | Mitigates the impact of very large claim payouts | The surplus arrangement rationale | | 2 | Mitigates NEW BUSINESS STRAIN | New business strain = the negative cash flows in the first 2–3 years of the policy term. It can be financed either by raising equity capital or by taking a LOAN FROM A REINSURER. That loan carries NO fixed repayment schedule and NO specified rate of interest — it is repaid only out of the surpluses/profits arising on the insurance portfolio, so it behaves very much like EQUITY | | 3 | Reinsurers have a GLOBAL PRESENCE and product expertise | They have already reinsured products not available in the domestic market, so the insurer can borrow their design and pricing expertise. The Indian example: CRITICAL ILLNESS products (paying out on diagnosis of cancer, heart attack, renal failure) were new to India until 2000–2001; when private insurers entered, they drew on reinsurers' expertise to design and price them |

    The reason AGAINST reinsurance: it costs money. Reinsuring a substantial proportion means transferring a significant part of premium income as reinsurance premium, which adversely affects the insurer's profitability.

    The four major reinsurers operating in India (life) list MCQ

    1. Swiss Reinsurance — "Swiss Re"
    2. Munich Reinsurance — "Munich Re"
    3. Reinsurance Group of America — "RGA"
    4. General Insurance Corporation of India (GIC) — also reinsures Indian insurers' term assurance portfolios

    6.14Managing expense risk and withdrawal risk1

    Expense risk management — the two levers

    Lever Actions
    Control expenses Focus on DISTRIBUTION COSTS — move from traditional channels to DIGITAL PLATFORMS to cut commission expense
    Increase expense revenue (a) increase the NUMBER of policies sold; (b) increase the TICKET SIZE per policy — e.g. move average premium from ₹50,000 to ₹1–2 lakh by seeking richer product structures

    Withdrawal risk management — the FOUR ways guaranteed MCQ| # | Tool | How it works |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | SURRENDER VALUE SCALE | Pre-computed surrender values at different durations, disclosed to policyholders. It cannot be too tight-fisted (no value for money) nor too generous (it would motivate surrender) — "a fairly complex calculation". For ULIPs, a surrender penalty is deducted from the fund value | | 2 | PAID-UP VALUE | Instead of surrendering, keep the policy in force with a REDUCED SUM ASSURED. Example: 10-year EA, SA ₹10 mn, premiums stop after the 5th of 10 → SA reduced by 50% to ₹5 million but protection continues for the full 10-year term | | 3 | POLICY LOAN | A loan against the surrender value — typically up to 80% of it. Example: surrender value ₹5,00,000 at the end of year 5 → loan up to ₹4,00,000. Interest is charged, and loan + interest are recovered from the maturity or death payout. The policyholder does NOT lose the protection benefit | | 4 | LOYALTY BONUS | An addition to the sum assured if the policyholder stays for the entire policy term — e.g. 10% of ₹10 mn, giving a maturity benefit of ₹11 million. Used to encourage PERSISTENCY |

    6.15Managing investment risk7

    The broader definition and the primary objective

    Broad definition of investment risk: the risk of NOT BEING ABLE TO ACHIEVE THE PRIMARY INVESTMENT OBJECTIVE.

    The PRIMARY INVESTMENT OBJECTIVE of a life insurer is TO MEET THE LIABILITIES AS AND WHEN THEY FALL DUE FOR PAYMENT. MAXIMISING INVESTMENT RETURN IS NOT THE PRIMARY GOAL — that's the key takeaway. classic MCQ

    Principles of INSTITUTIONAL investment

    An institutional investor (life insurer, general insurer, bank, NBFC) differs from an individual investor, for whom the primary objective may simply be maximising return.

    For a life insurer: 1. Select investments appropriate to the TERM, NATURE and CURRENCY of the liabilities 2. The investment strategy must match the insurer's RISK APPETITE (high risk aversion → mostly government bonds; low risk aversion → more equities) 3. Subject to the above, aim at maximising the expected return

    Attribute of liabilities What it means for a life insurer
    TERM Liabilities are LONG-TERM (typically > 5 years); assets should match. Problem: the term is UNCERTAIN — a 10-year endowment can pay out at year 4 if death occurs
    NATURE NOMINAL liabilities are denominated in monetary terms and do not change with inflation; REAL liabilities move in line with inflation. By and large a life insurer's liabilities are NOMINAL (the sum assured is a fixed money amount). Inflation-linked immediate annuities exist but are rare
    CURRENCY A mismatch would arise if liabilities are in rupees but assets in, say, pound sterling. Not a serious problem in India — the regulator mandates investment in the Indian capital market barring a few exceptions

    Therefore, in the Indian context the only real concern out of "term, nature and currency" is THE TERM.

    The three techniques for managing investment risk guaranteed MCQ

    1. PURE MATCHING · 2. IMMUNIZATION · 3. PRODUCT DESIGN

    Technique 1 — PURE MATCHING (a theoretical construct)

    Ensure the income and maturity proceeds from investments are exactly equal to the NET LIABILITY OUTGO UNDER ALL CIRCUMSTANCES.

    Net liability outgo: L(t) = B(t) + E(t) − P(t) where B(t) = benefit outgo, E(t) = expense outgo, P(t) = premium inflow at time t.

    The four reasons pure matching is impossible in practice: 1. Uncertainty about the TIMING of the benefit outgo (death can occur anywhere in the term) 2. Uncertainty about the MAGNITUDE of the benefit outgo — for EA there is NO magnitude uncertainty (₹10 mn either way), but for pure TERM assurance there IS (₹0 if he survives, ₹10 mn if he dies) 3. Mismatch between the term of the liabilities and the term of AVAILABLE investments — "it's very difficult to find a Government of India bond with a term of 40 years" 4. REINVESTMENT RISK on investment income — we don't know at what rate coupon income can be reinvested

    Technique 2 — IMMUNIZATION

    Interest rate risk, generally: the change in the value of a bond arising from a change in market rates of interest. The basic bond value theorem: when interest rates go UP, bond values DECLINE, and vice versa. More precisely, interest rate risk = the PERCENTAGE change in the market price of a bond.

    Interest rate risk FOR A LIFE INSURER is defined DIFFERENTLY: it arises when, for a given change in interest rates, THE CHANGE IN THE VALUE OF THE LIABILITIES IS NOT EQUAL TO THE CHANGE IN THE VALUE OF THE INVESTMENTS. this distinction is a likely MCQ Why interest rate risk dominates for a life insurer: most life insurers invest a substantial portion in government bonds or high-quality corporate bonds. It affects both sides of the balance sheet because both are present value calculations: - Value of liabilities = PV(future benefit outgo) + PV(future expense outgo) − PV(future premium inflows) - Value of a bond = PV(interest income) + PV(redemption proceeds)

    THE THREE CONDITIONS FOR IMMUNIZATION guaranteed MCQ| # | Condition | |---|---| | 1 | PV of the INVESTMENT cash flows = PV of the LIABILITY cash flows | | 2 | DURATION of the investment cash flows = DURATION of the liability cash flows | | 3 | CONVEXITY of the investment cash flows is GREATER THAN the convexity of the liability cash flows |

    The duration/convexity worked example
    Bond feature Value
    Face value ₹1,000
    Coupon rate 8% (₹80 for years 1–7; ₹1,080 in year 8 = coupon + redemption)
    Term to maturity 8 years
    Current market price ₹945
    Yield to maturity 9% p.a.

    Check: 80 × PVIFA(9,8) + 1,000 × PVIF(9,8) = ₹945. YTM definition: the market rate of interest that equates the PV of the cash flows from the bond to its current market price.

    The table columns: (1) t · (2) cash flow · (3) PV factor at 9% · (4) PV of cash flow · (5) t × PV of cash flow · (6) PV of cash flow × t(t+1).

    Measure Formula used Answer
    DURATION Σ[t × PV(CF)] ÷ market price = 5,813 ÷ 945 6.15 years (≈6.1)
    CONVEXITY Σ[PV(CF) × t(t+1)] ÷ market price = 47,496 ÷ 945 50.3 — it has NO units

    DURATION = the WEIGHTED AVERAGE TERM TO MATURITY of a bond, where the weights are the RELATIVE PRESENT VALUES of the cash flows. The duration of a bond is always LESS THAN its term (6.15 < 8 years).

    Duration and convexity as measures of interest rate risk

    If YTM rises 9% → 10% (+100 bps): new price = 80 × PVIFA(10,8) + 1,000 × PVIF(10,8) = ₹894. Interest rate risk = (945 − 894) ÷ 945 = 51 ÷ 945 = 5.4%.

    The approximation formula:

    ΔP = P × { −[D × ΔYTM ÷ (1 + YTM)] + [0.5 × C × (ΔYTM)² ÷ (1 + YTM)²] }

    Plugging in P = 945, D = 6.15, C = 50.3, ΔYTM = 1% → change = 51, exactly matching the equation-of-value approach.

    INFERENCE: interest rate risk is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL TO THE DURATION of the bond. A bond with a LONGER DURATION has HIGHER interest rate risk.

    The SIX limitations of immunization "which is NOT a limitation" MCQ
    1. Works well for NOMINAL liabilities but not for liabilities denominated in REAL terms (inflation-linked payouts)
    2. Because the change in asset value is set equal to the change in liability value, there is NO POSSIBILITY OF MAKING A PROFIT OR A LOSS — profits and losses are removed
    3. Works only for a SMALL change in interest rates (9% → 10%). For an abnormal change (9% → 14%) it does not provide credible results
    4. It is predicated on the assumption of a FLAT YIELD CURVE — but yield curves in practice are typically UPWARD SLOPING. (Yield curve = the relationship between YIELD TO MATURITY and TERM TO MATURITY; flat means a 1-year and a 10-year bond have the same YTM — "very unrealistic")
    5. Requires REBALANCING every time interest rates change → frequent rebalancing entails TRANSACTION COSTS
    6. There aren't sufficient LONG-DURATION assets to match long-duration liabilities; plus the uncertainty of the liability outgo itself makes liability duration and convexity hard to compute

    Despite the limitations, immunization is the technique WIDELY USED by insurers to achieve at least a partial hedge.

    Immunization IN PRACTICE — the three steps
    1. Most insurers IGNORE CONVEXITY and focus only on DURATION (a simpler measure)
    2. Classify liabilities into PAR and NON-PAR. They are not unduly concerned about UNIT-LINKED liabilities since that investment risk has been transferred to policyholders
    3. Allocate the LONGEST-duration assets to the NON-PAR liabilities (where investment risk is most significant), and the lower-duration assets to PAR liabilities

    The worked allocation: duration of non-par liabilities = 12 years; the highest-duration asset bucket has a weighted-average duration of 11 years → allocated to non-par. The remaining assets, weighted-average duration 10 years, → allocated to par. A mismatch is inevitable, but it is MINIMISED where investment risk matters most.

    The DURATION–INTEREST RATE MATRIX very likely MCQ| | Interest rates RISE | Interest rates FALL |

    |---|---|---| | Duration of ASSETS > Duration of LIABILITIES | % fall in assets > % fall in liabilities → LOSS ← THIS IS WHERE A BANK SITS | % rise in assets > % rise in liabilities → PROFIT | | Duration of ASSETS < Duration of LIABILITIES | % fall in assets < % fall in liabilities → comfortable / no loss | % rise in assets < % rise in liabilities → LOSS ← THIS IS WHERE A LIFE INSURER SITS |

    Institution Position Loses when
    LIFE INSURER D(assets) < D(liabilities) — liabilities are long-term and matching long assets don't exist INTEREST RATES DECLINE
    BANK D(assets) > D(liabilities) — deposits run from a few days to ~3 years but banks lend long INTEREST RATES RISE

    Technique 3 — PRODUCT DESIGN

    Guideline Rationale
    Sell LESS non-par business Non-par carries the highest investment risk
    If you must sell non-par, REDUCE THE POLICY TERMS Prefer 10-year endowments over 30-year endowments
    Within non-par, increase exposure to PURE PROTECTION business Term premiums are so low that little is invested, so exposure is small
    Sell MORE PAR business Investment risk is shared with policyholders. And within par, sell products with LOW REGULAR bonuses and a SUBSTANTIAL TERMINAL bonus — this gives maximum leeway to alter bonus levels if experience is worse than expected
    Sell MORE UNIT-LINKED products Risk is fully transferred to the policyholder — but sell them WITHOUT INVESTMENT GUARANTEES. A ULIP with, say, a 3% interest rate guarantee forces the insurer to credit 3% even if the fund earns less, making the product more onerous

    Default risk — the other component of investment risk

    Default risk is NOT a very significant component for a life insurer, because life insurers prefer to invest heavily in government bonds given the guaranteed nature of their liabilities.

    Mitigants: - The mandated investment pattern itself - EXPOSURE NORMS set by the regulator: (a) maximum exposure by CREDIT RATING — e.g. only AAA or AA rated bonds, no speculative bonds; (b) exposure limits to a SINGLE COUNTERPARTY (e.g. not more than 10% of total funds); (c) limits on RELATED counterparties (same group of companies); (d) limits by INDUSTRY OR SECTOR, which minimises exposure to cyclical risk - CREDIT DEFAULT SWAPS (CDS)

    How a CDS works: the BUYER (the life insurer) buys protection from the SELLER (the counterparty) on a REFERENCED BOND. The buyer pays an annual default risk premium over the swap term. If no default → no cash flow from seller to buyer. If default → the seller pays the DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE FACE VALUE AND THE MARKET PRICE at the time of default (face ₹100, market ₹10 at default → seller pays ₹90), ensuring the buyer receives the full face value. CDS have "just made a beginning" in India; transactions are few and far between.

    The MANDATED INVESTMENT PATTERN (IRDAI) certain numerical MCQ

    Life insurance business is segmented into two lines: (1) life insurance business (protection + savings products like whole life and endowment) and (2) annuities and pension business.

    Asset class Life insurance business Pension & annuity business
    Central government securities NOT LESS THAN 25% NOT LESS THAN 20%
    Central + State government securities together NOT LESS THAN 50% NOT LESS THAN 40%
    Infrastructure bonds NOT LESS THAN 15% —
    Other approved investments NOT MORE THAN 35% —
    Approved investments (total cap) 50% 60% — the pension pattern is MORE LIBERAL

    "Approved investments" = anything other than central and state government securities, which must satisfy prudential norms laid down by the regulator (corporate bonds, equities).

    6.16Capital requirements and solvency4

    The FIVE reasons a life insurer needs capital guaranteed MCQ| # | Reason | Detail |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | To cushion UNEXPECTED LOSSES from exposure to different sources of risk (insurance risk, credit risk, operational risk) | This is what the regulator legislates for | | 2 | To finance NEW BUSINESS STRAIN | The negative cash flows in the initial years of the policy term | | 3 | To have more INVESTMENT FREEDOM | Capital cushions the loss if the insurer deliberately mismatches asset and liability terms to chase a higher return | | 4 | To pursue ORGANIC growth | New operations, expanding the branch network | | 5 | To pursue INORGANIC growth | Mergers and acquisitions to add to the product portfolio |

    The STATUTORY (regulatory) balance sheet

            ASSETS                     |            LIABILITIES
  ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------
  STATUTORY VALUE OF ASSETS       |  3. FREE CAPITAL / EXCESS CAPITAL
                                  |  2. REGULATORY CAPITAL (= Required Solvency Margin)
                                  |  1. PRUDENTIAL ESTIMATE OF POLICYHOLDER LIABILITIES

    Statutory value of assets must be AT LEAST EQUAL TO (prudential value of liabilities + regulatory capital). Any excess is FREE CAPITAL.

    GAAP balance sheet REGULATORY / statutory balance sheet
    Prepared for INVESTORS — generally accepted accounting principles THE REGULATOR — to assess how much capital is needed to support the business
    Asset side All assets Not all assets qualify — e.g. assets in the nature of miscellaneous expenditure are EXCLUDED
    Liability side Accounting basis Policyholder liabilities estimated per the regulator's norms

    What free capital may be used for: writing new business · gaining investment freedom · pursuing growth opportunities. The regulatory capital chunk CANNOT be used for these purposes.

    The THREE LEVELS of capital requirement in India ← the highest-yield block in this module

    LEVEL 1 — Minimum paid-up capital

    Item Value
    Minimum paid-up capital to start a LIFE insurance company ₹1,000 million = ₹100 crore
    Maximum total foreign investment 74% — the Union Budget 2025 announced a raise from 74% to 100%
    Stock exchange listing Possible, but only after a LOCK-IN PERIOD of around 10 YEARS

    LEVEL 2 — the REQUIRED SOLVENCY MARGIN (RSM)

    RSM = MAXIMUM of { [K₁ × Policyholder Liabilities] + [K₂ × Sum At Risk] , ₹500 MILLION } For most lines of insurance business in India: K₁ = 4% and K₂ = 0.3%

    Component Economic rationale
    K₁ = 4% applied to POLICYHOLDER LIABILITIES Even estimated on prudential norms, liabilities can be MISSTATED (understated). The 4% provides for that misstatement
    K₂ = 0.3% applied to the SUM AT RISK Provides for the unexpected loss that arises because the policyholder liability does not equal the sum assured

    SUM AT RISK = SUM ASSURED − POLICYHOLDER LIABILITY

    where Policyholder liability = PV(future benefit outgo) + PV(future expense outgo) − PV(future premium inflows).

    The illustration: a 10-year EA, SA ₹10 million, now in year 4. The policyholder liability computed is only ₹5 million — so you hold assets of ₹5 mn. But if he dies at the end of year 4 you must pay ₹10 million. The ₹5 million difference is the SUM AT RISK — and NO liability has been provided for it.

    Reinsurance credit — can risk mitigants reduce the RSM? YES. To the extent policyholder liabilities have been reinsured, you exclude them and attach K₁ only to the un-reinsured liabilities. BUT: not more than 50% of the policyholder liabilities can be treated as reinsured for this calculation. (Otherwise, with 100% reinsurance, both PHL and SAR would be zero and no RSM would emerge.)

    The RSM worked example:

    Step Figure
    Policyholder liabilities ₹700 million
    Sum assured ₹8,400 million
    Sum at risk = 8,400 − 700 ₹7,700 million
    K₁ × PHL = 4% × 700 ₹28 million
    K₂ × SAR = 0.3% × 7,700 ₹23.1 million
    Formula-based RSM = 28 + 23.1 ₹51.1 million
    Monetary minimum ₹500 million
    ⟹ REQUIRED SOLVENCY MARGIN ₹500 MILLION (the monetary minimum wins)

    LEVEL 3 — the minimum SOLVENCY RATIO

    AVAILABLE SOLVENCY MARGIN (ASM) = Paid-up equity share capital + Reserves and surplus − Accumulated losses

    SOLVENCY RATIO = ASM ÷ RSM, and it must be ≥ 1.5 AT ALL TIMES (i.e. ASM ≥ 150% of RSM)

    Why 1.5? Because the RSM formula is focused entirely on the LIABILITY side (policyholder liabilities and sum at risk). There is NO safety mechanism in that formula for unexpected losses on the ASSET side (defaults, investment losses). The 1.5 factor provides for those.

    The solvency ratio worked example (continuing the RSM example):

    Item Figure
    Paid-up equity share capital ₹1,250 million
    Reserves and surplus Nil (start-up phase)
    Accumulated losses ₹200 million
    Available solvency margin = 1,250 − 200 ₹1,050 million
    Required solvency margin ₹500 million
    ⟹ SOLVENCY RATIO = 1,050 ÷ 500 2.1 — comfortably above the 1.5 control level

    All three tests are met: paid-up capital ₹1,250 mn > ₹1,000 mn required; RSM ₹500 mn maintained; solvency ratio 2.1 > 1.5.

    Actual Indian solvency ratios as of March 2024 (from IRDAI's Annual Report 2024-25) possible direct MCQ| Company | Solvency ratio | |---|---| | Bajaj Allianz | 4.32 — significantly the highest | | LIC of India (public sector) | 1.98 | | SBI Life | 1.96 | | ICICI Prudential | 1.9 | | HDFC Life | 1.8 |

    Interpretation: the HIGHER the solvency ratio, the GREATER the FINANCIAL STRENGTH of the insurer — because it implies more FREE CAPITAL for writing business, investment freedom and growth. (Context: there are 25 Indian life insurance companies.)

    Sources of capital

    Category Instruments
    Internal equity RETAINED EARNINGS, captured as reserves and surplus
    External equity Capital infused by the promoter, a public issue, a private placement, or a rights issue

    Indian life insurers have an UNLEVERAGED (ungeared) capital structure — minimal debt. WHY? Because debt instruments (debentures, bonds) DO NOT COUNT towards the AVAILABLE SOLVENCY MARGIN — ASM is only paid-up share capital + retained earnings. So there is little incentive to raise debt from a solvency standpoint. Mature markets, by contrast, have LEVERAGED life insurance capital structures.

    The three ALTERNATIVE RISK TRANSFER (ART) instruments guaranteed MCQ| Instrument | How it works | Indian status |

    |---|---|---| | FINANCIAL REINSURANCE | A reinsurer provides a CONDITIONAL LOAN to the life insurer. Repayment is conditioned on profits emerging from a SPECIFIED BLOCK OF BUSINESS (e.g. a whole life block). The reinsurer projects the profits, takes their present value, and sets the loan equal to that PV. If actual profits exceed the projection, the reinsurer gets more than the loan; if the block underperforms, no part of the loan is returned. Because it behaves like EQUITY, some developed-market jurisdictions allow it to count towards the ASM | Nascent | | CATASTROPHE EQUITY PUTS | Allows the insurer to issue equity at a PREDETERMINED PRICE to the option seller IF a specified catastrophic event occurs — e.g. a mass-casualty event hitting a large group term assurance book | Developed markets | | CREDIT DEFAULT SWAPS | Cushions losses arising from DEFAULT on the ASSET side | A few Indian life insurers |

    The global trend — RISK-BASED CAPITAL and SOLVENCY II

    India's RSM is a formula predicated on policyholder liabilities and sum at risk. Globally, insurers have moved to a RISK-BASED CAPITAL framework which is far more comprehensive — it looks at BOTH the asset side and the liability side.

    Calibration: the risk capital is set at the amount needed for the insurer to remain solvent with a very high probability over a specified period — e.g. solvent with a probability of 99.5% over the next 1 year.

    SOLVENCY II is the popular global risk-based capital framework — and it is "very similar to the BASEL II framework applicable to banks."

    The three steps under Solvency II: 1. Calculate the risk capital for EACH source of risk: mortality risk · credit risk · market risk · OPERATIONAL RISK (= the risk of failure of people, systems or processes) 2. Aggregate the risk capital, ALLOWING FOR CORRELATIONS between the risks — e.g. operational risk is empirically correlated with market risk 3. Ensure at all times: AVAILABLE CAPITAL > REQUIRED RISK CAPITAL (the Solvency Capital Requirement, SCR**)

    Two levels of capital under Solvency II likely MCQ| Level | If available capital falls below it | |---|---| | SCR — Solvency Capital Requirement | The regulator INTERVENES and asks the company for a RECAPITALISATION PLAN | | MCR — Minimum Solvency Capital Requirement (analogous to India's ₹500 million floor) | The insurer may LOSE ITS LICENCE to transact insurance business |

    6.17Accounting and reporting2

    The structure — two income statements, one balance sheet

    Statement Also called Contents
    POLICYHOLDERS' ACCOUNT The TECHNICAL ACCOUNT The income statement from the policyholder's perspective
    SHAREHOLDERS' ACCOUNT The NON-TECHNICAL ACCOUNT The income statement from the shareholder's perspective
    Balance sheet — Sources of funds and applications of funds

    The POLICYHOLDERS' (technical) account

    INCOME side:

    NET EARNED PREMIUM = (a) Premium on business sold − (b) Premium on REINSURANCE CEDED + (c) Premium on REINSURANCE ACCEPTED

    • Reinsurance ceded = premium paid to a reinsurer → shown as an offset
    • Reinsurance accepted = premium received because this life insurer has itself reinsured part of another life insurer's business → an income item (possible in some markets where an insurer acts both as direct insurer and reinsurer)

    Total income = Net earned premium + Income from investments + Other income (other income is fairly insignificant).

    EXPENSE side — three heads:

    # Head Detail
    1 Operating expenses Expenses of managing the company AND the commissions paid to distributors
    2 Benefits paid (NET) "Net" = total benefit payout LESS the amount recovered from the reinsurer. Benefits have three components: death benefits · withdrawal benefits · maturity benefits
    3 CHANGE IN VALUATION OF POLICYHOLDER LIABILITY The difference between the policyholder liability at (say) 31 March 2025 and at 31 March 2024, both being forward-looking present-value calculations using assumptions such as the discount rate

    Total income − Total expenses = the AMOUNT AVAILABLE FOR APPROPRIATION, which is transferred to the shareholders' account.

    The SHAREHOLDERS' (non-technical) account

    Line Note
    + Profit transferred from the policyholders' account
    + Income from shareholders' investments The share capital plus reserves are themselves invested
    − Expenses other than those related to insurance e.g. interest expense
    = Profit before tax
    − Provision for tax Life insurance profits are subject to a DIFFERENT TAX REGIME from the normal corporate 30% — the example assumes ~20% of PBT likely MCQ
    = Profit after tax ₹140 million in the worked example

    The BALANCE SHEET

    SOURCES OF FUNDS APPLICATIONS OF FUNDS
    1. Shareholders' funds — ₹1,750 mn 1. Shareholders' investments
    2. Borrowings — ₹300 mn (SUBORDINATED DEBT, repayable only after all policyholder liabilities have been paid out) 2. Policyholders' investments
    3. Policyholder liabilities — the dominant liability 3. Fixed assets
    4. Net current assets = current assets − current liabilities
    Total = ₹34,000 million Total = ₹34,000 million
    • Current assets for a life insurer: cash and bank balances and money market instruments
    • Current liabilities: policyholder amounts due because the insured event has happened but the payout has not
    • Shareholders' investments back the shareholders' funds; policyholders' investments back the policyholder liabilities

    Minimum capital sanity check: ₹1,000 mn (minimum to start) + ₹500 mn (minimum RSM) = ₹1,500 million. The example's shareholders' funds of ₹1,750 mn clear that bar.

    The financial ratios — worked value vs industry standard ← very high-yield table

    # Ratio Definition This company Industry standard / interpretation
    1 SOLVENCY RATIO ASM ÷ RSM 1.95 Minimum 1.5. The difference (1.95 − 1.5) represents the FREE CAPITAL — usable for new business or for mismatching investment positions
    2 Net profit margin PAT ÷ (total income in technical account + investment income in non-technical account) = 140 ÷ (9,585 + 120) 1.4% ~2.5%
    3 Premium income as % of technical-account income ~73% Premium is the dominant income source
    4 Investment income as % of total income ~27% Second major component
    5 REINSURANCE RATIO Reinsurance premium ceded ÷ premium received = 145 ÷ 7,100 ~2% ~10%. Low ratio → BETTER PROFITABILITY but WEAKER safeguards against very large death payouts
    6 Operating expenses ÷ premium income ~20% Standard ~20%. For a START-UP, typically HIGHER THAN 50%
    7 Benefits paid ÷ premium income 3,600 ÷ 6,955 (premium net of reinsurance) 52% Typically 30–35%. A high value probably means many policies MATURED this year → large maturity payout. Confirm by comparing with prior years
    8 Change in policyholders' liability ÷ premium income 4,500 ÷ 6,955 65% Typically 60–70%. CAUTION: a gradual DECLINE is NOT necessarily efficiency — it may mean the insurer is DILUTING THE ASSUMPTIONS used to calculate policyholder liabilities (i.e. under-reserving)
    9 External debt-to-equity Borrowings ÷ shareholders' funds = 300 ÷ 1,750 ~17% Manufacturing companies run 2:1 or 3:1. Insurers keep debt low to avoid diluting the solvency position
    10 Policyholders' liability as % of shareholders' funds 1,825% Expected — policyholder liability is the dominant balance-sheet liability
    11 Investments as % of total application of funds 99.7% ~90% typical
    12 RETURN ON EQUITY PAT ÷ shareholders' funds = 140 ÷ 1,750 ~8% A life insurer at MATURITY earns around 12%

    The TWO balance sheets issue likely MCQ

    A life insurer must prepare financial statements under: 1. Indian GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles), and 2. The IRDAI (ACTUARIAL, FINANCE AND INVESTMENT FUNCTIONS OF INSURERS) REGULATIONS, 2024 — used to demonstrate solvency

    FORTUNATELY, IN INDIA THE INDIAN GAAP CLOSELY FOLLOWS THE IRDAI REGULATIONS — so an Indian insurer needs to produce only ONE set of financial statements that satisfies both.

    6.18Organisational structure and distribution channels (life)2

    Organisational structure

    CEO reports to the Board of Directors. The main functions:

    Function Responsibilities
    Sales and marketing Managing distribution channels, assessing customer needs, and designing products appropriate to those needs
    Operations Underwriting · Claims management · Reinsurance · Customer service
    Actuarial and compliance Pricing · Valuation · Regulatory compliance
    Investments Managing investments and investment risk
    Accounting Financial accounting and preparing the financial statements
    IT Platforms for pricing, valuation and holding policyholder information
    HR Primary role in a life insurer: RECRUITING THE INTERMEDIARIES who distribute the products

    The IRDAI-prescribed regulatory roles list MCQ

    APPOINTED ACTUARY (mandatory for every life insurer) — monitors compliance with IRDAI regulations, is responsible for PRICING products and for VALUING them to determine policyholder liabilities. Plus: Chief Investments Officer · Chief Financial Officer · Chief Risk Officer · Company Secretary.

    Corporate governance guidelines (IRDAI)

    1. The CEO CANNOT be the CHAIRPERSON of a life insurance company
    2. Board-constituted committees are required: Audit · Corporate Governance · Investment · Asset-Liability Management (ALM) · Risk

    Distribution channels

    TRADITIONAL channels Detail
    Individual TIED agents Tied to one insurance company; cannot sell another life insurer's products. Compensated by commission: first-year commission ≈ 40% of the first premium; renewal commission ≈ 2.5% of the premium on an annual-premium policy ← memorise
    BANCASSURANCE Insurers partnering with banks
    Non-bank corporate agents NBFCs, microfinance institutions, large retail chains
    Insurance BROKERS They do NOT act on behalf of insurance companies — they act on behalf of the PROSPECTIVE POLICYHOLDERS, helping them choose appropriate products, and are compensated by the prospective policyholders
    MODERN channels Detail
    Online platforms Company website, mobile app, or an AGGREGATOR PORTAL such as PolicyBazaar (compare quotes across companies; some allow paperless onboarding)

    The constraint on modern channels: only SIMPLIFIED products can be sold through them — a pure term assurance or a simple endowment assurance. A complicated UNIT-LINKED product CANNOT be sold online because such products require "EYEBALL-TO-EYEBALL CONTACT", possible only through traditional channels. classic MCQ IRDAI regulates: the insurer's choice of distribution channels, the compensation payable to each channel, and the market conduct processes of each channel.

    PART B — NON-LIFE (GENERAL) INSURANCE AND INSURTECH (Sanath Kumar)

    6.19Life insurance vs Non-life insurance — the fundamental distinction

    Other names for non-life insurance: in the US it is called PROPERTY AND CASUALTY (P&C) insurance; liability insurance is part of it. In India, "general insurance" and "non-life insurance" are used interchangeably.

    THE ONE-LINE DISTINCTION: LIFE INSURANCE COVERS CERTAINTY; NON-LIFE INSURANCE COVERS UNCERTAINTY.

    Dimension LIFE insurance NON-LIFE / general insurance
    Nature of the event CERTAIN — natural death is certain; or survival to a specified age/period is a defined outcome FORTUITOUS / UNCERTAIN — payment is triggered only when a specified accident happens. If something is certain, it is NOT covered under non-life
    Payment Money comes back either on death or on survival If the event doesn't happen, NOTHING comes back
    Property damage NOT covered Core business — persons against accidents, buildings, cargo in transit, vehicles, ships, aircraft, and liability
    Savings element Yes — index-linked, unit-linked or regular savings; money returned with bonus/interest NO savings in India. (Japan has some savings-linked householders' insurance; India has not yet adopted it — "there is a lot of talk about it")
    Typical policy duration LONG-TERM — 20/30/40 years TYPICALLY 1 YEAR MAXIMUM (long-term home, health and motor TP policies now exist). Some are far shorter: a transit policy expires the moment the cargo reaches its destination; a travel policy expires when the travel is over
    Pension / annuity Yes — life insurers offer pension and group annuity schemes (also the National Pension System under PFRDA) NO pension scheme, NO annuity scheme
    Overlap Accidental death riders; critical illness riders Critical illness cover; personal accident

    Health insurance — the meeting ground

    LIFE insurer's health cover NON-LIFE insurer's health cover
    Payment form LUMP SUM — the full sum insured on diagnosis of a specified critical illness (stroke, cancer, heart attack, specified cardiac/neuro conditions) INDEMNITY — reimbursement of the actual expenditure incurred in hospital
    Hospitalisation reimbursement LIFE INSURERS IN INDIA DO NOT COVER REIMBURSEMENT OF HOSPITALISATION — cashless or otherwise. THEY ARE NOT ALLOWED BY THE REGULATOR Yes — this is their core business

    INDEMNITY = exactly compensating for the financial loss suffered. Around 22 to 25 specified CRITICAL ILLNESSES are commonly covered by both life and non-life insurers.

    Composite licences

    In India a LIFE insurer CANNOT do general insurance, and a GENERAL insurer CANNOT do life insurance — IRDAI issues SEPARATE LICENCES. There is NO COMMON LICENCE.

    BUT: a Government of India proposal to amend the Insurance Act to permit COMPOSITE (common) LICENCES is pending — expected in the monsoon session. Many countries already allow it.

    6.20The global non-life market1

    The world league table — 2024 gross premium number-matching MCQ| Rank | Company | Country | Premium (US$ bn) |

    |---|---|---|---| | 1 | State Farm | USA | 78 | | 2 | People's Insurance Company of China (PICC) | China | 70 | | 3 | Allianz | Germany | 65 | | 4 | AXA | France | 60 | | 5 | Berkshire Hathaway (Warren Buffett) | USA | 58 | | 6 | Ping An | China | 50 | | 7 | Liberty Mutual | USA | 48 | | 8 | Progressive | USA | 47 | | — | THE ENTIRE INDIAN NON-LIFE INDUSTRY | India | ~35–40 (≈38) |

    THE TOP 10 GROUPS ACCOUNT FOR ABOUT 25% OF GLOBAL NON-LIFE PREMIUM. The Indian industry as a whole is SMALLER THAN ONE of the largest single companies.

    Why? These giants operate across the world (Allianz is in Germany, India, the Gulf, Singapore…), whereas Indian non-life insurers are almost entirely domestic. The exception is NEW INDIA ASSURANCE, a public-sector company operating in about 24 countries, though its foreign premium is small relative to its domestic premium. About 95–96% of India's non-life premium comes from within India.

    Trend note: a decade ago the list was almost entirely US and Europe; today it includes two from China and one from Japan (Tokio Marine was already large earlier).

    6.21The current state of general insurance in India ← dense with examinable numbers3

    The headline figures (FY2025, i.e. 1 April 2024 – 31 March 2025)

    Metric Value
    Indian NON-LIFE premium ₹3.04–3.34 lakh crore (≈ US$38 billion)
    Indian LIFE premium ₹8.30 lakh crore
    Health insurance premium ₹1.30 lakh crore — now the LARGEST component of non-life
    Total assets under management (all insurers) ₹82.50 lakh crore, of which LIC alone accounts for ~₹60–62 lakh crore
    Non-life insurance DENSITY US$25 per capita — "quite low"
    Non-life insurance PENETRATION ~1% of GDP (stuck at 0.7–1% for several years)
    India's world RANK by non-life size 10th
    FDI cap 74% for insurers; 100% already allowed for BROKERS/intermediaries
    Growth rate ~8–11% p.a., poised to continue at 10–11%
    Minimum capital to start a GENERAL insurance company ₹100 crore

    THE THREE INDICATORS used to gauge any country's non-life industry guaranteed MCQ 1. TOTAL SIZE OF PREMIUM · 2. DENSITY (premium per capita) · 3. PENETRATION (premium ÷ GDP)

    Benchmarks for penetration: emerging economies (Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Korea) run 2–2.5%; advanced Western countries ~3%. India needs to break through 1% and reach 2–2.5% — "that is where FinTech comes in."

    The count of players certain "how many" MCQ| Type | Count |

    |---|---| | General (non-life) insurers | 25 (out of 30-plus non-life entities in total) | | Standalone Health Insurers (SAHI) | 7 | | Crop insurers (Agriculture Insurance Company) | 1 | | Credit insurer — ECGC (Export Credit and Guarantee Corporation of India) | 1 | | Reinsurers | 2 — GIC Re plus a newly licensed Fairfax-sponsored reinsurer | | Life insurers | ~25, roughly equal in number to non-life |

    SAHI = STAND-ALONE HEALTH INSURER. Why do they exist? Because health insurance is a complex SPECIALTY business — it involves medical terminology, dealing with hospitals, medicines/pharmaceuticals and diagnostic centres. High specialisation is needed to take health insurance to every corner of the country. More licences are being applied for and granted.

    Why health overtook motor very likely MCQ

    • As recently as 3–4 years ago, MOTOR was the largest component of Indian non-life (because third-party liability insurance is compulsory), with health second.

    • TODAY HEALTH IS THE LARGEST COMPONENT. The same shift is happening across emerging economies.

    • Premium composition last year: HEALTH ≈ 39%, MOTOR ≈ 32% — together ~71%. Everything else (fire, transit, engineering, construction, liability, personal accident, aviation, crop) = ~30%.

    The economics — the crucial insight

    MOST INDIAN NON-LIFE INSURERS DO NOT MAKE A PROFIT FROM THE INSURANCE BUSINESS ITSELF. Their balance sheets turn green ONLY because of INVESTMENT RETURNS.

    UNDERWRITING PROFIT = the profit that comes from doing the business (underwriting = the process of accepting risk). Only about 3 or 4 out of ~30 non-life insurers make an underwriting profit. Most public sector insurers have been running underwriting losses for 6–7 years.

    Why do investors still enter? Because you get access to a large investable corpus, and profits arrive after 4–5 years once investment returns reach a trigger point — plus a little underwriting profit if management and distribution expenditure are controlled very carefully.

    Why the AUM is so large: premiums are collected upfront but claims arrive later or never, so insurers invest the float — strictly per IRDAI's investment regulations (government bonds, state government bonds, housing and infrastructure securities). Insurance companies are among the largest institutional investors in India; banking is only secondary to them.

    Why FDI at 74% has not filled up

    Even at 74%, many FDIs are at much lower levels, because the Indian partner is itself a strong corporate, and foreign insurers want more confidence, more stabilised premium rates and higher penetration before committing capital. Health insurance is the one area with a queue for FDI. There is a clamour to raise the cap to 100%, though many feel it would not immediately translate into a flood of investment.

    COVID and the growth curve

    • 2020–21 shows a DIP — during COVID the country was down and buying insurance was not a priority
    • Post-COVID growth accelerated because of higher awareness of health insurance (people experienced hospitalisation costs, plus lingering lung/immune-related conditions), SMEs and MSMEs insuring against fire, and intense competition/advertising and new aggregators like Policy Bazaar
    • The drivers of growth remain MOTOR and HEALTH; the instructor personally would like FIRE, ENGINEERING and LIABILITY to grow

    6.22Indian business houses in insurance

    Why do large business houses enter insurance? They have corporate image and brand equity, substantial presence across the country, distribution platforms, management capability, and foreign technical partners — and being in both credit and insurance establishes their presence in the financial sector as a whole.

    Group Position
    Tata Life and non-life — partnered with AIG and AIA
    Axis Bank Recently took shares in a life insurer, which was renamed after them
    Aditya Birla Life, and a STANDALONE HEALTH insurer (SAHI) — has not entered general non-life
