    Reliance (Anil Ambani group) Life sold to NIPPON of Japan; non-life reportedly on the block; HINDUJAS to take over Reliance Capital
    ICICI Strong in both — non-life with LOMBARD (driven by the FAIRFAX group); life with PRUDENTIAL
    State Bank of India Life and non-life, with foreign partners (partners have changed from the originals)
    Bajaj Under Bajaj Capital — Bajaj Life and Bajaj Non-Life, partnered with ALLIANZ. Recent news: Bajaj is PARTING WITH ALLIANZ, and ALLIANZ is going with JIO to create a non-life insurer
    Shriram Finance Life, non-life and a broking unit
    Sundaram Partnered with the British ROYAL SUN ALLIANCE
    HDFC Life and non-life
    Patanjali Reported to be buying Poonawalla's stake in Magma General Insurance
    Central Bank of India Acquiring the FUTURE group's stakes in its life and non-life ventures (Future went insolvent)

    The instructor stresses this list is a snapshot — groups constantly enter, exit and swap partners.

    6.23The regulator — IRDAI2

    Attribute Detail
    Full name Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI)
    Headquarters HYDERABAD
    Constituted under The IRDA Act, 1999; originally empowered by the INSURANCE ACT, 1938
    Composition A CHAIRMAN + 4 to 5 WHOLE-TIME MEMBERS — including members for non-life, life, health, distribution, actuary, and finance & investment
    Scope COMMON for life AND non-life — this is the one meeting point between the two industries
    Peer financial-sector regulators RBI (banking) · SEBI (capital market) · PFRDA (pensions). TRAI is NOT a financial sector regulator — it is telecom ← classic "which of these is NOT" trap

    IRDAI's functions

    1. Issue and cancel LICENCES for insurance companies and all intermediaries
    2. Regulate the functioning of insurers and intermediaries — including how and where they may invest
    3. PROTECT THE INTEREST OF THE POLICYHOLDER — the FOREMOST objective. "What I buy is a PROMISE" — the regulator exists to ensure the promise is kept, whether the claim comes tomorrow or in 20 years
    4. Promote and regulate PROFESSIONAL ORGANISATIONS connected with insurance (brokers, surveyors, actuaries)
    5. Resolve DISPUTES among licensed entities (e.g. an insurer vs a surveyor)
    6. Call for information and conduct inspections
    7. PENAL / PUNITIVE POWERS — IRDAI can impose monetary penalties (news items about insurers being penalised ₹1–2 crore). "Not only the regulatory power — they have penal punitive powers as well." Beyond the money, the reputational cost is another cost to pay
    8. Handle policyholder complaints — IRDAI forwards the complaint to the insurer, which must treat it as high priority

    The THREE types of regulatory instrument guaranteed MCQ

    1. REGULATIONS (a GAZETTED NOTIFICATION) · 2. CIRCULARS (issued from time to time, amplifying a provision) · 3. GUIDELINES

    A circular is "as good as a regulation" — e.g. after the recent aircraft accident, IRDAI issued a circular that all claims arising out of that accident be given higher priority and settled within a specified number of days.

    The AREAS regulated ← "which of the following is NOT regulated" trap; the answer is almost always "none — everything is"

    Area What the regulation does
    Registration/licensing of insurers Minimum qualifications and criteria
    Products Design, wording, filing
    Investments Where premium money may be invested
    EXPENSE OF MANAGEMENT A FIXED CAP: "your expense of management shall not exceed this percentage." Purpose: to stop insurers going spendthrift and to keep the money intact for claims. Before the Insurance Act, insurers "made merry" and money was siphoned off to promoter families.
    Intermediaries and distribution Agents, brokers, corporate agents — "one area where a lot of FinTech activity is seen these days"
    Third Party Administrators (TPAs) Health claims administration
    CYBERSECURITY Detailed guidelines; tightened further after a highly publicised hacking of major insurers. "Data is more precious than gold now."
    RURAL AND SOCIAL SECTOR obligations A MANDATORY PERCENTAGE of business must be sourced from RURAL areas — insurers cannot make money only from cities. Failure attracts a penalty
    Risk management / RISK-BASED SUPERVISION Moving from a fixed capital norm to RISK-BASED CAPITAL — capital commensurate with the risk taken (low-risk book → lower capital). Draft guidelines issued. Flagged as "a potential area for InsurTech players"
    Corporate governance
    Protection of policyholders' interests "The foremost interest of the regulator"
    Reinsurance and foreign reinsurer branches How foreign reinsurers bring business and repatriate money
    REGULATORY SANDBOX A facility to introduce a new/creative technology on a TEST BASIS (e.g. 1 year) in partnership with an insurer, with the freedom to withdraw it, fine-tune it and reintroduce it. The RBI also has a sandbox; most global regulators allow it. "As a FinTech aspirant you should be quite familiar with this." guaranteed MCQ
    Finalisation of accounts Standardised, transparent format: claims received, claims paid, claims outstanding pending documents. Same logic as RBI standardising bank accounts so nothing can be hidden. India is moving to the IFRS regime
    Electronic marketplace An IRDAI-created e-marketplace
    ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING (AML) Prevents converting black money into white via fictitious claims. ## A premium of more than ₹50,000 CANNOT be paid in CASH — it must be electronic or by cheque ← memorise the number

    Why the course spends time on regulation: "if you aspire to run a FinTech organisation… the FIRST thing you should look at is the extent of relevant IRDAI regulations on that part of the area where you're going to come in."

    6.24The ecosystem, Part 1 — DISTRIBUTION intermediaries1

    The framing: the insurance company is the MANUFACTURER of the product. Somebody must distribute it to the last mile. The instructor's core argument:

    India's low non-life penetration is NOT caused by inadequacy of products. "Almost every eventuality has a product in the market" — 30 competing general insurers offer the most modern products available anywhere in the world. ## THE GAP IS IN DISTRIBUTION. The next generation of non-life explosion will happen in the DISTRIBUTION PLATFORM — done electronically, digitally, and using AI.

    Distribution platforms are COMMON to both life and non-life — an agent or broker sells both.

    The seven distribution intermediaries the single most likely "match the description" MCQ in Part B| # | Intermediary | Who they are | Key limits / facts |

    |---|---|---|---| | 1 | AGENT (individual) | "The friendly neighbourhood" individual who lives near you and approaches you. Must PASS AN EXAMINATION; the LICENCE is given by the individual insurance company | Can represent up to FOUR companies: ONE life + ONE general + ONE standalone health (SAHI) + ONE crop insurer. Has limits on maximum risk acceptance (cannot insure a ₹100-crore factory). ## She is the CUSTOMER'S representative, though she is paid an AGENCY COMMISSION by the insurer. The customer pays NOTHING extra — the commission is built into the premium, exactly like a travel agent's commission being built into the ticket price. MOST BUSINESS IN INDIA IS STILL SOLD BY AGENTS, because of personal connect | | 2 | CORPORATE AGENT | "An agent in a corporate format" — a partnership, firm, proprietary concern, BANK, or a large company | Higher risk-acceptance limits. Can represent TWO companies in each category (2 life, 2 general, 2 health, plus a credit or specialty insurer). ## MOST BANKS have converted into CORPORATE AGENTS — because they lend heavily, and both their customers and the properties created out of their lending need insurance. It is a major FEE-BASED INCOME stream for banks (SBI, HDFC, ICICI…). IRDAI imposes controls — you cannot place everything with your own group insurer, you must also place business outside | | 3 | INSURANCE MARKETING FIRM (IMF) | A MINOR/smaller version of the corporate agent, created by the regulator because corporate agents chase only larger customers | Serves those with no banking or credit requirement — e.g. a farmer insuring his cow or tools, a small shop. Can operate only within ONE STATE; limited number of policies and limited sum insured | | 4 | MISP — MOTOR INSURANCE SERVICE PROVIDER | EVERY MOTOR VEHICLE DEALER who wants to sell insurance must be registered as an MISP of an insurer or a broker | Created because dealer fees were previously uncontrolled; IRDAI stepped in to fix the maximum amount they can take, the promises they can make, and their roles and responsibilities. MISPs are effectively part of the broker channel | | 5 | POSP — POINT OF SALES PERSON | Kirana shops and the Common Service Centres (CSCs) you visit for Aadhaar verification, PAN updation, paying call tax or water tax | Many are also insurance agents who can sell simple personal accident and health policies. Not a major layer | | 6 | WEB AGGREGATOR | A distributor with NO OFFICE but a WEBSITE that compares many companies' policies and offers a review/suggestion on the insurer's claim-settling capability | The largest web aggregator WAS POLICY BAZAAR — which LATER BECAME A BROKER. 29 web aggregators remain, not very active, largely overshadowed by brokers who run the aggregation business themselves | | 7 | BROKER | "The ULTIMATE distribution platform" — a specialist COMPANY (or partnership), globally the largest, most professional and most complete distributors | 683 brokers registered as on 31 March 2024, though many are inactive or small-scale. They do NOT manufacture any product — they sell. Must employ underwriters, claims specialists, premium-acceptance specialists. ## Capital requirement for REINSURANCE broking ≈ ₹5 crore. ## MARSH is the LARGEST BROKER IN INDIA and is 100% FOREIGN-OWNED (100% FDI is allowed for brokers). Globally it is the second or third largest. Other global names: Gallagher, the Lloyd's platform |

    What brokers actually do — the illustrations

    • Air India with a fleet of ~150 aircraft cannot itself find the best combination of cover; it goes to the international market (Marsh, Gallagher, Lloyd's), who negotiate with aviation insurers and present the best option.
    • IPL is insured through brokers, who bring 3 or 4 insurance companies together to jointly offer the best cover.
    • A state agricultural scheme (e.g. Rajasthan) is too big for one insurer — the broker "stitches the cover", drafts excellent wordings, suggests coverage, and nudges insurers to offer it at the recommended pricing.

    Why Policy Bazaar succeeded: large data capture mechanisms, data analytics, call centres and CRM skills allowing it to sell the products of multiple insurers across the country.

    6.25The ecosystem, Part 2 — NON-DISTRIBUTION intermediaries1

    Two broad classes of intermediary: (1) those connected with DISTRIBUTION (§6.24) and (2) those who "keep the lights on" — settling claims, collecting data, developing KYC.

    The LICENSED non-distribution intermediaries

    Player Role Critical exam points
    SURVEYOR AND LOSS ASSESSOR The independent adjudicator of the quantum of loss — inspects the damage and independently arrives at the loss amount, producing a SURVEYOR AND LOSS ASSESSMENT REPORT THEY ARE NOT EMPLOYEES OF THE INSURANCE COMPANY — they are INDEPENDENT LICENSED PERSONS. ## THE INSURER PAYS THE SURVEYOR'S FEES, NOT THE CUSTOMER. They must pass an examination and take a licence from IRDAI, and are typically trained civil or mechanical engineers, licensed by class (motor / fire / burglary etc.). Courts have repeatedly held the report to be an important document — if the insurer wants to differ, the insurer must clearly establish why. Usually the assessment is accepted, except in very rare cases. The customer can get a copy
    THIRD PARTY ADMINISTRATOR (TPA) The intermediary between the patient, the hospital and the health insurer, processing health/hospital claims. Employs doctors, understands lines of treatment and medicines, runs portals interfacing with hospitals, checks for fraud and overcharging TPAs are ESSENTIALLY ONLY FOR HEALTH INSURANCE — NOT for motor (they are not surveyors). ## THEY DO NOT SETTLE THE CLAIM — CLAIMS ARE SETTLED BY THE INSURANCE COMPANY. They only administer/process it. Many health insurers settle claims in-house without a TPA
    ACTUARY / APPOINTED ACTUARY Employed by the insurer but REPORTING TO IRDAI. Every insurer must have at least ONE APPOINTED ACTUARY who tells IRDAI the true facts — that provisions are correct, accounts are clean, and product pricing is based on scientific, mathematical and statistical data The examination is notoriously difficult — harder than chartered accountancy — so there are very few actuaries in India; the Institute of Actuaries keeps the market tight. IRDAI cannot examine every product's pricing itself — it relies on the actuary's report. A chartered accountant certifies from a statutory audit perspective; the actuary certifies from the regulatory/actuarial perspective

    The UNLICENSED ecosystem players — "You do NOT have to take a licence from IRDAI to be an InsurTech/FinTech offering services to an insurer" likely MCQ| Player | What they do |

    |---|---| | Investigators | Go around discreetly checking with neighbours and others whether a claim is genuine; appointed over and above a surveyor when an anonymous letter or suspicion arises | | Hospital aggregators | Provide an agglomeration of doctors/hospitals with cashless arrangements — e.g. for an OPD product, so a policyholder travelling to another city can be directed to a covered doctor and the insurer pays directly | | Diagnostic and pharmacy aggregators | e.g. 1MG — agglomerations of diagnostic laboratories that insurers tie up with | | Internal auditors | | | FORENSIC SPECIALISTS | Determine whether a fire was accidental (electrical short, cigarette butt) or deliberately set (chemical, timer); whether a jewellery burglary was stage-managed; whether a natural death was dressed up as an accidental death for a personal accident claim. ## The insurer CANNOT reject a claim citing the forensic report alone — it is an INPUT to the decision. Police investigate separately, but insurers do not rely wholly on the police machinery | | Weather / meteorological data providers | Forecast monsoon, drought or excess rain before writing crop cover; feed mathematical models predicting a year's agricultural outcome. Reinsurers use the same satellite and weather-aggregator data, and the premium is decided on this basis | | CREDIT MONITORS | For credit insurance — track the financial performance of the insured's buyers and give early warning signals that a buyer may not pay | | Drones and satellite surveillance | Used where a surveyor cannot physically approach — a burning godown (drone with infrared/video feed), and for catastrophe/flood claims, measuring the extent of water, river and typhoon damage far more precisely than before |

    6.26The ecosystem, Part 3 — industry and professional bodies rich "match the body to its function" MCQ1

    Body Function
    GENERAL INSURANCE COUNCIL (and its twin, the LIFE INSURANCE COUNCIL) An INDUSTRY BODY mandated by the INSURANCE ACT — "all the general insurers shall constitute a General Insurance Council." Has a Secretary General and an executive governance council; all CEOs of insurers are members by rule. It discusses industry issues, new products, problems faced, and communicates the industry's concerns to IRDAI — "one of the major sources for IRDAI to know the pulse of the industry." Two new initiatives: (a) a FRAUD MITIGATION facility collecting data from insurers and outsourcing analysis to identify fraudulent patterns; (b) ## becoming the APEX/NODAL AGENCY for EMPANELMENT OF HOSPITALS for health insurance across ALL non-life insurers — eliminating duplicate applications by hospitals to each insurer. ~25,000–30,000 hospitals are currently networked; maybe 60,000 exist. Expected to take 1–2 years to stabilise. It also forms sub-committees on individual issues
    INSURANCE INFORMATION BUREAU (IIB) The WAREHOUSE / CUSTODIAN of the ENTIRE insurance data of the country — EVERY SINGLE POLICY AND EVERY SINGLE CLAIM is forwarded to it, for BOTH life and general insurance. ## It is CONSTITUTED BY IRDAI — it is NOT a private company; some insurer CEOs sit on its board. It provides data on a need basis, for a prescribed fee, under confidentiality, to licensed insurers — e.g. the last 5 YEARS of claims history of a person who is PORTING his health policy from insurer A to insurer B, or the prior accident history of a car. It also publishes statistics handbooks and an annual report with aggregate data (flood claims paid in Maharashtra, Rajasthan…) and never divulges individual details
    PORTING The technical term for moving one's HEALTH INSURANCE policy from one company to another
    INSTITUTE OF ACTUARIES OF INDIA Professional body for actuaries; sets standards of actuarial practice; hosts the Mortality and Morbidity Investigation Bureau
    INSTITUTE OF INSURANCE SURVEYORS AND LOSS ASSESSORS Sponsored by IRDAI; a SELF-CONTROLLING institution with its own professional code of conduct. It conducts the licensing examination for surveyors and hears and adjudicates complaints that a surveyor has not been neutral. IRDAI sits on its board
    GENERAL INSURANCE CORPORATION OF INDIA (GIC Re) The national reinsurer — see §6.29
    NATIONAL HEALTH AUTHORITY (NHA) The driver of AYUSHMAN BHARAT. Vision: HEALTH FOR ALL BY 2047. Funds medical facilities, sets standards; does NOT enter medical education
    WORKMEN COMPENSATION COURTS Under the Workmen Compensation Act, a deceased/injured worker's family files a case with the Workmen Compensation Court, which makes an award; the insurer then remits that amount to the court
    EMPLOYEE STATE INSURANCE (ESI) For employees above a wage level (about ₹25,000 per month). ESI provides hospitalisation and medical compensation through its own hospitals and tie-ups. An employee under ESI generally does not need separate health insurance; when they cease to be employees they must shift from ESI to health insurance
    INSURANCE INSTITUTE OF INDIA (formerly the Federation of Insurance Institutes) Conducts the QUALIFYING EXAMINATIONS for insurance employees, agents, distributors and brokers. ## THREE levels: LICENTIATE (basic) → ASSOCIATE (more specialised) → FELLOWSHIP (highly specialised) — analogous to the banking CAIIB. Also offers diplomas in health insurance and in investigation. It is only an examination body with very small training facilities
    INSTITUTE OF INSURANCE AND RISK MANAGEMENT (IIRM) Based in HYDERABAD, sponsored by IRDAI. Runs a certified, well-recognised course in RISK MANAGEMENT (identifying risks, threats, and ways to mitigate, avoid and control them) — sought by corporates well beyond the insurance industry — plus proprietary courses for actuarial examinations
    NATIONAL INSURANCE ACADEMY (NIA), PUNE The CENTRE OF EXCELLENCE for insurance EDUCATION, with a large residential campus near Pune. Runs 1–2 week residential programmes for executives on health insurance, fire claims, risk management, mathematical foundations of insurance, and for the past several years an MBA with insurance as a specialisation. Sponsored by the industry, with industry representatives on the governing board

    6.27Segments of general insurance2

    First, two definitions that WILL be tested

    PERIL = the EVENT insured against. RISK = the PROPERTY insured. Example: a house is covered against fire → FIRE is the PERIL, the HOUSE is the RISK. In insurance parlance "a risk" means a factory, a car, a property — "when I insure you, you are a risk acceptance."

    INDEMNIFY = compensating for the ACTUAL loss. What is covered: PHYSICAL loss to the insured property on the happening of a peril. NOT covered: BUSINESS/consequential losses — "my wife went into shock, I am depressed, my creditors are shouting at me" are not covered. Loss of profits is NOT automatically covered, though it can be covered by a separate loss-of-profits cover.

    FIRE insurance

    • Fire is a NOMENCLATURE covering a BASKET OF PERILS under the STANDARD FIRE POLICY
    • Origin: the great LONDON FIRE of the 1600s. "The origin of almost all general insurance policies can be attributed to BRITAIN" — the then kings of international commerce and shipping
    • Perils covered: fire, EXPLOSION, IMPLOSION (e.g. a geyser collapsing inwards under vacuum pressure), lightning, storm, hurricane, landslide, and RIOT, STRIKE AND CIVIL COMMOTION

    • WAR IS NOT COVERED. "If Pakistan shells a property near Kashmir, insurers do not pay" — war risk compensation is the forte of the GOVERNMENT of India. World over, TERRESTRIAL/territorial war risk is covered by governments; what insurers cover is INTERNATIONAL TRANSPORT war risk while goods are at sea

    • Two valuation bases likely MCQ| Basis | How it pays | |---|---| | MARKET VALUE | A house built for ₹1 crore is worth ₹60–70 lakh after 5 years → you are compensated proportionate to the depreciated value | | REINSTATEMENT VALUE | You insure the anticipated higher reinstatement value → you are compensated for RECONSTRUCTING the damaged portion |

    • Fire insurance is very CHEAP — about ₹8,000 a year for ₹1 crore of house cover — yet most home fire insurance in India is effectively COMPULSORY (insisted on by the bank/financier); voluntary fire insurance is "far and few between." After the Bombay floods and the Chennai floods, everyone predicted a surge in fire insurance — nothing happened

    • Covers: factories, SMEs, houses, shops, shopping complexes, movie houses. ## The LARGEST INSURED ASSET IN THE WORLD is the RELIANCE HAZIRA project — about ₹1 LAKH CRORE of fire insurance (obviously heavily reinsured)

    The full list of general insurance segments ← "which of these is NOT a general insurance segment" trap

    Segment What it covers / memorable detail
    Burglary and cash Cash at premises and in transit (armoured ATM-filling vans); jewellers' stock; gold-loan financiers' gold
    FIDELITY GUARANTEE Covers FRAUD/defalcation BY AN EMPLOYEE. "That is how banks are so happy when somebody picks up and takes away the money — the insurer pays"
    Animal insurance Cattle, horses, poultry, HONEYBEES, DUCKS, pet dogs, ELEPHANTS. ## The 80 elephants of the GURUVAYUR temple in Kerala are insured — for the elephant's death and for third-party damage the elephant causes. Dog-bite third-party liability is covered under a dog policy. BLOODSTOCK insurance: race horses insured for ₹60–70 lakh, covered while racing AND while being transported between racecourses. Insurers employ veterinary doctors to inspect animals before cover
    EVENT insurance The IPL example. Can be bought by the stadium, the BCCI, or the sponsor. Covers cancellation due to rain, an accident to a player, a hartal/strike, lightning/heavy rain, demolition or collapse of the stadium, plus PUBLIC LIABILITY. Two variants: (a) pay if the ENTIRE match is washed out; (b) do NOT pay if the first few hours have already been bowled. ## A MAJOR buyer of event insurance is the MEDIA (e.g. Sony Television) — they lose huge advertising revenue if a match is cancelled. Music concerts are also insured (singer's accident en route, fire at the venue)
    MOTOR insurance THIRD-PARTY LIABILITY IS ABSOLUTELY COMPULSORY under the MOTOR VEHICLES ACT before a vehicle is used in public — the cheapest policy available; police can fine you. ## A Supreme Court committee found 40% OF INDIA'S VEHICLES ARE UNINSURED even for this. The Act makes liability UNLIMITED — a ₹190 two-wheeler premium can generate a ₹2–3 crore death claim paid entirely by the insurer with nothing from the owner — but in practice it is limited because the MOTOR ACCIDENT CLAIMS TRIBUNAL (MACT) decides the amount using a matrix of income, age, future income potential and family
    Health and Personal Accident See §6.28. Personal accident is very cheap — about ₹800 a year for ₹1 lakh of cover, family included
    Aviation and SATELLITE Covers damage to the craft, passenger legal liability, and damage to third parties/property on the ground. ## ISRO insures ALL COMMERCIAL satellite launches with Indian insurers (then reinsured) — but NOT EXPERIMENTAL satellites. The FAILURE OF THE LAUNCH is also covered
    MARINE / transit ("transport of goods") Still called MARINE INSURANCE because it originated in the British days of sailing — the word survives even for road/air/container transit. Covers ships (oil leakage, POLLUTION LIABILITY), cargo, household goods on transfer. ## RANSOM PAID TO SOMALI PIRATES IS PAID BY THE INSURER, NOT THE SHIPPING COMPANY. Banks insist on marine cover before negotiating documents
    DIGITAL / CYBER Cyberattacks, hacking, ransomware, virus infection, deliberate damage. Costly but available. Also covers LOSS OF PROFIT during the interruption — e.g. a website down for 5 days, or a factory shut for repairs after a fire/explosion. Ransomware payments are covered
    KIDNAPPING AND RANSOM (K&R) Originating in tea plantations in Assam, where terrorists kidnapped senior executives. ## Insurers employ PROFESSIONAL RANSOM NEGOTIATORS (very few in India), acting FOR THE INSURER, and the insurer pays the negotiated ransom. It is a HIGHLY CONFIDENTIAL cover — insurers never disclose who holds one
    Specialised body-part / talent cover Footballers (Ronaldo) insure their legs; dancers and singers insure their ability to perform. Specialised insurers do only this
    LIABILITY — a huge segment See the sub-table below
    CROP insurance PRADHAN MANTRI FASAL BIMA YOJANA (PMFBY) — "the largest crop insurance scheme, most probably in the world." Frequently reinsured with specialist global crop reinsurers
    PACKAGE policies Householder's package (house + electronic equipment + domestic servants' personal accident + a little health + a tree falling on a neighbour's house + dog bite), shopkeeper's, farmer's, office package

    The liability sub-segments likely MCQ| Liability cover | Detail |

    |---|---| | PRODUCT LIABILITY | A geyser explodes and injures you → claim against the manufacturer. ## PRODUCT LIABILITY COVER IS ABSOLUTELY A MUST FOR EXPORTS TO THE US, THE WEST AND JAPAN — many countries insist on it for imported goods. Common for exports of garments, electronic instruments, automobile and aviation spare parts | | DIRECTORS AND OFFICERS (D&O) LIABILITY | Covers directors/officers accused in their corporate capacity (the Chanda Kochhar / ICICI Bank example). ## Insurers have even PAID BAIL AMOUNTS to courts — PROVIDED there is NO CRIMINAL ACTIVITY. Criminal cases are NOT covered; only FINANCIAL liability is | | PROFESSIONAL INDEMNITY / negligence | Covers doctors (e.g. a gynaecologist whose surgery goes wrong), engineers, consultants. ## It SPECIFICALLY COVERS NEGLIGENCE — "no accident can happen without negligence"; an insurer will not refuse a motor claim merely because the driver was negligent | | GENERAL / PUBLIC LIABILITY | The BHOPAL DISASTER (gas leak) is the classic case — there was NO general liability policy in India then; UNION CARBIDE was insured in the US and paid from there. Also libel/defamation cover taken by media houses (Hindustan Times, Times of India, The Hindu, Indian Express); the instructor cites Trump's ~₹1,000 crore suit against a US news organisation — the money is insured, but the loss of reputation is not | | WORKMEN'S / EMPLOYEE'S COMPENSATION | Statutory cover for employees; the award comes from the Workmen Compensation Court |

    6.28Health insurance and Ayushman Bharat2

    Why health is the story

    Metric Value
    Share of non-life premium ~39–40% — the largest component (motor ~32%)
    Premium crossed ₹1.06 lakh crore (₹1.30 lakh crore in FY2025), growing at 10.20%
    People covered last year 57.30 crore
    — of which through GOVERNMENT SCHEMES 26 crore
    — of which GROUP (employer) health insurance 25.59 crore
    — of which VOLUNTARY INDIVIDUAL/retail cover only 5.60 crore ← the striking number
    The gap Out of ~140 crore people, ~100 crore are insurable; even excluding ~10 crore who cannot afford it, 30–40 crore people remain to be covered

    "See the potential — that's why foreign insurance companies are making a beeline to come to India."

    The two claim routes certain MCQ| Route | How it works |

    |---|---| | CASHLESS at a NETWORK hospital | The hospital verifies the policy and bills the insurer directly; you pay only the balance (diet charges, extra tests). Insurers pre-negotiate PACKAGE RATES with hospitals for common procedures — angioplasty, hernia, cataract, knee replacement, shoulder replacement. A hospital may have 120–130 procedures, of which insurers have package agreements on the most common 60–70. If no other treatment is involved, you walk out paying almost nothing | | REIMBURSEMENT at a NON-NETWORK hospital | You pay, collect the bills, and submit them to the insurer or the TPA — online, at the nearest office, or via your agent |

    A third structure — CRITICAL ILLNESS: cover for (say) 21 specified procedures/conditions; on diagnosis of cancer or a heart attack a LUMP SUM is paid — no bills, no hospital documents required. Combined "critical illness + hospitalisation" policies exist.

    IRDAI's health regulations are extremely tight — prescribing how the hospital must submit bills, WITHIN HOW MANY HOURS the insurer must give approval, when the final approval must come, and within how many days reimbursement must be made.

    AYUSHMAN BHARAT (PM Jan Arogya Yojana) guaranteed MCQ block| Feature | Detail |

    |---|---| | What it is | The LARGEST PUBLIC HEALTH INSURANCE SCHEME IN THE WORLD, run by the NATIONAL HEALTH AUTHORITY (NHA) | | Goal | UNIVERSAL HEALTH COVERAGE BY 2047 — the centenary of Independence | | Sum insured | ₹5 LAKH PER FAMILY, on a FLOATER basis, for SECONDARY AND TERTIARY CARE HOSPITALISATION | | Beneficiaries | 50 CRORE, identified from the SOCIO-ECONOMIC CASTE SURVEY (SECC) of 2011 (earlier identification was by ration card colour). "There is no such thing as a below-poverty line any more" — selection is automatic from the survey | | The senior citizen extension | EVERY SINGLE SENIOR AGED ABOVE 70 IS INCLUDED — RICH OR POOR, IRRESPECTIVE OF INCOME — for ₹5 lakh cover | | Beneficiary contribution | Almost free — about ₹40 a year; the rest is met by the central and state governments | | Funding split | The ₹5 lakh base is funded predominantly by the CENTRE (60%+) with the STATE contributing ~20–40%. ## Where a state ENHANCES the cover (e.g. Karnataka to ₹15–20 lakh), the ENTIRE premium on the ENHANCED PORTION is paid by the STATE government | | Delivery | Each state calls for a TENDER; the LOWEST-QUOTING insurer runs the scheme for 1 year. Some states run it directly without insurers. Completely paperless — swipe a SMART CARD; no documents to submit; settlement happens digitally between hospital and insurer |

    Why this matters for the course: "it provides immense potential for intervention by technology" — either a large institutional IT organisation or an agile, incisive FinTech. Cost is the binding constraint — insurers do not make money out of insurance, so they are reluctant to spend on technology without clear perceivable benefit.

    6.29Reinsurance (non-life)

    Why: a fleet of Air India aircraft, the Reliance Hazira project, a container ship, a satellite — no single Indian insurer can retain these; a single loss "in tens of thousands of crores" would demolish the company forever.

    Concept Detail
    Definition The process by which an insurer transfers the risk it has accepted to another insurer (a reinsurer)
    Two ways to arrange it CASE BY CASE (facultative) or YEAR-WISE (treaty) — e.g. "across all my fire policies I will retain a maximum loss of ₹100 crore per event; anything above goes to reinsurers"
    The chain in India First to GENERAL INSURANCE CORPORATION OF INDIA (GIC Re); whatever GIC cannot accept goes to foreign reinsurers
    GIC Re The NATIONAL REINSURER; HQ MUMBAI; for a long time the ONLY reinsurer in India. ~50–60% of its business is Indian, ~40% foreign. Presence in Moscow, South Africa, Dubai, contemplating the US. Also supports NUCLEAR insurance and TERRORISM insurance pools
    COMPULSORY CESSION IRDAI requires 4% OF EVERY SINGLE PREMIUM WRITTEN IN THE COUNTRY to be placed with GIC Re — for CAPACITY BUILDING ← memorise the 4%
    New entrant A second reinsurer, sponsored by FAIRFAX, licensed about 6 months ago
    Foreign presence 10 branches of foreign reinsurers in India, plus the LLOYD'S market
    Retention in India About 72% of the total risk is retained/insured within India; of the remainder only about 10% actually goes outside India — India has developed considerable capacity
    What still goes abroad Major oil refineries, major aircraft, large ships, satellites, large industrial complexes — and CROP insurance, which is frequently reinsured with specialist global crop reinsurers
    Specialisation Aviation reinsurers examine the history of that aircraft type, the pilots, the territories flown, riot/strike exposure. In the recent Air India crash, insurers will go by the REINSURANCE SPECIALIST'S report
    Coverage nuance WAR is not paid. TERRORISM and SABOTAGE ARE paid. ## TERRORISM is one of the most commonly covered risks in India, though claims are very few — the TAJ HOTEL attack was fully compensated because it was clearly terrorism

    6.30Acceptance of business and issuance of the policy (non-life)3

    THE TWO PILLARS OF THE INSURANCE BUSINESS: UNDERWRITING (acceptance of the policy and issuing it) and CLAIMS (the delivery of the promise) — "the moment of truth." guaranteed MCQ Origin of the word "underwriting": in early London, a ship sailing to Portugal or India carried merchandise from many shop owners. A rich man would say "if something happens to it, I will pay up" and WRITE UNDER the document and sign it — hence underwriting. In the trade the short form is simply "writing" ("Do you write fire? Do you write motor?").

    The underwriting process

    Step Detail
    1. UNDERWRITING PHILOSOPHY IRDAI insists every insurer have an underwriting philosophy, APPROVED BY ITS BOARD and PUBLISHED ON ITS WEBSITE. It decides: which geographies, whether to accept commercial vehicles, godowns in congested areas, riot/strike losses, fresh health business from an 80-year-old, a person who has already had a heart attack. All products and processes must follow it
    2. PROPOSAL FORM The applicant declares name, nominee, prior health issues, current medication
    3. Evaluation and acceptance UNDERWRITING = the process of EXAMINING THE PROPOSAL FORM, ACCEPTING THE BUSINESS AND CHARGING A PREMIUM. The person who does it is the UNDERWRITER
    4. STP where possible STRAIGHT-THROUGH PROCESSING (STP) — a standard Maruti/WagonR/Honda City is a class, so it is underwritten automatically with pre-fixed premiums and need never reach an underwriter; motor dealers can issue the policy themselves. Home insurance likewise
    5. Manual underwriting where needed Required for: a person with an existing health condition, an older person, a person PORTING from another insurer, long travel to the US/Canada, mountaineering, a high-value imported car (outside standardised models), an industrial risk, a cricket event during the monsoon (high rain probability → charge a very high premium and reinsure), transport through Naxalite areas
    6. COLLECTION OF PREMIUM THE LAW IN INDIA: UNLESS THE PREMIUM IS PAID, THE RISK DOES NOT START. The worked example: a house quoted ₹8,000; the party intends to pay on Monday; a fire occurs on Saturday → NOT COVERED, even though the proposal was filled and accepted guaranteed MCQ
    7. BIMA-ASBA IRDAI's equivalent of the IPO's ASBA — the bank BLOCKS/freezes the premium amount (e.g. ₹15,000) against an assurance, so the excess over the final premium (say ₹12,000) is not stuck with the insurer
    8. RENEWAL Automatic if there are no changes; every payment mode accepted (GPay, credit card, handover)
    9. UPSELLING AND CROSS-SELLING UPSELLING = persuading the customer to INCREASE THE SUM INSURED on the same product. CROSS-SELLING = selling a DIFFERENT product (a critical illness policy, a personal accident policy). Both happen intensively at renewal classic definitional MCQ
    10. ENDORSEMENTS Changes made DURING THE CURRENCY of a policy — address change on transfer, adding 3 rooms to the house, buying another flat, changing the car
    11. IT systems Run the whole chain: proposal collection → underwriting → premium collection → accounting → policy issuance → endorsements. The robustness of the IT system contributes to the reputation of the insurer. ## READY-MADE, OFF-THE-SHELF, END-TO-END insurance products are QUITE RARE — systems are largely BUILT TO REQUIREMENT and take time
    12. Online and mobile app Good for home, travel, simple health and motor renewal; avoids a lot of cost, is quick and appealing. ## THE FLIP SIDE: "I cannot ask so many questions in a mobile app" — if the applicant declares a heart disease, the app cannot process further and must refer to an underwriter. An industrial risk (stock policy, loss-of-profit cover, machinery cover) can never be bought through an app

    6.31Claims handling (non-life)1

    The claims process — in order

    Step Detail
    1. IMMEDIATE REPORTING The FIRST BASIC RULE: report immediately to the insurer — and to the POLICE and FIRE SERVICES in criminal or fire cases. Why? So the insurer gets a chance to examine the scene BEFORE evidence is destroyed or the situation changes. Insurers want to see the scene within about 24 HOURS; today you can upload a WhatsApp/app photograph and the insurer may settle straight away or send a surveyor
    2. Check whether liability exists Is it covered? Was the policy renewed? Was the person actually hospitalised (tests-and-go-home is not hospitalisation)? Only then is a claim registered
    3. Claim registration and communication A claim number is communicated by SMS, WhatsApp, email or telephone. "Many insurers claim this is very smooth, but I find a lot of hindrances here" — customer says "I informed", insurer says "we received nothing"
    4. Appointment of specialists Surveyor/investigator (fire, motor, burglary); a CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT for a burglary claim (to look into the books); a weather specialist for crop; police for burglary/murder; the motor vehicle authority for a liability claim; fire force; a TPA for hospitalisation
    5. COLLECTION OF DOCUMENTS "A very simple sentence, but still a BIG ELEPHANT IN THE ROOM" — the perennial dispute over what was and was not submitted. "I am yet to see a 100% smooth interaction here"
    6. Claim processing By a CLAIM SPECIALIST (the claims analogue of an underwriter) covering liability, quantification and surveyor assessment. If an anonymous letter alleges the claim was engineered, an INVESTIGATOR is appointed OVER AND ABOVE the surveyor and checks discreetly with neighbours
    7. Communication, acceptance and payment

    THE CUSTOMER-EXPERIENCE INSIGHT worth memorising: "There are many customers who would be happy getting ₹8,000 or ₹9,000 against a ₹10,000 claim PROVIDED it is done expeditiously and smoothly. The problem is insurers keep fighting, dilly-dallying and delaying, and ULTIMATELY PAY THE SAME ₹8,000 — the claim is paid but the DISSATISFACTION PERSISTS. You pay the claim and still end up with an unhappy customer."

    The grievance/dispute escalation ladder guaranteed sequence MCQ| Level | Detail |

    |---|---| | 1. The insurer's GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL OFFICER | Every insurer must have one per IRDAI. ## They must RESPOND WITHIN 3 DAYS | | 2. The INSURANCE OMBUDSMAN | You only need to WRITE A LETTER — NO ADVOCATE, and you need not even attend. ## IRDAI requires EVERY CLAIMS COMMUNICATION to CONTAIN THE ADDRESS OF THE OMBUDSMAN for that area — the settlement letter must say "if not satisfied, approach our grievance redressal officer, and if still not satisfied, the ombudsman at this address" | | 3. CONSUMER COURT | | | 4. MACT | For MOTOR THIRD-PARTY LIABILITY it is INVARIABLY the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal — insurers will NOT settle it directly. Only AFTER the tribunal's AWARD can the claim be settled | | 5. Arbitration, then civil and High Court | |

    "INSURANCE COMPANIES ARE THE LARGEST LITIGATORS IN THIS COUNTRY" — because every single motor accident leads to a case under MACT.

    6.32Fraud in insurance2

    Fact Detail
    Scale Globally, FRAUD ACCOUNTS FOR ABOUT 10% OF THE CLAIM AMOUNT — "and India is no different." Context: on ~₹3,04,000 crore of premium, claims payouts run ₹2,50,000–2,70,000 crore a year, so 10% is enormous
    The regulator's DEFINITION of fraud "An ACT OR OMISSION intended to gain advantage through DISHONEST OR UNLAWFUL MEANS, IRRESPECTIVE OF THE MEDIUM USED — for a party committing the fraud or for RELATED PARTIES." ← memorise this wording

    The taxonomy of fraud examples (in ascending severity)

    Type Example
    "Light" fraud A pre-existing dent on a car claimed as a fresh accident — the surveyor says "this dent doesn't look fresh". Non-disclosure of diabetes/BP on the health proposal form (people simply draw a line through the question). Not disclosing a prior ANGIOPLASTY — "very interesting to forget an angioplasty"
    Hospital fraud During COVID, patients admitted and given only a drip were billed for antibiotics and costly equipment never administered (₹20,000–30,000) — "the insured doesn't mind because he isn't paying". Fraud rings in Nagpur spotted only by pattern analysis — the same diagnostic parameters across all patients, same ages (35/45), inflated blood counts
    Fire/stock fraud A genuine fire where old, outdated, expired stock is destroyed but claimed as new live stock worth crores — detectable because there are no purchase bills for bringing that stock in. Common in TEXTILE factory claims
    Marine fraud A fishing vessel (₹30–40 lakh) reported sunk in deep sea where no surveyor can go. An anonymous letter revealed it had been renamed and repainted and was operating elsewhere; the police found it
    Burglary fraud Jewellery-shop burglaries proven to be deliberate when the jeweller was in financial trouble
    Murder for personal accident Wives killed in Rajasthan and Haryana to claim ₹50–70 lakh personal accident policies, with death within a month of the policy
    Bank/NBFC-linked "If a bank gives credit and it cannot be repaid, it's a good idea to set fire to the industry" to make the insurer pay the bank

    The dimensions along which fraud is classified likely MCQ

    Fraud may be: OUTRIGHT CREATION OF A NON-OCCURRING EVENT, or INFLATION OF THE COST OF LOSSES when an event did occur. Sources: EXTERNAL · agents/DISTRIBUTION CHANNELS in collusion · GARAGES (doing earlier repairs under the guise of an accident) · collusion with GOVERNMENT AGENCIES · INDIVIDUAL · GEOGRAPHICAL (e.g. Haryana) · SECTORAL (textiles, hospitals, electronics, second-hand goods, transport, banks and NBFCs).

    The response

    • Insurers spend crores on software intelligence systems to identify patterns. "Companies come flaunting their anti-fraud detection systems, but they are only scratching the surface — not very reliable."
    • IRDAI has issued a FRAUD MONITORING TEMPLATE; the General Insurance Council is building an industry-wide fraud mitigation facility
    • Insurers check CIBIL ratings before writing some policies — "but that alone may not be an input in preventing fraud"
    • The industry is lobbying the Government to make CHEATING AN INSURANCE COMPANY A PENAL/CRIMINAL OFFENCE, as cheating a bank already is under the Indian Penal Code, to create a fear element likely MCQ

    • THE MORAL ARGUMENT: out of 100 health policyholders about 10 claim and 90 do not. What is paid to the 10 sets the premium for the 90. "You are affecting the UNCLAIMING population by this fraud" — claim costs rise, so premiums rise for people who had nothing to do with it

    6.33Insurance and information technology1

    The FINANCIAL SECTOR in India (banking + insurance + pension + capital markets) is THE LARGEST CONSUMER OF INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY in the country, and insurance is a very large component of it. Insurance is still a "SUNRISE INDUSTRY" growing at a DOUBLE-DIGIT rate. All the large IT firms — TCS, Infosys, HP, Wipro, HCL, Accenture — have separate insurance wings for services, product support and consulting.

    INSURTECH = a FinTech company working in insurance technology — "a SUBSET of FinTech."

    Why many FinTechs fail in insurance: "they could not scale up because they do not understand the fundamentals — of the business, the regulations, the requirement, the customer's perception, the gap between what is delivered and what could be delivered, the need of the country, and the huge unchartered territory — and delivering all that at LOW COST."

    Where technology is already working

    Area What is happening
    WELLNESS AND HEALTH programmes Health insurers (≈40% of general insurance) accept that reimbursement of hospitalisation alone is not good enough. Offerings: TELEMEDICINE (introduced widely during COVID — a doctor answers, advises paracetamol/hydration/rest, and many recovered without hospitalisation; now used for diabetes and BP management); obesity, diabetic, BP and DEPRESSION consultants; post-oncology counselling during chemotherapy. ## Insurers now offer telemedicine to NON-CUSTOMERS too, as a way of attracting them. Wellness is bundled free into the base product, because if one insurer charged for it a competitor would not, and it would lose customers. Diabetes-management apps: upload a photo of your food, report glucose and BP levels; nutritionists, group counsellors, exercise and physical-fitness specialists engage with the patient — "this has been a major success"
    Data collection and analytics For a state crop tender the insurer must know the crops grown in those districts, past claims, agricultural practices (good and bad), irrigation availability, weather patterns — all outsourced to IT/agri-FinTech firms. To insure 1 million farmers an insurer cannot collect the data itself; an outsourced firm can aggregate ration cards, KISAN CREDIT CARDS and bank details
    KYC / onboarding VIDEO-BASED KYC — say your PAN number in front of a camera; done by an EXTERNAL OUTSOURCED TECHNOLOGY AGENCY, not the bank/insurer
    EMBEDDED RISK / EMBEDDED INSURANCE Insurance embedded into other transactions: credit card holders, vehicle loans, small finance, FERTILISER SUBSIDY, RATION CARDS. Requires innovation, high-speed technology and LOW-skill interfaces — in many areas it must be SMS-BASED, since GPay-style apps need internet. "Digital cash so prevalent in AFRICA works through SMS, not the internet"
    BUSINESS CORRESPONDENTS A person carrying a mobile device to a village, collecting deposits as low as ₹10–30 a day and allowing withdrawals up to ₹100 — because travelling to the nearest bank would cost the villager ₹30–40 in bus fare. ## Called RURAL MITRA; the health-data variant is AROGYA MITRA. If the device is offline, she carries it to a connected place in the evening and the data is uploaded that night. This channel can carry insurance requirements, premium collection, policy issuance, SMS and claims details
    PARAMETRIC COVERS A cover that pays on a PARAMETER BEING CROSSED — e.g. a drought threshold — with NO SURVEYOR and NO ASSESSMENT; a flat agreed payout. "Catching on in popularity", but can only be driven through an external IT technology vendor guaranteed MCQ
    Underwriting technology AI analysing a customer's PHOTOGRAPH in health insurance — "face scan… very high probability of identifying fraud or a potential claim situation. I did not believe this previously, but it was shown that they have a high level of accuracy." Also geographical/CRISIL data, financial background and integrity checks, terrorism or political-unrest exposure, whether the workshop is in an illegal location
    STP, bots and pricing software STP for standardised motor/home; intelligent BOTS answering the routine share of 1,000 daily call-centre calls so only genuine queries reach a human; agent onboarding checks trawled from SOCIAL MEDIA; automatic PRICING SOFTWARE for a ₹5–10 lakh jeweller's burglary cover without an underwriter
    Claims technology Drones and infrared video for an inaccessible fire; satellite data for floods; digital/VC verification of the hospital — whether it is equipped for that case, or whether the patient was even admitted ("there are cases where the hospital doesn't exist and claims have been made"); uploading 10–12 claim documents from a mobile while travelling
    CHANGE IN RISK PROFILE — post-policy monitoring A genuinely interesting frontier: on a storm warning, inform customers to secure trees and tarpaulins; in Europe, HAILSTONES on cars (front sensors, reverse sensors, solar roofs all destroyed) — insurers warn customers to garage their cars. For a hurricane travelling from Odisha through Chennai to the Andhra coast, ## plot the hurricane route by SATELLITE IMAGERY and overlay the insured values in that corridor — factories, cargoes, stock — to identify high-value exposure. Same for a pandemic/Nipah outbreak (who is covered in that area, at what sum insured, alert them and put a medical team on surveillance), earthquake warnings, and INDUSTRY DOWNTURNS ("a depression in the chemical industry typically produces a lot of fire claims — genuine or fraudulent")
    Compliance / RegTech Tracking IRDAI regulations, GST and tax laws, personal laws, municipal building laws, the Shop and Establishment Act, call centre rules, distance and digital marketing regulations, provident fund and employee benefit regulations. IT firms are offering 24×7, 360-degree regulation tracking
    HR Recruitment, background verification, genuineness of records, resume cross-verification, onboarding, training
    Finance Premium collection; preserving HIGH-FIDELITY, HEAVILY ENCRYPTED data. ## The tension to remember: "increasing security should NOT increase the handling difficulty for the customer and employees" — smooth at the user end, very high at the encryption level. Plus correct MIS, actuarial validations, balance sheet and P&L tracking, and AI-driven PROFITABILITY PROJECTION — knowing the Q2 profitability trend BEFORE the quarter closes under multiple scenarios, so management can make midterm corrections "while it is hot." And IFRS reporting, now required alongside the old format, being addressed by Oracle, Accenture and others

    6.34Current LIMITATIONS of IT in the insurance industry a classic list MCQ1

    # Limitation Detail
    1 OUTDATED LEGACY SYSTEMS A 10-year-old system that everyone is comfortable with and that has crossed its teething troubles — but is inadequate for current and future requirements as the insurer scales in volume, products, claim types, customers, geographies and distribution channels. Replacement is resisted because it is costly and painful (proof of concept → pilot → scale), diverts focus from day-to-day business, and the disruption period is UNPREDICTABLE — 6 months to a year. ## "No insurer can afford to interrupt the customer experience, because the competitive market is very cruel — it will not wait for anybody to stabilise their system"
    2 SIGNIFICANT SHORTAGE OF PROFESSIONALS Despite India's IT depth, there is a shortage of insurance-specialised cybersecurity, data analytics and modern insurance IT specialists. Upskilling existing employees or attracting new talent is costly or not up to the mark, and new hires arrive with no idea about insurance — a learning curve that is "a little taxing"
    3 CYBER THREATS Increasing reliance on digital platforms and cloud-based systems. ## FOUR large insurance companies have been hacked — all had good IT and security systems; the criminals keep getting better, so security standards must be raised continuously
    4 INCONSISTENT DATA QUALITY Data arrives from individual agents, corporates, brokers, digital channels, banking platforms, online, apps and paper proposal forms — with inherently different quality (a bank dumping thousands of customer records in one batch vs a shabbily filled rural proposal form). This flows into the data lakes and MIS output. Also note: ## SOCIAL MEDIA is now a MEASURING FACTOR of an insurer's performance — one mistake can go VIRAL, and once viral IT CANNOT BE RETRACTED; it stays
    5 SLOW ADOPTION OF AI, IoT AND BLOCKCHAIN "You keep hearing about it, but real usage in insurance is slow" — because of COST, COMPLEXITY AND REGULATORY HURDLES
    6 TELEMATICS not caught on A "PAY AS YOU USE" motor product exists — why pay a full premium for a car mostly kept in the shed? — but people still prefer the flat premium
    7 WEARABLES not operationalised A person who jogs and eats moderately, all tracked by a wearable, should pay a lower health premium. "It looks scientific, it looks reasonable" — but it needs authentic wearables, authentic incoming data, and rebuilt underwriting systems. "This is something we are really struggling with"
    8 URBAN BIAS IT systems are primarily designed for URBAN, TECH-SAVVY customers. In a remote village in Madhya Pradesh only 4 or 5 people use IT systems — yet they too must be brought into the digital underwriting platform, which forces reliance on external agencies expert in data collection, standardisation and transferring data with integrity

    6.35Opportunities for FinTech / InsurTech in insurance ← the closing block of the course

    Fact Value
    India's insurance market TODAY US$38.7 billion
    Projected BY 2030 US$88.4 billion
    Demographic driver 68% of the population is UNDER 35
    The gap Despite all the products, IT, branches and regulators, 30–40 crore people remain uncovered
    Where the growth is TIER-II and TIER-III CITIES and RURAL AREAS — the "underserved populations"

    The specific opportunity areas named

    Opportunity The illustration given
    EMBEDDED COVERS A farmer's daily milk yield recorded by the milk collection society → embed cattle insurance at low cost. A vegetable vendor buying from a mandi and paying by GPay → embed a cover at the point of payment. Fertiliser purchase → inject a staggered-payment insurance cover into agricultural pricing
    PARAMETRIC COVERS Pay on the parameter (drought), no surveyor, no assessment
    MICROFINANCE-linked cover "Lakhs of women make their livelihood through weaving, making baskets, selling vegetables." If she is hospitalised, ## "there is no point in asking them to submit documents and come back later — CAN WE PAY SOME AMOUNT SO THAT THE CHILDREN CAN EAT THAT DAY? This is NOT a wish list; it is being actively debated in various fora." Microfinance channels exist but are not standardised; a premium-payment technique can be embedded in them
    Riding existing digital rails ITC's e-CHOUPAL — the farmer brings produce to a collection centre which weighs, qualifies and classifies it and pays immediately, with no deposit and no waiting, leaving a digital track. "Can we ride that? We have tried — but with existing costly IT platforms we could not make it commercially viable"
    Fixing the core pain points "The traditional Indian insurance industry has been OFFLINE-ORIENTED, COMPLEX AND AGENT-DRIVEN, leading to INEFFICIENCIES AND LACK OF TRANSPARENCY." FinTech can address FRAUD, HIGH OPERATIONAL COST and INEFFICIENT CLAIM PROCESSING using blockchain, AI and IT

    THE RECURRING REFRAIN OF THE WHOLE COURSE, worth quoting: insurers will only adopt technology that is "AGILE, LIGHT, HIGH-SPEED AND LOW-COST" — because "already they are not running a very profitable business, so would they willingly put more money into it? I doubt it."

    Digital Product Management

    Digital Product Management (DPM)

    (Instructor: Prof. Shankhadeep Banerjee , Associate Professor of Information Systems, IIM Bangalore; Chairperson, Centre for Software and IT Management. Formerly a Product Manager at Microsoft , and worked closely with PMs at eBay .)

    Course structure (Modules 0–7): Introduction to the role and domain → Product strategy → Product improvement → Product metrics → Product UX design (incl. start-ups and MVPs) → Product planning / roadmaps → Product development (agile). Why the course exists: the instructor observed "a big gap between the B-school curriculum and the practical industry requirements for this role."

    7.1What is a digital product?4

    A DIGITAL PRODUCT is any item or service which uses DIGITAL TECHNOLOGY for serving customers.

    Technically it can be software or hardware ("even a digital clock can be a digital product"), but the scope of this course is limited to SOFTWARE — mobile apps, desktop apps and web apps.

    The three ways to classify digital products likely MCQ| Basis | Categories |

    |---|---| | By INDUSTRY | Retail products, healthcare products, FinTech products | | By CUSTOMER TYPE | B2C (business-to-consumer, e.g. Amazon) · B2B (business-to-business) · G2C (government-to-consumer) | | By MODEL | SaaS (Software as a Service, cloud-based) · platform-based products |

    Product vs FEATURE definitional MCQ

    FEATURES are DISCRETE CAPABILITIES, COMPONENTS AND DESIGN ELEMENTS of a product that can deliver value to customers.

    "In your career practically, you will be MANAGING FEATURES AND NOT ENTIRE PRODUCTS. Entire products are managed by the LEADERS of the product who are higher up in the product management team."

    The definition of digital product management

    Digital product management is the END-TO-END process of CONCEIVING, DEFINING, DELIVERING, MONITORING, REFINING and also WITHDRAWING digital products in a market to MAXIMISE BUSINESS RESULTS. It covers the whole lifecycle of the product.

    The other way to see it — the bridge:

    Building the RIGHT product Building the product RIGHT
    Research, connecting with users, data analytics Engineering: development, quality assurance, design

    Product management is the BRIDGE between "building the right product" and "building the product right."

    Where the PM function sits — the famous Venn diagram guaranteed MCQ

    PM lies at the INTERSECTION OF THREE CIRCLES: TECHNOLOGY · BUSINESS · UX (user experience/design).

    The PM need not be an expert in any one of them — a UX team, a technology team of developers and QA, and business leaders all surround the PM. The PM is the BRIDGE between all of them.

    An alternative framing used by some companies: PM lies at the intersection of PRODUCT DESIGN, DEVELOPMENT and MARKETING — in those companies a lot of PM work sits inside the product marketing function (marketing, advertising, creating awareness, training salespeople).

    The end-to-end PM process (a cycle, not a line)

    BUSINESS STRATEGY → PRODUCT STRATEGY → DESIGN & DEVELOPMENT → USER TESTING
     → PRODUCT RELEASE → PRODUCT MARKETING & GROWTH STRATEGY → MEASURE WITH METRICS
     ↺ feedback loop back into product strategy / business strategy / design

    The product strategy must be ALIGNED with the business strategy, and product objectives must be ALIGNED with business objectives. The process is ongoing and continuous — there is a FEEDBACK LOOP.

    PM stakeholders ← "who is NOT a stakeholder" trap; the answer is that everyone is

    Stakeholder What the PM does with them
    Development team (engineering + QA) Build
    UX / design team Design
    Product team (other PMs) Plan upcoming releases, curate ideas, define features
    Executive team Share high-level progress towards goals and initiatives
    Marketing team Collaborate on buyer personas, product messaging, upcoming launches
    Sales and support teams Review customer requests; familiarise the team with new features
    Research team, Finance (product pricing), Legal (IP — intellectual property rights)
    Users / customers

    "PM is often called THE THREAD THAT CONNECTS ALMOST EVERY FUNCTION OF THE BUSINESS."

    PM tools possible match-the-tool MCQ| Task | Tools |

    |---|---| | Wireframing / prototyping | Figma · Sketch · Adobe XD | | Tracking users | Hotjar | | Documenting | Notion | | Visual product management | Miro |

    7.2The product manager — role, responsibilities, competencies7

    Who is a PM? "People involved in managing PARTS OR WHOLE of the product." Managing just a feature already makes you a product manager.

    PMs are called "the VOICE OF THE CUSTOMER" — but the instructor adds the nuance: they can equally be the voice of the executives or the voice of the engineers, depending on whom they are talking to. Talking to business executives → wear the engineer's hat and discuss technical feasibility; talking to engineers → discuss business goals and objectives. "The PM has to be versatile."

    The three properties of a product — and who owns each guaranteed MCQ| Property | Owned by |

    |---|---| | FEASIBILITY | The TECHNOLOGY team / developers | | USABILITY | The DESIGN / UX team | | VALUE | THE PRODUCT MANAGER |

    But a PM cannot ignore feasibility and usability — they must understand enough technology to know whether a requirement is buildable, and must wear the user's hat as a LAYMAN, not as a technical expert, to judge usability.

    The FIVE key buckets of PM responsibility ← "please keep these five in mind throughout this entire course, because all topics map to these five"

    # Bucket What it contains
    1 SETTING THE PRODUCT STRATEGY Understanding the business, the market and the competition; positioning for target segments; defining the product vision; creating product goals aligned to business goals; pricing the product; envisioning a long-term strategic roadmap (3–4 years)
    2 DEFINING AND PLANNING THE PRODUCT User research (interviews, surveys, feedback, user reviews, social media reviews); product discovery (finding user needs and turning them into prioritised requirements); MVPs to test assumptions; sourcing feature ideas (from users, employees, competition) and — very importantly — VALIDATING AND DISCARDING ideas; feature prioritisation; the short-term/TACTICAL product roadmap (a few weeks to a few months)
    3 GUIDING DESIGN AND DEVELOPMENT Writing product requirements; creating EPICS and USER STORIES (agile artefacts); creating LOW-FIDELITY MOCKUPS / wireframes — skeleton forms giving an idea of the design; providing design inputs (final design remains the UX team's responsibility); managing the agile development process (sometimes as product owner or scrum master); TESTING THE FEATURES — "PMs are often called the FIRST USER of the features being released"; learning the technical constraints
    4 SUPPORTING THE PRODUCT RELEASE Inputs to the GO-TO-MARKET (GTM) plan and content (social media, advertising, email marketing); creating and giving product demos (at Microsoft and Google it is a PM who demos new products); training the sales team; GROWTH HACKING — "how do you market and advertise your product and scale it up with MINIMAL RESOURCES"
    5 TRACKING PERFORMANCE Monitoring product and business metrics day to day; tracking goals using OKRs; identifying which features succeeded/failed and why; noting feedback and refining the product. "The whole PM lifecycle is an ITERATIVE FEEDBACK LOOP"

    PM goals CHANGE across the product lifecycle very likely match-the-stage MCQ| Lifecycle stage | The PM's goal | Focus |

    |---|---|---| | INTRODUCTION | Getting the right PRODUCT-MARKET FIT | Adjusting and adapting RAPIDLY to new insights from customers and the market | | GROWTH / SCALING | Expanding reach and scale; staying competitive (new and old players appear) | Supporting more users while optimising to accelerate growth | | MATURITY / PLATEAU (e.g. Microsoft Office) | RETENTION — sustain market share, don't lose customers | Evolving the value proposition; customer satisfaction and customer delight; ## BATTLING CHURN — churn = users moving OUT of your product. The PM is a "retention strategist" | | DECLINE | Decide the best outcome: ## PIVOT · RESURRECT · or PHASE OUT/withdraw | |

    Which stage should a new PM join? (a reflection question, but the trade-offs are examinable)

    Stage Upside Risk
    Introduction Define the product and strategy from scratch; huge learning The product may not work out — career risk
    Growth Scaling experience, many new features Many start-ups lose out in the scaling-up phase
    Maturity Stability of career and product Fewer learning opportunities
    Decline If you turn around a failing product you are regarded as a SUPERSTAR PM The product/project will close in a short time

    The SIX skills required in a PM role guaranteed MCQ| # | Skill | Why |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | CUSTOMER EXPERIENCE GROUNDING | Be customer-centric; keep the customer decision journey and experience in mind. "In a business, NOBODY ELSE would be thinking about the users and customers apart from you" | | 2 | MARKET ORIENTATION | Competition, ecosystems, partners, trends; will it scale and gain market share? | | 3 | BUSINESS ACUMEN | Business processes, strategies, portfolios, pricing, KPIs, financial metrics | | 4 | TECHNICAL SKILLS | Technology trends, software architecture, how software is built — "you do not want to be taken for a ride" when a developer says a feature takes three months and you suspect three weeks (or vice versa). ## "Too much DEPTH is NOT mandatory for PMs" | | 5 | SOFT SKILLS (the most emphasised) | Communicating with a diverse group of stakeholders, leading, influencing change. ## "NOBODY REPORTS TO A PRODUCT MANAGER. The PM is in charge of the PRODUCT, but NOT the PEOPLE" → INFLUENCING WITHOUT AUTHORITY | | 6 | ENABLING SKILLS | Enabling innovation across the organisation; identifying talent, enriching career paths, creating a learning and innovation culture, championing practices like design thinking and user-centric thinking |

    How PM time is actually spent: alongside the technical/operational work (defining requirements, roadmap, strategy, reviewing metrics, market and competitor research, pricing and packaging), roughly HALF the time goes to collaborating with technical and design functions, collaborating with sales/marketing/legal/support, coaching, team management, recruiting, and engaging with customers and partners.

    The two PM ORIENTATIONS and the three resulting roles likely MCQ| | "HEADS-UP" / MARKET-FACING PM | "HEADS-DOWN" / TECHNICAL PM |

    |---|---|---| | Focus | Outside — product vision, product opportunity, strategic roadmap 2–3 years out | Inside — creating product requirements, working closely with developers | | Owns | Business metrics, KPIs, business goals and outcomes; talks to customers and watches market trends | Is the SCRUM PRODUCT OWNER; launch/release planning; managing the requirements backlog |

    The three role types: TECHNOLOGIST (technical-facing) · BUSINESS-ORIENTED PM (market-facing) · GENERALIST (in between). In most companies you will find PMs who are GENERALISTS.

    The competency map — two axes

    Axis 1: STRATEGIC (long-term, abstract, high-level) vs TACTICAL (operational, day-to-day). Axis 2: EXTERNAL-FACING (users and market) vs INTERNAL-FACING (technical and business).

    Quadrant Strategic examples Tactical examples
    External (users & market) Creating market/user segments, finding product-market fit, analysing competitors, positioning Monitoring feedback day to day, talking to users, collecting requests, user wireframes
    Internal — technical Innovation, technical partnerships Writing SQL queries, writing API specifications
    Internal — business Portfolio planning, sitting on the product council Sales support, analysing business, creating and tracking metrics
    CORE PRODUCT COMPETENCIES (the centre — apply to ALL PMs) Product vision · Product roadmapping · Feature prioritisation Backlog grooming · Writing detailed product requirements · Creating acceptance testing criteria and testing

    Use of the map: no single PM is an expert in all of it. When you later manage a PM team, you need a combination of product managers covering all the competencies together.

    PM career path likely sequence MCQ

    Associate/Assistant Product Manager → Product Manager (~4–5 years' experience) → Senior / Principal Product Manager → Director or VP of Product → CHIEF PRODUCT OFFICER (CPO)

    Level Skills that matter
    Entry level Technical: agile software development, ML/AI, core PM practices, working with data, SQL
    VP level Strategy creation, leadership, strategic planning — plus core product management throughout

    The PM interview rounds likely MCQ, and note they mirror the six skills| Round | What it tests | Sample questions given |

    |---|---|---| | 1. PROBLEM SOLVING | Structured thinking, use of clear frameworks on vague macro-level problems | "How do you guess the number of potholes in Bangalore?" · "How do you increase engagement on Flipkart?" · "What would improve Flipkart's profitability?" | | 2. PRODUCT THINKING | Customer empathy; creating a product vision with strategy and roadmap | "How do you launch grocery at Flipkart?" · "How is Netflix different from YouTube in product philosophy?" · "Your favourite product, and one feature enhancement you'd add — and why?" | | 3. BUSINESS UNDERSTANDING | Business strategy, industry landscape, competitors, business problems | "Explain the ad-technology market — key players, what drives customer success, revenue model, profit drivers" · "Comment on the future of e-commerce and payments in India" | | 4. ENGINEERING (more so for tech-oriented PM roles) | SDLC (software development lifecycle), system design, tech trade-offs | "Create a Google Photos-like product with mobile and web backup — how would you proceed?" · Draw a system diagram / functional view — frontend, backend, databases, servers · "What is the difference between a product, a feature and a platform?" · Data flow diagrams. ## NO questions on coding or programming | | 5. Culture / HR fit | Soft skills | |

    The TEN career MYTHS extremely likely "which of the following is a myth" MCQ| # | The myth | The reality |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | PMs are managers with employees/teams under them | MYTH — they manage the PRODUCT, not people | | 2 | PMs are PROJECT managers | MYTH — product managers ≠ project managers. Project managers own on-time, on-budget delivery and resourcing | | 3 | PMs work in the marketing department | Not a myth everywhere — in some companies PMs sit in marketing, a legacy of PM's origins in the consumer industry at companies like P&G, where the PM was effectively a BRAND MANAGER owning product lines. It came to software much later. Most tech companies now have a separate product department | | 4 | PMs are product owners | Not entirely a myth — in agile SCRUM there is a role called product owner, and PMs typically take it up during a sprint. But they are not the same thing | | 5 | PMs must think of all the feature ideas | Partly true only. Their real job is to SOURCE ideas (users, employees, social media) and PRIORITISE what gets included and excluded | | 6 | PMs find a way to put everyone's ideas into the product | MYTH. ## "It is an important responsibility of a PM to SAY NO to people, say no to many ideas, EVEN IF THEY COME FROM WAY TOP" | | 7 | PMs are responsible for designing cool products | Partly a myth — design belongs to the UX/product design team; the PM supplies inputs and initial skeletal wireframes | | 8 | A PM just hands over the product specs and is done | MYTH — the PM stays engaged through development, testing, launch and post-launch monitoring | | 9 | PMs definitely need a technical degree | MYTH. You need a high-level understanding of technology and the building blocks of software (APIs, microservices architecture) — not a degree, not in-depth coding | | 10 | PMs are hired to coordinate meetings | MYTH — ## "They're supposed to LEAD the meetings, set the direction... believe me, as a PM, all you have to do day in and day out is meetings" | | 11 | PM roles, concepts and processes are standardised across the industry | MYTH — even Agile Scrum is implemented differently everywhere; role names vary (Product Marketing Manager, Technical Product Manager/TPM) and mean different things in different companies | | 12 | "PMs are the CEOs of their product" — "the BIGGEST myth" | There is an element of truth (they own the product and the value delivered) BUT the one thing missing is AUTHORITY. CEOs have power over people; PMs must influence without authority. Counterpoint: Sundar Pichai (Google) and Satya Nadella (Microsoft) were both PMs — PMs are extremely well placed to become CEOs precisely because they delivered on goals without any formal power |

    7.3The FOUR approaches to developing digital products10

    WATERFALL · AGILE · DESIGN THINKING · LEAN PRODUCT MANAGEMENT ← memorise the set

    1. WATERFALL — the traditional "STAGE-GATE" process

    It is called a STAGE-GATE process because there are clear stages and you must CLEAR ONE STAGE BEFORE ENTERING THE NEXT.

    The five stages in order sequence MCQ

    REQUIREMENTS → DESIGN → IMPLEMENTATION → VERIFICATION (testing) → RELEASE AND MAINTENANCE

    Stage Detail
    Requirements Collect from all users/clients and write ONE detailed PRD — Product Requirements Document — which can run to HUNDREDS OF PAGES. Takes about 4 to 6 months. "Nothing can be missing, because once you have cleared this stage there is no going back"
    Design Software architecture — how databases and components fit and communicate; the technical design of the whole product
    Implementation Developers code and program
    Verification Testing by the QA (quality assurance) team
    Release and maintenance

    A CHANGE REQUEST (CR) is the industry term for going back a stage — "a DREADED TERM. Nobody likes a change request."

    Pros of waterfall Cons of waterfall
    Cost known clearly in advance Very limited scope for any changes
    Timelines known clearly Heavy dependency on the initial requirements
    Requirements very clearly known NO working prototypes for users to test at any stage → no user feedback until verification or release → HIGH RISK AND UNCERTAINTY
    Operationally poor: only ONE TEAM is engaged at any time (while development runs, the testing team idles, and vice versa)

    2. AGILE

    History ← guaranteed MCQ: in 2001, 17 SOFTWARE DEVELOPERS met at a resort in UTAH, USA to discuss a lightweight, flexible development method and published THE MANIFESTO FOR AGILE SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT, containing the Agile principles on which the many agile methods are based.

    At its centre, Agile is an ITERATIVE AND INCREMENTAL development methodology. - ITERATIVE = repeating the development cycle again and again. Each cycle is "like a mini waterfall" and is called a ## SPRINT — typically 2 to 4 weeks. Within a sprint you plan, analyse/design, implement AND test the requirements — testing both with QA and with users - INCREMENTAL = adding block by block, module by module. After several sprints you make a RELEASE — e.g. 3 months of sprints → V1 release; 3 more months → V2 release at 6 months

    Pros of Agile Cons of Agile
    Very adaptable to changing requirements (build in sprint 1, users dislike it, change it in sprint 3) Lack of concrete PLANNING AND ESTIMATION — you don't know how long the sprints will run, so budgeting is hard "because the requirements themselves may keep changing BY DESIGN"
    Immediate feedback from users after every cycle (feedback from even 4–5 users) Less emphasis on proper DOCUMENTATION — instead of a several-hundred-page PRD you may have one line: "as a user I want to have this ride-sharing feature"
    LESS RISK and LOW TIME-TO-MARKET — you can ship the first 20 core features rather than waiting for all 100 NOT suitable for MONOLITHIC products whose features are all interconnected. The example: sending CHANDRAYAAN to the moon — you want all the requirements ready before you start; WATERFALL is better there
    Not suitable when QUALITY/brand reputation is paramount — a big brand will not release incrementally; internal development may be agile but release happens only when the whole thing is finished, like the end of a waterfall

    3. LEAN PRODUCT MANAGEMENT — and the story of "Mr X"

    The trivia story (the exam may ask who "Mr X" is): - His first co-founded company, ## "CATALYST RECRUITING" — an online forum for university students to network with potential employers — failed because he and his colleagues did not understand the wants or needs of their target customers; they focused on the initial product requirements and launch rather than customer needs. ## This is the PROBLEM-SOLUTION FIT (PS-fit) problem - He then joined ## "THERE INCORPORATION" as a software engineer — a classic Silicon Valley start-up with ## $40 million in financing and nearly 200 employees at product launch. In ## 2003 it launched THERE.COM, which got some early adopters but could not scale. The most important mistake: ## "THE VISION WAS ALMOST TOO CONCRETE" — it would not flex or change direction to meet market demand. ## This is the PRODUCT-MARKET FIT (PM-fit) problem - The shared origin of both failures: ## "trying to work FORWARD FROM THE TECHNOLOGY instead of BACKWARD FROM THE BUSINESS RESULTS AND THE USER NEEDS you are trying to satisfy"

    Mr X is ERIC RIES, who wrote the bestselling book "THE LEAN START-UP" (2008), built on Lean and Agile principles and on ## STEVE BLANK's ideas on customer development in his book "THE FOUR STEPS TO THE EPIPHANY." This began the entire lean start-up / lean product development / lean product management movement.

    PS-fit vs PM-fit — the scale distinction subtle, likely MCQ| | Problem-Solution fit | Product-Market fit | |---|---|---| | How you validate it | Talk to maybe 15–20 users | Launch into the larger market and get a few hundred to a few thousand users |

    Why start-ups fail the statistic MCQ| Rank | Reason | Share |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | NO MARKET NEED FOR THE PRODUCT | 42% | | 2 | RAN OUT OF CASH | close to 30% | | then | Not the right team · got out-competed · pricing issues · poor product quality · features users don't like | |

    The five lessons drawn: 1. Ensure a clear problem-solution fit 2. Validate product-market fit 3. ## FAIL FAST AND CHEAP — a waterfall build takes 1–1.5 years and loses the market and all the money 4. Build competing products — what do you have that others don't (patents, delightful features, embedded AI)? 5. Discover the right product strategy and BUSINESS MODEL — "they may have a cool product with wonderful features, but there is no business model; customers are not willing to pay, or costs exceed profits"

    The lean loop

    IDEAS (= your assumptions/hypotheses) → BUILD an MVP → MEASURE by testing with real users → LEARN
                                                  → then PIVOT or PERSEVERE
    Concept Definition
    MVP — Minimum Viable Product A very skeletal product with ONLY AS MANY FEATURES AS REQUIRED TO TEST YOUR ASSUMPTIONS AND HYPOTHESES. Takes a few days, versus months for the full product. ## THE MVP IS NOT THE ACTUAL PRODUCT
    PIVOT vs PERSEVERE If the assumption fails → change/refine the idea (PIVOT) — you have FAILED FAST BUT CHEAP. If validated → PERSEVERE
