    VALIDATED LEARNING The core lean principle — learning that is validated from real customers and the real market using MVPs. It is an experiment-based, scientific method: formulate the hypothesis, test it in the market
    A/B TESTING Build version A and version B of a feature as MVPs and test both with users; ship whichever they prefer. Can extend to A, B, C, D

    The other lean characteristics: iterative product releases · well-defined success metrics set in advance ("if customers rate it more than 3.5 out of 5 stars, I will consider it a success") · continuous market feedback · openness to repeated pivoting.

    The two famous pivots likely MCQ| Product | Original idea | Pivot | |---|---|---| | YOUTUBE | A platform to upload DATING PROFILES in video form | Any kind of video | | TIKTOK | An EDUCATIONAL platform for short educational videos | Short ENTERTAINMENT videos for the young generation |

    The criticism of lean — the "Like A Little" story likely MCQ

    • Prasanna Shankar followed lean principles to build ## "LIKE A LITTLE", an anonymous flirting app which reached ## 20 million page views in the first 6 weeks and attracted $7 million of funding — then engagement declined
    • The founders pivoted unsuccessfully, then pivoted again, and ## folded up after 4 years
    • What went wrong: "switching ideas until a small group of users showed interest" — the pivoted ideas were not fundamentally exciting to the founders, so they did not know how to keep growing them
    • His verdict: ## "I would NEVER do the lean start-up thing again. I don't think ideas are brainstormed. You need to have a DEEP COMMITMENT AND DOMAIN KNOWLEDGE… the guys who do not switch ideas too frivolously may not be the VC-level hit stories, but they are the ones actually doing well for themselves."

    Other criticisms of lean given: users may dislike the half-baked MVP but would have liked the real product → you pivot wrongly. And a big brand cannot release a half-baked first product.

    The improved lean approach — PRODUCT DISCOVERY likely MCQ| | Traditional lean | PRODUCT DISCOVERY approach |

    |---|---|---| | The team | Product team | PRODUCT DISCOVERY TEAM | | What is tested with users | MVPs built by developers — takes days/weeks | TESTABLE PROTOTYPES built by UX + PM, requiring NO CODING — buildable in a FEW HOURS | | What reaches the delivery team | Validated ideas | Only the ideas validated in the prototype cycle |

    4. DESIGN THINKING

    Origin ← guaranteed MCQ: started in 2005 by STANFORD'S DESIGN SCHOOL (d.school). It was not meant only for technology product development but as a general approach to any social and technological innovation — it is even taught in primary schools.

    Design thinking solves the PRODUCT-MARKET FIT but MORE THAN THAT the PROBLEM-SOLUTION FIT.

    The five stages in order certain sequence MCQ

    EMPATHISE → DEFINE → IDEATE → PROTOTYPE → TEST (then loop back)

    Stage What you do
    EMPATHISE Understand people; user research, user interviews, going to the field and OBSERVING how users solve their problems today
    DEFINE State the 5 or 6 most important problems clearly
    IDEATE Generate many different ideas for each problem
    PROTOTYPE Build interactive prototypes users can touch and feel on mobile or desktop — proofs of concept/demos. "Even sketches" work: showing a wallet idea visually gets far better feedback than describing it
    TEST Refine the ideas and the product; then loop

    THE TWO PILLARS OF DESIGN THINKING: (1) CUSTOMER EMPATHY and (2) PROTOTYPING (having something VISUAL to test on real users).

    The DOUBLE DIAMOND framework guaranteed MCQ

         PROBLEM SPACE                    |            SOLUTION SPACE
  ◇ DIVERGE → CONVERGE                |         ◇ DIVERGE → CONVERGE
  DISCOVER      DEFINE                |         DEVELOP        DELIVER
 (find 30-50   (reframe to 3-5        |      (10 ideas per   (prototype, test,
  problems)     problems)             |       problem)        converge to 1 solution)
    Half Diamond Movement
    Problem space Diamond 1 DIVERGE — empathise, understand needs and challenges, surface 30, 40, 50 problems → CONVERGE — define a reframed set of 3–5 problems to tackle
    Solution space Diamond 2 DIVERGE — ideate, "get as wild and creative as possible", e.g. 10 solutions per problem → CONVERGE — screen on feasibility and desirability, prototype the top 1–2, test with users, converge to the ONE solution to release

    How the three modern approaches FIT TOGETHER guaranteed MCQ| Approach | What it delivers | Which fit it solves |

    |---|---|---| | DESIGN THINKING | Exploring the PROBLEM and finding good solutions | PROBLEM-SOLUTION FIT | | LEAN | Building the RIGHT THING for the market | PRODUCT-MARKET FIT | | AGILE | Building the THING RIGHT — the structured engineering process | SCALING the product |

    The Gartner integration: start in the problem space with design thinking (empathise, define, ideate) → move into the LEAN START-UP build–measure–learn loop to test the assumptions → and the BUILD part of that loop is executed using AGILE (planning, product backlog, sprints).

    "This is the INTEGRATED PM METHODOLOGY. Don't think you will be doing only design thinking, or only lean, or only agile in a company — you will be working with all three."

    When to use which — the decision rule very likely MCQ| Do you know WHAT customers want? | Do you know HOW to deliver it? | Use |

    |---|---|---| | YES | YES | WATERFALL | | YES | NO | AGILE SCRUM | | NO | NO | LEAN (the start-up situation) |

    7.4Product strategy — the landscape and the seven questions2

    The strategy hierarchy likely MCQ| Level | Contents |

    |---|---| | 1. BUSINESS STRATEGY | Company vision, target markets, competitive strategies and advantages, unique capabilities | | 2. PORTFOLIO STRATEGY (only if the business has multiple products) | Product dependencies among portfolio products, investment decisions on which product to pursue, portfolio adjustments (removing products) | | 3. PRODUCT STRATEGY | How the product will succeed — the positive change it creates for market/business/people/customers, the value proposition, standout features, and how product goals connect to business goals | | 4. PRODUCT ROADMAP | How the strategy will be implemented — short- and long-run product goals, time frames, key deliverables/features, release dates, milestones, success criteria | | 5. KPIs | How performance will be measured — e.g. NPS (Net Promoter Score), market share, financial metrics (revenue, cost); product, business, financial and operational metrics | | 6. BUSINESS MODEL | How the product achieves its goals and monetises — customer relationships, channels, cost factors, revenue drivers |

    Definition: ## "Product strategy defines WHAT THE PRODUCT WANTS TO ACHIEVE. It provides a CONTEXT around the market it operates in and guides the LARGE THEMES OF WORK that will help accomplish concrete product goals."

    Product strategy is NEVER in isolation — always in alignment with the business strategy. And it is NOT STATIC — review it regularly (half-yearly or yearly) for change/no-change decisions, because the industry, competitors, customers and positioning change (AI disruption, new blockchain-based technology in FinTech).

    THE SEVEN QUESTIONS OF PRODUCT STRATEGY the organising spine of the whole module; guaranteed MCQ

    1. WHY does this product exist? (value proposition / vision) 2. WHO are its target customers? 3. HOW is it powering the business? (business model) 4. WHAT is the macro view of its industry? 5. WHICH are the key competitors? 6. WHERE is it positioning itself in the market? (differentiation) 7. DOES it have strategic goals? (goals and the 2–3 year roadmap)

    7.5Question 1 — Why does the product exist? (Vision, overview, business goals)2

    Product VISION

    Rule Detail
    Same as company vision? YES if the company has a SINGLE product; NO if it is a MULTI-PRODUCT company — each product then has its own vision
    Time frame IDEALLY 3 TO 5 YEARS. NOT 6–7 years or beyond (too far) and NOT 1–2 years (that becomes tactical, not strategic)
    Form ONE TO TWO INSPIRING SENTENCES on WHY THIS PRODUCT EXISTS
    Purpose Clear understanding of the value provided to target customers, and to align everyone across the company with shared clarity of purpose

    The five properties of a good vision likely MCQ

    PURPOSEFUL · ASPIRATIONAL · ACHIEVABLE · CUSTOMER-FOCUSED · CONCISE

    The vision template:

    "To [VERB — empower / unlock / enable] [TARGET CUSTOMER] to [BENEFIT / GOAL / FUTURE STATE]."

    Example — LinkedIn: "To CONNECT the world's professionals and make them more productive and successful."

    The PRODUCT OVERVIEW — the elements

    Key concept → key value proposition → main features → what it looks like (images, videos, demos) → how successful it is (testimonials, download and rating stats) → pricing (tiers; one-time vs subscription) → team, history, financials.

    Worked examples:

    Product Overview content
    Signal Value proposition condensed to "Speak Freely" — signalling data privacy and protection
    Playo "A one-step solution for sports enthusiasts to book sports venues"; stats: 1 million downloads, 4.4 star rating, 9,000 reviews, annual sales ₹35 crore; key features: book venue, events
    Hotstar "A video experience like none other" — seamless video playback, smart search, friendly user interface, plus revenue and paid-subscriber stats and pricing tiers

    THE PRODUCT MANAGEMENT ONION guaranteed MCQ (an ordering question)

    Company/business VISION → Business STRATEGY and business GOALS → Product VISION → Product STRATEGY and product GOALS → Product BACKLOG → SPRINT GOALS and SPRINT PLANNING → DAILY PLAN

    The inner layers are the agile development mode. The onion shows how a daily task connects up to a decade-scale vision.

    The BUSINESS GOAL of a product — three questions

    1. How does this product serve the company?
    2. How does it fit into the portfolio? — the Microsoft Copilot example: it could have been standalone, but was integrated with Word, PowerPoint and Excel, creating integrations and dependencies across portfolio products
    3. Which KPIs does it target? — ## not all products exist for profitability. The Facebook/Oculus Rift example: buying the VR headset maker had no immediate revenue goal; the long-term goal became clear only when Zuckerberg renamed Facebook to META and focused on the metaverse

    Worked example — Mercedes-Benz business goals (vision: "We will build the world's most desirable cars"): - Think and act like a LUXURY BRAND — note this is NOT profit-focused; even if there is an opportunity to make money selling low-end cheap cars, they won't, because it is not aligned to the business goal - Profitable growth - Expand the customer base by growing the top-end luxury market - Embrace customers, be more customer-centric, and grow lifetime revenues - Lead in the electric car drive and in digital experiences - Lower the cost base, improve the industrial footprint, increase supply chain resilience

    7.6Question 2 — Who are the target customers? (Segmentation and personas)3

    The FOUR bases of segmentation guaranteed MCQ| Basis | Variables |

    |---|---| | GEOGRAPHIC | City, region, size of region, climate, communities, countries, rural vs urban | | DEMOGRAPHIC | Age, gender, race, religion, income, education, languages | | PSYCHOGRAPHIC | Budget attitude (conservative vs liberal about expenditure), beliefs, values, pain points, attitudes, social and cultural norms, roles, activities | | BEHAVIOURAL | Hobbies, habits, purchasing styles and behaviours, social media usage, mobile phone usage, media consumption |

    Worked example — Mercedes-Benz EV:

    Basis Segment
    Demographic Affluent millennials aged 27–40 and Gen X aged 41–56; income: high-income individuals earning above $200,000 annually
    Geographic Urban and suburban areas in Europe, America, China where EV infrastructure is developed; moderate-climate regions where EVs perform optimally year-round
    Psychographic Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritise sustainability and will pay more for it; tech-savvy; value luxury, innovation and status — see the car as a reflection of success
    Behavioural Heavy users who drive frequently and benefit from EV cost savings (fuel efficiency, lower maintenance)

    The PERSONA

    The problem with raw segments: "Do you feel any connect or empathy with customers if you just say their age is this, their income is this? Not exactly."

    A PERSONA is a COMPOSITE SKETCH of a key segment of the target market. Its PURPOSE is TO CREATE EMPATHY for customers among ALL the product-related teams.

    Rule Detail
    How many? Multiple personas per product — typically 3 or 4, depending on the number of target segments
    How built? On a MIX OF QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE RESEARCH — a survey for wants, needs, motivations, frustrations, attitudes and behaviours, followed by qualitative interviews for insight; then all the insights go into one composite sketch
    Tools Canva, Xtensio
    Contents Name, face, age, occupation, income, location · personality · goals and motivations · challenges and pain points

    Worked example — "John Harrison" for Mercedes-Benz EV: age 50+, CEO, income $500,000+, New York; personality high-powered, fast-paced, focused on sustainability and innovation, values work-life balance, enjoys luxury travel and fine dining; goal — drive a vehicle that symbolises success, innovation and environmental stewardship; pain points — balancing luxury with genuine sustainability, and transitioning to EV without compromising performance and prestige.

    USER persona vs CUSTOMER persona guaranteed MCQ

    A USER is somebody who USES the product. A CUSTOMER is somebody who PURCHASES the product.

    The Mercedes example: the customer is John (CEO); the USER of the car's app may be a DRIVER who is not highly educated, not high-income, not tech-savvy and not seeking a luxurious lifestyle → "if you are building an app it better be very intuitive and easy to use."

    MARKETING AND ADVERTISING TEAMS LOOK AT CUSTOMER PERSONAS; DEVELOPMENT TEAMS LOOK AT USER PERSONAS.

    The two-sided example — PhonePe (two main players, so two personas):

    Persona Wants / needs Frustrations
    Harshad — the store owner Easy scan and pay for customers, investment suggestions, best deals on service payments Managing and keeping records of all cash payments; unnecessary rewards/notifications that distract from work
    Srikanth — the consumer Easy money transfer, bank transfers with no additional charges and no limits; recharge, bill payment, reminders and offers Managing expenses; the bank account getting automatically unlinked

    The PRODUCT VISION BOARD likely MCQ on its five sections

    A one-shot snapshot of product strategy containing: 1. VISION (top) · 2. TARGET GROUP (users and customers, plus personas) · 3. NEEDS (what the target group wants) · 4. PRODUCT (key value proposition, concept and key features) · 5. BUSINESS GOALS (and metrics)

    Example content: vision — "helping teams create great UX-rich products"; users — product managers and product owners; customers — mid-sized to large enterprises; need — "easily integrate the UX artefacts into the product backlog"; product — "a tablet application that looks like a physical canvas, very intuitive, provides guidance and templates"; business goals — "opening a new revenue stream, developing our main brand."

    7.7Question 3 — How is it powering the business? (Business models and analysis frameworks)2

    The BUSINESS MODEL CANVAS — the 9 blocks guaranteed MCQ| Position | Block | The question it answers |

    |---|---|---| | Centre | VALUE PROPOSITION | What value do we deliver? What problem are we solving? Which customer needs, wants and desires are satisfied? (Key features go here, concisely) | | Right | CUSTOMER SEGMENTS | Who are the target segments and personas? | | Right-middle | CHANNELS | How do we reach those segments? | | Right-middle | CUSTOMER RELATIONSHIPS | How are relationships built and maintained? | | Left | KEY PARTNERS | Who is involved in developing/delivering this? | | Left | KEY ACTIVITIES | What activities deliver the value? | | Left | KEY RESOURCES | People, technology, data required | | Base-left | COST STRUCTURE | What are the cost drivers / high-cost elements? | | Base-right | REVENUE STREAMS | How does the product earn money? |

    Worked example — Disney+ Hotstar:

    Block Content
    Value proposition 24×7 video-on-demand, HD quality, popular TV shows and movies from across the world, streaming of sports, unlimited access for premium customers, no commercials, original videos and shows, content for kids
    Customer segments Sports enthusiasts, regional content viewers, kids (Disney-owned content), youth seeking premium content from Bollywood/Hollywood
    Channels Apps, websites, social media, word-of-mouth advertising
    Customer relationships On-demand usage, self-service, ease of use (streaming instead of DVDs and CDs)
    Key partners Investors, media production houses, filmmaker guilds, TV networks, cloud service providers, content regulators
    Key activities Technology R&D, content licensing, content production, distribution, data analysis, recommendations
    Key resources The app/platform, employees, developers, the CONTENT itself, and the BRAND
    Cost structure Production, marketing, R&D, licensing, infrastructure
    Revenue streams Subscriptions, broadcasting fees, movie premieres, content hosting, advertising

    The LEAN CANVAS — and how it DIFFERS from the Business Model Canvas guaranteed comparison MCQ

    Blocks that are the SAME: cost structure, revenue streams, value proposition (plus a high-level concept), customer segments, channels.

    Business Model Canvas block REPLACED IN THE LEAN CANVAS BY
    Key partners PROBLEM — the top 1 to 3 problems you are solving, plus ## EXISTING ALTERNATIVES (how the segment solves it today = who the competitors are)
    Key activities SOLUTION — the key features
    Key resources KEY METRICS — "this was sort of MISSING in the business model canvas" — the key success metrics
    Customer relationships UNFAIR ADVANTAGE — unique resources competitors cannot easily replicate or gain control over: e.g. patents, or founders with many years of domain experience

    Worked example — "Mingout" (a dating app):

    Block Content
    Problem Existing dating apps focus on discovery and discussion but give no aid in taking it forward into EXPERIENCES — "the onus of making the date successful comes to the user"
    Solution An app that assists users to have experiences with their matches and find people with similar interests
    Customer segment 18–35 year-olds, primarily 21–25, living in metro cities
    Value proposition A real connect on dates based on activities that interest both parties; curated experiences usable after matching; one chat at a time (so no ghosting); selfies for security; Facebook and Instagram verification
    Channels Instagram, word of mouth, publicising through partners for offline experiences
    Key metrics % of dating invites accepted · ## the FEMALE-TO-MALE GENDER RATIO (critical for dating apps) · number of experiences converted into IRL (in-real-life) dates
    Cost structure Payroll, advertising, app development, design, testing, rent, equipment
    Revenue streams Partnerships with entities that want to be listed and provide shared experiences; advertising; paid subscriptions

    The two supplementary business analysis frameworks

    Framework Elements
    SWOT Strengths (unique assets and resources the business is good at) · Weaknesses (lacking talent, lacking patents, dependency on partners) · Opportunities (new revenue streams) · Threats (competing products, market, industry technology trends)
    THE 5 Ps (a MARKETING framework — "if you are a PRODUCT MARKETING MANAGER you may lean towards the 5 Ps") PRODUCT (functionality, appearance, quality, packaging) · ## PRICE (selling price, discounts, credit terms) · ## PROMOTION (advertising, sponsorships, messaging, media, PR) · ## PLACE (= channels: distribution, logistics, locations, market coverage) · ## PEOPLE (attitude of people, customer service, how employees are perceived)

    The PM's toolkit rule given: use either the Business Model Canvas or the Lean Canvas ("just one of them is fine"), and analyse the business with SWOT or the 5 Ps.

    Worked SWOT — the LIC app (LIC: a public sector company serving over 250 million people with revenue over $800 million**):

    Content
    Strengths Dominant market position in India, variety of products, very loyal customer base, channel partnerships
    Weaknesses High government control → reduced returns/revenue/profit-making and slower growth and innovation
    Opportunities Continued growth of the Indian insurance market — huge untapped potential; good short-term economic outlook; more people entering the middle class; increasing life expectancy (people live longer → less insurance payout)
    Threats Competitive pressure from ACKO Insurance, HDFC Life etc.; economic issues such as interest-rate fluctuations affecting operating performance

    7.8Question 4 — The macro view of the industry3

    The worked industry snapshot — Indian insurance (the LIC app's market) possible number MCQ| Metric | Value |

    |---|---| | Total market size | $280 billion | | Segments | Life insurance vs non-life | | Life insurance CAGR (2018–2023) | 7.1% | | Life insurance penetration | 2.82% | | LIC's market share | ~66% (private sector ~33%) — LIC is number one in Indian life insurance |

    The FUTURE OUTLOOK items ("what is in the future is also very important for PMs who are building products for the future"): - Robust demand — life insurance expected to rise 14–15% annually for the next 3–5 years - Increasing investment — the finance ministry announced an infusion of ₹3,000 crore into state-owned insurance companies - New opportunities — ## India is the SECOND LARGEST INSURANCE TECHNOLOGY MARKET IN ASIA-PACIFIC, accounting for 35% of $3.6 BILLION of InsurTech-focused venture investments - Policy support — ## the FDI limit in insurance raised from 49% to 74%; DigiLocker issuance for digital insurance policies; privatisation of some state-run insurers

    "As a product manager, you are supposed to be an EXPERT IN YOUR INDUSTRY as well."

    PORTER'S FIVE FORCES guaranteed MCQ

    At the CENTRE: RIVALRY AMONG EXISTING COMPETITORS, shaped by four surrounding forces: 1. THREAT OF NEW ENTRANTS · 2. THREAT OF SUBSTITUTE PRODUCTS · 3. BARGAINING POWER OF SUPPLIERS · 4. BARGAINING POWER OF BUYERS

    The substitution example given: in banking you had NEFT transfers; now you have UPI-based wallet transfers — UPI has SUBSTITUTED bank transfers to a large extent.

    PESTEL guaranteed MCQ on the six letters| Letter | Element | What you examine |

    |---|---|---| | P | POLITICAL | Policy, regulations, government funding, political stability, trade policy, corruption, taxation | | E | ECONOMIC | Economic growth, interest rates, inflation, labour costs, disposable income, middle-class consumers | | S | SOCIAL | Age/population distribution, population growth, workforce trends | | T | TECHNOLOGICAL | Emerging technologies, research, copyrights, who holds the patents, who controls production and distribution (big tech vs smaller players) | | E | LEGAL | Company registration, taxation policies, audit policies, regulations, legal processes to set up | | L | ENVIRONMENTAL | Climate impact, environmental policies, CSR goals, sustainability practices |

    (Note the instructor's order: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, L for Legal, and the final E for Environment.)

    MARKET OUTLOOK

    Describe the market → list your product and competing products → state whether the market is growing, shrinking or stable → and for each choice provide a RATIONALE sourced from industry reports and news articles, not an intuitive guess.

    Example: virus protection for desktops (Norton, McAfee) is a SHRINKING market because the desktop market itself is shrinking as people move to mobile — while virus protection for MOBILES** may be stable or growing.

    7.9Market sizing — TAM, SAM, SOM guaranteed MCQ1

    Acronym Full form Definition
    TAM Total Available Market (also Total Addressable Market) The MAXIMUM POSSIBLE size of the market — an IDEAL, THEORETICAL potential number only
    SAM Serviceable/Service Addressable Market How big is the segment WITHIN the TAM that can ACTUALLY BE TARGETED — within reach if given all the resources
    SOM Serviceable/Service Obtainable Market The REALISTIC portion within SAM that your company can CAPTURE with its services IN 4 TO 5 YEARS — after considering competitors and your limited sales and distribution resources (e.g. you operate in only 2–3 countries)

    Worked example — "LeanCase" accounting SaaS (helps users who currently do accounting in Excel):

    Layer Figure
    TAM 60 million corporations + 600 million Excel users
    SAM Only ~1% of Excel users — those using it specifically for accounting → 600,000 corporations, 6 million Excel users
    SOM ~10% of that → 6,000–10,000 companies, and only 1% of the SAM users fitting the target groups and regions

    TOP-DOWN estimation — the air-conditioner example

    Total population of India (~1.5 bn)
   → split URBAN vs RURAL (different purchase behaviour)
      → split by CLASS (upper / upper-middle / lower-middle / lower)
         → number of FAMILIES × ACs PER FAMILY  (e.g. upper class 2.5 ACs/family; lower-middle 0.2)
            → total existing ACs ≈ 40 million
               + new demand at 10% market growth = 4 million
               + replacement demand (based on average AC lifespan) = 5 million
                  = TOTAL AC DEMAND 9 MILLION
                     × average price ₹30,000
                        = TOTAL MARKET SIZE ₹270 BILLION

    BOTTOM-UP estimation — the burger outlet example

    7 operating hours; 8 burgers ordered every 10 minutes
   → 48 orders per hour
      → 48 × 7 = 336 orders per day
         → × average 2 burgers per order = 672 burgers per day
            → × average price ₹40 = ₹26,880 SALES PER DAY
               → × 365 = yearly revenue for ONE outlet
                  → × number of outlets in the city / country = the market

    The distinction to memorise: TOP-DOWN starts from the TOTAL POPULATION and segments downwards; BOTTOM-UP starts from the SMALLEST OBSERVABLE UNIT (orders in 10 minutes) and extrapolates upwards.

    7.10Question 5 — Competitor analysis2

    Strategic competitor analysis — the five questions

    1. Who are the other companies vying for customers in your market?
    2. What products and services do they offer?
    3. What is each competitor's market share?
    4. What are their strengths and weaknesses?
    5. How do your own products and services compare?

    "A product manager MUST understand the competition very well… you should be the GO-TO PERSON in your company who can talk about your key competitors, their products, their strengths and weaknesses, and where your product is positioned among them."

    How to SCAN the competition likely "which of these is a competitor-scanning method" MCQ| Method | Detail |

    |---|---| | Conventional | Google, competitor websites, industry reports, asking your customers who also use their products, directly interviewing their customers | | Product directory / review sites | Product Hunt · alternativeto.net · G2.com — leaders vs niche players, key features, revenues, side-by-side comparisons | | Q&A and social | Quora (many PMs post questions about their product or competitors) · social media · App Store user reviews · complaint sites like MouthShut | | Traffic analysis | similarweb.com |

    The SimilarWeb worked example — amazon.in ← the insight matters more than the numbers:

    Metric Value
    Visits 233 million
    Average visit duration 5 minutes
    Pages per visit 6
    Traffic from India / outside India 89% / ~11% — the 11% are NRIs sending gifts or purchasing in India (US, UK, UAE, Canada) → a competing product could position itself as an NRI-focused e-commerce platform
    Traffic sources ~50% DIRECT · ~38% SEARCH · ~5% SOCIAL · ~2% referrals and mail → a competitor must invest in SEO and sponsored search ads**
    Within social The majority comes from YOUTUBE — not Facebook or Instagram → ensure a good YouTube presence

    The COMPETITOR PROFILE

    A one-page snapshot per key competitor. Worked example — ET Money profiling Paytm Money: 100+ employees, founded 2018, 10 million+ downloads, 3.8 star rating, $19 million funding; mission and description; financial products (mutual funds, stocks); key features (one-stop portfolio insights, fully transparent tracking and data privacy, fingerprint and PIN-protected login, fully digitalised account opening); strength — part of the core Paytm app so higher awareness; weakness — no telephonic support, no investment recommendations; differentiator — buy and sell digital gold.

    THE FEATURE COMPARISON TABLE ← "this is THE MOST IMPORTANT CONCEPT for a product manager"

    Rows = features; columns = competing products; tick where the feature exists.

    The worked example — the LIC app has multiple insurance categories, a user dashboard and an in-app calculator, but lacks features other apps have: HDFC Life offers social sign-up/sign-in, request-a-callback for consultation, in-app document scanner, push notifications, service requests through WhatsApp; SBI Life and ICICI Prudential offer live chat consultation.

    "If LIC does not have push notifications and ALL other products do, users will not take it well — they will EXPECT these features in your product." The table is a key input for the PM's future product ROADMAP.

    The COMPETITOR SCORECARD

    Goes beyond features to weighted metrics: customer experience, market awareness, personalisation, product variety, number of downloads, number of features. Assign weights (e.g. downloads 15%, basic features 20%), rate each product, and compute a weighted average. Worked example: Splitwise vs Settleup, Splitr, Tab — Splitwise scores 4–5 across criteria; Tab lags on downloads, product breadth and customer experience; Splitwise still has room on basic features and personalisation. Ratings come from user surveys plus objective data (app rating, downloads, feature counts).

    THE IMITABILITY LADDER guaranteed MCQ (four rungs, bottom to top)| Rung | Level | Examples |

    |---|---|---| | 4 (top) | CANNOT BE IMITATED | Legal copyrights and PATENTS · unique locations and leases · unique physical assets (e.g. data centres) · unique partnerships that cannot be given to anyone else | | 3 | DIFFICULT TO IMITATE | Brand image and reputation · customer loyalty · company culture and employee motivation · networks and alliances (partners of 10 years, exclusive rights) — all take years to build | | 2 | CAN BE IMITATED, BUT AT A COST | Skilled workforce (better training, higher salaries) · good customer service · product development capabilities · physical resources (office space in a good area, sales locations, distribution channels) | | 1 (bottom) | EASY TO IMITATE | Unskilled workforce · generic, undifferentiated products and services — "you don't want to be here" |

    The WhatsApp illustration: technologically WhatsApp is "nothing hard to build", and many have tried and failed — because of assets that are hard to imitate: the networks and alliances, the partnership with Meta/Instagram/Facebook, and above all the ## NETWORK ADVANTAGE — the more users there are, the more valuable WhatsApp becomes and the harder it is to imitate.

    7.11Question 6 — Product positioning and pricing4

    The SIX positioning strategies guaranteed MCQ| # | Strategy | Detail / example |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | PRICE | Position as the more affordable option; out-compete by offering a lower-cost option | | 2 | QUALITY | Convey high quality or a niche luxury product. Apple in phones — "we don't want to compete in the sub-₹15,000–20,000 market" | | 3 | USER GROUP / DEMOGRAPHIC | Target a specific demographic relevant to the product (e.g. environmentally sustainable users) | | 4 | PRODUCT TYPE | Shift customer perceptions by selecting an ALTERNATIVE CATEGORY — the smartwatch created by Samsung and Apple out of the watch category | | 5 | COMPETITORS | Place yourself directly against a competing product — Signal vs WhatsApp on PRIVACY: everything else is similar, but one key value proposition is much better | | 6 | DIFFERENTIATION | A completely unique offering that cannot be easily duplicated — Bitcoin/crypto when it arrived |

    The PERCEPTUAL MAP: plot competitors on two dimensions that matter for your market. Worked example — streaming, on value for money vs content quality: Netflix — high content quality but costly, so lower value for money; Zee5 — high value for money but lower content quality.

    The SIX pricing MODELS likely MCQ| Model | How it works |

    |---|---| | FLAT FEE | One price, no tiers | | PER-USER | Charge by number of users — the typical cloud/SaaS user-based licence | | TIER-BASED | Basic tier vs premium tier with more features | | FREEMIUM | Basic plan free; pay for certain features | | USAGE-BASED | The more you use, the more you pay — again typical of cloud | | FEATURE-BASED / add-ons | Pay for feature bundles or add-ons — e.g. games where you buy tools or coin packs |

    The THREE ways to DETERMINE the price guaranteed MCQ| Method | How |

    |---|---| | COST-PLUS PRICING | Compute the TOTAL COST of creating the product (technology, people, marketing) → add a margin (e.g. 20% profit) → derive the price point | | TARGETED RETURN PRICING | ROI-based — based not on cost but on what return you expect on your INVESTMENT (the investor's ROI question); a formula gives the required price | | RELATIVE VALUE-BASED PRICING | Compare against competing products. If competitors sit at $20–28, price at $30 if your quality is better, or $19–20 if you want to undercut and position as low-cost. "Users expect prices similar to your competitors, not too high or low compared to them." Worked example: a product priced at $12/user/month where competitors charge $19–20, and $29 / $49 for team and pro tiers where competitors are much higher |

    The UNIQUE VALUE PROPOSITION (UVP)

    A UVP is a statement explaining (a) how your products and services SOLVE YOUR CUSTOMERS' PROBLEMS or improve their situations, (b) what SPECIFIC BENEFITS customers can expect, and (c) WHY customers should buy from you and not from your competitors — in two to three statements.

    MCQ trap: a UVP is NOT A SLOGAN. "Think Different" or "We are the number one targeting platform" are NOT value propositions. State the VALUE PROVIDED TO THE CUSTOMER, not a slogan or a boast about the company.

    A good example — Campaign Monitor: "Create and send unforgettable email. Connecting with your audience has never been easier with Campaign Monitor's straightforward email marketing and automation tools."

    THE VALUE PROPOSITION CANVAS guaranteed MCQ

    Two halves, three boxes each, mapped across:

    CUSTOMER PROFILE (right) maps to VALUE MAP (left)
    CUSTOMER JOBS — the activities/needs the customer wants done. This is the ## JTBD = JOBS TO BE DONE framework: "the customers are giving you some jobs to do, and your product gets those done" ← PRODUCTS AND SERVICES
    PAINS — the real pain points (e.g. transferring money India→US: high transaction charge, many forms to fill, takes 2 days) ← PAIN RELIEVERS — targeting specific pains
    GAINS — the DELIGHT factors. Not pain points: if absent there is no problem, but if provided, customers love it. "All competing products are supposed to focus on the pain points — so how will you differentiate? Have MORE GAIN CREATORS." ← GAIN CREATORS

    Worked example — Tesla:

    Element Content
    Customer jobs (JTBD) Commute to work · convey an image of success · personal mobility to go anywhere · occasional long-distance trips · be different from others
    Pains Lack of charging infrastructure · need to charge frequently · fear of a dead battery or the battery blowing up in an accident · mileage
    Products and services Model X, Model 3 …, plus an 8-year battery warranty
    Pain relievers Their OWN charging network (solves charging-station scarcity) · high mileage — a Tesla goes ~600–800 km without charging, so no frequent charging
    Gain creators The 17-inch touchscreen · autonomous/self-driving · the interior design and styling — "not what the customer was looking for as a pain point, but a DELIGHT factor"

    7.12Question 7 — Strategic goals, initiatives and OKRs5

    The goal hierarchy

    Product VISION → high-level STRATEGIC GOAL → what the team PRIORITISES ON THE ROADMAP.

    SMART goals guaranteed MCQ

    S = SPECIFIC · M = MEASURABLE · A = ATTAINABLE · R = RELEVANT · T = TIME-BOUND

    Example goal Verdict
    "Be a top-rated social fitness cycling app within 12 months, metric: number-one rated in both the iOS and Android marketplaces" ✅ Fully SMART
    "Double revenue year over year — add $100 million more in revenue" ✅ SMART
    "Create the largest partner ecosystem with 100+ partners" ⚠️ Specific, measurable, attainable and relevant — but NOT TIME-BOUND. Fix by adding "in 1 year" classic MCQ

    Goal-setting is a COLLABORATIVE PROCESS between the BUSINESS LEADERSHIP and the PRODUCT TEAMS, because product goals must align with business goals.

    INITIATIVES and the two roadmaps

    Concept Detail
    INITIATIVE A high-level effort of roughly 3 to 15 months created so that it meets a specific product goal. Initiatives cross multiple releases and sprints and include many features. Examples: adding new features, providing better security
    STRATEGIC roadmap Maps the initiatives over 1 to 2 years (elsewhere stated as 3–4 / 3–5 years for the long-range strategic roadmap)
    TACTICAL / features roadmap Guides the low-level planning at a weekly or monthly level

    THE VALUE–EFFORT MATRIX guaranteed MCQ| | LOW effort | HIGH effort |

    |---|---|---| | HIGH value | QUICK WINS — do these FIRST | STRATEGIC INITIATIVES — take longer but ultimately deliver high value | | LOW value | PM's judgement call — "sometimes low-value items can act as DIFFERENTIATORS" | CUT THESE — "more loss-making, more cons than pros" |

    OKRs — Objectives and Key Results guaranteed MCQ

    OKR = OBJECTIVES AND KEY RESULTS. It was popularised by INTEL and GOOGLE as the goal-setting and tracking system.

    Element Definition — the question it answers
    OBJECTIVES The product goals that INSPIRE AND SET DIRECTION (the SMART goals) — ## "WHERE DO I NEED TO GO?"
    KEY RESULTS The deliverables and METRICS connected to the objective — ## "HOW DO I KNOW I AM GETTING THERE?"
    INITIATIVES The TASKS required to drive progress on the key results — ## "WHAT DO I NEED TO DO TO GET THERE?"

    How OKRs work in a company: organisation-wide alignment — every employee has their own OKRs, aligned to their manager's OKRs, to their manager's manager's OKRs, right up to the company's business vision; all tracked continuously, on a scale of 0 to 1 or 0 to 100%, and visible transparently to managers, employees and other teams.

    Worked OKR — Hotstar: - Objective: "Create an awesome engagement experience on mobile" - Key results: increase average time spent on the platform by 25% · improve NPS (Net Promoter Score) by 10% · raise upgrades from the free tier to the premium account by 5%

    Worked OKR — the LIC app: - Goal: become the top-rated app in the next 12 months in the life insurance segment on Android and iOS - Metrics: number-one rating, and at least 60% of rated reviews in the next 12 months with a rating above 4 - Initiatives: complete UI refresh · mobile app upgrade · improving the mobile experience

    Alignment worked example: company objective — increase revenue and optimise the sales process to double annual revenue → Susan, VP of Sales: increase new product sales from $12 million to $15 million → her two directors of sales: close $1.5 million and $700,000 in new deals respectively. Progress rolls UP from the bottom to the company level.

    THE NESTED CADENCE OF OKRs guaranteed MCQ

    "Cadence" = the rhythm/regularity at which OKRs are tracked.

    Cadence Level Frequency
    STRATEGIC cadence High-level, long-term OKR for the COMPANY ANNUAL
    TACTICAL cadence Shorter-term OKR for the TEAMS QUARTERLY
    OPERATIONAL cadence Daily/weekly OKRs, or per sprint WEEKLY / PER SPRINT

    The drill-down example: strategic objective "increase customer satisfaction" (key results: improve NPS from 20 to 50, reduce lead time to ~10 minutes) → tactical quarterly objectives "make the demo process better", "improve infrastructure scalability" → operational features and user stories (e.g. a "program board" feature and the user stories enabling it). Progress rolls up; objectives roll down.

    7.13The ART of product strategy (module recap)

    Knowing all seven questions and every framework does NOT make you a master product strategist. ## What is missing is the "X FACTOR" — STRATEGIC WISDOM, gained only through the experience of yourself and others. That is the ART of product strategy, which cannot be taught.

    The five illustrative puzzles the instructor poses (each is a memorable exam anecdote):

    Puzzle The example
    Why do some ORDINARY products become so successful, while good products fail? WhatsApp — "hardly anything in the UI/UX" — beat ## HIKE MESSENGER, which was better in user experience, had stickers, was more colourful and looked better
    How do you predict what customers may not like now but will prefer in future? E-BOOKS — many leaders and PMs said "let's not get into this, users still prefer physical books"; others predicted that once users saw the advantages of storing and carrying e-books, they would adopt them
    How do you think beyond what customers say they want? HENRY FORD: "If I had asked customers what they wanted, they would have said FASTER HORSES."
    How and when do you SHOCK AND AWE the market and competitors? The iPhone REMOVING THE HEADPHONE JACK altogether — customers protested, competitors were shocked; Apple could have kept it as an extra feature alongside Bluetooth, but removed it entirely and changed the dynamics of the market
    How do you create a completely NEW market and revolutionise an industry? CRYPTO — which created an entirely new FinTech market

    The prescription: read the many websites that share product stories on why products succeeded or failed — "more you go through these stories, the more wisdom you gain for your own product strategy."

    MODULE 3 — PRODUCT IMPROVEMENT (improving EXISTING products)

    "Most of the companies you may work with will work on EXISTING products and try to improve them, instead of building completely new products from scratch."

    CONTINUOUS DISCOVERY: product discovery is a continuous process — on regular intervals (weekly, bi-weekly or monthly customer interactions) the PM team surfaces ideas, problems and opportunities, tests whether a good solution exists, and — if it is FEASIBLE, DESIRABLE and VALUABLE — it goes into the development team's backlog.

    The module is structured on the DOUBLE DIAMOND:

    Space Phase Purpose
    PROBLEM DISCOVER Research and identify a diverse set of problems and opportunities
    PROBLEM DEFINE Converge on a clearly defined set of problem statements
    SOLUTION DEVELOP Develop solutions for each problem
    SOLUTION DELIVER Select the solutions that go into development/coding

    7.14DISCOVER — the I-SEE-MUCK framework for sourcing problems guaranteed MCQ1

    Mnemonic: "I SEE MUCK" — MUCK means problems, so "I see problems."

    Letter Source Detail
    I I — the PM myself "As a PM I am supposed to be the FIRST AND BEST CUSTOMER of my own product" — for an existing product you should find problems by regularly using it
    S SOCIAL CHATTER Reviews, tweets, complaints scattered across social platforms. A very good source, because the issues are strong enough for users to complain publicly → should be tackled on a priority basis**
    E EMPLOYEES AND TEAMS Customer service, sales, marketing (they work closest to users) and QA (they do end-to-end analysis of use cases). Keep a continuous dialogue going with them
    E EXTERNAL sources News, blogs, books, research — not specific to your product; they reveal new technologies (e.g. how AI is being used in your product space)
    M MELT — telemetry data and analytics Behaviour captured while users interact with the product: where are they getting stuck? where can't they complete a flow? — "a goldmine of information"
    U USERS, CUSTOMERS AND CLIENTS The PRIMARY source. Interviews, surveys, other user research methods, and group settings such as focus group discussions
    C COMPETITORS Analyse competing products — features they have that you don't; problems they solve that you don't. The FEATURE COMPARISON TABLE is the tool
    K KINGS People higher up: the company owner, board members, executives, and GOVERNMENT REGULATORS — e.g. if you must implement the Data Privacy Act, you must

    MULTI-SOURCING: never depend on one source. Worked example — NTES (National Train Enquiry System): - From the PM (I): chatbot support, station-name recommendations, platform numbers with incentivised user inputs - From social chatter (S): linking the user profile with the IRCTC account; a drop-down to segregate arrivals and departures in the live-station train list - From users (U): layout enhancement/user-friendliness; smart search in "Spot Your Train"; integrating IRCTC features into NTES - From competitors (C): regional language support, PNR status notifications, a train speedometer, coach position, an alarm before arrival

    Analysing USER REVIEWS

    Now easy with AI-based tools that summarise a review database. ET Money example → the key problem surfaced was lack of proper customer support (solutions: a chatbot, an AI agent, or more support staff). MLympics (e-sports) example → player matching, bonus cash restrictions, limited game types, poor pricing structure, lack of statistics/data on games played.

    The practical tip: filter the App Store to ONE- AND TWO-STAR reviews. "I can bet you will see a lot of problems which are actually very easy to solve — it is just that the PMs did not look there."

    7.15USER RESEARCH METHODS — the 2×2 matrix guaranteed MCQ2

    Axis 1: QUANTITATIVE (data, numbers, statistics) vs QUALITATIVE (text — interviews, discussions). Axis 2: ATTITUDINAL (what users THINK/FEEL/SAY) vs BEHAVIOURAL (what users actually DO).

    Method Quant/Qual Attitudinal/Behavioural Notes
    SURVEYS Quantitative ATTITUDINAL Rate satisfaction 1–7, rate problem intensity. Advantage: hundreds or thousands of users. ## Shortcoming: you capture only what users SAY they might do — they may behave differently in the real world
    INTERVIEWS and FOCUS GROUP DISCUSSIONS Qualitative ATTITUDINAL Focus group = 6 or 7 users from different targets (lower/higher age, urban/rural) mixed together. "In an interview a user may say something but behave differently in the real world"
    ANALYTICS (product analytics) Quantitative BEHAVIOURAL "Now a major source of behavioural analysis." Example: on Amazon, if a user searches for an item that is not available, the PM can be informed
    A/B TESTING Quantitative BEHAVIOURAL Or divert 10% of traffic to version A and 10% to version B and compare the success metric — without even asking users
    MODERATED TESTING (incl. REMOTE moderated) Qualitative Behavioural The user is given a goal ("transfer this much money to another wallet") and the PM observes — remotely via online tools — then asks "why did you click that?"
    UNMODERATED TESTING Behavioural Observe only; do not engage or control
    DESIRABILITY STUDIES Level of desirability of different features
    CARD SORTING How features should be ORGANISED/STRUCTURED — what goes on the homepage, what goes on pages below
    FIELD STUDIES / ETHNOGRAPHIC STUDIES Qualitative Behavioural Observing the user in his or her NATURAL HABITAT — "let me accompany you, let me see how you call for cabs" — taking notes in the field

    Conducting a USER INTERVIEW — the question set

    "What led you to using our product in the first place? · Why would you recommend or not recommend us? · What do you like MOST / LEAST about the product and why? · What do you wish you could do that you can't right now? · Can you SHOW me how you are doing this right now? · What are your thoughts if we change this feature/user flow to this? · Where does this problem fall in your priorities — a big problem or a little problem? · How much would you be willing to pay to solve this?" ← ## WTP = WILLINGNESS TO PAY**

    The four interviewing rules guaranteed MCQ

    1. ASK OPEN-ENDED QUESTIONS · 2. AVOID LEADING QUESTIONS (don't feed them the answers you want to hear) · 3. LISTEN MORE — let the USERS do all the talking · 4. When you find something interesting, DIG DEEP (ask "why" to find the ROOT CAUSE)

    The LIC app interview structure: collect demographics (name, age, gender, location, profession, marital status, family) → devices used → where they access LIC information → frequency of use → primary use → how they check policy information and problems faced → "Name 3 things you LIKE and 5 things you DISLIKE" → missing basic requirements → features that should be included ("a good way of CROWDSOURCING features from users") → which other apps they use → pros and cons vs competitor apps.

    After divergence: collate the 30–50 problems into a STRUCTURED FORMAT — categorise into buckets (user-experience problems, performance issues, security/privacy concerns…).

    7.16TELEMETRY AND ANALYTICS — the MELT framework guaranteed MCQ3

    Letter Data type What it is
    M METRICS Product metrics — users who bought, users who upgraded from basic to premium, DAU/MAU
    E EVENTS A user action you have MARKED as an event — e.g. clicking the purchase button. Lets you count how many people passed each step
    L LOGS The detailed technical record on the back end behind each event (connecting to the database, fetching information). Used to check whether there was a technical issue — e.g. why payments are failing
    T TRACES For a user journey that CUTS ACROSS DIFFERENT COMPONENTS AND EVEN OTHER PRODUCTS — e.g. a payment that redirects to Paytm or Google Pay and comes back. ## A TRACE ID covers the whole transaction as one unit even when it goes externally — used to diagnose EXTERNAL faults (e.g. the bank server was down)

    The power of telemetry: "PMs are able to solve actual user problems WITHOUT EVEN TALKING TO CUSTOMERS" — you can see between which events users drop off.

    FEATURE USAGE analysis

    Track how many users activate each feature daily/monthly. The ideal graph shows all features well-adopted; reality shows a few features used heavily and others not at all.

    RULE: EXCLUDE ADMINISTRATIVE FEATURES (account creation, password reset) from feature usage analysis.

    Worked example — Mingout: 36 Questions, Truth or Dare and Work Dates are the popular experiences; GeoGuesser and Higher or Lower are much less used.

    THE FEATURE AUDIT MATRIX guaranteed MCQ

    Axis 1: HOW MANY people use it (few → some → most → all). Axis 2: HOW FREQUENTLY / how much TIME they engage (very little → some → most → all the time).

    Quadrant Diagnosis Fix
    Most/all people, most/all the time (top-right) SUPERSTAR FEATURES Nothing — performing well
    FEW people, but ALL/MOST of the time (top-left) AN AWARENESS PROBLEM — "those who are aware of it use it and like it; many others don't even know it exists" — or only a particular segment is interested Awareness campaigns, helpful tips, training
    MANY people, but VERY LITTLE time (bottom-right) A USAGE FREQUENCY PROBLEM Use the HOOK FRAMEWORK and notifications to bring users back
    FEW people, VERY LITTLE time (bottom-left) THE BIG PROBLEM — poor adoption AND poor frequency Dig deep into what went wrong — and CONSIDER DROPPING the feature, since resources are limited
    Low usage BY DESIGN NOT A PROBLEM — "results as expected" The example: the SOS BUTTON in the Uber app — you WANT it used by very few people for very little time

    Worked example — NTES: "Spot Your Train" and "Live Station" are used by most people all the time; cancelled / rescheduled / diverted train lists are used by only some people — ## which is NOT a problem, because cancellations and rescheduling are infrequent events; but message alerts being barely used (or turned off) IS a problem — probably too many messages, or alerts that are not valuable.

    THE ETHICAL DILEMMA the instructor raises: "Is it right to keep hooking users on certain features so they keep going back like an addict?" — kids and adults get addicted to doomscrolling reels and short videos. ## "There is an ETHICAL LINE we should not be crossing, and it is the PM's call where the boundary is" — hence features like "you have been doing this for a lot of time, do you want to stop?" and user-set time limits.

    FEATURE FUNNEL ANALYSIS guaranteed MCQ

    A FUNNEL is the step-by-step journey of the user through the product — e.g. log in → browse products → click a product and view details → click "Buy Now" → make payment → done/thank you.

    It is called a FUNNEL because of its SHAPE: the number of people at each successive step is smaller, so it is fat at the top and narrow at the bottom.

    The funnel SHAPE is EXPECTED and normal. THE PROBLEM IS A BIG DROP at any one step. A small drop at checkout is fine (people leave items in the basket to return later); a big drop from checkout to payment means there may be issues with the PAYMENT PAGE.

    COHORT ANALYSIS (also called GROUP ANALYSIS): divide users into GROUPS THAT SHARE A COMMON CHARACTERISTIC ("cohorts") and check whether the drop is concentrated in one group — e.g. payment failing only for Paytm users, or only for one bank.

    Worked example — Mingout: 937 users sign up successfully → a 44% drop to those sending date invites → an even bigger drop at the matching stage → only 5% of total users create a virtual date plan. 55% of users send no invites at all after signing up.**

    7.17Cause analysis and the USER JOURNEY MAP1

    Telemetry tells you WHAT the problem is and WHERE it happens — it does NOT tell you WHY. For the ROOT CAUSE you must dig deeper with interviews and the "5 WHYs" analysis.

    The worked 5-Whys chain (fact from analytics: users are not using our new Reports feature):

    Step Answer
    Why? They don't see any value
    Why? They can't share it with their teams or boss
    Why? They can't get it in a nice shareable format like PDF or Excel
    Why? Our export tools are not good enough
    Why? Our BACK-END APIs don't even generate that kind of output — they don't support PDF and Excel formats ← THE ROOT CAUSE

    The insight: the root cause was NOT that the Reports feature is un-valuable — it was the back-end APIs. Each "why" can branch into 3–4 answers, so a full exercise yields 10–20 root causes — "a goldmine of data for product managers."

    THE USER JOURNEY MAP — "one of the MOST USED artefacts in the discovery process" guaranteed MCQ

    Its components in order:

    # Component Detail
    1 PERSONA Who the user is
    2 SCENARIO What the persona is trying to do — goals and expectations (e.g. book a cab from A to B and pay at the end)
    3 PHASES of the journey e.g. for Uber: logging in → finding a cab → tracking the cab → the ride → the payment
    4–6 ACTIONS, THOUGHTS and EMOTIONS in each phase EMOTIONS GO UP AND DOWN across phases — happy logging in, frustrated when the cab cancels, happy during the ride, unhappy when the preferred payment method isn't accepted
    7 OPPORTUNITIES (zone C — the INSIGHTS) WHEREVER EMOTIONS GO DOWN AND FRUSTRATION APPEARS, THERE LIES THE OPPORTUNITY TO IMPROVE THE PRODUCT — this is the point of the whole map

    How it is built: by talking to a number of users and mapping their end-to-end journey.

    Worked examples: - Splitwise — users are unhappy at stages 1, 3 and especially 4: "I want to pay my friends via Google Pay or Paytm, but Splitwise only allows the Splitwise wallet" → opportunity: integrate/allow other wallets - Playo — stages: searching for the venue → selecting venue, sport and timing → booking confirmation → payment → going to the venue / post-booking experience. Pain points: cannot filter by sport; cannot sort by price (so you can't find the cheapest court) → opportunity: improved sorting and filtering

    The map need NOT follow a fixed standard template — the Playo example is informal (stage · activity · pain point · opportunity).

    7.18DEFINE — converging on the problems to solve

    Step Tool Detail
    1. Organise AFFINITY MAP Group the scattered problems into CATEGORIES/buckets. Splitwise example buckets: personal financial assistance · customisation/personalisation of the interface · expense tracking and budget management · seamless integration across applications
    2. Vote DOT VOTING Each team member gets dots ("just like bindis") and places them on the opportunities they think most important for users and business. ## More dots = higher priority. Common in start-ups, small companies and idea workshops in big companies
    3. Score on user impact THE USER IMPACT GRAPH — INTENSITY × FREQUENCY FREQUENCY = how often users encounter the problem. INTENSITY = how much it affects them / how much they care. "It can be a frequent problem people don't care much about, or a very intense problem they hardly ever encounter." Score = frequency × intensity
    4. Score on business impact The user-impact vs business-impact 2×2 The top-right quadrant (important to BOTH user and business) holds the top opportunities. Something "very important to the user but LEAST important to the business" may be deprioritised; something important to neither is not even looked at
    5. Screen on feasibility THE FDV CRITERIA F = FEASIBILITY (technically implementable) · D = DESIRABILITY (to the customer) · V = VIABILITY (to the business) — "very popular in industry". A problem may be desirable and viable but NOT TECHNICALLY FEASIBLE — throw it out

    Splitwise user-impact worked example:

    Problem Frequency Intensity
    Cannot sort or filter expenses HIGH HIGH
    Limited options of payment apps HIGH (faced every single time you pay) Moderately high — "not a make-or-break, you can still make payments"
    Cannot add splits with friends who are not on Splitwise MEDIUM LOWER — "they can just get their friends to install Splitwise"
    Cannot settle balances selectively MEDIUM MEDIUM

    Opportunity-tracking tools hold, per opportunity: a description, a category, the CONNECTED GOALS AND OKRs ("never forget that these problems must be connected to product/business goals and OKRs"), scores for prioritisation, user VOTING and COMMENTS, and status tracking (under consideration → solutioning → prototyped and tested → shipped).

    7.19DEVELOP — generating solutions2

    The "HOW MIGHT WE" (HMW) format guaranteed MCQ

    State each selected problem as a short question: ## "HOW MIGHT WE create multiple patient profiles?" · "HOW MIGHT WE keep the layout simple?"

    Why each word matters: - ## "HOW" — we do NOT know how to do this; we have no solution yet - ## "MIGHT" — we are UNCLEAR; we are clear on the problem, NOT the solution. It stops the PM falling into the trap of assuming there is only one possible solution and never looking for better alternatives - ## "WE" — this is NOT the PM's job alone; it is done as a TEAM

    The team: a design team / discovery team / design sprint team of typically 5 to 7 members — the PM plus a developer, someone from QA/testing, someone from marketing, someone from business — bringing different perspectives and expertise.

    The four IDEATION techniques guaranteed MCQ| Technique | How it works | The key point |

    |---|---|---| | BRAINSTORMING | State the problem clearly, state the constraints (technical feasibility, budget), then every team member generates ideas; favourite ideas are selected after discussion | The most common method. ## Its ONE MAJOR ISSUE: you cannot BUILD UPON anybody else's ideas | | BRAINWRITING | Round 1 — everyone writes their own ideas on chits/sticky notes (same as brainstorming). ## Round 2 — the chits are EXCHANGED and each person BUILDS UPON someone else's idea. Round 3 — build on round 1 and 2 ideas | Yields ideas that are richer and more holistic. ## Worked example: Yang — "why not add an ANDROID version?" → Grace — "why not INCENTIVISE downloading it?" → Billy — "why not create an entire REWARDS PROGRAM around it?" | | MIND MAPPING | A hierarchy of concepts — centre → categories → subcategories → ideas | Used to ORGANISE 10–13 ideas into a structured category/subcategory format | | CRAZY 8s | SKETCH 8 IDEAS IN 8 MINUTES on an 8-panel chart, each panel a different idea | Called crazy because of the time pressure. With 5 team members that is 8 × 5 = 40 IDEAS for one problem. "Even if 30–35 are useless, you may get 4–5 good ideas — the BEST ideas can come out of this." Engages the VISUAL mind — common among UX teams, who are more visual thinkers |

    7.20DELIVER — feature prioritisation the densest MCQ area of the module6

    Prioritisation is "a mix of a science and an art." You do NOT need to apply multiple methods — MASTER ANY ONE.

    QUALITATIVE techniques QUANTITATIVE techniques
    MoSCoW · FEATURE BUCKETS · STORY MAPPING KANO MODEL · VALUE–EFFORT · ICE · RICE · WSJF · BUY A FEATURE ("PIE feature")

    MoSCoW ← "the EASIEST way to prioritise features"

    Letter Bucket Meaning Example
    M MUST HAVE Absolutely vital requirements A login page for authentication
    S SHOULD HAVE High-priority; not a must, but users EXPECT it A way to sort products by price
    C COULD HAVE OPTIONAL Filtering products by a specific colour
    W WON'T HAVE Will NOT be implemented

    Worked example — NTES (built from a survey of 135 respondents rating feature importance — "you can have a quantitative dimension while deciding the qualitative buckets"): - Must have: coach position · GPS location tracking · IRCTC account linkage · layout enhancement - Should have: languages · chatbots · alarms - Could have: smart train search · train notifications · PNR notifications - Won't have: speedometer · IRCTC app features

    FEATURE BUCKETS — four different buckets easily confused with MoSCoW; likely MCQ| Bucket | Definition | Grocery-app example |

    |---|---|---| | METRIC MOVERS | Features that increase the CORE METRICS of the product — activation rate, retention rate, revenue | The list of stores (more stores = better) · notifications (bring users back to buy → moves revenue) | | CUSTOMER REQUESTS | Features users EXPECT to see, whether or not they move your metrics | User profile · order history · more payment gateway options · order status tracking | | DELIGHTS | Exciting and attractive features with a WOW factor that increase engagement | Voice-based chatbots · good ratings and reviews | | STRATEGIC | Neither short-term metric movers nor delighters — features that expand the horizons of the business in the LONG TERM (a 2–3 year timeframe) | LIBRA — the crypto coin for Facebook |

    STORY MAPPING

    Divide the user journey into phases (e.g. find shoes → buy shoes → manage orders → receive orders), place each ideated feature under the phase it targets, and prioritise within each phase.

    CRITICAL: keep FEATURE DEPENDENCIES in mind. If a priority-one feature in "manage orders" REQUIRES a low-priority feature in "find shoes", that dependency must ALSO be raised to priority one — they go together.

    THE KANO MODEL guaranteed MCQ| Category | Definition | Satisfaction behaviour |

    |---|---|---| | MUST-HAVES / BASIC features | Without them, customers won't even consider your product as a solution | Providing them fully gives NEUTRAL emotion — users are NOT satisfied, they merely EXPECT it. NOT having them makes DISSATISFACTION RISE EXPONENTIALLY | | PERFORMANCE features | The more you invest, the higher the satisfaction — a LINEAR relationship | Examples: number of payment wallet options · security · page loading time / app speed | | EXCITEMENT features / DELIGHTERS | Pleasantly surprise customers because they don't expect them — used to DIFFERENTIATE from competitors | Absence causes NO dissatisfaction (they weren't expected); presence makes satisfaction rise EXPONENTIALLY | | INDIFFERENT | Users don't care whether it is there or not | | | REVERSE | If you HAVE it, people HATE it; if you DON'T have it, they LIKE it | THE CLASSIC EXAMPLE: ADS (e.g. on YouTube). They exist for business goals and profitability, not user impact |

    Splitwise Kano example: payment reminders, expense tracking, quick UPI payments = BASIC expectations; friends' profile settings, selective balance settlement, bad debts = DELIGHTERS.

    THE KANO QUESTIONNAIRE — the pair of questions to memorise: 1. The FUNCTIONAL question: "How do you feel IF YOU HAVE this feature?" 2. The DYSFUNCTIONAL question: "How do you feel IF YOU DON'T HAVE this feature?" Each answered on the same five options: ## "I like it · I expect it · I don't care · I can live with it · I dislike it."

    Reading the response matrix:

    Functional answer Dysfunctional answer ⟹ Category
    "I like it" "I don't care" ATTRACTIVE / DELIGHTER
    "I like it" "I dislike it" PERFORMANCE feature
    "I expect it" "I dislike it" BASIC feature
    "I don't care" "I don't care" INDIFFERENT
    "I dislike it" "I like it" REVERSE

    THE VALUE–EFFORT MODEL

    SCORE = VALUE ÷ EFFORT (rate each on a scale of, say, 1 to 5)

    High value + low effort = the highest score; low value + high effort = the lowest.

    Input What it covers
    VALUE Impact on the user · impact on the business · benefits to potential customers · developing relationships · revenue
    EFFORT Not just development/programming effort but also OPERATIONAL costs, the NUMBER OF RESOURCES, TIME taken, RISK and COMPLEXITY

    Worked example — LIC: the "compare products" feature scored impact 4, effort 2 → value/effort = 2; 14 features were scored, with red = worst and green = the top ideas.

    I.C.E. guaranteed formula MCQ

    ICE SCORE = IMPACT × CONFIDENCE × EASE

    Letter Meaning
    I — IMPACT How does this contribute to the goal / OKR / metric? (scale 1–10)
    C — CONFIDENCE How CONFIDENT are you that this will work and deliver the assigned impact? ("Are you 80% confident? Then mark confidence 8") — "could you have calculated it wrong, over- or under-estimated?"
    E — EASE How easy is it to implement — the REVERSE of effort (so it is MULTIPLIED, not divided)

    Hotstar example: a curated watchlist feature scored impact 8/10, ease 9/10.

    R.I.C.E. ← "very, very popular in industry"; guaranteed formula MCQ

    RICE SCORE = (REACH × IMPACT × CONFIDENCE) ÷ EFFORT

    Note the differences from ICE: EFFORT DIVIDES (you cannot multiply by "ease"), and REACH is added.

    Letter Meaning The STANDARD VALUES
    R — REACH HOW MANY PEOPLE WILL THIS FEATURE AFFECT IN A GIVEN PERIOD — e.g. how many customers per quarter will use it. A very important feature that affects few users may rank below a lesser feature that affects many. Estimate from similar features in your product or competitors', or industry reports A number/estimate
    I — IMPACT Contribution to the goal MASSIVE = 3 · HIGH = 2 · MEDIUM = 1 · LOW = 0.5 · MINIMAL = 0.25
    C — CONFIDENCE Confidence in your impact score HIGH = 100% · MEDIUM = 80% · LOW = 50%
    E — EFFORT Cost to deliver Divides the numerator

    W.S.J.F. — Weighted Shortest Job First guaranteed formula MCQ

    WSJF = (BUSINESS VALUE + TIME CRITICALITY + RISK REDUCTION) ÷ ESTIMATED SIZE (effort)

    Used in bigger companies such as MICROSOFT. Its distinguishing element is ## TIME CRITICALITY — urgency, fixed deadlines and DEPENDENCIES. In a big company a mega-feature releasing in 3 months may depend on 3–4 other features — those must therefore be released first. RISK REDUCTION asks: is there a NEGATIVE IMPACT TO DELAYING this task? The higher that negative impact, the less you want to delay it.

    BUY A FEATURE likely MCQ

    A "fun" prioritisation game: give 5–6 users a fixed amount of MONEY and a menu of features; they BID for, or BUY, the features they want.

    Why it works: "when there is MONEY involved, users subconsciously make BETTER decisions — they are putting money to the value."

    Variants: a bidding game, or a fixed price per feature based on the effort it takes to develop it ("this is a $5 feature — do you want to buy it?"). Especially useful for features that will be sold as ADD-ON BUNDLES or subscription charges.

    CUSTOM SCORECARD

    Define your own criteria and weights — e.g. PR/marketing effort required, customer retention impact, effort required, operational efficiency improvement — standardised across the organisation. Tools: ## Aha!

    7.21Demonstrating and validating solutions3

    The three FIDELITY levels of prototype guaranteed MCQ

    HAND SKETCHES → (tool-based) WIREFRAMES / medium fidelity → HIGH-FIDELITY INTERACTIVE MOCK-UPS

    High-fidelity mock-ups look like the real product but are just interactive mock-ups users can use. Tool: ## FIGMA (with AI features that generate basic interactive mock-ups from a feature idea) — "easy to use and freely available."

    Validating prototypes with real users

    Interview users, have them use the prototype, and ask whether it solved the problem the feature was designed to solve, and how well. Collect positive and negative comments ("Gene said something positive; Rachel has two negative comments"), reiterate, re-prototype, then finalise.

    The NTES validation: a survey shown with the prototype, asking users to rate features (coach position, GPS, IRCTC linkage) on ease of navigation, user comfort and aesthetics, plus the NPS.

    THE SYSTEM USABILITY SCALE (SUS) guaranteed number MCQ

    SUS = SYSTEM USABILITY SCORE — a STANDARD scale used by PMs and UX teams. TEN survey items — some POSITIVELY worded, some REVERSE-CODED (negative). THE INDUSTRY AVERAGE IS 68 OUT OF 100. Above 68 (e.g. 75+) means you are doing a good job on usability.

    Other usability testing tools (e.g. Maze) provide ## HEAT MAPS based on EYE TRACKING — "where are the users looking? are they even looking at your feature?" — plus feature usage, usability scores, design metrics and reports.

    THE FEEDBACK GRID — four quadrants likely MCQ

    1. WHAT WORKED · 2. WHAT REQUIRES CHANGING · 3. OPEN QUESTIONS (that you could not answer when users asked) · 4. IDEAS (that users gave)

    The closing rule of the module: "Hardly any of the discovery process is based on your intuitive sense. It's all about research and DATA-DRIVEN DECISION-MAKING." PRIMARY research = interviews, surveys. SECONDARY research = Play Store data, industry reports, comparing apps.

    MODULE 4 — PRODUCT METRICS

    The categories of metrics: revenue and monetisation · customers and users · financial management · product experience. Metric FRAMEWORKS (combinations of metrics): ## the HEART framework and the PIRATE metrics. Prioritising metrics (what the whole business rallies around): ## the NORTH STAR METRIC and GROWTH LEVERS. Ways of analysing metrics: ## DASHBOARDS and PRODUCT ANALYTICS.

    7.22Revenue metrics1

    Metric Formula Notes
    RRR — REVENUE RUN RATE Annual RRR = Revenue in the short period × Number of such periods in a year (e.g. monthly revenue × 12) Forecasts ANNUAL revenue from a SHORTER period (a month or a quarter)
    MRR — MONTHLY RECURRING REVENUE Beginning MRR = Σ (subscription plan price × number of subscribers on that plan) last month, summed over all tiers (bronze/silver/gold) "Recurring" = PREDICTABLE revenue, typical of SaaS/cloud products with monthly subscription charges
    MRR — the movement formula MRR = Beginning MRR + NEW MRR − CHURNED MRR + UPGRADES − DOWNGRADES Churn = subscribers who left; upgrade = silver→gold; downgrade = silver→bronze guaranteed formula MCQ
    ARR — ANNUAL RECURRING REVENUE Same as MRR but computed on an ANNUAL/yearly scale

    7.23Monetisation metrics

    Metric Full form Formula
    ARPU (in SaaS also ## ARPA) Average Revenue Per User (per Account) Total revenue in a period ÷ Number of users in that same period
    CLV / CLTV / LTV Customer Lifetime Value Definition: the PRESENT VALUE OF THE FUTURE CASH FLOWS attributed to the customer during his or her ENTIRE RELATIONSHIP with the company
    CLTV — computed CLTV = ARPU per month × Average customer lifetime in months
    CLTV — via churn CLTV = ARPU per month ÷ MONTHLY CHURN RATE ← the trick for getting average lifetime
    CLTV profit CLTV profit = CLTV × MARGIN (e.g. a 20% margin)

    7.24Customer metrics

    Metric Formula / definition
    Number of visitors How many potential customers explored the website/app
    CONVERSION RATE The percentage of potential customers that turn into real customers. ## Visitor-to-signup = signups ÷ visitors; ## FREE-TO-PAID = paid signups ÷ total free signups (the free vs paid ChatGPT Plus example). 20 visitors, 1 sale → 5%**
    CUSTOMER GROWTH (monthly) (Customers this month ÷ Customers last month) × 100
    CAC — CUSTOMER ACQUISITION COST Total SALES AND MARKETING cost ÷ Number of NEW customers added — "the average business expense of acquiring a new customer"
    UNIT ECONOMICS — the LTV : CAC comparison A SUCCESSFUL model has LTV > CAC. An UNSUCCESSFUL model has LTV < CAC — you spend more to acquire the customer than you earn from them. ## "This is where many product start-ups FAIL." It is acceptable early on while spreading awareness, but should be corrected within 2–3 years
    DAU / MAU Daily / Monthly Active Users — ENGAGEMENT metrics. "Unique users who are ACTIVE — have logged in or performed some action"
    STICKINESS RATIO DAU ÷ MAU. If it equals 1, every monthly user logs in every single day. In the real world it is less than 1 — the CLOSER TO 1, the STICKIER your users (e.g. a news app checked daily)
    CHURN RATE (monthly) Customers lost in the month ÷ Total customers at the BEGINNING of the month. "Ideally you would want to reduce the churn rate to zero"

    7.25Financial management metrics

    Metric Formula Meaning
    BURN RATE (monthly) (Starting cash − Ending cash) ÷ Number of months How QUICKLY a business is spending its cash reserves
    CASH RUNWAY Current cash ÷ Monthly burn rate How many MONTHS the business can sustain itself on existing cash reserves
    OPERATIONAL EFFICIENCY Operating expense ÷ Total revenue Reveals whether the cost of running the business is lower than the revenue. ## If operating expense > revenue it is a LOSS-MAKING product — so operational efficiency should be AS LOW AS POSSIBLE

    7.26Product experience metrics3

    Type Examples
    INTERNAL (trackable inside your product) Product sign-ins · usage · user actions and engagement · session tracking · FUNNELS and conversions · FEATURE USAGE and frequency (the feature audit matrix) · usability and TASK COMPLETION · QUALITY metrics (bugs, crashes, page loading speed)
    EXTERNAL (must look outside your product) User satisfaction surveys · APP STORE RATINGS · NPS (recommendations/referrals) · usability metrics

    THE NET PROMOTER SCORE (NPS) guaranteed MCQ

    The question: "HOW LIKELY ARE YOU TO RECOMMEND OUR PRODUCT TO A FRIEND OR COLLEAGUE?" An 11-POINT SCALE, 0 to 10 (0 = not likely at all, 10 = extremely likely)

    Score range Group
    0 – 6 DETRACTORS
    7 – 8 PASSIVES
    9 – 10 PROMOTERS

    NPS = % PROMOTERS − % DETRACTORS. THE PASSIVES ARE IGNORED. Worked example: 37% promoters, 48% passives, 13% detractors → NPS = 37 − 13 = 24%**

    BENCHMARKS: above 30% is considered GOOD. TOP WORLD-CLASS PRODUCTS are typically ABOVE 70%.

    THE AAARRR "PIRATE METRICS" guaranteed MCQ

    Called pirate metrics "because of the sound that triple-A triple-R makes" (AAARRR!). It is shaped as a FUNNEL — the number of users shrinks at each successive stage.

    Letter Stage The question How it is measured
    A AWARENESS How many people did you REACH? An advertising/brand-building metric used by marketing teams: people who saw your ad, received your emails
    A ACQUISITION How many customers have you ACQUIRED? Downloads · installs · website visits — they clicked through, not merely saw the ad
    A ACTIVATION How many users did you get to actually TRY the product? Registrations · 1-DAY RETENTION · users who spent 30+ minutes exploring
    R RETENTION How many buyers COME BACK? N-DAY RETENTION (15-day, 30-day) · MAU · SESSION FREQUENCY
    R REFERRAL How many customers become ADVOCATES? Referrals · app store ratings and reviews · social media shares · page likes
    R REVENUE How much revenue do you generate from them? ARPU and CLV as the top revenue metrics; also app purchases, subscription value, in-app transactions, ad revenue

    GOOGLE'S HEART FRAMEWORK guaranteed MCQ

    Originated at GOOGLE, now adopted widely. Five aspects:

    Letter Dimension What it measures Example metrics
    H HAPPINESS User experience — how satisfied/happy they are App store rating · NPS · ease of use (via customer survey ratings)
    E ENGAGEMENT The FREQUENCY or INTENSITY of interaction over a time frame — the level of user involvement Time spent (via back-end analytics) · number of uploads · videos watched · shares
    A ADOPTION How many NEW users are adopting the product Signups · new usages per day · new subscribers · upgrades to the latest version · purchases by new users
    R RETENTION How many users stick around vs churn Active users · N-day retention · repeat purchases · subscription renewal rate · churn rate
    T TASK SUCCESS The EFFICIENCY, EFFECTIVENESS, QUALITY and ERROR RATES when users try to accomplish a task Task success rate (e.g. how many payments failed due to a bug or UI confusion) · search result success · time to upload · time to complete a profile

    7.27The NORTH STAR METRIC (NSM) guaranteed MCQ3

    The NORTH STAR METRIC is THE ONE CUSTOMER GROWTH METRIC that EVERY TEAM in the company can look at to guide their goals and priorities.

    Teams keep their own metrics (developers track code quality and delivery time; marketing has its own), but all of them must ultimately be LINKED to the North Star.

    The three benefits likely MCQ 1. ## A COMMON GOAL for all teams 2. ## CLARITY — everyone can see AT A GLANCE how well the company is doing 3. ## CUSTOMER FOCUS — an NSM is USUALLY NOT profit, revenue or number of sales; it is about ADDING VALUE FOR THE CUSTOMER, which signals to every employee that customer value matters

    The canonical NSM examples certain match-the-company MCQ| Company | North Star Metric | |---|---| | Facebook | Monthly Active Users | | Spotify | Time spent listening | | Amazon | Number of purchases per month | | Airbnb | Number of booked nights | | WhatsApp | Number of messages sent | | Uber | Number of rides per week |

    The GALAXY of metrics around the North Star

    North Star (the single focus) → L1 metrics that CONTRIBUTE to it → L2 metrics that contribute to each L1.
