    Worked example — NSM = Weekly Active Subscribers (WAS): - L1 = reach / activation / engagement / retention — e.g. number of subscribers (owned by marketing) - L2 under it = retained subscribers, reactivated subscribers, new subscribers - L1 activation (owned by the growth team) → L2 = subscription within 7 days, time to subscription - L1 engagement (owned by the product/content team) → minutes of content viewed → L2 = video starts and completions

    7.28GROWTH EQUATIONS AND GROWTH LEVERS guaranteed MCQ1

    A GROWTH EQUATION combines several related metrics MULTIPLICATIVELY; each component is a GROWTH LEVER — improve ANY ONE of them and overall growth improves.

    Amazon's revenue growth equation:

    Number of CATEGORIES/VERTICALS × Number of PRODUCTS per vertical × TRAFFIC PER PRODUCT PAGE × PURCHASE CONVERSION × AVERAGE PURCHASE PRICE × REPEAT PURCHASE BEHAVIOUR

    Which is exactly why e-commerce companies keep adding verticals (vertical expansion is a growth lever), advertise to raise page traffic, and offer discounts, credits and cashbacks to lift the visitor-to-buyer conversion.

    Airbnb's booking growth equation:

    Number of HOSTS × Number of ROOMS LISTED per host × Number of USERS × Number of BOOKINGS per user × REPEAT BOOKINGS

    7.29Dashboards1

    All PMs monitor dashboards refreshed in real time or daily, showing every metric in one snapshot — e.g. customer lifetime of 79 months with a customer lifetime value of $2,600.

    Product analytics — the FOUR analyses PMs run regularly likely MCQ| Analysis | The question it answers |

    |---|---| | COHORT ANALYSIS | Groups sharing common characteristics (young vs older users, male vs female, highest-repeat-purchase customers). ## "Who are my MOST VALUABLE customers, and what ACTIONS do they take?" | | CHURN / RETENTION ANALYSIS | Who is churning out, and what actions did they take before leaving? (performance issues, incomplete tasks, payment failures) | | FUNNEL / CONVERSION ANALYSIS | At which stage of the user flow are users dropping off? A drop-off is expected — "but it should not be TOO HIGH between any two stages" | | A/B TESTING / EXPERIMENTS | Which features should be introduced (A or B, C or D)? Product analytics tools also allow PERSONALISED OFFERS to a cohort (e.g. a 10% loyalty discount to your most valuable customers) |

    Dashboard reading example: LTV : CAC of 2.9 — healthy, since a successful model needs the ratio above 1; 99% account retention; plus internal dashboards for DAU vs MAU, new vs repeat active users, number of CRASHES, network response time, transactions, network errors, logouts and app slowness over the last 24 hours / week / month.**

    MODULE 5 — PRODUCT DESIGN (UX)

    7.30UX vs UI — and the opening trap

    The two-picture question: "Which design is better?" Most say the elegant one. ## The answer given: BOTH designs are BAD — because in the elegant one there is CONFUSION about which is the UP button and which is the DOWN button.

    STEVE JOBS: "DESIGN IS NOT JUST WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE AND FEELS LIKE — IT IS ALSO HOW IT WORKS."

    UI — User Interface UX — User Experience
    What the product LOOKS like — the interface the user sees How it LOOKS and HOW IT FUNCTIONS
    A SURFACE-LEVEL thing only The whole experience

    The ketchup bottle example: the traditional bottle may have better UI, but you must thump it and it splashes everywhere; the inverted, squeeze bottle has far better UX.

    DEFINITION: UX design is the process of designing products that are USEFUL, ATTRACTIVE, EASY TO USE, and overall DELIGHTFUL to interact with.

    The module covers three things: ## 1. UX ARTEFACTS AND DELIVERABLES · 2. UX DESIGN PRINCIPLES (incl. psychological biases) · 3. THE UX DESIGN PROCESS (the design sprint).

    7.31The key elements and the FIVE LAYERS of UX guaranteed MCQ2

    Element Meaning Artefacts
    USABILITY How easy it is to use User flow diagrams, usability reports
    INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE Whether the hierarchy of pages makes sense Sitemaps
    INTERACTION DESIGN How you interact/engage with the product Interactive wireframes and prototypes
    WIREFRAMES The basic skeleton form Hand-sketched and tool-sketched wireframes
    VISUAL DESIGN How the finished product looks High-fidelity UI mock-ups and STYLE GUIDES

    The five layers — bottom (most abstract) to top (most concrete) certain ordering MCQ| Layer | What it is | Deliverables |

    |---|---|---| | 1. STRATEGY (bottom-most, most abstract, the CORE) | "Where it all begins — what do users want? Why does this product exist?" — the product strategy module | User personas · customer journey maps · lean canvas | | 2. SCOPE | Transforming strategy into REQUIREMENTS — what features must be included (the product improvement module) | List of features · user story maps | | 3. STRUCTURE | = INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE. Gives shape to the scope — how the different pages and pieces fit together | UFDs (User Flow Diagrams) · SITEMAPS | | 4. SKELETON | Makes the structure CONCRETE — how the components look and enable use | WIREFRAMES | | 5. SURFACE (uppermost — what the user interacts with) | Brings everything together VISUALLY | MOCK-UPS · high-fidelity INTERACTIVE PROTOTYPES |

    Structure-layer deliverables

    Deliverable Definition Tools
    USER FLOW DIAGRAM (UFD) A FLOWCHART outlining the STEPS users must take in the product to meet their goals — e.g. log in (→ forgot-password branch) → locate address by GPS or manually → list of nearby stores (or "no store in your area") → choose store → search/browse items → select items and quantity → add to cart → view/edit cart → select payment method → redirect to bank/wallet → confirmation → track delivery → delivered Microsoft Visio · Lucidchart
    SITEMAP How PAGES are organised HIERARCHICALLY — Home → (UX courses, Community, Literature, About) → Course page → Lesson items; Community → discussions, local groups, external events

    7.32Prototyping — the two axes guaranteed MCQ2

    Axis Meaning
    LOW vs HIGH INTERACTIVITY How much users can actually interact — click, swipe, navigate. Hand sketches, static wireframes and static mock-ups are LOW interactivity; interactive wireframes/mock-ups are HIGH
    LOW vs HIGH FIDELITY How CLOSELY it represents the REAL product. Hand sketches = low fidelity; mock-ups = high fidelity

    THE QUOTE TO REMEMBER: "IF A PICTURE IS WORTH A THOUSAND WORDS, A PROTOTYPE IS WORTH A THOUSAND MEETINGS." This is why prototype is one of the two pillars of design thinking, and why in modern product development you build a wireframe/prototype and TEST IT WITH USERS BEFORE any real coding.**

    Prototype type Detail Tools
    HAND-SKETCHED WIREFRAMES UX designers start with rough sketches on charts with sketch pens of each screen. Cardboard MOBILE CUTOUT SLIDERS are used to make the sketches feel like a real phone Paper
    TOOL-SKETCHED / INTERACTIVE WIREFRAMES A SCHEMATIC or BLUEPRINT to help the PM, developers and designers think and communicate about the STRUCTURE. Built with drag-and-drop components (icons, text boxes, rectangles) and reusable templates in minutes to hours; pages can be LINKED via button actions to make them interactive Balsamiq · Mockplus · Wireframe.cc
    WIRE FLOW DIAGRAMS COMBINING user flow diagrams WITH wireframes — lines connect a button to the next screen, giving an accurate visual representation of the interaction
    HIGH-FIDELITY UI MOCK-UPS Visual design, colour, images, text, size — how charts, calendars, time displays will look. ## "This is usually NOT the job of a product manager, but of the UX team" Sketch · Photoshop
    INTERACTIVE PROTOTYPES Mock-ups plus interactions — "very similar to real products, except you cannot enter data because it is not connected to any database or server. It is ultimately a FAKE PRODUCT." Built by importing mock-ups and adding HOTSPOTS linked to other pages; can be downloaded onto actual devices for testing Figma · InVision · ProtoPie

    Consistency artefacts

    Artefact What it does
    STYLE GUIDE Documents how the product's LOOK AND FEEL, COLOURS and TYPOGRAPHY are STANDARDISED across all features and pages
    PATTERN LIBRARY A set of REUSABLE UI COMPONENTS — charts (bar, line), calendars, icons — not just images but drag-and-drop components, saving time and ensuring all UX teams build with the same components

    THE FIVE DIMENSIONS OF INTERACTION DESIGN guaranteed MCQ| Dimension | What it covers |

    |---|---| | 1D — WORDS | All the text in the design | | 2D — VISUAL | All the images | | 3D — PHYSICAL OBJECT / SPACE | WHICH DEVICE the design is for — a mobile (swipe, touch), a laptop (mouse, keyboard shortcuts), or a television app (a remote). The interaction changes with the device | | 4D — TIME | ANIMATIONS AND VIDEOS — the non-static elements, e.g. the spinner showing "saving" or "loading" | | 5D — BEHAVIOUR | What HAPPENS when the user clicks, swipes, pinches, zooms in/out |

    7.33The USABILITY REPORT2

    Evaluation type Measures
    QUALITATIVE Give the user a goal/task ("find and purchase a pair of orange running shoes" — requiring colour filters, type filters and sorting by price), then observe their behaviour, note insights, and ask "why did you do that? why did you make this mistake? why are you giving up?"
    QUANTITATIVE EFFECTIVENESS = % of users completing the task · TIME TAKEN to complete · NON-CRITICAL ERRORS (errors the participant RECOVERS from and still completes the task) · CRITICAL ERRORS (errors the participant CANNOT recover from — they ABANDON the task) · user satisfaction, ease of use and ease of finding information on a LIKERT SCALE

    The most common UX deliverables (from a survey of UX teams and PMs) likely list MCQ

    STATIC WIREFRAMES (the most common) · flowcharts/activity diagrams · sitemaps · usability reports · style guides and pattern libraries · user journey maps · competitive analysis reports · visual mock-ups

    Division of labour likely MCQ| Exclusively the UX TEAM's domain | What the PM does | |---|---| | Visual design · UI sketches · usability testing reports | WIREFRAMING (and increasingly prototyping) · user personas · user stories · competitor analysis · user research and feedback, plus the normal PM functions: feature prioritisation, business modelling, stakeholder input, scope planning, product-market fit, roadmapping, KPI monitoring |

    The instructor's career advice: "Creating interactive wireframes — and nowadays prototypes too, since Figma AI lets you write a prompt and generate high-fidelity wireframes and prototypes — is becoming a more and more important function for PMs. Learn Balsamiq and Figma."

    7.34The basic aspects of good UX design likely list MCQ1

    Aspect Detail
    USER FOCUS User empathy, design thinking, usability research, more user control
    VISUAL Aesthetics, symmetry, colours, contrasts
    CONSISTENCY INTERNALLY within the product AND EXTERNALLY with similar/competing products — "users become ACCUSTOMED to a certain kind of UX; they expect the checkout cart to look a particular way"
    HIERARCHY Different font sizes, bold/colour, borders to distinguish heading vs subheading vs content
    TEXT Typography, simple language, NO typos or grammatical errors — "if you see a typo on the front page you don't have a good opinion of the quality of the app"
    USER COMFORT Minimal user effort; intuitive; no frustrations; help when required; usable by OLDER audiences too, not just the young
    ACCESSIBILITY Inclusive design for people with low vision — high contrast, increased font size

    Two dimensions of UX design principles: ## (1) PSYCHOLOGICAL BIASES — studied under ## HCI (HUMAN–COMPUTER INTERACTION), a subset of engineering, computer science, psychology, sociology, ethnography and design — and ## (2) DESIGN HEURISTICS (best practices / rules of thumb).

    7.35The psychological design principles extremely high-yield; each is a likely MCQ1

    The GESTALT principles

    Principle Statement Application
    LAW OF SIMILARITY Elements that are VISUALLY SIMILAR are perceived as RELATED and likely to share a common meaning or functionality All "Edit" buttons pink, all "Remove" buttons white → users instantly infer shared functionality. Headings must look visually different from subheadings and body text
    LAW OF COMMON REGION Elements are perceived as a GROUP if they share an area with a CLEARLY DEFINED BOUNDARY — or a COMMON BACKGROUND behind them (it need NOT be a border) News/content CARDS with clear boundaries — without it users get confused about where one card ends and the next begins
    LAW OF PROXIMITY The brain GROUPS objects that are NEAR each other — proximity helps users organise information faster A form where the "Name" label sits close to the name field and the "Email" label close to the email field, with distance separating the two groups

    The other four principles

    Principle The experiment/illustration The rule
    AESTHETIC–USABILITY EFFECT Two computers: people assume the better-looking one performs better, even if the plainer one is more powerful "USERS OFTEN PERCEIVE AESTHETICALLY PLEASING DESIGN AS THE DESIGN THAT'S MORE USABLE. People are MORE TOLERANT OF MINOR USABILITY ISSUES when the design is aesthetically pleasing."
    PEAK–END RULE The cold-water experiment: Round 1 = 60 seconds at 14°C. Round 2 = the same 60 seconds at 14°C FOLLOWED BY 30 MORE SECONDS AT 15°C (one degree warmer). Round 3 = choose which to repeat. ## Logically you'd repeat Round 1 (shorter pain) — but MORE PEOPLE CHOSE TO REPEAT ROUND 2 "People judge their experience largely based on HOW THEY FELT AT ITS PEAK AND AT ITS END, rather than the total sum or average of every moment." → ## Pay close attention to the MOST INTENSE POINTS and the FINAL MOMENTS of the user journey. Application: DUOLINGO's course-completion screen — "You have conquered the Spanish skill tree, you are awesome" + an award — making the END feel great so users start another course
    GOAL-GRADIENT EFFECT The coffee loyalty card: Card A requires 9 purchases but ARRIVES WITH 2 STAMPS ALREADY MARKED (so 10 boxes with 2 pre-filled); Card B requires the same 9 purchases with none pre-filled. MORE PEOPLE COMPLETE CARD A "The tendency to approach a goal INCREASES WITH PROGRESS — REAL progress OR EVEN THE ILLUSION OF PROGRESS." Applications: PROGRESS BARS, and ARTIFICIAL progress — surveys showing "page 2 complete, halfway through page 3"; checkout flows showing progress beyond what you have actually filled
    HICK'S LAW The JAM-TASTING STUDY: one stall with 24 varieties, another with 6. 60% of shoppers stopped at the 24-jam stall vs 40% at the 6-jam stall, and on average only 2 flavours were sampled at each. BUT only 3% of shoppers BOUGHT at the 24-jam stall vs 30% at the 6-jam stall — A TEN-FOLD DIFFERENCE "THE TIME IT TAKES TO MAKE A DECISION INCREASES WITH THE NUMBER AND COMPLEXITY OF CHOICES." → Minimise choices when response time is critical; BREAK COMPLEX TASKS INTO SMALLER STEPS to reduce COGNITIVE LOAD. Applications: offer 3 pricing plans (bronze/silver/gold) not 100; replace a 20–30 option drop-down with a 4-option multiple choice
    VON RESTORFF EFFECT (the "isolation effect") The single RED tomato among dozens of green ones captures your attention first "When MULTIPLE SIMILAR OBJECTS are present, the one that DIFFERS from the rest is most likely to be NOTICED AND REMEMBERED." → Make important information or KEY ACTIONS VISUALLY DISTINCTIVE. Application: HIGHLIGHTING one pricing plan (e.g. the Gold plan bounded by a border — law of common region — and coloured orange against the others' blue) to NUDGE customers towards it

    7.36JAKOB NIELSEN'S USABILITY HEURISTICS guaranteed MCQ (the instructor calls them "Jacob's usability heuristics")1

    # Heuristic What it means Examples given
    1 VISIBILITY OF SYSTEM STATUS Always keep users informed about what is going on through APPROPRIATE, TIMELY FEEDBACK Loading indicators, progress bars, status messages ("loading…", "your file is being uploaded"). Otherwise the user wonders whether to click again
    2 MATCH BETWEEN THE SYSTEM AND THE REAL WORLD Speak the USER'S LANGUAGE — words, phrases and concepts familiar to them, NOT internal jargon A TRASH CAN icon for delete · the word "CART" · a digital calendar that mimics a paper calendar
    3 USER CONTROL AND FREEDOM Users perform actions by mistake, so they need a clearly marked "EMERGENCY EXIT" UNDO options · a CANCEL button in any multi-step process · an accessible BACK button
    4 CONSISTENCY AND STANDARDS Users should not have to wonder whether different words/situations/actions mean the same thing. FOLLOW PLATFORM CONVENTIONS Consistent navigation menus and button styles across screens; adhering to ANDROID or iOS design standards
    5 ERROR PREVENTION "Good error messages are important, but the BEST DESIGNS CAREFULLY PREVENT PROBLEMS FROM OCCURRING IN THE FIRST PLACE" CONFIRMATION DIALOGUES for critical actions ("are you sure you want to delete your entire account?") · DISABLING the submit button until all mandatory fields are filled
    6 RECOGNITION RATHER THAN RECALL Minimise memory load by making elements, actions and options VISIBLE "People are more likely to correctly answer 'IS LISBON THE CAPITAL OF PORTUGAL?' than 'WHAT IS THE CAPITAL OF PORTUGAL?'" → auto-suggestions in search · drop-down menus · tooltips · previous searches · frequently used options · "repeat your last purchase"
    7 FLEXIBILITY AND EFFICIENCY OF USE Shortcuts HIDDEN from novice users can SPEED UP interaction for EXPERT users Keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+B instead of clicking the B in the toolbar) · personalised shortcuts · customisable toolbars · swipe-to-archive in email apps
    8 AESTHETIC AND MINIMALIST DESIGN "EVERY EXTRA UNIT OF INFORMATION IN AN INTERFACE COMPETES WITH THE RELEVANT UNITS OF INFORMATION" Clean, uncluttered interfaces; effective use of WHITE SPACE. A long form should show 3–4 questions per page with a "Next" button, not 20 questions crammed onto one page
    9 HELP USERS RECOGNISE, DIAGNOSE AND RECOVER FROM ERRORS Error messages in PLAIN LANGUAGE — NOT error codes (101, 104) — precisely stating the problem and constructively recommending a solution "Incorrect password. Please try again" · highlighting the erroneous form field, e.g. "missing an @ symbol in the email address"

    The good-vs-bad design examples given: a Save button that gives no indication vs one that shows "saving… saved" (heuristic 1) · "Initiate autonomous control sequence" vs "Launch vehicle" (heuristic 2) · a technical database-connectivity error message vs one stating the exact problem and fix (heuristic 9) · a screen where text and buttons all merge together vs one with a clear hierarchy and Cancel/Create buttons in separate colours.

    7.37THE DESIGN SPRINT guaranteed MCQ4

    A DESIGN SPRINT is a DESIGN THINKING METHOD used to solve user problems through CO-CREATION, RAPID PROTOTYPING and QUALITATIVE TESTING with TARGETED USERS within a VERY SHORT, CONTINUOUS TIMEFRAME — typically 2 to 5 DAYS.

    The GOOGLE VENTURES 5-day format certain sequence MCQ

    DAY 1 UNDERSTAND · DAY 2 DIVERGE · DAY 3 DECIDE · DAY 4 PROTOTYPE · DAY 5 VALIDATE (mapping directly onto design thinking's empathise → define → ideate → prototype → test)

    DAY 0 — planning

    Item Detail
    Assemble the team AT LEAST 6 TO 8 PEOPLE from different functions: a PM · UX · development · QA · marketing/sales (a customer-facing team) · business/executive (someone who can make business decisions) — so that design, technical FEASIBILITY, user DESIRABILITY and business VALUE are all covered
    The leader The PM usually LEADS the design sprint and is called the SPRINT MASTER (not mandatory, but typical, because the PM owns the ultimate value delivered)
    The sprint briefing State the ## SPRINT CHALLENGE (the problem area) and the expected deliverables
    Share the research artefacts UPFRONT User personas · journey maps · survey and interview reports. ## The user research is NOT part of the sprint — it must already be done
    Logistics Sticky notes, sticky dots, pens, sketch pens, boards

    DAY 1 — UNDERSTAND (identify problems and opportunities)

    Clarify the sprint goals (first 10–15 min) → LIGHTNING TALKS, discussion and clarification of questions → EMPATHISE with users using the user persona, user journey map and EMPATHY MAP → define the BUSINESS SUCCESS METRICS → post the HMW ("How Might We") cards → AFFINITY MAPPING → DOT VOTING → a PRIORITISED list of problems to solve.

    THE EMPATHY MAP — its four quadrants: WHAT DOES THE USER SAY? · THINK? · DO? · FEEL? guaranteed MCQ

    DAY 2 — DIVERGE (explore multiple solutions)

    BRAINSTORM and note ideas for the prioritised HMW problems → CRAZY 8s sketching → share ideas across the team → DOT VOTING on the ideas.

    DAY 3 — DECIDE (finalise a solution)

    An "ART MUSEUM" display of the top ideas on whiteboards → PRIORITISE using value-vs-effort or other criteria → refine the winning idea → create a HEAT MAP — team members place red dots on the parts of the storyboard/screens they see problems with, so that portions of the solution are critiqued and improved until the end-to-end solution is acceptable to the whole team.

    Dot-voting rule to remember: ## each team member gets a LIMITED number of dots — typically 4 to 5.

    DAY 4 — PROTOTYPE

    Create the UX deliverables: user flow diagrams · mock-ups · a CLICKABLE, HIGH-FIDELITY prototype · and prepare for the usability study. "Most of this work is done by the UX team member."

    DAY 5 — VALIDATE

    Conduct the usability study with just FIVE USERS — "it has been shown that 85% OF PROBLEMS CAN BE FOUND BY TALKING TO JUST 5 USERS." guaranteed MCQ Observe and take notes on each solution (positive/negative, excited/unimpressed, suggested improvements) → UPDATE the final designs → STAKEHOLDER REVIEW (product heads/business stakeholders SIGN OFF) → CLOSE the sprint → the finalised designs go to the developers for coding.

    MODULE 6 — PRODUCT START-UPS AND MVPs

    7.38Start-up development models2

    Model Structure
    THE LEAN START-UP MODEL BUILD an MVP → MEASURE with real customers → LEARN → PIVOT or PERSEVERE
    THE CUSTOMER DEVELOPMENT MODEL (Steve Blank) TWO PHASES: the SEARCH phase and the EXECUTION phase

    The customer development model in detail guaranteed MCQ| Phase | Stage | What you are doing |

    |---|---|---| | SEARCH (searching for a REPEATABLE AND SCALABLE business model) | 1. CUSTOMER DISCOVERY | PROBLEM-SOLUTION FIT — are we tackling the right problem with the right solution? Propose an MVP; propose funnels based on market awareness | | SEARCH | 2. CUSTOMER VALIDATION | PRODUCT-MARKET FIT — is there enough demand? will people pay when alternatives exist? what is the business model? what is the sales and marketing roadmap and the channels? | | — | (iterate) | Discovery and validation repeat iteratively until you reach product-market fit | | EXECUTION | 3. CUSTOMER CREATION | SCALE UP — more customers, new markets, geographies | | EXECUTION | 4. COMPANY BUILDING | "You can start in a garage with two or three friends, but BUILDING A COMPANY is a very different thing" — scaling the organisation and operations. Many start-ups FAIL exactly here |

    The CUSTOMER DEVELOPMENT FUNNEL likely MCQ

    GET customers → KEEP customers → GROW customers

    Stage Sub-stages and tactics
    GET ACQUIRE (paid media, organic/word-of-mouth, emails) then ACTIVATE (they actually purchase or take a plan). ## A VIRAL LOOP runs from ACTIVATION back to ACQUISITION — activated customers bring in friends via rewards programmes
    KEEP Loyalty programmes · contests and events · updating the product on feedback AND telling customers you did · outreach programmes · blogs
    GROW UPSELL · NEXT-SELL · CROSS-SELL · REFERRALS. Upsell = get them to upgrade to a higher plan. Cross-sell = the Amazon example — buying baby oil or shampoo and being recommended diapers

    7.39The four phases of this module

    1. FINDING a start-up opportunity · 2. The GO / NO-GO decision · 3. Conducting MVP EXPERIMENTS · 4. LAUNCHING the real MVP

    7.40Phase 1 — Finding a start-up opportunity3

    THE FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLE: OPPORTUNITIES ALWAYS ARISE FROM PROBLEMS.

    The seven kinds of problem likely MCQ| Problem type | Opportunity | Example |

    |---|---|---| | COST | Provide a lower-cost solution | | | TIME / EFFORT | Reduce time or effort | Paytm — eliminated carrying cash, the time to pay, and finding change | | QUALITY | A higher-quality product with better features | Apple / Google phones | | EXPERIENCE | Improve the user experience | | | CAUSE | Sustainability, donating to children's healthcare — "it is not easy to find apps that do that" | | | HEDONIC (fun/entertainment) | | Netflix, sports apps, gaming apps | | USER/CONSUMER PSYCHOLOGY | | See below |

    The psychology chain to memorise:

    A SITUATION OR CONTEXT TRIGGERS the problem → the problem MANIFESTS THROUGH SYMPTOMS, OFTEN MISTAKEN FOR THE ROOT CAUSE → it causes an IMMEDIATE EMOTIONAL REACTION (frustration, irritation, concern) which reveals the INTENSITY → it must have a MEASURABLE IMPACT (metrics) → the customer LOOKS FOR EXISTING SOLUTIONS or IMPROVISES A WORKAROUND → THE SHORTCOMINGS OF THOSE ALTERNATIVES ARE WHERE YOUR START-UP PITCHES IN.

    "The DEEPER the problem intensity, the BETTER it is for the start-up."

    The four stages of finding problems

    1. SOURCING the problems · 2. RESEARCHING the problems · 3. DEFINING the opportunities · 4. EVALUATING the opportunities

    Sourcing — ORGANIC vs INORGANIC vs TRANS-ORGANIC guaranteed MCQ| Type | Definition | Examples |

    |---|---|---| | ORGANIC | The problem is OBSERVED — by the founder/PM personally, reported by people around them, or seen as having no solution or only unsatisfactory solutions | RATAN TATA seeing a family of 4–5 packed onto one scooter → the ₹1 lakh car, TATA NANO. ## UBER — call taxis existed, but were an UNSATISFACTORY solution | | INORGANIC | You ACTIVELY FISH/SEARCH for the problem | Fishing with CUSTOMER JOURNEY MAPS of an existing product (where is the customer unhappy?) · ## the SCAMPER framework | | TRANS-ORGANIC | Neither searched NOR observed — the problem is INTUITED. It requires a VISION OF THE FUTURE — not a current or emerging problem but one 2–3 years away | Emerging technologies — AI, AGENTIC AI, blockchain. Enables ## BLUE OCEAN INNOVATION — a product category that did not exist at all, e.g. e-books |

    THE SCAMPER FRAMEWORK guaranteed MCQ with the examples| Letter | Strategy | The question | Example |

    |---|---|---|---| | S | SUBSTITUTE | What elements of this product/service can we substitute? | NETFLIX — substituted the DVD and DVD player with an online streaming app. ## UBER — substituted phoning a call-taxi number with an app (which also tracks the driver and takes payment) | | C | COMBINE | Can we combine two or more product ideas/services? | INSTAGRAM = SOCIAL PLATFORMS + CAMERA/PHOTO-EDITING APPS (filters, enhancement) | | A | ADAPT | What idea from elsewhere can we alter or adapt? | RAPIDO — did what Uber did with cars, but with AUTOS AND TWO-WHEELERS. ## SWIGGY GENIE — did what Dunzo was doing | | M | MAGNIFY / MODIFY | How can we greatly ENLARGE or greatly REDUCE any element? | LICIOUS — while other grocery apps sell everything, Licious magnified ONE element: only MEAT AND ANIMAL PRODUCTS, at the highest quality | | P | PUT TO OTHER USE | What completely different use is there for an existing product? | CAMSCANNER — camera apps put to use for SCANNING DOCUMENTS (tilting, lighting, text extraction). ## FACEBOOK SHOPPING — a social platform put to use as a SOCIAL MARKETPLACE | | E | ELIMINATE | What elements can be eliminated? | CHROME OS — eliminated the need for a separate OPERATING SYSTEM ("maybe the browser is good enough"). ## BITCOIN — eliminated the FINANCIAL INTERMEDIARY / central bank that prints currency, replacing it with a peer-to-peer mining network | | R | REARRANGE | How can we rearrange the existing process? | GOOGLE PAY / PAYTM — rearranged the money-transfer process (NEFT, RTGS, IMPS) into UPI. ## AIRTEL PREPAID — rearranged POSTPAID billing into PREPAID, solving the problem of unexpectedly high bills |

    7.41Researching the problems — the THREE RISKS a problem interview addresses guaranteed MCQ1

    Risk The interview goal
    PRODUCT RISK "WHAT is the problem?" — how do customers rank their top three problems? Are we solving the right one?
    MARKET RISK "WHO is the competition?" — what existing alternatives do customers use? How do customers solve this problem TODAY?
    CUSTOMER RISK "WHO exactly has this pain point?" — identifying the right customer segment; is it viable; will they pay to have the pain solved?

    Interview asks: rank the top three problems · rate urgency/pain on a 1–5 or 1–7 scale (a 2 or 3 out of 7 is not worth pursuing; a 5 out of 5 is) · "what is your current solution/workaround, and why are you satisfied or dissatisfied with it?"

    7.42Defining problems — THE PROBLEM STATEMENT CANVAS likely MCQ on its boxes1

    Its elements: ## WHO (customer) · CONTEXT · THE PROBLEM · EMOTIONAL IMPACT · QUANTIFIABLE/MEASURABLE IMPACT · EXISTING ALTERNATIVES · SHORTCOMINGS OF THOSE ALTERNATIVES.

    The worked example:

    Box Content
    Who Young men aged 25–35, middle-to-low income, living in suburban São Paulo, working in a corporate office
    Context Every workday, morning and evening, an average of 2–3 hours a day lost in traffic instead of doing something valuable
    Emotional impact Frustrated and bored
    Quantifiable impact They lose an average of 40 hours per month
    Existing alternative They sign up as UBER DRIVERS and accept rides to and from work, earning money on the commute
    Shortcoming of the alternative Driving for Uber requires more waiting time, because the trip origin and destination may NOT COINCIDE with their home–work itinerary
    ⟹ The start-up idea it suggests A HOME-TO-OFFICE ride app that matches riders along the driver's fixed route, rather than a general ride app like Uber

    7.43Evaluating problems the densest MCQ area of this module4

    VITAMIN vs PAINKILLER

    A PAINKILLER solves an URGENT pain; a VITAMIN is nice but not urgent. THE START-UP RULE: THE MORE IT IS A PAINKILLER, THE BETTER.

    THE 4 U FRAMEWORK guaranteed MCQ| U | The question |

    |---|---| | UNWORKABLE | Is the problem UNWORKABLE — i.e. there is NO good workaround? | | UNAVOIDABLE | Is it UNAVOIDABLE — the user cannot simply sidestep it? | | URGENT | Is it URGENT — important to solve right now from the user's perspective? | | UNDERSERVED | Is it UNDERSERVED — other players in the market are not solving it? |

    If the answer to all four Us is YES, it is a great problem to solve.

    THE BLAC FRAMEWORK guaranteed MCQ| Letter | Meaning |

    |---|---| | B — BLATANT | Very obvious and open to all — anyone can see it is a problem | | L — LATENT | Could be a big problem, but hard to see; users are NOT AWARE of it — e.g. certain security issues | | A — ASPIRATIONAL | Not critical — e.g. ## NETFLIX solves an ASPIRATIONAL problem (entertainment) — and is still a good product idea | | C — CRITICAL | Users will do anything and PAY ANYTHING → user adoption is much easier |

    THE BEST PROBLEMS ARE BLATANT AND CRITICAL — "you don't need to sell it to them, they already know about it."

    The worked evaluation — METTL's online exam platform during COVID:

    Test Verdict
    Unworkable? ✅ YES — no workaround; classes were online, pen-and-paper was impossible
    Unavoidable? ✅ YES — you cannot avoid taking exams, for 1–2 years
    Urgent? ✅ YES — every institute needed it immediately
    Underserved? ✅ YES — few online examination platforms existed then
    Blatant? ✅ YES — obvious to institutes, faculty and students
    Critical or aspirational? ✅ CRITICAL
    ⟹ "Mettl checked all these boxes, which is why it became a very successful product — and continued after COVID."

    MICHAEL SEIBEL'S THREE CRITERIA guaranteed attribution MCQ

    MICHAEL SEIBEL, CEO of Y COMBINATOR (one of the biggest incubators in the world), evaluates start-up problems on THREE things: 1. FREQUENCY — how OFTEN does the customer experience this problem? (a frequent problem means a definite need for a solution and possibly repeated payment = continuous revenue) 2. INTENSITY — how PAINFUL is the problem? (low intensity → they won't pay) 3. WILLINGNESS TO PAY — how much will the customer pay to make the problem go away?

    The sweet spot = frequent + high intensity + willing to pay.

    The OPPORTUNITY SCORE (where solutions already exist)

    OPPORTUNITY SCORE = IMPORTANCE × DISSATISFACTION, where dissatisfaction = 1 − satisfaction with the existing solution. Higher importance and higher dissatisfaction with the existing alternatives → higher opportunity score.

    7.44Phase 2 — The GO / NO-GO decision1

    MARTY CAGAN'S 10 QUESTIONS (from the book "INSPIRED") guaranteed attribution MCQ| # | Question | What it establishes |

    |---|---|---| | 1 | What exactly will this problem solve? | The VALUE PROPOSITION | | 2 | For whom do we solve this problem? | The TARGET MARKET | | 3 | How big is the opportunity? | MARKET SIZE | | 4 | What alternatives are out there? | The COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE | | 5 | Why are we best suited to pursue this? | Our DIFFERENTIATOR / assets | | 6 | Why now? | The MARKET WINDOW — right time? too early? too late? do we have FIRST-MOVER ADVANTAGE? | | 7 | How will we get this product to market? | The GO-TO-MARKET strategy — channels, distribution, marketing, advertising | | 8 | How will we measure success / make money? | METRICS and REVENUE STRATEGY | | 9 | What factors are critical to success? | The required FEATURES in the solution | | 10 | Given all the above, what's the recommendation? | GO or NO-GO |

    Note the link: these are essentially the PRODUCT STRATEGY questions. "For the GO opportunities, treat this assessment as the OPPORTUNITY HYPOTHESIS for setting your product strategy — then test it in the market."

    THE R-W-W FRAMEWORK ← guaranteed MCQ ("proposed in a Harvard Business Review article")

    Letter Question The two sub-questions
    R — IS IT REAL? Is the MARKET real (is there actual demand)? Is the PRODUCT real (does it solve the right pain point — does the solution FIT the problem)?
    W — CAN WE WIN? Can the PRODUCT win in this market given the competition? Can our COMPANY win (do we have the resources)?
    W — IS IT WORTH DOING? Will the product be PROFITABLE in the short and long run? Does it FIT OUR PORTFOLIO STRATEGY and business goals?

    7.45Phase 3 — Conducting MVP experiments2

    The two categories of experiment guaranteed MCQ| Category | Tests | Formats | Do you need a product? |

    |---|---|---|---| | MARKET TESTS | Mostly ## PRODUCT-MARKET FIT | Landing page · explainer video · ad campaigns · crowdfunding | NO — not even a wireframe or mock-up is required | | PRODUCT TESTS | The product itself — are the features accepted? | Wireframes · mock-ups · interactive prototypes · WIZARD OF OZ · CONCIERGE · a beta version of the live product | YES — some form of product is needed for users to give feedback on |

    The six benefits of MVP experiments likely list MCQ

    1. CUT COSTS (no need to build the whole product) · 2. SAVE PRODUCTION TIME AND RESOURCES · 3. BUILD AN INITIAL CLIENT BASE (the people who showed interest become your first customers at launch) · 4. GET EARLY MARKET FEEDBACK · 5. COLLECT INSIGHTS ON THE FOCUS FEATURES and how to improve them · 6. ATTRACT EARLY INVESTMENT (a successful test supports a seed/Series-A raise)

    How to set up an MVP experiment — the four steps

    Step Detail
    1. LIST YOUR ASSUMPTIONS Written as: ## "For my start-up idea to be successful, the following MUST BE TRUE" — e.g. my customers have these problems · customers will pay at least this much · there are no satisfactory substitutes in the market
    2. Identify the HIGH-RISK assumptions "Do you need to test ALL the assumptions with MVPs? NO — only the HIGH-RISK assumptions WITHOUT WHICH THE PRODUCT WILL FAIL."
    3. Hypothesise on the RISKIEST assumptions and choose the right MVP format
    4. Set the ## MCS — MINIMUM CRITERIA FOR SUCCESS The specific METRIC that tests the hypothesis, fixed IN ADVANCE — e.g. "I will test demand using signups/ad clicks, and my MCS is AT LEAST 1,000 SIGNUPS IN 1 MONTH"

    The MVP EXPERIMENT CANVAS contains: the MCS · the experiment format · the RISKIEST ASSUMPTIONS · how you will reach the customers · the customer segments targeted, and so on.

    THE TYPES OF MVP ← the highest-yield table in this module

    MVP type How it works The famous example
    LANDING PAGE MVP No product at all — just a landing page stating the VALUE PROPOSITION and the PRICING TIERS. Clicking a plan leads to "you've caught us before we're ready — sign up and we'll let you know" → an email waiting list BUFFER — "Tweet more consistently with Buffer", with a $0 free tier, a $5 plan and a $20 plan. It revealed (a) that demand existed, (b) WHICH PLAN people preferred, and (c) an initial client list — all with just TWO WEB PAGES
    EXPLAINER VIDEO MVP A simple, story-like video explaining how the idea would work, with a registration field for the waiting list DROPBOX — received 10,000 REGISTRATIONS IN JUST ONE DAY, telling the founders the idea had huge potential
    A/B TESTING MVP Create different versions and compare which scores higher on the success metric The Highrise headline test: "Start a Highrise account" (with a small subheading "pay as you go, 30-day free trial") vs a version whose HEADLINE was "30-day free trial on all accounts", plus options C and D
    CROWDFUNDING MVP Upload the idea with a detailed description, images and an explainer video; backers get discounts at launch. ## You validate demand AND RAISE MONEY — "your initial customers are also becoming your investors", without banks or angel investors PEBBLE — the e-paper watch for iPhone and Android: a goal of ~$100,000, but it raised ALMOST $10 MILLION FROM 68,000 BACKERS
    CONCIERGE MVP The founder performs the service MANUALLY for the customer — AND THE CUSTOMER KNOWS IT IS MANUAL FOOD ON THE TABLE — the founder physically accompanied homemakers to the grocery store, made their weekly meal plan and gave them the grocery list by hand, for 10–20 customers
    WIZARD OF OZ MVP The founder performs the service manually TOO — BUT THE CUSTOMER DOES NOT KNOW. Named after the novel's "scientist pulling the levers behind the curtain" ZAPPOS — the shoe e-commerce site had NO WAREHOUSE. For every order the founder went to a NEARBY SHOE STORE, bought the shoe and couriered it out

    THE CONCIERGE vs WIZARD OF OZ DISTINCTION — a near-certain MCQ: in CONCIERGE the customer KNOWS the service is being provided manually by a person; in WIZARD OF OZ that is HIDDEN BEHIND THE CURTAIN.

    The learning step: after the experiment, record the result · whether the MCS was met · learnings and insights · and the DECISION: PERSEVERE or PIVOT.

    The Dropbox worked write-up: persona ## "Tom the Techie" — an early adopter working on projects requiring the swapping of many files with a fluid network of collaborators; problem — hard to share files, especially big or frequently changing ones, and the alternatives are poor; value proposition — ## "a file-sharing service that truly feels TRANSPARENT to the user across all major platforms"; key assumptions — people like Tom exist, and they will adopt a genuinely easy way to share files; experiment — handcraft a demo (the explainer video); validation criteria — substantial traffic on the video and sign-ups; result — ## strong preliminary validation → PERSEVERE.

    7.46Phase 4 — Launching the real MVP5

    THE ACRONYM, EXPANDED: M = MINIMUM — the minimum number of features: the key features plus maybe some delightful, differentiating ones V = VIABLE — sufficient to ATTRACT THE EARLY ADOPTERS. The rule of thumb: "20% OF FEATURES ARE USED BY 80% OF ADOPTERS" — build at least those 20%, so the END-TO-END USER JOURNEY is taken care of P = PRODUCT — something TANGIBLE customers can touch, feel and use — an actual app or website

    DEFINITION: an MVP is the MOST BASIC VERSION of a product with JUST ENOUGH FEATURES TO SATISFY EARLY CUSTOMERS AND PROVIDE FEEDBACK FOR FUTURE PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT.

    Position on the spectrum: prototypes and POCs (proofs of concept) come first; ## the MVP sits JUST BEFORE the actual product and can be developed further into the full-scale product. An MVP takes a FEW WEEKS TO A COUPLE OF MONTHS; the full product then takes months or years via agile.

    MVP vs MMP vs MLP guaranteed MCQ| Acronym | Full form | Definition |

    |---|---|---| | MVP | Minimum VIABLE Product | Just enough to satisfy early customers and generate feedback | | MMP | Minimum MARKETABLE Product | The minimum features to actually SELL it in the market — may not be focused on UX/UI, but needs decent features and aesthetics to be sold | | MLP | Minimum LOVABLE Product | SLOWER to develop than an MVP or MMP. The minimum features not just to sell it but to GAIN A USER FOLLOWING — good early WORD OF MOUTH and feedback. The focus is on a LOVABLE, ATTRACTIVE UX |

    The ranking given: MMP is better than MVP, and MLP is better than both.

    THE DEVELOPMENT ORIENTATION — the classic diagram guaranteed MCQ

    WRONG: build one tyre → a second wheel → the chassis and body → the steering wheel → only at stage 4 does the user get a working car. RIGHT: SKATEBOARD → SCOOTER → BICYCLE → MOTORCYCLE → CAR — AT EVERY SINGLE STAGE THE USER CAN ALREADY TRAVEL FROM POINT A TO POINT B. "MVP 1 is just the skateboard — the user may not be that happy with it, but it still solves the problem better than walking. That is a valid MVP solution."

    What a GOOD MVP must still contain likely MCQ

    An MVP is NOT "just some features and that's it." The right way focuses on the key functionality AND still ensures the early product is RELIABLE, has decent DESIGN and some USABILITY — otherwise early adopters get turned off and complain about design, usability and reliability.

    The four advantages of an MVP

    1. Proves or DISPROVES the viability of an idea with MINIMUM RISK · 2. MINIMUM COST — "an MVP can cost TENFOLD LESS than creating a full app" · 3. MUCH SHORTER TIME — weeks instead of months · 4. Demonstrates viability TO INVESTORS much sooner (Caveat noted: with no-code/low-code and AI you can now build higher-quality MVPs, but it should still cost far less than a full app built by a hired development team.)

    Real MVP examples likely MCQ| Product | Its first MVP |

    |---|---| | UBER | "An ON-DEMAND CAR SERVICE VIA iPHONE AND SMS" | | AIRBNB | Called "AIR BED AND BREAKFAST" — targeted at CONFERENCE PARTICIPANTS who needed only "a bed to lie on and some breakfast", using INFLATABLE AIR BEDS in someone's spare room, far cheaper than hotels. Once validated it scaled beyond conferences to vacation and business travellers — and from air beds to actual beds |

    MVP planning — the three steps likely MCQ| Step | Name | What you do | Source |

    |---|---|---|---| | 1 | PRODUCT IDENTIFICATION | Explicitly state the GOAL of the product/MVP | from PRODUCT STRATEGY | | 2 | | Specify the MAIN USER FLOW and its stages | from the USER PERSONA and CUSTOMER JOURNEY MAP | | 3 | PRIORITY IDENTIFICATION | List the features stage-wise, CATEGORISE and PRIORITISE them, and finalise the MVP feature set | |

    The Zappos worked example: goal — enable online purchase of shoes; stages — find shoes → buy → manage orders → receive order; then per stage, categorise features into must-haves, nice-to-haves/performance features and delighters, and cut the line such that:

    THE MVP MUST CONTAIN ALL THE MUST-HAVE FEATURES (none may be missing), PLUS SOME KEY PERFORMANCE/NICE-TO-HAVE FEATURES to compete, PLUS SOME DELIGHTERS to set you apart — while keeping the END-TO-END USER FLOW INTACT. Competitors will all have the must-haves — so the differentiators are the performance features and the delighters.** MVP v2 then adds features from the lower-priority list, and so on to the full product.

    MODULE 7 — PRODUCT REQUIREMENTS, ROADMAPS AND DEVELOPMENT

    7.47The requirement hierarchy guaranteed MCQ5

    Level Requirement items Time horizon
    STRATEGIC INITIATIVES · THEMES More than one product release — 3 to 15 months / many months
    TACTICAL EPICS · FEATURES · USER STORIES Within a sprint or a couple of sprints, but WITHIN ONE RELEASE
    OPERATIONAL TASKS Within a single sprint — sometimes a few days or a few HOURS

    Caveat stated: "the definitions and hierarchies of these items MAY CHANGE in different frameworks, tools and companies."

    The standard hierarchy used in tools like JIRA (Atlassian) and Aha!

    INITIATIVE → EPIC → USER STORY → TASK

    Item Definition Example
    INITIATIVE Broad areas of INVESTMENT supporting the overall business and product goals, planned ACROSS MULTIPLE RELEASES; aligned to the strategic planning periods when BUDGETS are allocated (each initiative gets its own budget and release plan) Facebook's DIEM (formerly LIBRA) crypto initiative · Microsoft Office's COPILOT initiative
    EPIC (sometimes called a FEATURE SET) A composite chunk of product made of MULTIPLE FEATURES, planned ACROSS MULTIPLE SPRINTS (a sprint = 2–4 weeks). Focuses on ONE MAJOR AREA OF FUNCTIONALITY; takes a few weeks to a few months "As a RIDER, I want to SHARE A CAB WITH OTHERS, so that I can REDUCE MY TRAVEL EXPENSE" (ride-sharing on Uber)
    USER STORY (often equated with a FEATURE) A DISCRETE FUNCTIONAL UNIT providing benefit to the user that CAN BE DEVELOPED WITHIN A SINGLE SPRINT. If a feature cannot fit one sprint, break it into multiple stories "As the blogger BOBBY, I want to SHARE MY BLOG LINK ON WHATSAPP, so that MY FRIENDS CAN READ MY BLOG"
    TASK Detailed WORK ITEMS ASSIGNED TO INDIVIDUAL TEAM MEMBERS to complete a story — coding tasks to developers, design tasks to UX, testing to QA. Tracked on a DAILY/HOURLY basis. Also used for bug fixes and change requests "Design the WhatsApp share button" — assigned to the UI designer

    The user-story / epic TEMPLATE guaranteed MCQ

    "AS A [type of user], I WANT TO [perform some task], SO THAT I CAN [achieve some goal / get some benefit]." The three parts: ## the TARGET USER · the USER NEED/TASK · the USER BENEFIT/VALUE.

    THE "INVEST" PROPERTIES OF A USER STORY guaranteed MCQ| Letter | Property | Meaning |

    |---|---|---| | I | INDEPENDENT | Independent of future user stories — a discrete functional unit of its own; not spread across sprints | | N | NEGOTIABLE | HOW to implement it is NOT fixed — that is left to the DEVELOPERS. The story states only WHAT is required from the USER'S perspective | | V | VALUABLE | Valuable to users/customers | | E | ESTIMABLE | The development team must be able to precisely ESTIMATE how long it will take | | S | SMALL | Small enough to be completed WITHIN A SINGLE SPRINT | | T | TESTABLE | Testable for completion and sign-off — there must be clear sign-off criteria |

    ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA guaranteed MCQ

    A user story REQUIRES ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA describing the conditions to be fulfilled to mark it COMPLETE. EPICS DO NOT HAVE THEM.

    The WhatsApp-share worked acceptance criteria: 1. The user should SEE a WhatsApp sharing button in the list of sharing options on published blogs 2. Clicking it should take the user to WhatsApp contacts and groups for selection 3. The selected contacts/groups receive a link with the text "Sharing my latest blog with you"

    Hierarchy rule: one epic contains multiple related user stories; ## when ALL the user stories under an epic are complete, the EPIC is marked done.

    THEMES easily confused with initiatives; likely MCQ

    THEMES are HIGH-LEVEL, STRATEGIC requirement items that SPAN EPICS OR USER STORIES SHARING A COMMON CHARACTERISTIC OF INTEREST ACROSS RELEASES — e.g. "improving customer experience" or "enhancing product security". They can be SPECIFIC TO A SINGLE PROJECT or CROSS-PROJECT, and are used to ## TRACK A HIGH-LEVEL OKR OVER MULTIPLE EPICS AND STORIES ACROSS MULTIPLE RELEASES.

    Usage How it works
    Type 1 The theme is almost equivalent to an INITIATIVE — broken into epics, then stories
    Type 2 (the better way) Themes X, Y, Z are TAGGED (colour-coded) ONTO initiatives, epics and stories that cut across them, so leaders can track progress on, say, product security across all sprints and releases

    7.48The PRODUCT ROADMAP3

    DEFINITION: a HIGH-LEVEL VISUAL SUMMARY that maps out the VISION AND DIRECTION of your product offering OVER A PERIOD OF TIME.

    The four goals of a roadmap likely MCQ 1. Describe the VISION AND STRATEGY of the product clearly (what it looks like over the next 1–3 years) 2. Provide a GUIDING DOCUMENT for EXECUTING the strategy across teams — everyone sees what others are doing and what the dependencies are 3. Align INTERNAL stakeholders and facilitate options discussion and SCENARIO PLANNING 4. Communicate with EXTERNAL stakeholders, including customers

    The seven key elements of a roadmap likely MCQ

    1. PRODUCT REQUIREMENT ITEMS (at whichever level) · 2. TIME FRAMES (quarter/month/week) OR KANBAN BUCKETS (now / short-term / long-term categories) · 3. ACTORS (individuals or teams the roadmap is for) · 4. MILESTONES (releases, MVP versions, sprint identifiers) · 5. DEPENDENCIES across sprints and releases · 6. TRACKING METRICS

    Roadmaps VARY by: AUDIENCE (internal — developers, executives, sales/marketing; or external — users/customers) · REQUIREMENT LEVEL (initiatives/themes vs epics/features — strategic vs tactical) · FORMAT · SCOPE AND PURPOSE (product planning, portfolio planning, release planning, sprint planning, goal tracking, launch planning) · PLATFORM (online tools vs a physical whiteboard with sticky notes).

    The roadmap FORMATS guaranteed MCQ| Format | Description |

    |---|---| | GANTT CHART (timeline-based) | Quarters Q1–Q4 explicitly shown, with work items, MILESTONES and DEPENDENCIES shown as arrows | | KANBAN BOARD (no dates, category/bucket-based) | Columns such as ## BACKLOG · IN DESIGN · IN PROGRESS · COMPLETED. "Much simpler and often used by START-UPS" | | NOW / NEXT / LATER | A Kanban variant: what the team is working on RIGHT NOW · what comes NEXT · what is taken up LATER. "Very simple and easy to understand" | | LEAN format | Teams (product design, engineering, mobile, operations) on one axis and NEAR-TERM / MID-TERM / LONG-TERM on the other — creates alignment and shows dependencies | | USER STORY MAP format | Typically used when creating MVPs — the end-to-end user journey across the top, features per stage per release. ## The rule it enforces: in release 1 you CANNOT pick features only from the first half of the journey — the END-TO-END JOURNEY MUST BE COMPLETE in every release | | HYBRID format | A timeline across the top PLUS Kanban categories within it, PLUS progress indicators PLUS links to product/strategic goals — used by tools like Aha! |

    Real and specialised roadmaps

    Roadmap Audience / purpose
    Buffer A public Trello roadmap where users can VOTE on and COMMENT on features, with colour tagging by THEME
    Slack A Kanban product-category roadmap: near-term / mid-term / long-term, ongoing improvements, and already-released features
    PORTFOLIO roadmap Multiple products and their dependencies in one snapshot — e.g. Microsoft Office releasing Word, PowerPoint, Excel and Copilot together; shows planning, beta and pre-launch phases
    STRATEGIC roadmap For BUSINESS EXECUTIVES — goals and long-running initiatives cutting across months and quarters; "they may not be interested in every individual feature's progress"
    RELEASE PLAN What shipped in release 1, 1.1, 1.2 — "like the update notes on Android or iPhone"
    DEVELOPMENT roadmap For the development teams — a detailed SPRINT-WISE plan per team (security, front-end, back-end)
    LAUNCH roadmap For SALES AND MARKETING — the go-to-market plan: what sales, PR and marketing do PRE-LAUNCH, DURING LAUNCH and POST-LAUNCH
    CUSTOMER-FACING roadmap Keeps customers aware of short-, mid- and long-term releases

    7.49THE PRODUCT REQUIREMENTS DOCUMENT (PRD) guaranteed MCQ1

    "THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT DOCUMENT OWNED BY THE PRODUCT MANAGER." The PM creates and maintains it, and it is given to all teams involved in managing or developing the product.

    Its five questions ← memorise the set:

    Question Contents
    1. WHY are we doing this? Work objectives, OKRs, goals, initiatives, the problem being solved, the strategy
    2. WHO are we doing this for? Target users, the USER PERSONA, user needs and problems
    3. WHAT are we doing? (the BULK of the PRD) The proposed EPICS AND STORIES · the USER FLOW AND DESIGN (mock-ups and wireframes) · and the ## NON-FUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS — not features, but criteria such as PERFORMANCE (page loading under 1–2 seconds) and SECURITY
    4. HOW will we measure success? Metrics / KPIs / success metrics
    5. WHEN will we release? Release information and the planned ROADMAP

    A PRD template's sections (the Nuclino example): overview (goals, stakeholders, owner, design owner, development contact) → background and STRATEGIC FIT (why the initiative is worth the effort, how it links to goals) → customer/user research → success criteria → SCOPE (user stories and requirements) → FUTURE ENHANCEMENTS → ## OUT OF SCOPE for this release → embedded FIGMA designs (user flows, mock-ups, interactive prototypes) → the TIMELINE/roadmap.

    The historical contrast: in the WATERFALL days PRDs ran to HUNDREDS OF PAGES; today a PRD can be just a FEW PAGES, LINKING OUT to Jira user-story numbers, Figma designs and Miro roadmapping boards.

    7.50The GO-TO-MARKET (GTM) PLAN likely MCQ1

    An EXTERNAL-facing document — "preparing for the product launch." A Confluence-style template contains:

    Product launch details and OBJECTIVE · MARKET RESEARCH including COMPETITIVE ANALYSIS · overall SUCCESS METRICS ("when would you consider this release a success?") · TARGET PERSONAS · MESSAGING AND POSITIONING (a one-line positioning statement plus a detailed one giving benefits/values) · PRICING STRATEGY (subscription? feature bundle?) · the PRODUCT RELEASE ROADMAP · DISTRIBUTION CHANNELS AND LAUNCH ACTIVITIES (PR, email, social strategy, blogging, advertising — each with an OWNER, a TIMELINE and a DUE DATE) · a SUPPORT PLAN (who owns support, plus reference materials).

    7.51Agile product development3

    Iterative vs incremental — the definitions

    ITERATIVE = building the product through SUCCESSIVE AND REPEATED CYCLES OF REFINEMENT (making it better and better). INCREMENTAL = building the product PIECE BY PIECE, adding new features. Agile is BOTH.

    STACEY'S MATRIX — when to use what guaranteed MCQ

    Axes: REQUIREMENTS (certain ↔ uncertain) and TECHNOLOGY / "how to do it" (certain ↔ uncertain).

    Situation Region Method to use
    Requirements CLEAR and technology CLEAR KNOWN-KNOWN Traditional methods — WATERFALL
    One of the two is fuzzy KNOWN-UNKNOWN or UNKNOWN-KNOWN (the grey area) AGILE
    Both requirements AND technology uncertain UNKNOWN-UNKNOWN Experimentation-based LEAN START-UP or DESIGN THINKING

    THE AGILE MANIFESTO — the four values guaranteed MCQ

    1. INDIVIDUALS AND INTERACTIONS over PROCESSES AND TOOLS 2. WORKING PRODUCT (working software) over COMPREHENSIVE DOCUMENTATION 3. CUSTOMER COLLABORATION over CONTRACT NEGOTIATION 4. RESPONDING TO CHANGE over FOLLOWING A PLAN

    THE CRUCIAL CAVEAT — a classic MCQ trap: "WHILE THERE IS VALUE IN THE ITEMS ON THE RIGHT, WE VALUE THE ITEMS ON THE LEFT MORE." Agile does NOT discard documentation, contracts, plans or processes.

    (History recap: 17 developers, Utah, 2001 — the waterfall model was "too heavy, too rigid, too documentation-based", so they wrote a manifesto for a lighter, more adaptable method.)

    The Agile family of methods

    Agile is an UMBRELLA of HUNDREDS of methods: SCRUM · KANBAN · CRYSTAL · XP (EXTREME PROGRAMMING) · RUP · FDD.

    Agile is a SPECTRUM measured by NUMBER OF RULES: KANBAN has only 3 or 4 rules; SCRUM has 8 or 9; RUP HAS ABOUT 120 RULES — so RUP is highly prescriptive and LESS agile. ## The MOST POPULAR are the MOST FLEXIBLE: SCRUM and KANBAN. guaranteed MCQ

    7.52THE AGILE-SCRUM FRAMEWORK the densest MCQ area of this module7

    Why the name?

    "SCRUM" comes from AMERICAN FOOTBALL / RUGBY, where the entire team HUDDLES TOGETHER — mirroring the DAILY SCRUM MEETING, which is what gives the methodology its name.

    The three roles guaranteed MCQ| Role | Responsibility |

    |---|---| | PRODUCT OWNER | The BRIDGE between the Scrum team and the business — TYPICALLY THE PRODUCT MANAGER, because they understand the requirements best. Responsible for the FEATURES and for GROOMING THE PRODUCT BACKLOG, taking inputs from executives, teams, stakeholders, customers and users | | SCRUM MASTER | Responsible for the SMOOTH FUNCTIONING of the agile development process and RESOLVING CONCERNS AND ROADBLOCKS at each stage; runs the daily scrums and keeps the sprint on track | | DEVELOPMENT TEAM | Responsible for the DELIVERY AND QUALITY of the product. Varied skills and expertise, and THERE IS NO HIERARCHY — they all work as one team. Can include a UX/design person, a testing person, and connected subject-matter experts |

    THE SCRUM TEAM IS CROSS-FUNCTIONAL AND IDEALLY CONSISTS OF 7 MEMBERS (a rule of thumb).

    The five phases of the Scrum cycle certain sequence MCQ

    1. Create the PRODUCT BACKLOG (by the PRODUCT OWNER) → 2. SPRINT PLANNING and creating the SPRINT BACKLOG → 3. SPRINT EXECUTION with DAILY SCRUM MEETINGS → 4. TESTING and DEMONSTRATING the sprint's features to users and business executives (the SPRINT REVIEW) → 5. SPRINT RETROSPECTIVE and planning the next sprint — repeating over dozens of sprints.

    Ceremony Detail
    SPRINT 2 to 4 WEEKS — "typically 3 weeks is a good number." Each sprint contains planning, design, development, testing and user feedback
    SPRINT PLANNING A specific, achievable sprint GOAL is set; the product owner and team select user stories from the product backlog to form the SPRINT BACKLOG
    DAILY SCRUM A very short meeting of 15 to 20 minutes, MANDATORY EVERY 24 HOURS, where the whole team discusses past progress and any ROADBLOCKS, so they are resolved upfront. This embodies the Agile value of "individuals and interactions"
    SPRINT REVIEW After the sprint, the FINISHED WORK IS DEMOED TO THE USERS (and business stakeholders) for FEEDBACK; required changes go into future sprints
    SPRINT RETROSPECTIVE The team reflects on the sprint itself: "what could we have done better? did we OVER- or UNDER-ESTIMATE stories? did we miss dependencies or technologies? were more resources needed?" — the learnings feed the next sprint

    THE PRODUCT BACKLOG

    "The ORDERED LIST OF EVERY REQUIREMENT needed to develop the product." Formats: a FLAT list · a USER STORY MAP (best for keeping the end-to-end journey intact) · a KANBAN backlog (backlog / in progress / done / closed).

    THE UNIT OF THE PRODUCT BACKLOG IS THE USER STORY, but the backlog can also contain: BUGS to fix from previous sprints · TECHNICAL TASKS (e.g. database changes, upgrading an old architecture to MICROSERVICES) · KNOWLEDGE TASKS (time to research a new technology such as AI or to build a new ML model)

    STORY POINTS — effort estimation guaranteed MCQ

    STORY POINTS capture THREE things: the AMOUNT OF WORK, the COMPLEXITY of the work, and the ASSOCIATED UNCERTAINTIES (unknowns, dependencies, unfamiliar technology) — NOT just hours.

    RULE OF THUMB: 1 STORY POINT ≈ 4 TO 12 HOURS. E.g. 1 point = 4 hours (half a day), so an 8-hour day of one developer's work = 2 story points.

    STORY POINTS FOLLOW THE FIBONACCI SERIES — 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, … — where every number is the sum of the previous two, NOT 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. classic MCQ| Technique | How it works | |---|---| | T-SHIRT SIZING | First size the story roughly as ## S / M / L / XL, then convert: S ≈ 1–3 points, M ≈ 5–8, L ≈ 13+ | | PLANNING POKER | Done in the SPRINT PLANNING meeting. Every sprint team member simultaneously assigns their own story points to a story; the MAJORITY view is taken. If one person is a big OUTLIER (e.g. says 13 when others say 3 or 5), ANOTHER ROUND OF DISCUSSION happens — that person explains the complexity or uncertainty they see — and then a FRESH ROUND OF PLANNING POKER is played so people can readjust; the final number is the estimate |

    CRUCIAL DISTINCTION: STORY POINTS give the EFFORT only — they say NOTHING about PRIORITY. For priority you use the feature prioritisation techniques (Kano, value–effort, ICE, RICE).

    Building the SPRINT BACKLOG — the subtle rule likely MCQ

    You do NOT simply take the top-priority items in order. ## Because a sprint holds only a LIMITED NUMBER OF STORY POINTS, if the 3rd-priority item is TOO BIG to fit, you SKIP it and pull in a LOWER-PRIORITY item with FEWER story points instead — combining high-priority large stories with low-priority small ones to fill the sprint. This decision is taken in the SPRINT PLANNING MEETING.

    THE TWO SCRUM METRICS guaranteed comparison MCQ| Metric | What it shows |

    |---|---| | SPRINT BURNDOWN CHART | How quickly the team is "BURNING DOWN" (completing) the story points WITHIN A SPRINT — the remaining story points plotted over the days of the sprint. Example: 30 story points on day 0 falling to 0 by the end of a 10-day sprint | | VELOCITY CHART | The AVERAGE RATE OF STORIES COMPLETED ACROSS SPRINTS — indicating the work that can be EXPECTED in a sprint. It should RISE and then SATURATE, because teams get better: "in sprint 1 the team was new and cautious; by sprint 2 they have experience and can take on more points" |

    THE ONE-LINE DIFFERENCE: the BURNDOWN chart shows story points completed WITHIN a sprint; the VELOCITY chart shows story points completed ACROSS sprints.

    7.53KANBAN

    "KANBAN means CATEGORIES." "One of the SIMPLEST agile methodologies possible — there are hardly any more rules than this."

    The four typical columns: ## BACKLOG · PRIORITISED (for right now) · IN PROGRESS · DONE. Flow: as an item finishes it moves from IN PROGRESS to DONE; as "in progress" empties, items move from the priority list into progress; as the priority list empties, items move from the backlog into priority. Can be run on a whiteboard, a Miro board, or even an Excel sheet.

    7.54SAFe and Agile DevOps

    Framework Definition
    SAFe — THE SCALED AGILE FRAMEWORK "A set of ORGANISATION AND WORKFLOW PATTERNS intended to guide ENTERPRISES in SCALING lean and agile practices." Used by big corporations with many interdependent teams (billing, selling, back-end, front-end). Certifications are offered in it
    DevOps "A combination of CULTURAL PHILOSOPHIES, PRACTICES AND TOOLS that increases an organisation's ability to DELIVER APPS AND SERVICES AT HIGH VELOCITY by enabling the formerly SILOED roles" — development, IT operations, QA and security — to work as one team
    DevSecQAOps The extended name: DEV (developers) + SEC (security) + QA (quality assurance/testing) + OPS (IT operations)
    The DevOps flow CONTINUOUS INTEGRATION (agile development is continuously integrated into the production version) → CONTINUOUS TESTING (in a production/QA environment) → CONTINUOUS DELIVERY (features released to users)

    The parallel to remember: ## AGILE brings the BUSINESS/PRODUCT team closer to the DEVELOPMENT team; ## DevOps brings the DEVELOPMENT team closer to IT OPERATIONS and SECURITY.

    Quick-fire revision — Digital Product Management

    Item Answer
    Digital product Any item/service using digital technology to serve customers; scope here = mobile, desktop and web apps
    Feature Discrete capabilities, components and design elements of a product
    DPM defined End-to-end conceiving, defining, delivering, monitoring, refining and WITHDRAWING digital products to maximise business results

    PM interview rounds Problem solving · product thinking · business understanding · engineering · culture fit

    The 4 development approaches Waterfall · Agile · Lean · Design thinking
    Waterfall stages Requirements → Design → Implementation → Verification → Release & maintenance; a STAGE-GATE process; PRD of hundreds of pages, 4–6 months; CR = change request, "a dreaded term"
    Agile origin 2001, 17 developers, a resort in UTAH → the Manifesto for Agile Software Development

    Famous pivots YouTube (video dating profiles) · TikTok (educational videos)
    Lean's critic Prasanna Shankar of "Like A Little" — 20 mn page views in 6 weeks, $7 mn funding, folded after 4 years: "I would never do the lean start-up thing again"

    Design thinking origin / stages Stanford d.school, 2005 / Empathise → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test
    Design thinking's two pillars Customer empathy and prototyping
    Double diamond Problem space (Discover→Define) + Solution space (Develop→Deliver); diverge then converge in each
    Which fit each method solves Design thinking = problem-solution fit · Lean = product-market fit · Agile = building it right / scaling
    When to use which Know what + know how → Waterfall · Know what, not how → Agile · Know neither → Lean

    PESTEL Political · Economic · Social · Technological · Legal · Environmental

    Imitability ladder (bottom→top) Easy to imitate → imitable at a cost → difficult to imitate → CANNOT be imitated (patents, unique assets)

    UVP rule NOT a slogan — state the value delivered
    Value proposition canvas Customer jobs (JTBD) ↔ products & services · Pains ↔ pain relievers · Gains ↔ gain creators
    SMART Specific · Measurable · Attainable · Relevant · Time-bound
    Value–effort matrix High value/low effort = QUICK WINS; high value/high effort = STRATEGIC; low value/high effort = CUT
    OKR Objectives ("where do I need to go") · Key Results ("how do I know I'm getting there") · Initiatives ("what do I need to do"); popularised by ## Intel and Google
    OKR nested cadence Strategic = ANNUAL · Tactical = QUARTERLY · Operational = weekly/per sprint
    Problem sourcing mnemonic I-SEE-MUCK: I · Social chatter · Employees & teams · External · MELT telemetry · Users · Competitors · Kings
    User research 2×2 Quantitative/qualitative × attitudinal/behavioural. Surveys & interviews = attitudinal; analytics and A/B testing = behavioural
    MELT Metrics · Events · Logs · Traces (traces use a trace ID across external systems)
    Feature audit matrix Few people/all the time = AWARENESS problem · many people/little time = FREQUENCY problem (Hook framework) · few/little = drop it · low-by-design (Uber SOS button) = fine
    Funnel Shape is expected; a BIG DROP is the problem; segment via ## COHORT ANALYSIS
    Root cause tool THE 5 WHYs
    User journey map components Persona · scenario · phases · actions/thoughts/EMOTIONS · OPPORTUNITIES (where emotions dip)
    Define-phase tools Affinity map · dot voting · intensity × frequency user impact · user-vs-business impact · ## FDV (feasibility, desirability, viability)
    Solution framing HMW — "How Might We"
    Ideation techniques Brainstorming (can't build on others' ideas) · BRAINWRITING (chits exchanged, ideas built on) · mind mapping · ## CRAZY 8s (8 sketches in 8 minutes)
    Qualitative prioritisation MoSCoW (Must/Should/Could/Won't) · Feature buckets (metric movers, customer requests, delights, strategic) · Story mapping (mind DEPENDENCIES)
    Kano categories Basic/must-have (absence → exponential dissatisfaction) · Performance (linear) · Delighter (presence → exponential satisfaction) · Indifferent · ## REVERSE (e.g. ADS)
    Kano questionnaire The FUNCTIONAL question ("how do you feel if you HAVE it?") and the DYSFUNCTIONAL question ("if you DON'T have it?")
    ICE / RICE / WSJF ICE = Impact × Confidence × Ease · RICE = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort · WSJF = (Business value + Time criticality + Risk reduction) ÷ Estimated size
    RICE standard values Impact: massive 3, high 2, medium 1, low 0.5, minimal 0.25 · Confidence: high 100%, medium 80%, low 50%
    Buy a Feature Users spend real money/bids — "when money is involved, users make better decisions"
    Prototype fidelity ladder Hand sketch → tool wireframe → high-fidelity interactive mock-up
    SUS System Usability Scale — 10 items, some reverse-coded; the INDUSTRY AVERAGE IS 68/100
    Feedback grid What worked · what to change · open questions · ideas
    Revenue metrics RRR = short-period revenue × periods per year · MRR = beginning + new − churn + upgrades − downgrades · ARR
    Monetisation ARPU = revenue ÷ users · CLTV = ARPU ÷ monthly churn rate · CLTV profit = CLTV × margin
    Customer metrics Conversion rate · customer growth · CAC = sales+marketing ÷ new customers · ## LTV must EXCEED CAC · DAU/MAU · stickiness = DAU ÷ MAU · churn rate
    Financial metrics Burn rate = (starting − ending cash) ÷ months · CASH RUNWAY = current cash ÷ burn rate · operational efficiency = opex ÷ revenue (LOWER is better)
    NPS 11-point 0–10 scale; detractors 0–6, passives 7–8, promoters 9–10; ## NPS = %promoters − %detractors; >30% good, world-class >70%
    Pirate metrics AAARRR: Awareness · Acquisition · Activation · Retention · Referral · Revenue
    HEART (Google) Happiness · Engagement · Adoption · Retention · Task success
    North Star examples Facebook = MAU · Spotify = time spent listening · Amazon = purchases per month · Airbnb = booked nights · WhatsApp = messages sent · Uber = rides per week
    Growth levers Amazon: verticals × products × traffic per page × purchase conversion × avg price × repeat purchase
    UX vs UI UI = what it looks like (surface); UX = looks AND how it works. ## Steve Jobs: "design is also how it works"
    The 5 UX layers Strategy → Scope → Structure (UFDs, sitemaps) → Skeleton (wireframes) → Surface (mock-ups, prototypes)
    The 5 dimensions of interaction design Words · Visual · Physical object/device · Time (animations) · Behaviour
    Usability report errors NON-CRITICAL = recoverable; CRITICAL = task abandoned
    Gestalt principles Similarity · Common region (boundary or background) · Proximity
    Aesthetic-usability effect Pretty designs are perceived as more usable; users tolerate minor issues
    Peak-end rule The cold-water experiment (60 s at 14°C vs 60 s + 30 s at 15°C — people repeat the LONGER one); application: Duolingo's completion screen
    Goal-gradient effect The coffee card with 2 free stamps — real OR ILLUSORY progress increases goal-seeking; application: progress bars
    Hick's Law The jam study — 24 jams: 60% stopped but only 3% bought; 6 jams: 40% stopped and 30% bought; decision time rises with number of choices
    Von Restorff effect The single red tomato — make key actions visually distinctive; application: the highlighted pricing plan
    Nielsen's heuristics Visibility of status · match with the real world · user control & freedom · consistency & standards · error PREVENTION · recognition rather than recall (Lisbon/Portugal) · flexibility & efficiency · aesthetic & minimalist · recognise/diagnose/recover from errors
    Design sprint 2–5 days; Google Ventures: ## Understand → Diverge → Decide → Prototype → Validate; team of 6–8; the PM is the SPRINT MASTER; 4–5 dots per voter; ## 5 USERS FIND 85% OF PROBLEMS
    Empathy map SAY · THINK · DO · FEEL
    Customer development model SEARCH (customer discovery → customer validation) then EXECUTION (customer creation → company building)
    Customer development funnel GET (acquire → activate, with a viral loop) · KEEP · GROW (upsell, next-sell, cross-sell, referrals)
    Opportunity sourcing types Organic (observed — Tata Nano, Uber) · Inorganic (searched — journey maps, SCAMPER) · Trans-organic (INTUITED — blue ocean, e-books)
    SCAMPER Substitute (Netflix, Uber) · Combine (Instagram) · Adapt (Rapido, Swiggy Genie) · Magnify/Modify (Licious) · Put to other use (CamScanner, FB Shopping) · Eliminate (Chrome OS, Bitcoin) · Rearrange (Google Pay, Airtel prepaid)
    The 3 interview risks Product risk (what) · Market risk (who is the competition) · Customer risk (who has the pain)
    Problem statement canvas Who · context · problem · emotional impact · quantifiable impact · alternatives · shortcomings
    Vitamin vs painkiller Painkillers are what you want
    4 U Unworkable · Unavoidable · Urgent · Underserved
    BLAC Blatant · Latent · Aspirational · Critical — best = blatant + critical; Netflix = aspirational
    Michael Seibel (Y Combinator) Frequency · Intensity · Willingness to pay
    Opportunity score Importance × Dissatisfaction
    Marty Cagan's book "INSPIRED" — the 10 opportunity-assessment questions
    RWW (HBR) Is it REAL? · Can we WIN? · Is it WORTH doing?
    MVP experiment types Landing page (Buffer) · explainer video (Dropbox — 10,000 registrations in ONE DAY) · A/B test (Highrise) · crowdfunding (Pebble — ~$10 mn from 68,000 backers) · CONCIERGE (Food on the Table — customer KNOWS) · WIZARD OF OZ (Zappos — customer does NOT know)
    MCS Minimum Criteria for Success — the metric fixed in advance
    MVP / MMP / MLP Minimum Viable / Minimum MARKETABLE / Minimum LOVABLE product; MLP is slowest and best
    The 20/80 rule for MVPs 20% of features are used by 80% of adopters — build those
    Development orientation Skateboard → scooter → bicycle → motorcycle → car (NOT wheel → chassis → car)
    First MVPs Uber: "on-demand car service via iPhone and SMS" · Airbnb: "Air Bed and Breakfast" for conference attendees
    Requirement hierarchy Initiative → Epic → User story → Task (strategic / tactical / operational)
    Story template "As a [user], I want to [task], so that I can [benefit]"
    INVEST Independent · Negotiable · Valuable · Estimable · Small · Testable
    Acceptance criteria Required for USER STORIES; NOT for epics
    Themes Span epics/stories across releases; used to track a high-level OKR; applied by TAGGING
    Roadmap formats Gantt · Kanban · Now/Next/Later · Lean · User story map · Hybrid (Aha!)
    PRD The single most important document owned by the PM: WHY · WHO · WHAT (incl. NON-FUNCTIONAL requirements) · HOW measured · WHEN released
    GTM plan External-facing launch plan: objective, market research, success metrics, personas, messaging & positioning, pricing, roadmap, channels & activities with owners and dates, support plan
    Stacey's matrix Known-known → Waterfall · the grey area → Agile · Unknown-unknown → Lean/design thinking
    Agile Manifesto's 4 values Individuals & interactions > processes & tools · working product > documentation · customer collaboration > contract negotiation · responding to change > following a plan — "while there is value in the items on the right, we value the left more"
    Agile methods & rule counts Kanban 3–4 rules · Scrum 8–9 rules · RUP ~120 rules; also Crystal, XP, FDD
    Scrum roles Product owner (= the PM; grooms the backlog) · Scrum master (removes roadblocks) · Development team (no hierarchy); ideal team size ## 7
    Scrum ceremonies Sprint planning · DAILY SCRUM (15–20 min, every 24 hours) · sprint review (demo to users) · sprint retrospective (team learnings)
    Scrum's name origin The rugby/American football huddle
    Story points Work + complexity + uncertainty; ## 1 point ≈ 4–12 hours; ## FIBONACCI series (1,2,3,5,8…); T-shirt sizing; ## PLANNING POKER with a re-vote when there is an outlier
    Scrum metrics BURNDOWN = points completed WITHIN a sprint · VELOCITY = points completed ACROSS sprints
    Kanban columns Backlog · prioritised/to-do · in progress · done
    SAFe Scaled Agile Framework — organisation and workflow patterns for scaling lean and agile in ENTERPRISES
    DevOps / DevSecQAOps Dev + Security + QA + IT Operations working as one team; continuous integration → continuous testing → continuous delivery
